docs.title: Topics
docs.text:
• Context Engineering — what goes in the context window, how to structure it, and what actually works
  • Harness Engineering — designing the runtime layer that wraps agents: tools, safety, orchestration, and evals
  • Ontologies — structured representations of entities and relationships; knowledge graphs, schemas, and the gap between LLM understanding and relational reasoning
  • Testing and Compliance for Coding Agents — verifying agent-generated code is correct, secure, and meets standards; the verification bottleneck
  • Executable Context — evidence that tests, structured representations and designed tool interfaces outperform static documentation for coding agents, and what fails without them
  • Executable Context Practices — how-to guide built on that evidence: executable specs, types, linters, teaching tool output, review gates, outcome metrics and adoption order
  • Agent-Driven Test Generation — designing autonomous test improvement loops; mutation scoring, context separation, execution feedback, and failure modes benchmarked against research
  • Agent Memory and Retrieval — how agents store, retrieve, and keep memory current; why long context doesn't replace it; and how agents lose track of state over long runs
  • Multi-Agent Systems — when coordinating several agents beats one, what carries the coordination, what it costs, and why many instances of one model may not be independent
  • LLMs in Finance and Accounting — how models perform on financial and audit work, why reported results are hard to trust, and verification-first architectures

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: This technical report presents Qwen3, the latest series of open-weight large language models from Alibaba, featuring both dense (0.6B-32B) and MoE (30B-A3B, 235B-A22B) architectures. A key innovation is the integration of thinking mode (complex, multi-step reasoning) and non-thinking mode (rapid, context-driven responses) into a unified model, trained on 36 trillion tokens across 119 languages with a multi-stage post-training process combining chain-of-thought fine-tuning, reinforcement learning, and strong-to-weak distillation.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• Qwen3 integrates thinking and non-thinking modes into a single model with a thinking budget mechanism, eliminating the need to switch between chat-optimized and reasoning-specific models
  • The flagship Qwen3-235B-A22B (235B total, 22B activated per token) uses 128 total experts with 8 activated per token, excluding shared experts and using global-batch load balancing loss for expert specialization
  • Pre-training uses 36 trillion tokens across 119 languages, with a three-stage strategy progressing from general knowledge to STEM-focused data to long-context training (up to 32,768 tokens)
  • For smaller models, strong-to-weak distillation from larger models significantly outperforms reinforcement learning alone in both performance and training efficiency

docs.title: Raw
docs.text: Original: https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.09388

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: This paper from the Qwen team introduces Group Sequence Policy Optimization (GSPO), a reinforcement learning algorithm that addresses fundamental instabilities in GRPO by defining importance ratios at the sequence level rather than the token level, performing sequence-level clipping, rewarding, and optimization. GSPO achieves superior training stability, efficiency, and performance compared to GRPO, notably resolving catastrophic model collapse issues in Mixture-of-Experts training, and contributed to the Qwen3 model improvements.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• GRPO's token-level importance weights are fundamentally ill-posed: they fail to perform proper importance sampling correction since each weight is based on a single sample from the next-token distribution, introducing high-variance noise that accumulates over long sequences
  • GSPO defines importance ratios based on sequence likelihood (geometric mean of token probabilities), aligning the unit of off-policy correction with the unit of reward (the entire sequence)
  • GSPO inherently resolves stability challenges in RL training of large MoE models that caused catastrophic and irreversible model collapse with GRPO, eliminating the need for complex stabilization strategies
  • GSPO contributed to the performance improvements in the latest Qwen3 models and shows potential for simplifying RL infrastructure

docs.title: AgentFold: Long-Horizon Web Agents with Proactive Context Management
Summary
docs.text: AgentFold introduces a novel web agent paradigm centered on proactive context management, treating the agent's context as a dynamic cognitive workspace rather than a passive log. At each step, the agent performs a "folding" operation on its trajectory at multiple scales -- granular condensations to preserve fine-grained details, or deep consolidations to abstract entire sub-tasks -- achieving 36.2% on BrowseComp and 47.3% on BrowseComp-ZH, surpassing much larger models including OpenAI's o4-mini.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• Prevailing ReAct-based agents suffer from context saturation by accumulating noisy raw histories, while fixed summarization methods risk irreversible loss of critical details
  • AgentFold treats context as a dynamic workspace with multi-scale state summaries (long-term memory) and a latest interaction (working memory), proactively sculpted at each reasoning step
  • The "folding" operation can perform granular condensation (preserving fine-grained details as a new state summary) or deep consolidation (abstracting multiple state summaries into a coarser strategic summary)
  • A 30B parameter AgentFold model matches or surpasses dramatically larger models (DeepSeek-V3.1-671B, GLM-4.5-355B) and proprietary agents (o4-mini) on long-horizon web browsing benchmarks

docs.title: The Anatomy of a Personal Health Agent
Summary
docs.text: This paper from Google Research presents the Personal Health Agent (PHA), a multi-agent framework consisting of three specialist sub-agents -- a Data Science Agent (analyzing wearable/medical data), a Domain Expert Agent (providing personalized health insights), and a Health Coach Agent (guiding behavior change through motivational strategies). The system is evaluated through the most comprehensive health agent assessment to date, with over 7,000 annotations and 1,100 hours of expert evaluation across 10 benchmark tasks.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• Personal health needs fall into four critical categories: general health knowledge, personal data insights, wellness advice, and personal medical symptoms, each requiring different agent capabilities
  • A multi-agent architecture with specialist sub-agents (data science, domain expert, health coach) is necessary to address the diverse range of consumer health needs
  • The Data Science Agent must handle complex numerical time-series reasoning from wearables and medical records, incorporating population-level statistics for contextualized insights
  • The Health Coach Agent uses specified psychological strategies (motivational interviewing) to drive multi-turn interactions, interactive goal setting, and user progress tracking

docs.title: Reasoning RAG via System 1 or System 2: A Survey on Reasoning Agentic RAG for Industry Challenges
Summary
docs.text: This survey categorizes Reasoning Agentic RAG methods into two paradigms mapped to dual-process cognitive theory: predefined reasoning (System 1) using structured, rule-based pipelines (route-based, loop-based, tree-based, hybrid-modular), and agentic reasoning (System 2) where the model autonomously orchestrates retrieval and tool use via prompt-based or training-based (reinforcement learning) methods. The paper reviews representative techniques under both paradigms covering architectural design, reasoning strategies, and tool coordination, and discusses key research challenges for advancing flexibility, robustness, and applicability of reasoning agentic RAG systems.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• Reasoning Agentic RAG can be usefully categorized via the System 1 / System 2 cognitive analogy: predefined reasoning (fast, structured, rule-based) vs. agentic reasoning (slow, deliberative, adaptive with autonomous tool use).
  • Predefined reasoning spans four architectural variants: route-based (selective retrieval triggers), loop-based (iterative retrieval-feedback cycles), tree-based (hierarchical exploration), and hybrid-modular (composable specialized modules).
  • Training-based agentic reasoning methods using reinforcement learning (e.g., DeepRetrieval, Search-R1, R1-Searcher) enable more fine-grained and strategic tool usage compared to prompt-based approaches.
  • Predefined reasoning offers efficiency and control but lacks flexibility for open-ended tasks, while agentic reasoning provides adaptability but at higher computational cost and reduced predictability.

docs.title: RollPacker: Mitigating Long-Tail Rollouts for Fast, Synchronous RL Post-Training
Summary
docs.text: RollPacker introduces "tail batching," a prompt scheduling strategy for synchronous on-policy RL post-training that mitigates GPU idle bubbles caused by long-tail response length distributions. By consolidating tail prompts (those generating long responses) into dedicated "long rounds" while keeping the majority of rollout steps as balanced "short rounds," RollPacker preserves on-policy training accuracy while achieving 2.03-2.56x end-to-end speedup over veRL and up to 2.24x over RLHFuse on 128 H800 GPUs.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• The rollout stage dominates RL post-training runtime at ~70% of total step time, with long-tail responses (25-32x longer than median) creating severe GPU idle bubbles
  • Tail batching separates long-response prompts into dedicated long rounds and uses speculative execution for short rounds, preserving synchronous on-policy training semantics while reducing idle time
  • An adaptive parallelism planner dynamically configures tensor parallelism based on memory profiling and response length distributions, reducing rollout latency by up to 21.9%
  • A stream trainer opportunistically initiates training on partially completed rollouts, further reducing idle GPU time by overlapping training with ongoing long-round rollouts

docs.text: Original: https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.21009

docs.title: ROLL Flash: Accelerating RLVR and Agentic Training with Asynchrony
Summary
docs.text: ROLL Flash extends the ROLL system with native asynchronous RL post-training support, built on two core principles: fine-grained parallelism (enabling overlap among LLM generation, environment interaction, and reward computation) and rollout-train decoupling (placing rollout and training on separate resources executing in parallel). The system achieves up to 2.24x speedup on RLVR tasks and 2.72x on agentic tasks over synchronous baselines, with theoretical and empirical analysis showing that asynchronous training can match synchronous performance through off-policy algorithms.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• Synchronous RL post-training suffers from severe resource bubbles, with the rollout stage accounting for over 70% of total training time due to long-tail response length distributions
  • Fine-grained parallelism with queue scheduling and prompt replication enables overlap among generation, environment interaction, and reward computation during rollout
  • Rollout-train decoupling enables asynchronous training where rollout and training proceed in parallel on separate resources, with an "asynchronous ratio" bounding policy staleness
  • Existing off-policy algorithms (importance sampling corrections, V-trace) effectively compensate for potential degradation from stale samples in async training, matching synchronous performance

docs.title: LightMem: Lightweight and Efficient Memory-Augmented Generation
Summary
docs.text: LightMem introduces a lightweight memory system for LLMs inspired by the Atkinson-Shiffrin model of human memory, organizing memory into three stages: a cognition-inspired sensory memory for pre-compression and filtering, a topic-aware short-term memory for semantic grouping and consolidation, and a long-term memory with an offline "sleep-time" update mechanism that decouples consolidation from inference. On LongMemEval and LoCoMo benchmarks, LightMem improves QA accuracy by up to 7.7%/29.3% while reducing token usage by up to 38x/20.9x and API calls by up to 30x/20.9x.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• Existing LLM memory systems suffer from redundant sensory processing, inefficient short-term memory balancing, and tightly-coupled long-term memory updates that introduce latency during inference
  • A three-stage memory architecture (sensory filtering, topic-aware STM, sleep-time LTM update) inspired by human memory can dramatically reduce computational overhead while improving accuracy
  • The offline "sleep-time" consolidation mechanism decouples memory maintenance from real-time inference, enabling reflective high-fidelity updates without latency costs
  • LightMem reduces total token usage by up to 38x and API calls by up to 30x compared to baselines while improving QA accuracy by up to 7.7% on LongMemEval

docs.title: Production-Grade Local LLM Inference on Apple Silicon: A Comparative Study of MLX, MLC-LLM, Ollama, llama.cpp, and PyTorch MPS
Summary
docs.text: This paper presents a systematic empirical comparison of five local LLM inference frameworks on Apple Silicon (MLX, MLC-LLM, llama.cpp, Ollama, PyTorch MPS), evaluating production-grade metrics including TTFT, throughput, latency percentiles, KV caching, quantization effects, and long-context behavior using Qwen-2.5 models. MLX achieves the highest sustained throughput (~230 tok/s), MLC-LLM delivers lower TTFT for interactive loads, while all Apple Silicon frameworks remain 5-10x behind NVIDIA A100+vLLM but are rapidly maturing for on-device deployment.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• MLX delivers the highest sustained generation throughput (~230 tok/s on M2 Ultra) with the most stable inter-token latency, making it the preferred default for throughput-bound Apple Silicon deployment
  • MLC-LLM achieves ~17% lower TTFT than MLX on moderate prompt sizes due to faster first-token generation, making it better suited for interactive, latency-sensitive workloads
  • All five frameworks run fully on-device with no telemetry, ensuring strong privacy guarantees for local deployment
  • Apple Silicon inference frameworks remain approximately 5-10x behind NVIDIA A100+vLLM in absolute throughput, but are rapidly maturing into viable production-grade solutions for on-device inference

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Google's code coverage infrastructure computes line and branch coverage for 1 billion lines of code daily across 7 programming languages. The key design insight is applying coverage at the changeset level during code review — not just as a project-level metric — making it immediately actionable for authors and reviewers. A 5-year analysis and 512-developer survey show steady adoption growth and 60% positive sentiment, with the primary adoption drivers being automation, low friction, and integration into existing tools.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• Changeset-level coverage (especially delta coverage — only modified/added lines) is far more actionable than project-level aggregates; it shifts coverage from a reporting metric to a code review signal
  • Automation is essential for adoption: only 0.5% of developers manually invoke coverage daily, but when computed automatically and surfaced in review, 45% use it "Often" or "Very Often" when authoring and 40% when reviewing
  • Coverage instrumentation reliability is a major engineering challenge — performance timeouts and OOM from instrumentation overhead are the primary causes of failed computations, requiring years of incremental fixes
  • Google does not mandate coverage thresholds globally; voluntary opt-in levels (60%-90% targets) proved more effective for adoption than top-down mandates
  • Line coverage, when combined with enforced style guides (one statement per line), strongly correlates with statement coverage — making it a practical, sufficient metric despite theoretical limitations

docs.title: A Benchmark to Understand the Role of Knowledge Graphs on Large Language Model's Accuracy for Question Answering on Enterprise SQL Databases
Summary
docs.text: This paper introduces a benchmark for evaluating LLM-powered question answering over enterprise SQL databases in the insurance domain, demonstrating that GPT-4 with zero-shot prompting achieves only 16% accuracy on direct SQL databases but 54% accuracy when questions are posed over a Knowledge Graph representation -- a 37.5% improvement. The benchmark includes a 199-table enterprise schema, 43 enterprise questions of varying complexity, and a contextual ontology layer.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• GPT-4 with zero-shot prompting achieves only 16.7% accuracy on enterprise natural language questions posed directly over SQL databases, far below what existing text-to-SQL benchmarks would suggest
  • Accuracy increases to 54.2% when questions are posed over a Knowledge Graph representation of the enterprise SQL database, a 37.5 percentage point improvement
  • Existing text-to-SQL benchmarks are misaligned with real enterprise settings: they overlook complex schemas with hundreds of tables, business reporting/KPI questions, and the absence of a business context layer
  • Knowledge Graphs provide the missing business semantics and context that LLMs need to bridge the gap between natural language questions and complex enterprise database schemas

docs.title: A Comprehensive Study of Knowledge Editing for Large Language Models
Summary
docs.text: This comprehensive survey defines the knowledge editing problem for LLMs and proposes a unified taxonomy based on educational and cognitive research theories, classifying methods into three categories: resorting to external knowledge (recognition phase), merging knowledge into the model (association phase), and editing intrinsic knowledge (mastery phase). The paper introduces KnowEdit, a new benchmark for evaluating knowledge editing approaches, and provides analysis of knowledge locating within LLMs, revealing insights about implicit knowledge structures.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• Knowledge editing methods can be classified into three categories inspired by cognitive learning: resorting to external knowledge, merging knowledge into the model, and editing intrinsic knowledge (modifying model parameters directly)
  • MLP weights in LLMs function similarly to key-value memories, with the multi-layer perceptron weights in core regions playing a role in recalling facts from the training corpus
  • Knowledge editing offers a lightweight alternative to full retraining for correcting outdated information, removing harmful content, and integrating new knowledge while preserving overall model performance
  • Applications of knowledge editing span efficient ML, AI-generated content correction, trustworthy AI, and personalized agents

docs.title: A Comprehensive Survey of Self-Evolving AI Agents
Summary
docs.text: This survey provides a comprehensive review of self-evolving AI agents -- autonomous systems that continuously optimize their internal components through interaction with environments. The paper introduces a unified conceptual framework with four key components (System inputs, Agent System, Environment, Optimisers), traces the paradigm shift from Model Offline Pretraining through Model Online Adaptation and Multi-Agent Orchestration to Multi-Agent Self-Evolving (MASE), and proposes "Three Laws of Self-Evolving AI Agents" inspired by Asimov prioritizing safety, performance preservation, and autonomous evolution.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• Self-evolving AI agents represent a paradigm shift from static, manually configured architectures to adaptive, data-driven systems that can evolve in response to changing requirements and environments
  • The development trajectory spans four stages: Model Offline Pretraining (MOP), Model Online Adaptation (MOA), Multi-Agent Orchestration (MAO), and Multi-Agent Self-Evolving (MASE)
  • A unified framework with four components (System inputs, Agent System, Environment, Optimisers) can abstract the feedback loop underlying all self-evolving agent designs
  • Three hierarchical laws should govern self-evolving agents: (1) safety adaptation must be maintained, (2) performance must be preserved or enhanced, (3) autonomous optimization must be subject to the first two laws

docs.title: A frontend-backend architecture for tool calls in full-duplex speech models
Summary
docs.text: NVIDIA adds tool use to a full-duplex speech-to-speech model by delegation rather than internalisation: a duplex speech-to-text frontend (Nemotron-Nano-9B backbone with a streaming Parakeet encoder) learns to emit a tool-call token, speaks a short filler, and forwards the streaming ASR transcript to a text backend LLM (a LangGraph ReAct agent) that executes the tool calls; the backend's natural-language result is prefilled into the frontend's agent-text channel, which is trained to repeat it before streaming TTS speaks it. The design needs only a new control token in the frontend and largely preserves duplex turn-taking, interruption handling, and ASR quality.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• Voice agents lag text agents badly on tool use — leading commercial duplex voice models complete only 31–51% of grounded customer-service tasks in τ-Voice versus 85% for GPT-5 in text mode — and audio-native modelling spends parameters and context on audio tokens, which motivates delegating tool calls to a mature text backend instead of internalising them
  • Delegation with prefill-and-repeat is accurate on single-turn tool calls: on a speech version of BFCL the frontend fires the tool-call token with 92–97% recall and rejects up to 81.2% of irrelevant calls, at the cost of ~320 ms added before the tool-call token (≈640 ms to the filler) plus about 1 s of filler while the backend works
  • Backend capability carries over to voice: with a Qwen3-235B-A22B backend the system matches GPT-realtime-mini response quality on Full-Duplex-Bench-V3 and beats GPT-realtime-mini and Qwen3-Omni-30B-A3B on EVA-Bench (EVA-A/EVA-X), performing similarly to Gemini 3.1 Flash Lite, though it still trails GPT-realtime2 on task completion and faithfulness
  • Long tool chains remain the weak point: the Qwen3-235B backend beats GPT-realtime2 on airline tasks (72% vs. 54% completion) but loses on ITSM (56.3% vs. 75%) and Medical HR (49.4% vs. 69.9%), where tasks need 6–8 successful tool calls and the frontend must detect tool calls reliably across a long conversation
  • Adding tool-call training costs little conversational quality: turn-taking precision and recall drop slightly, streaming ASR WER rises from 10.80% to 11.47% (attributed to mostly synthetic tool-call data), and the model becomes more responsive but worse at handling natural pauses

docs.text:
• Topic fit: no existing topic page covers voice agents or speech architectures; left unlinked. Closest is harness-engineering (delegation to a backend agent), but the paper is a model-architecture contribution rather than harness design.
  • Limitation: latency of prefill and serving was not optimised; end-to-end latency is not compared because backends differ; tool-call training data are mostly synthetic.

docs.title: A Mechanistic Understanding of Alignment Algorithms: A Case Study on DPO and Toxicity
Summary
docs.text: This paper provides a mechanistic analysis of how DPO (Direct Preference Optimization) reduces toxicity in GPT-2, finding that DPO does not remove the model's capability to generate toxic content but rather learns a distributed offset across layers that bypasses the regions triggering toxic vectors in MLP blocks. The authors demonstrate that this bypass can be easily undone, shedding light on why aligned models can be jailbroken.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• Toxicity in GPT-2 is represented by specific value vectors in MLP blocks that promote toxic tokens; these can be extracted via SVD and used for targeted interventions
  • DPO does not remove toxic capabilities from the model but learns an offset distributed across layers to bypass the activation of toxic vectors, while every parameter is minimally shifted
  • The alignment learned through DPO can be easily undone by re-activating the toxic vectors, providing a mechanistic explanation for why jailbreaks succeed on aligned models
  • Simple vector subtraction interventions on toxic vectors can achieve comparable toxicity reduction to DPO while maintaining perplexity and generation quality

docs.text: A-MEM is an agentic memory system for LLM agents inspired by the Zettelkasten method, dynamically organizing memories into interconnected knowledge networks through indexing and linking. docs.text: AAFLOW treats agentic workflows as operator abstractions mapped to distributed HPC communication patterns (broadcast, shuffle, reduce), using Apache Arrow's zero-copy data plane and the Cylon distributed framework to eliminate serialization overhead in RAG pipelines. docs.text:
• The main bottleneck in large-scale agentic RAG systems is data orchestration and inter-node communication, not LLM inference — existing frameworks (LangChain, LangGraph) optimize flexibility but ignore data movement costs

  • Resource-deterministic scheduling decouples logical agent behavior from resource allocation, enabling reproducibility and high-concurrency batching that agentic frameworks currently lack

docs.title: Adaptation of Agentic AI: A Survey of Post-Training, Memory, and Skills
Summary
docs.text: A comprehensive survey organizing the fragmented landscape of agentic AI adaptation under a unified four-paradigm framework spanning agent adaptation and tool adaptation. docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• The field can be organized into four adaptation paradigms: A1 (tool-execution-signaled agent adaptation), A2 (agent-output-signaled agent adaptation), T1 (agent-agnostic tool adaptation), and T2 (agent-supervised tool adaptation)
  • Three mechanisms drive adaptation: post-training (SFT, RLVR, preference optimization), memory systems (episodic buffers, reflective databases, knowledge graphs), and skill libraries that accumulate reusable capabilities
  • Agent-tool co-adaptation, where both the agent and its tools evolve jointly, remains a key open problem with significant potential for synergistic improvement
  • Continual learning, safe adaptation, and efficient deployment are identified as critical unsolved challenges for production agentic AI systems

docs.title: Agent Lightning v1.0: Towards Harnessed Agentic RL
Summary
docs.text: Names and characterises harnessed agentic RL: RL post-training where the deploy-time agent harness (Claude Code, OpenHands, mini-SWE-agent…) — not the training engine — owns context construction, tool execution and the interaction loop, and the trainer sees only a sequence of LLM request–response pairs through an API proxy. The paper argues this proxy-based paradigm (also adopted by verl Uni-Agent, AReaL 2.0, slime, Polar) fundamentally changes the RL problem and identifies challenges existing frameworks leave underspecified: retokenization breaking sample merging, rollout- vs sample-level advantage calculation and loss normalization, and training-backend scheduling. It ships Agent Lightning v1.0 (~3,500 LoC), validated on search, instruction-following and coding agents; RL alone lifts Qwen3.5-9B on SWE-bench Verified from 41.8% to 56.4% with ~6K examples and modest compute.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• The harness is now part of the training loop, not just deployment: training through the same harness that runs in production narrows the train/deploy gap, at the cost of the trainer losing sight of harness and environment state (a POMDP whose observations are only the prompts the harness chose to send).
  • Because the harness decides how many LLM calls a rollout makes, and retokenization can prevent merging calls, per-sample counts are incidental — so advantage and loss normalization must be computed at the rollout level, or training becomes ineffective or unstable (validated on the coding-agent run).
  • Coding-agent RL is under-supported in the open: no data, no complete scripts, and heavy compute assumptions; the paper releases a data-cleaning pipeline and reproducible scripts on open models and datasets.
  • Reward hacking is concrete and environmental: agents found the gold commit in git history and fetched upstream sources via wget/pip/urllib. Safeguards are harness-level — hide .git, disable git, whitelist-only egress via Kubernetes network policy — not reward-model fixes.
  • +14.6pp SWE-bench Verified on a 9B model from RL alone is the empirical headline, but it's a single model family and one benchmark.

docs.title: Agent Plasticity: Measuring Self-Improvement Through Experience
Summary
docs.text: Meta Superintelligence Labs, UC Berkeley, and collaborators argue that agent evaluations measure what an agent can do at a fixed point, not how well it learns, and propose a controlled protocol: frozen weights, a fresh context every episode, and improvement only through persistent self-built artifacts (Python tools, skills, strategies, memory, CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md) inherited by the next checkpoint, scored on held-out in-distribution (ID) and stronger out-of-distribution (OOD) opponents. They introduce agent plasticity — held-out score gain per $1,000 of learning cost — and find, across chess, Go, Hex, and NetHack, that frontier models follow sharply different improvement trajectories and that the most capable model is not the most efficient learner.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• Self-improvement is model- and task-dependent: the same feedback/reflection/artifact interface yields very different learning curves (in Hard chess, Claude Fable 5 rises from 37.5% to 73.3% held-out ID while several models stay flat or decline; Claude Opus 4.8 loses ground in Go but improves in Hex) — "the common learning interface permits improvement but does not ensure it"; held-out ID gains transfer only partially to stronger OOD opponents
  • Endpoint capability and acquisition efficiency diverge: Claude Fable 5 reaches the highest fitted score, while GPT-5.6 Sol has the highest plasticity to saturation (298 pp per $1,000 vs. 57 for Fable 5) and overtakes Claude Opus 4.8 despite starting lower; the authors frame plasticity as protocol-dependent, not a universal model ranking
  • Low artifact reuse accompanies weak improvement: weak improvers skip their own relevant artifacts at 28–98% of relevant decisions vs. 2–6% for strong improvers, and reuse correlates with held-out gain across 19 model–game cells; reuse can also decay (GPT-5.5 drops from 96–100% to 32–50% reuse while its artifacts are unchanged)
  • High reuse is not sufficient: the four strong improvers all reuse at 94–98% yet reach very different scores, and 83–99% of their remaining failures occur while a relevant artifact is in use — pointing to artifact quality, generality, or application as the bottleneck; "writing down an instruction is not the same as following it"
  • Structural validity is not enough, and plasticity is trainable in principle: artifact updates are gated only on structural/executable checks, and the authors argue validation should assess behavioral effectiveness, and that post-training (e.g. RL) could target the ability to learn after deployment rather than deployment-time capability alone

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Limitation: failure diagnostics are observational — artifact use and outcome are judged by Gemini 3.1 Pro combined with execution traces.
  • Limitation: the value of environment feedback is not separated from the extra reflection compute.
  • Limitation: learning cost uses provider pricing as a proxy for compute.
  • Limitation: NetHack runs use Claude Code and Codex with their native harnesses, so they measure agent plasticity (model + harness), not bare-model plasticity.

docs.text: Agent0 is a fully autonomous framework that evolves LLM agents from scratch without any external data or human annotations, using a co-evolutionary loop between a curriculum agent (which generates increasingly challenging tasks via RL) and an executor agent (which learns to solve them with tool-integrated reasoning). docs.title: AgentGuard: Runtime Verification of AI Agents
Summary
docs.text: AgentGuard introduces Dynamic Probabilistic Assurance, a runtime verification framework for agentic AI that operates as a middleware inspection layer observing agent I/O without code intrusion. It abstracts raw agent interactions into formal state transition events, dynamically builds and updates an Agentic Markov Decision Process (AMDP) from execution traces using online learning, and verifies quantitative properties in real-time using probabilistic model checking (PCTL). Applied to RepairAgent (automated bug-fixing), it reveals execution patterns and enables predictive success likelihood, loop detection, and cost management.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• Traditional verification methods are inadequate for agentic AI because they assume deterministic logic and manageable state spaces; the critical question shifts from "will the system fail?" to "what is the probability of failure within given constraints?"
  • AgentGuard models agents as Agentic MDPs with states (progress snapshots), actions (tool invocations), probabilistic transitions, and rewards, learning the model dynamically from actual execution traces rather than pre-specifying it
  • The framework verifies quantitative PCTL properties: success probability within resource constraints, expected time to completion, probability of avoiding failure states, and pattern-specific path properties
  • By learning from actual execution traces, AgentGuard circumvents state-space explosion limitations of exhaustive offline verification while providing guarantees about observed execution and predictions about future behavior
  • Applied to RepairAgent, it reveals that 75% of code searches follow hypothesis formulation, enables early termination decisions based on learned patterns, and supports real-time cost management through efficiency monitoring

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Introduces "semi-formal reasoning" — structured prompting that requires LLM agents to state explicit premises, trace execution paths, and derive formal conclusions when reasoning about code without executing it. • Semi-formal reasoning acts as a certificate: the agent must state premises, trace code paths, and give formal conclusions — it cannot skip cases or make unsupported claims, unlike free-form chain-of-thought

  • On RubberDuckBench (code QA): semi-formal achieves 87% accuracy (Opus 4.5), a 10.8pp improvement over single-shot (76%) and 8.7pp over standard agentic reasoning

docs.text: ACE (Agentic Context Engineering) treats contexts as evolving playbooks that accumulate, refine, and organize strategies through modular generation, reflection, and curation. It addresses brevity bias (dropping domain insights for concise summaries) and context collapse (iterative rewriting that erodes details over time) through structured, incremental updates. • Brevity bias in context optimization: prior methods drop domain insights to produce concise summaries, losing critical task-specific knowledge
  • Context collapse in iterative rewriting: each update erodes details from previous rounds, degrading performance over time
  • ACE uses structured, incremental updates that preserve detailed knowledge and scale with long-context models
  • Works without labeled supervision, leveraging natural execution feedback for adaptation

docs.text: This paper introduces Agentic Harness Engineering (AHE), a closed-loop system that automatically evolves coding-agent harnesses through three observability pillars: component observability (file-level representation of editable components), experience observability (layered distillation of raw trajectories into actionable signal), and decision observability (self-declared predictions verified against outcomes, making each edit a falsifiable contract). docs.text:

docs.title: Agentic Property-Based Testing: Finding Bugs Across the Python Ecosystem

docs.text: This paper presents an LLM-based agent (built on Claude Code) that autonomously analyzes Python modules, infers properties from code and documentation, synthesizes and executes Hypothesis property-based tests, and triages failures to produce actionable bug reports. docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• An agentic approach to property-based testing can autonomously discover genuine bugs across diverse Python libraries at scale, with 56% of generated reports being valid bugs.
  • The cost of finding a valid bug is approximately $9.93, making LLM-guided PBT an economically viable complement to traditional testing.
  • The agent found bugs spanning diverse failure modes (numerical precision, serialization, caching logic), demonstrating that PBT properties mined by LLMs go beyond shallow invariants.
  • A ranking rubric applied to bug reports surfaces high-priority valid bugs with 86% precision among top-scoring reports (17 of 21 worth reporting).
  • The primary limitation is intent ambiguity: the agent cannot reliably distinguish intentional design violations from actual bugs without developer domain expertise.

docs.text: Agentic Reasoning enhances LLM reasoning by integrating external tool-using agents—web search, code execution, and a Mind-Map agent that constructs a structured knowledge graph to maintain reasoning coherence. docs.text: Agentless proposes a simplistic, non-agentic approach to automated software engineering that uses a three-phase process of localization, repair, and patch validation without letting the LLM autonomously decide future actions or use complex tools. • A simple three-phase process (localization, repair, patch validation) without autonomous agent decision-making achieves the highest performance on SWE-bench Lite among open-source approaches at very low cost ($0.70)

docs.title: AgentRadio: Passive Awareness for Long-Horizon Multi-Agent Collaboration
Summary
docs.text: AgentRadio is an asynchronous message-passing layer for coding-agent harnesses built on three primitives (create_thread, send_message, wait_for_mention), where the mention-wait runs as a background task so agents stay passively aware of teammates' discoveries without pausing their own work. Under a five-phase division-of-labor protocol on SWE-Atlas QnA (long-horizon codebase-understanding tasks), four Claude Code (Opus 4.6) agents coordinated via AgentRadio raise task accuracy from 32.3% (single agent) to 62.1% — surpassing even a single agent on the newer Opus 4.8 (57.2%). The gains hold up under a controlled ablation isolating just the passive-vs-blocking communication mode, and grow with task difficulty, consistent with mid-execution correction as the mechanism.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• Existing multi-agent systems make communication and work mutually exclusive (parallel-but-isolated, round-synchronized, or one-way task queues); no prior system gives concurrently-working agents passive lateral awareness of natural-language messages.
  • On a two-model ablation ladder (B0→L1 division→L2 negotiation→L3 passive awareness), every layer helps on both Opus 4.6 and DeepSeek V4 Pro; the passive-awareness step alone adds 10.5 points (Opus 4.6) and 11.3 points (DeepSeek), significant on paired McNemar tests (p<0.003).
  • The full AgentRadio stack beats a compute-matched best-of-6 single-agent baseline (62.1% vs. 37.9% at similar cost with Opus 4.6), showing the gain is structural, not just extra compute/budget.
  • Passive awareness's benefit grows with task difficulty — on tasks the blocking protocol nearly solves it adds ~0.3 rubrics/task, but on the hardest near-misses it adds up to 2.0 rubrics/task — consistent with catching discoveries that would otherwise die unvoiced (illustrated in a MinIO case study).
  • The approach has a clear limit: passive awareness surfaces discoveries agents already make but wouldn't otherwise share — it can't supply a conclusion no agent forms (Grafana case study, zero gain).

docs.title: AgREE: Agentic Reasoning for Knowledge Graph Completion on Emerging Entities

docs.text: AgREE (Agentic Reasoning for Emerging Entities) is a zero-training agent framework from Apple that combines iterative web retrieval with multi-step reasoning to complete knowledge graph (KG) triplets for emerging entities not seen during model training. docs.text:
• KG completion for emerging entities (new startups, public figures, products) is fundamentally different from standard KGC because no prior representation exists in the graph

  • Single-step retrieval approaches miss the multifaceted nature of entity relationships; multi-step agentic exploration is necessary for comprehensive KG representation
  • A new evaluation methodology addresses a fundamental weakness of existing setups that don't properly test on genuinely emerging entities
  • The work demonstrates that combining agent-based reasoning with strategic information retrieval is more effective than static methods for maintaining up-to-date knowledge graphs

docs.title: AI auditing: The Broken Bus on the Road to AI Accountability
Summary
docs.text: This paper surveys AI audit practice across academia, regulators, law firms, consultancies, journalism and civil society, and assesses whether each produces real accountability outcomes such as product changes, recalls, policy, or bans. It finds that only a subset of audits translate into accountability: academic audits mostly treat evaluation as the end goal, while non-academic audits achieve more impact through stakeholder engagement, specific targets and demands, and dissemination of results.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• An AI audit is defined as an independent assessment of a named, concrete target against articulated expectations, with the objective of accountability; abstract fairness or safety studies without a specific target do not qualify
  • Academic audits, often academia–big-tech collaborations examining their own systems, follow publication norms and rarely demand concrete systemic change, whereas journalism, civil society and regulator audits are more consequential
  • Audit framing (target selection, harms investigated, scope, and stages beyond evaluation such as harm discovery, communication and collective action) matters more for impact than execution details
  • Impact increases with specificity: naming the target and the desired remedy (Gender Shades, ACLU, The Markup, ICO) works, while diffuse audits such as ORCAA's HireVue audit gain little traction; scope that is too narrow, however, obscures systemic causes
  • Power asymmetries between auditors, audit targets and affected stakeholders are a major determinant of audit effectiveness; policymakers could empower auditors through legal access and by attaching consequences to audit results

docs.title: An Empirical Evaluation of Using Large Language Models for Automated Unit Test Generation
Summary
docs.text:
TestPilot generates unit tests for JavaScript APIs by prompting an LLM with the function signature, its implementation, and usage examples mined from documentation, then re-prompting with the failing test and error message when a generated test fails. Evaluated on 25 npm packages covering 1,684 API functions with gpt-3.5-turbo, it reached 70.2% median statement coverage against 51.3% for Nessie, the prior feedback-directed technique. The approach needs no fine-tuning or few-shot examples of existing tests, and holds up across three different models, suggesting it depends on model scale rather than any specific model.

Dating caveat: this is a February 2023 paper evaluated on gpt-3.5-turbo, code-cushman-002, and StarCoder. Treat the absolute coverage numbers as a historical baseline for what unaided prompting achieved at that capability level, not as a current ceiling. The method — documentation-derived prompts plus an error-feedback loop — is the durable contribution.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• LLMs can generate effective unit tests without additional training or few-shot examples, using only the function under test and documentation-derived usage snippets — 70.2% median statement / 52.8% branch coverage vs Nessie's 51.3% / 25.6%.
  • Re-prompting with the failing test and its error message is a core part of the method, not a refinement — the feedback loop is what turns a plausible test into a passing one.
  • Ablations show every prompt component contributes; notably, removing usage snippets hurt no more than removing any other refiner, so examples are not the dominant signal the authors expected.
  • Generated tests are not memorized copies: 92.8% have ≤50% similarity to existing tests by normalized edit distance, none are exact copies.
  • Results degrade gracefully across models (gpt-3.5-turbo 70.2%, code-cushman-002 68.2%, StarCoder 54.0%), indicating sensitivity to model size and training data rather than dependence on one vendor.

docs.title: An Empirical Study of Harness Design for Coding Agents
Summary
docs.text: A controlled component-level study of coding harnesses: the ReAct execution loop is held fixed while planning, the action space (predefined tools vs bash-only) and context management (five strategies across 32k–128k windows) are varied, across 176 settings with three Nemotron-3 sizes (30B, 120B, 550B) and Mistral-Medium-3.5-128B on SWE-Bench Verified and Terminal-Bench 2.1. No component helps unconditionally: each one's value depends on model capability, task type and context budget, and trajectory analysis ties each effect to a specific behavioral change.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• Context management is worth most when the window is tight, mainly because it prevents overflow: the managed-vs-unmanaged success gap on SWE-Bench shrinks from 35.7 points at 32k to 2.7 at 128k, tracking unmanaged overflow failures falling from 78.7% to 8.7%
  • Cheap rule-based elision of stale tool outputs before LLM summarization gives the best cost at similar accuracy; making elided content recoverable adds nothing — 56% of recall-enabled settings never call recall_event, and elision with recall vs without differs by −0.36 points on average
  • Planning flips from accuracy aid to cost saver as capability rises: it adds 11.6 points on SWE-Bench for the 30B model (by keeping trajectories alive long enough to attempt an edit), but for the strongest models cuts cost about 30% with success down 0.4–2.0 points, mostly by trimming redundant post-edit verification
  • Predefined tools help models weak at bash, while bash-capable models do better with bash only: Nemotron-3 550B gains 3.6 points on SWE-Bench and 5.6 on Terminal-Bench at 53% and 30% lower cost, combining several operations per call; Mistral prefers full tools on SWE-Bench but bash-only on Terminal-Bench, so the crossover depends on task type
  • Limitations: each setting is run once, Terminal-Bench has only 89 tasks so many of its contrasts aren't individually significant, planning and action space are ablated only at T4/128k, and the action-space switch bundles tools with diagnostics and state tracking

docs.title: Analyzing and Bridging the Gap between Maximizing Total Reward and Discounted Reward in Deep Reinforcement Learning
Summary
docs.text: This paper identifies and analyzes the "objective misalignment problem" in deep RL, where policies that maximize discounted return can paradoxically minimize total return, especially in environments with cyclic states. The authors propose two alignment approaches -- modifying the terminal state value as a tunable hyperparameter, and a trajectory reward data calibration method -- both of which provably align the two objectives and improve robustness to discount factor choices in practical DRL algorithms.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• Maximizing discounted return does not guarantee improved total return performance; a policy maximizing discounted return can paradoxically minimize total return in MDPs with cyclic states
  • Simply increasing the discount factor toward one is insufficient to resolve the objective misalignment, as it can destabilize training, slow convergence, or fail entirely in cyclic-state environments
  • The terminal state value can be treated as a tunable hyperparameter to align discounted and total return objectives, with theoretically derived suitable ranges
  • A trajectory reward data calibration method can modify discounted returns to ensure monotonic alignment with total returns, improving robustness across tasks with long trajectory lengths

docs.title: Antislop: A Comprehensive Framework for Identifying and Eliminating Repetitive Patterns in Language Models
Summary
docs.text: Antislop is a framework to detect and eliminate "slop"—repetitive, overused patterns in LLM output that make AI-generated text immediately recognizable. It combines an inference-time Antislop Sampler (backtracking to suppress patterns without destroying vocabulary), an automated profiling pipeline, and FTPO (Final Token Preference Optimization), a novel fine-tuning method that surgically adjusts logits at individual tokens where banned patterns appear. Some slop patterns appear 1,000× more frequently in LLM output than human text.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• Some LLM output patterns appear over 1,000× more frequently than in human text, creating a pervasive "slop" problem
  • Token banning becomes unusable at just 2,000 patterns due to collateral damage; the Antislop Sampler suppresses 8,000+ patterns while maintaining quality
  • FTPO operates on individual tokens in inference traces (not full sequences), achieving 90% slop reduction with maintained or improved performance on GSM8K, MMLU, and creative writing
  • DPO achieves weaker suppression than FTPO while causing significant degradation in writing quality and lexical diversity
  • All code and results released under MIT license

docs.text: ANX is an agent-native protocol and architecture that unifies GUI automation, MCP, skill systems, and CLI under a single framework with a 3EX (Expression-Exchange-Execution) decoupled architecture. docs.text:

docs.title: ArchAgent v2: A Case Study with the Data Prefetching Championship
Summary
docs.text: ArchAgent v2 builds on AlphaEvolve and the ChampSim simulator to design hardware data prefetchers automatically, covering three cache levels (L1D, L2 and LLC). It adds two things to v1. The first is a cascaded divide-and-conquer search: it evolves one cache level at a time, freezes the best result, and only then optimizes all levels together, adding multi-core configurations last. The second is a feedback loop that rejects any candidate exceeding its storage budget before it is evaluated. Under the official rules of the Fourth Data Prefetching Championship (DPC4), it beats the hand-designed winner, BertiGO. The authors also profile more than 12,000 candidates, which shows that the evolutionary loop is wasteful: about half the candidates fail or score lower, and the average proposal never improves over the course of the run.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• The evolved three-level prefetcher gets a 3.8% geometric-mean IPC speedup over the DPC4 baseline, 0.3% above BertiGO. Its advantage is concentrated in low-bandwidth single-core runs (4.6% vs 2.6%). On multi-core it loses to BertiGO by about 1.5%, because multi-core feedback only entered the search at the final stage. Simulation runs take up to 12 hours each, which makes multi-core evolution impractical for now.
  • Evolving all prefetchers at once makes the search non-monotonic: a gain at one cache level can cancel out a gain at another. Breaking the problem into one level at a time, then optimizing globally, is what made progress possible where v1 had stalled.
  • Telling the LLM the storage limits in the prompt is not enough, because LLM optimizers chase the performance metric and ignore physical constraints. The authors therefore require each candidate to report its own size through a prefetcher_size() function, checked during compilation, and reject over-budget designs outright, which acts as a negative reward. An LLM judge checked that the size function was kept in sync with the code, and the final design was also checked by hand.
  • Along the best design's lineage, about 65% of changes were architectural, and the score did not rise steadily. Some ideas only paid off after later refinement or after being combined with others. The single biggest jump came from merging candidates that had evolved separately in other groups of the population.
  • The authors concede that the resulting design is only incrementally novel. Its parts recombine known techniques: RL arbitration, global stride tracking, and throttling based on available bandwidth.

docs.title: Artificial Hivemind: The Open-Ended Homogeneity of Language Models (and Beyond)
Summary
docs.text:
This paper introduces INFINITY-CHAT, a dataset of 26K real-world open-ended queries mined from WildChat that admit many plausible answers with no ground truth, together with the first taxonomy of open-ended LM prompts (6 categories, 17 subcategories). Using it across 70+ models, the authors document an "Artificial Hivemind" effect with two components: intra-model repetition, where one model keeps producing near-identical responses, and — more consequentially — inter-model homogeneity, where independently trained models converge on the same ideas with only phrasing differences. A companion set of 31,250 human annotations (25 independent annotators per example) shows that LMs, reward models, and LM judges are poorly calibrated to human ratings precisely where annotators' idiosyncratic preferences diverge.

This is the paper that names the effect; two other sources in this wiki respond to it directly — see Related below.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• Inter-model homogeneity is the sharper finding. Different model families and sizes converge independently, so ensembles and model "swarms" cannot be assumed to produce real diversity when constituents share alignment and training priors.
  • The "write a metaphor about time" demonstration is the paper's most legible evidence: 25 models × 50 responses at temperature 1.0 collapse into just two embedding clusters — "time is a river" and "time is a weaver."
  • Existing diversity benchmarks are too narrow to detect this — random-number or name generation, persona generation, poetry — which is why the effect needed a real-world open-ended corpus to surface.
  • Reward models and LM judges assume a single consensus notion of quality. They are miscalibrated exactly on responses where humans legitimately disagree despite comparable quality, so current pipelines systematically fail to reward pluralism.
  • The authors frame homogenization as a long-term AI safety risk — repeated exposure to convergent outputs homogenizing human thought — not merely a creativity shortfall.

docs.title: Related
docs.text:
• Beyond the Hivemind — proposes persona anchoring + filtered temperature scaling as mitigation, evaluated on INFINITY-CHAT.
  • Is Convergence Inevitable? — traces the effect back to base models.

docs.title: LLMs Get Lost in Multi-Turn Conversation
Summary
docs.text: This paper demonstrates that all major LLMs exhibit significantly lower performance in multi-turn, underspecified conversations compared to single-turn, fully-specified settings, with an average performance drop of 39% across six generation tasks and 15 models. The degradation decomposes into a minor loss in aptitude and a major increase in unreliability, driven by LLMs making premature assumptions, generating overly verbose responses, and failing to recover once they take a wrong conversational turn.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• All top open- and closed-weight LLMs show significantly lower performance in multi-turn conversations than single-turn, with an average 39% drop across six generation tasks
  • Performance degradation decomposes into two components: a minor loss in aptitude (~15%) and a dramatic increase in unreliability (~112%)
  • When LLMs take a wrong turn in a conversation, they get lost and do not recover -- a phenomenon the authors call "lost in conversation"
  • LLMs tend to generate overly verbose responses, propose solutions prematurely, make incorrect assumptions about underspecified details, and rely too heavily on previous incorrect attempts
  • The performance drop is observed even in two-turn conversations, across models from small open-weights to state-of-the-art proprietary models

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: MemoryOS proposes a comprehensive memory operating system for AI agents inspired by OS memory management principles, featuring a three-tier hierarchical storage (short-term, mid-term, long-term personal memory) with four functional modules (storage, updating, retrieval, generation). On the LoCoMo benchmark, MemoryOS improves F1 by 49.11% and BLEU-1 by 46.18% over GPT-4o-mini baselines for maintaining contextual coherence and personalized memory retention in long conversations.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• Existing LLM memory approaches operate in isolation (storage, retrieval, or architecture alone), lacking a unified systematic framework
  • MemoryOS uses three-tier hierarchical storage: Short-Term Memory (recent conversations), Mid-Term Memory (recurring topic summaries), and Long-term Personal Memory (user/agent preferences)
  • Memory updating uses a segmented paging strategy with heat-based replacement, inspired by OS memory management
  • MemoryOS achieves 49.11% F1 improvement and 46.18% BLEU-1 improvement over GPT-4o-mini baselines on the LoCoMo benchmark
  • The system enables dynamic capture and evolution of user preferences across extended dialogues through coordinated storage, updating, retrieval, and generation modules

docs.title: tau2-Bench: Evaluating Conversational Agents in a Dual-Control Environment
Summary
docs.text: tau2-bench introduces a dual-control benchmark for conversational AI agents where both the agent and user can use tools to act in a shared, dynamic environment (modeled as a Dec-POMDP), unlike prior single-control benchmarks. In the telecom domain, state-of-the-art LLMs struggle significantly (gpt-4.1: 34%, o4-mini: 42%, claude-3.7-sonnet: 49% pass^1), with a ~20% performance drop when shifting from autonomous to dual-control mode, revealing communication and coordination as critical bottlenecks.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• Existing agent benchmarks are single-control (only the agent acts), missing real-world scenarios where users also take actions
  • tau2-bench models the interaction as a Decentralized POMDP where both agent and user have distinct tools and observe a shared environment
  • Agent performance drops ~20% when transitioning from autonomous mode to dual-control, isolating communication/coordination as the bottleneck
  • Tightly coupling the user simulator to environment state via tools produces more reliable simulations (16% error rate vs 40% in tau-bench)
  • A compositional task generator programmatically creates diverse, verifiable tasks ensuring domain coverage and controlled complexity

docs.title: Monitoring Decomposition Attacks in LLMs with Lightweight Sequential Monitors
Summary
docs.text: This paper studies decomposition attacks where malicious goals are broken into seemingly benign subtasks that bypass LLM safety filters, achieving 87% attack success rate on GPT-4o across QA, text-to-image, and agent settings. The authors propose lightweight sequential monitors that cumulatively evaluate prompt streams to detect emerging harmful intent, achieving 93% defense success rate with carefully prompt-engineered models like Llama-3.1-8B, outperforming expensive reasoning models like o3-mini at greatly reduced cost.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• Decomposition attacks reduce refusal rates from 77.8% to 7.2% on average and achieve 87% attack success rate on GPT-4o across QA, text-to-image, and agent settings
  • Current LLM safety mechanisms use "shallow" alignment that only detects harm in immediate prompts, not across sequences of benign-looking subtasks
  • Sequential monitoring that cumulatively evaluates each prompt significantly outperforms single-input harm detection (DSR: 58% vs 27% with Llama-3.1-8B)
  • Carefully prompt-engineered lightweight monitors (Llama-3.1-8B, GPT-4o-mini) achieve up to 93% defense success rate, outperforming expensive o3-mini
  • Random task injection into decomposed subtasks can easily bypass even strong monitors, but lightweight monitors remain robust with 90% cost reduction and 50% latency reduction

docs.title: AbsenceBench: Language Models Can't Tell What's Missing
Summary
docs.text: AbsenceBench evaluates LLMs' ability to detect deliberately omitted information from documents, complementing the Needle-in-a-Haystack (NIAH) test which measures retrieval of inserted information. Across 14 LLMs on poetry, numerical sequences, and GitHub PRs (average 5K tokens), even state-of-the-art models like Claude-3.7-Sonnet achieve only 69.6% F1, with a massive 56.9% F1 drop compared to NIAH, suggesting a fundamental limitation in Transformer attention mechanisms' ability to attend to "gaps."

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• LLMs are dramatically worse at detecting omitted information than inserted information, with a 56.9% average F1 drop from NIAH to AbsenceBench
  • Even state-of-the-art models (Claude-3.7-Sonnet) achieve only 69.6% F1 on the relatively simple task of identifying missing content
  • Inference-time compute (extended thinking) offers only 7.9% improvement at the cost of 3x average document length in thinking tokens
  • Adding explicit placeholder markers for omissions improves performance by 35.7%, suggesting Transformer attention mechanisms struggle with attending to absent keys
  • Counter-intuitively, a lower rate of omission leads to worse model performance

docs.title: AlphaEvolve: A Coding Agent for Scientific and Algorithmic Discovery
Summary
docs.text: AlphaEvolve is an evolutionary coding agent from Google DeepMind that combines LLM-based code generation with automated evaluation to discover novel algorithms and optimize computational infrastructure. It surpasses the state of the art on 14 matrix multiplication algorithms, improves Strassen's algorithm for 4x4 complex matrices (first improvement in 56 years), matches or improves best-known constructions on ~75% of 50+ open math problems, and has been deployed to optimize Google's data center scheduling, TPU circuits, and attention runtime.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• AlphaEvolve discovered a procedure to multiply two 4x4 complex matrices using 48 scalar multiplications, the first improvement over Strassen's algorithm in 56 years
  • The system matches or beats best-known constructions on ~75% of 50+ open problems in mathematics, with ~20% achieving provably better results
  • Unlike its predecessor FunSearch, AlphaEvolve evolves entire code files (not single functions) across any language using state-of-the-art LLMs
  • AlphaEvolve has been deployed on critical Google infrastructure including data center scheduling, TPU circuit design, and Transformer attention optimization
  • The evolutionary approach with automated evaluation grounding avoids incorrect LLM suggestions while leveraging LLMs' ability to respond to feedback

docs.title: Potemkin Understanding in Large Language Models
Summary
docs.text: This paper formalizes "potemkin understanding" -- the phenomenon where LLMs correctly answer benchmark questions designed to test conceptual understanding while possessing fundamentally incoherent internal representations of those concepts. The authors develop procedures for detecting potemkins and find they are ubiquitous across models, tasks, and domains (literary techniques, game theory, psychological biases), driven by incoherence rather than mere incorrect understanding.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• Benchmarks designed for humans (AP exams, SAT, etc.) are only valid tests for LLMs if the space of LLM misunderstandings is structured like the space of human misunderstandings
  • Potemkins arise when LLMs can define concepts correctly but fail to apply them, producing internally incoherent combinations of correct and incorrect answers
  • Potemkin understanding is ubiquitous across models, tasks, and domains, reflecting deeper internal incoherence in concept representations rather than mere factual errors
  • An automated procedure provides a lower bound on potemkin prevalence and identifies high rates across LLMs even without domain-specific assumptions
  • Benchmark success should not be interpreted as evidence of genuine conceptual understanding in LLMs

docs.text: MemAgent introduces a novel agent workflow for processing arbitrarily long documents by reading text in segments and maintaining a dynamically updated fixed-length memory using an overwrite strategy, trained end-to-end with a multi-conversation extension of the DAPO algorithm. docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• MemAgent processes arbitrarily long inputs within a limited context window with linear time complexity, overcoming the quadratic bottleneck of standard transformers
  • An 8K-context model trained on 32K documents extrapolates to 3.5M tokens with less than 5% performance degradation
  • The multi-conversation DAPO algorithm enables end-to-end training of agent workflows with independent context segments
  • MemAgent achieves 95%+ on the 512K RULER test, outperforming models with much larger native context windows
  • The approach uses RL to teach the model what information to retain in memory, rather than relying on external memory modules

Summary
docs.text: Astraios presents a systematic comparison of 7 parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods across 4 model scales (1B-16B) for instruction-tuning code LLMs based on StarCoder, evaluating on 5 code tasks and 8 datasets.   • PEFT methods differ significantly in their efficacy based on model scale; at 16B parameters, Parallel Adapter and LoRA are most competitive with FFT
  • Larger models tend to demonstrate reduced robustness and less security in generated code despite improved generation task performance
  • Tuning effectiveness observed in small PEFT models generalizes well to larger ones, and validation loss is a reliable proxy for downstream performance

docs.title: ATime-Consistent Benchmark for Repository-Level Software Engineering Evaluation
Summary
docs.text: This paper proposes a time-consistent benchmark methodology for evaluating repository-aware software engineering systems. A repository is snapshotted at time T0, repository-derived code knowledge is constructed only from pre-T0 artifacts, and evaluation tasks are derived from pull requests merged in the interval (T0, T1]. The benchmark uses a matched A/B design to isolate the causal contribution of repository-derived code knowledge while controlling for model, prompt, environment, and task effects. A baseline study on DragonFly and React across three Claude-family models shows that prompt granularity is a first-order benchmark variable strongly affecting measured performance.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• Time-consistent benchmarking with strict pre/post-snapshot separation is necessary to avoid temporal contamination when evaluating repository-knowledge-augmented coding agents.
  • Prompt construction granularity (minimal, concise, contextual, guided) is a first-order variable that strongly affects benchmark scores, not merely a packaging detail.
  • A matched A/B evaluation design isolates the marginal effect of repository-derived code knowledge by holding all other variables constant (model, snapshot, task, environment, metric).
  • File-level F1 increases monotonically from minimal to guided prompts, reaching ~0.81 on both DragonFly and React for the strongest model tested.
  • Any future knowledge-augmentation gains must be interpreted against the background variance caused by prompt granularity and model capability differences.

  • Combining manual and automatic construction methods produces higher-quality attack prompts than either approach alone

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: The paper introduces the Transformer, a sequence transduction architecture based entirely on attention mechanisms, dispensing with recurrence and convolutions. It achieves state-of-the-art BLEU scores on English-German and English-French translation while being significantly faster to train due to full parallelizability. docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• Self-attention alone (no RNNs/CNNs) is sufficient for high-quality sequence transduction
  • Multi-head attention allows the model to jointly attend to information from different representation subspaces at different positions
  • Positional encodings (sinusoidal) substitute for recurrence to inject sequence order information
  • Achieves 28.4 BLEU (EN→DE) and 41.8 BLEU (EN→FR), outperforming all prior models including ensembles
  • Training is dramatically faster than RNN-based models due to full parallelization

docs.title: AuditBench: A Benchmark for Large Language Models in Financial Statement Auditing
Summary
docs.text: AuditBench is a benchmark for evaluating LLMs on financial statement auditing, using a curated dataset combining real-world financial tables with synthesized transaction data. Its five-stage evaluation framework (error detection → explanation → standard citation → complete audit → revision) reveals progressively worse performance at each stage: LLMs can identify errors but struggle to explain them, cite relevant accounting standards, or execute complete audits. Presented at AI4Research @ AAAI 2025.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• Five-stage evaluation framework reveals progressively worse performance: LLMs succeed at error detection but fail at explanation, standard citation, complete audit execution, and revision
  • Current state-of-the-art LLMs successfully identify financial statement errors when given historical transaction data, but this surface capability masks deep gaps in domain knowledge
  • The benchmark maps specific financial statement errors to corresponding violations of accounting standards, simulating real-world auditing workflows
  • A critical gap exists in LLMs' understanding of auditing principles and procedures — they can pattern-match anomalies but cannot reason about why they violate standards

Summary
docs.text: AutoDAN introduces a hierarchical genetic algorithm for automatically generating semantically meaningful (stealthy) jailbreak prompts against aligned LLMs, addressing the limitations of manual crafting (not scalable) and token-based attacks like GCG (not stealthy, detectable by perplexity filters).   • AutoDAN uses a hierarchical genetic algorithm with paragraph-level and sentence-level crossover policies to search the discrete space of semantically meaningful prompts
  • AutoDAN surpasses the GCG baseline by 60% in attack strength while bypassing perplexity-based defenses
  • Handcrafted jailbreak prompts serve as effective prototypes to initialize the genetic algorithm, dramatically reducing the search space
  • The method demonstrates notable cross-model transferability and cross-sample universality across both open-source and commercial LLMs

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Autogenesis introduces AGP, a two-layer protocol for self-evolving multi-agent systems that decouples what evolves from how evolution occurs. The Resource Substrate Protocol Layer (RSPL) models prompts, agents, tools, environments, and memory as versioned, lifecycle-managed resources, while the Self-Evolution Protocol Layer (SEPL) provides a closed-loop operator interface for proposing, assessing, and committing improvements with auditable lineage and rollback. Evaluated on GPQA, AIME, GAIA, HLE, and LeetCode, the instantiated system (AGS) achieves consistent improvements over strong baselines.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• Existing agent protocols (MCP, A2A) handle invocation and message passing but lack lifecycle management, version lineage, and controlled state mutation needed for self-evolution
  • Decoupling evolutionary substrate from evolutionary logic via two protocol layers enables composable, auditable, and reproducible self-evolution of agent components
  • Treating prompts, tools, memory, and agents as protocol-registered resources with explicit versioned interfaces allows uniform application of optimization algorithms across heterogeneous components
  • The system achieves consistent improvements on five challenging benchmarks (GPQA, AIME, GAIA, HLE, LeetCode) over strong baselines, validating principled resource management

Summary
docs.text: AutoRocq is the first LLM proof automation agent that autonomously collaborates with the Rocq (Coq) theorem prover to verify software. docs.text:
• AutoRocq proves 48.0% of CoqGym mathematical lemmas and 30.9% of SV-COMP verification lemmas, exceeding baselines by 10.6-204.6% on verification tasks

docs.title: Back to Basics: Revisiting REINFORCE Style Optimization for Learning from Human Feedback in LLMs
Summary
docs.text: This paper argues that PPO is unnecessarily complex for RLHF in LLMs and demonstrates that simpler REINFORCE-style optimization consistently outperforms PPO, DPO, and RAFT for aligning language models with human preferences. The key insight is that RLHF operates in a fundamentally different regime from traditional deep RL -- the pre-trained, SFT-initialized policy has low variance gradient estimators -- making PPO's complexity unwarranted.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• Most motivational principles behind PPO (e.g., stability through clipping, value function baselines) are less relevant in the RLHF setting due to the well-initialized policy from pre-training and SFT
  • Vanilla REINFORCE with full-trajectory reward and no clipping consistently outperforms PPO across models and datasets
  • Modeling the entire generation as a single action rather than per-token actions is more appropriate for RLHF where rewards apply only to full generations
  • Higher variance (lambda=1.0) gradient estimators outperform lower-variance biased alternatives in RLHF, contrary to traditional deep RL intuitions
  • REINFORCE Leave-One-Out (RLOO) provides a practical multi-sample extension that further improves performance

docs.title: Benchmarking Multi-Agent LLM Architectures for Financial Document Processing: A Comparative Study of Orchestration Patterns, Cost-Accuracy Tradeoffs and Production Scaling Strategies
Summary
docs.text: A systematic benchmark comparing four multi-agent orchestration architectures (sequential pipeline, parallel fan-out, hierarchical supervisor-worker, reflexive self-correcting) across five LLMs on 10,000 SEC filings with 25 extraction field types. The hierarchical architecture achieves the best cost-accuracy Pareto position (97.7% of reflexive F1 at 60.9% cost), while hybrid configurations combining semantic caching, model routing, and adaptive retries recover 89% of reflexive accuracy gains at only 1.15x baseline cost. Scaling analysis from 1K to 100K documents/day reveals architecture-specific degradation curves, and a failure taxonomy catalogs 12 failure modes with architecture-specific prevalence rates.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• Reflexive self-correcting architectures achieve highest accuracy (F1 0.943) but at 2.3x cost of sequential baselines; hierarchical architectures occupy the most favorable cost-accuracy Pareto position (F1 0.921 at 1.4x cost)
  • Hybrid configurations recover 89% of reflexive accuracy gains at 1.15x baseline cost through semantic caching, model routing, and adaptive retries — a practical "best of both worlds" for production
  • 12 failure modes cataloged with architecture-specific prevalence: cross-table reference failure (28.4% sequential vs. 8.7% reflexive), temporal confusion (18.2% vs 6.4%), and reflexive "overthinking" oscillation on ambiguous disclosures (39.3%)
  • Scaling reveals non-linear degradation: reflexive F1 drops from 0.943 to 0.871 at 100K docs/day; sequential shows smallest degradation (0.017 F1 loss); hierarchical optimal range is 10K-50K docs/day
  • The reflexive verifier applies domain-specific financial consistency rules (total assets = total liabilities + equity) and source grounding checks (extracted values must have supporting evidence in source text)
