docs.title: Beyond Code Generation: Reliability, Verification, and Cost Economics in the Agentic Software Development Lifecycle
Summary
docs.text: A single-author (Northeastern) systems synthesis of 2024–September 2026 evidence — RCTs, university studies, benchmark audits, company production reports, telemetry, and cost data — arguing that coding agents move the software-delivery bottleneck from writing code to verifying, integrating, and operating it. It runs no new experiments and proposes four concepts: the Agentic SDLC Throughput Paradox, Production-Qualified Change (PQC), the Verification Tax, and an Agentic SDLC Control Plane that allocates autonomy under cost, reliability, and human-attention budgets.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• Throughput Paradox: gains shrink as work moves toward release — a study of 100,000+ GitHub developers found autonomous agents raised commit-level activity by 180% but project-level output by 50% and releases by only 30%, while pooled RCTs across 4,867 developers show a 26.08% increase in completed tasks; review, integration, testing, security, and operations remain the constraining stages
  • Agent output is heavily filtered and often worse: in Stanford's SWE-chat dataset of 6,000 real agent sessions only 44% of agent-produced code survived into user commits, users pushed back in 44% of turns, and agent-written code showed more security vulnerabilities; SWE-Marathon rollouts averaged 27.2M tokens with no configuration above 30% pass@1 and reward hacking in 13.8% of rollouts; DORA 2025 links higher AI adoption to higher throughput but lower delivery stability
  • Count Production-Qualified Changes, not generated patches: a change is output only after review, test, security, deployment, and operational gates; the Verification Tax makes the variable assurance cost explicit (CI, reviewer time, security analysis, rework, escaped failures), not just tokens
  • Harness quality is a hidden variable: tool permissions, retrieval, context compression, test selection, sandbox state, and retry logic materially change both success and cost, and a benchmark score can move because the harness changed rather than the model — so organisations need versioned harnesses and reproducible agent runs, not just a record of which model was called
  • Economics are shifting from per-seat licences to variable token, tool, sandbox, CI, and rework costs: token use varies by programming language even at equal difficulty (agents produce non-compiling attempts, revise passing solutions, distrust provided tests), 98% of surveyed FinOps practitioners now manage AI spend (up from 31%), and the paper proposes a control plane that sets autonomy per task by risk, reversibility, and budget

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Limitation: a structured synthesis, not a systematic review; many 2026 sources are preprints or company reports; the author notes the headline studies (RCTs, METR's 19% slowdown, the GitHub event study) differ in population and causal strength and should not be compared directly. PQC, Verification Tax, and the Control Plane are proposed hypotheses, not validated standards. Gartner's forecast that AI coding cost could exceed developer salary by 2028 is a planning signal, not evidence.
  • Numbers are attributed to their original studies; check the primary source before reusing any figure.

docs.title: Beyond Cognitive Load Theory: Why Learning Needs More than Memory Management
Summary
docs.text: A conceptual review in Brain Sciences arguing that Cognitive Load Theory, built to optimize instruction for novices learning well-structured material, is overextended when used as a general framework for K–12 education. Drawing on neuroscience and developmental psychology, it argues that working-memory capacity is malleable and that emotional, social and self-regulatory processes are intertwined with cognition. It proposes the Neurodevelopmental Informed Holistic Learning and Development Framework (NIHLDF) as a hypothesis-generating alternative. It is about human learning, not AI systems.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• CLT's core categories (intrinsic, extraneous and germane load) and its split between biologically primary and secondary knowledge are contested and weakly supported by evidence
  • Neuroscience suggests working memory is a distributed, context-sensitive and trainable system rather than a fixed-capacity bottleneck
  • Cognitive, emotional and social processes share neural substrates (e.g. prefrontal cortex, amygdala) and cannot be meaningfully isolated in real learning environments
  • Optimizing for short-term efficiency through load reduction gives an incomplete account of how learners develop the capacity to handle complexity and persist through challenge
  • NIHLDF is offered as a heuristic, not an empirically confirmed model; the authors call for studies testing it in classrooms

docs.title: Beyond Context: Large Language Models Failure to Grasp Users' Intent
Summary
docs.text: This paper argues that LLMs' inability to understand context and recognize user intent is a critical, underexplored safety vulnerability that enables systematic circumvention of safety mechanisms through emotional framing, progressive revelation, and academic justification techniques. Testing across ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, and DeepSeek reveals four categories of contextual blindness (temporal degradation, implicit semantic failure, multi-modal integration deficits, situational blindness), with current models achieving only 18% success in recognizing user-specific context.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• Contextual blindness -- not just harmful content detection -- is the most exploitable weakness in contemporary LLMs
  • Current state-of-the-art models achieve only 18% success in recognizing user-specific context
  • Reasoning-enabled configurations amplified rather than mitigated exploitation effectiveness, increasing factual precision while failing to detect underlying intent
  • Four categories of contextual blindness create exploitable vulnerabilities: temporal context degradation, implicit semantic context failure, multi-modal context integration deficits, and situational context blindness
  • Technical safeguards alone will remain insufficient without fundamental advances in contextual reasoning as a core architectural capability

docs.title: Beyond the Hivemind: Escaping LLM Homogeneity via Meta-Persona Anchoring and Sequential Temperature Scaling
Summary
docs.text: A mitigation framework for the Artificial Hivemind effect, combining Meta-Persona Anchoring — prompting the model to self-select an idiosyncratic persona before answering — with Filtered Temperature Scaling, a two-stage sieve that applies Top-p filtering to preserve grammatical validity and then extreme temperature (T >= 4.0) to the surviving candidates. Evaluated on INFINITY-CHAT with open-weight models under ~20B parameters, it drops average pairwise cosine similarity from roughly 0.85 to 0.65, putting a majority of questions below the 0.7 threshold. The authors release the implementation as an open-source framework.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• The two-stage design is the substance: Top-p first, extreme temperature second. Applying T >= 4.0 directly would destroy grammaticality; filtering to a valid candidate set first makes the high temperature survivable.
  • Persona anchoring is a starting-point intervention — the model self-selects an idiosyncratic persona to move its initial position in output space, rather than being handed personas from a fixed list.
  • Reported effect is a drop in mean pairwise cosine similarity from ~0.85 to ~0.65, narrowing but not closing the gap to human typological diversity.
  • Evaluation is confined to open-weight models under ~20B parameters, so it is untested on the frontier models where the hivemind effect was originally characterized.
  • The framing accepts Artificial Hivemind's diagnosis wholesale and attacks it at inference time only — no training-side intervention, which is also its main limitation as a remedy.

docs.title: Related
docs.text:
• Artificial Hivemind — the paper this mitigates; source of the INFINITY-CHAT dataset used here.
  • Is Convergence Inevitable? — argues the cause is upstream in pretraining, which would limit what inference-time fixes like this can achieve.

docs.title: Beyond the Imitation Game: Quantifying and extrapolating the capabilities of language models
Summary
docs.text: BIG-bench (Beyond the Imitation Game benchmark) is a collaborative benchmark of 204 tasks contributed by 450 authors across 132 institutions, designed to probe capabilities believed to be beyond current language models. The benchmark evaluates GPT models, Google-internal dense transformers, and Switch-style sparse transformers across model sizes spanning millions to hundreds of billions of parameters, with human expert raters providing baselines.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• Model performance and calibration both improve with scale, but remain poor in absolute terms compared to human raters
  • Performance is remarkably similar across model classes (dense vs. sparse transformers), with sparse models showing benefits from sparsity
  • Tasks that improve gradually with scale commonly involve knowledge or memorization, while "breakthrough" tasks involving multiple steps or brittle metrics show sudden capability jumps at critical scale
  • Social bias typically increases with scale in settings with ambiguous context, but this can be improved with prompting
  • Even large language models are brittle, with performance sensitive to task specification details

docs.title: Blending Is All You Need: Cheaper, Better Alternative to Trillion-Parameters LLM
Summary
docs.text: The paper introduces "Blending," a simple approach where multiple smaller chat AI models (6B-13B parameters) are combined by randomly selecting which model generates each response in a multi-turn conversation. Large-scale A/B testing on the Chai platform over 30 days shows that a Blended ensemble of three moderate-sized models can rival or outperform ChatGPT (175B+ parameters) in user engagement and retention at a fraction of the computational cost.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• Randomly selecting among smaller models per conversation turn produces an ensemble that takes on the "best of all" characteristics
  • A Blended ensemble of three 6-13B parameter models outcompetes OpenAI's 175B+ parameter ChatGPT on user retention metrics
  • Conditioning on the conversational history from mixed models causes individual models to learn abilities from other systems
  • Users find Blended chat AIs more engaging, entertaining, and useful compared to single-model ChatGPT-based systems
  • The approach requires only a fraction of the inference cost and memory overhead of trillion-parameter models

docs.title: Brain-Inspired Graph Multi-Agent Systems for LLM Reasoning
Summary
docs.text: BIGMAS (Brain-Inspired Graph Multi-Agent Systems) organizes specialized LLM agents as nodes in a dynamically constructed directed graph, coordinating through a centralized shared workspace inspired by Global Workspace Theory from cognitive science. A GraphDesigner agent constructs task-specific agent topologies per problem, while a global Orchestrator uses complete shared state for routing decisions. Experiments on Game24, Six Fives, and Tower of London across six frontier LLMs show consistent reasoning improvements for both standard LLMs and Large Reasoning Models, outperforming baselines like ReAct and Tree of Thoughts.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• Both standard LLMs and Large Reasoning Models suffer accuracy collapse beyond certain problem complexity thresholds, and providing explicit solution algorithms does not alleviate this -- the limitation lies in consistent logical execution, not solution discovery
  • Multi-agent architectural design provides complementary gains orthogonal to model-level reasoning enhancements, with the largest gains precisely where individual models struggle most
  • Dynamic, problem-adaptive agent topologies constructed per-task outperform fixed pre-specified topologies by enabling task-specific specialization and coordination
  • A centralized shared workspace maintaining globally consistent intermediate state overcomes the local-view bottleneck of reactive approaches like ReAct where agents only see their own context

docs.title: Breaking Models to Test the Judge: A Mutation Testing Approach for Semantic Evaluators of Domain Class Diagrams
Summary
docs.text: LLMs are now used as judges of domain class diagrams, but for that task there is often no single correct diagram to compare against. So the authors test the judge with mutation testing instead. They inject known defects into PlantUML diagrams using 11 operators, such as removing a class, reversing a relationship, or adding an implementation class or an off-domain class. A mutant counts as "killed" if any issue the judge reports is close in meaning to the defect's description, measured by sentence-embedding similarity. Across six judge configurations (3 LLMs × 2 prompts), the kill ratio ranks configurations mostly the same way as an expensive manual precision review. The two measures diverge in one important case: verbose judges.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• The kill ratio mostly agrees with manual review: Pearson r = 0.624 with manual precision across the six configurations, and the same ordering on 11 of 15 configuration pairs (73%). Both methods agree that gpt-5.3-codex is the best model and that the more detailed prompt (P2) beats P1.
  • Verbose judges can game the kill ratio. Listing many possible issues raises the chance of matching the injected defect. gpt-5-mini killed 86.6% of mutants yet had only 35.5% manual precision on unmutated diagrams. The kill ratio measures how often the judge catches defects; precision still needs human review.
  • Overall scores hide the judge's blind spots. Obvious defects such as off-domain classes or attributes were caught 96–98% of the time. Removed attributes (62%), removed classes (73%) and reversed relationships (76%) were caught much less often. Easy mutants inflate the total, so they should be reported separately as a basic sanity check.
  • The human baseline is itself shaky. Expert annotators agreed on only 65% of labels (Krippendorff's α = 0.32), and every disagreement had to be adjudicated. That is the oracle problem the method is meant to avoid. Mutants, by contrast, have known defects by construction.
  • Caveats: the method assumes the original diagram is good, so a mutation actually degrades it. In 10 of 79 hard cases inspected, the mutation barely hurt the diagram. The similarity threshold (τ = 0.55, F1 0.90) was calibrated on gpt-5-mini's output only, and each mutant contains just one defect.

docs.title: BrowseComp-Plus: A More Fair and Transparent Evaluation Benchmark of Deep-Research Agent
Summary
docs.text: BrowseComp-Plus improves upon BrowseComp by providing a fixed, human-verified document corpus with supporting and challenging negative documents, enabling fair and reproducible evaluation of deep-research agents by disentangling retrieval from reasoning. Results show GPT-5 achieves 55.9% accuracy while Search-R1 with BM25 achieves only 3.86%, and better retrievers both improve accuracy and reduce the number of search calls needed.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• Current deep-research benchmarks like BrowseComp lack fairness (dynamic web APIs) and transparency (opaque retrieval), hindering reproducible evaluation
  • With a fixed corpus, retrieval and LLM reasoning components can be evaluated independently for the first time
  • Deep-research agents mostly improve accuracy at the cost of more search calls, while better retrieval systems improve accuracy and reduce calls
  • Even state-of-the-art retrievers face substantial challenges consistently surfacing all necessary evidence for reasoning-intensive queries
  • GPT-5 with Qwen3-Embedding-8B retriever achieves 70.1% accuracy, significantly outperforming BM25-based configurations

docs.title: BrowseComp-ZH: Benchmarking Web Browsing Ability of Large Language Models in Chinese
Summary
docs.text: BrowseComp-ZH is the first benchmark for evaluating LLM web browsing agents in the Chinese information ecosystem, consisting of 289 multi-hop questions spanning 11 domains with natively Chinese-constructed queries verified on Baidu, Bing, and Google. Most models achieve below 10% accuracy, with only a handful exceeding 20% and OpenAI's DeepResearch reaching the best score of 42.9%, demonstrating that directly translating English browsing benchmarks is inadequate.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• Directly translating English browsing benchmarks into Chinese does not yield a meaningful evaluation framework due to structural, idiomatic, and information ecosystem differences
  • Most LLMs achieve below 10% accuracy on BrowseComp-ZH; only a handful exceed 20%
  • Models with inherent reasoning capabilities (e.g., DeepSeek-R1) consistently outperform non-reasoning counterparts
  • Agentic systems with external retrieval mechanisms (e.g., OpenAI DeepResearch at 42.9%) achieve the highest scores
  • Enabling web search can actually hurt some models (DeepSeek-R1 drops from 23.2% to 7.6%), showing retrieval integration is not uniformly beneficial

docs.title: Building Effective AI Coding Agents for the Terminal: Scaffolding, Harness, Context Engineering, and Lessons Learned
Summary
docs.text: OPENDEV is an open-source, terminal-native AI coding agent written in Rust — claimed to be the first comprehensive technical report for an interactive CLI coding agent. It employs a compound AI architecture with a dual-agent planning/execution split, per-workflow LLM routing, and adaptive context compaction to handle long-horizon development tasks. The paper focuses on design decisions and lessons learned rather than algorithmic novelty, positioning itself as a bridge between closed-source industrial practice and open research.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• Effective terminal agents require solving three problems: managing finite context windows over long sessions, preventing destructive shell operations, and extending tool capabilities without prompt bloat
  • Context engineering is a first-class concern: adaptive compaction, event-driven system reminders to counter instruction fade-out, and cross-session memory accumulation
  • A five-layer defense-in-depth safety architecture handles dangers at progressively lower levels: prompt guardrails → schema-level tool gating → runtime approval → tool validation → lifecycle hooks
  • Per-workflow LLM configurability lets different cognitive tasks (planning vs. execution vs. compaction) independently bind to different models, making the system model-agnostic by construction
  • The key architectural organizing principle is separating scaffolding (agent assembly before first prompt) from harness (runtime orchestration)

docs.title: C++ Design Patterns for Low-latency Applications Including High-frequency Trading
Summary
docs.text: This paper bridges the knowledge gap in optimizing latency-critical C++ code for high-frequency trading (HFT) systems through three contributions: a Low-Latency Programming Repository, optimization of a market-neutral statistical arbitrage pairs trading strategy, and implementation of the Disruptor pattern in C++. docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• Cutting-edge HFT research remains largely confidential due to competitive advantage concerns, creating a public knowledge gap
  • Cache Warming and Constexpr are the most impactful techniques for latency reduction among those evaluated
  • The Disruptor pattern shows significant performance enhancement over traditional queuing methods in Order Management Systems
  • Optimization of the pairs trading strategy led to substantial improvements in both speed and profitability
  • The Low-Latency Programming Repository provides reproducible benchmarking as a practical guide for practitioners

docs.title: Can LLMs Perform Deep Technical Comprehension of Computer Architecture Papers?
Summary
docs.text: Gauntlet is an open-source pipeline that analyzes a research paper through five independent expert-persona reviewers plus an adversarial synthesis stage, aiming at structured critique rather than summarization — naming the core mechanism, surfacing buried assumptions, and connecting a contribution beyond its own scope. On 20 ISCA 2025 and HPCA 2026 papers, ten researchers wrote their own analyses and then blind-judged human against machine output on papers other than their own; evaluators preferred Gauntlet in 15 of 20 comparisons (human in 4, one tie), significant on per-analyst totals at p < 0.01. A 98-paper ablation attributes the gain to the multi-agent structure and specifically the synthesis pass.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• Defines deep technical comprehension operationally — the structures built, the non-obvious insight, the evaluation assumptions, the connections to related work — rather than leaving 'understanding' vague.
  • The multi-agent structure is doing the work: the pipeline beats the same model run as a single rich-persona agent on 96% of papers, isolating the synthesis pass as the source.
  • Evaluation design is unusually careful — authors judge analyses of papers other than their own, against analyses they themselves wrote.
  • Gauntlet's advantage is largest on Critical Rigor and vanishes on Calibration, which is the honest boundary of the result.
  • Where humans win it is on trust and usefulness, not depth: a confident wrong claim, a mechanism described but not taught, unprioritized breadth.

docs.title: Related
docs.text: • Formalizing Fermat's Last Theorem — multi-agent structure applied to producing verified mathematics rather than critique.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: This paper identifies and analyzes twelve key communication challenges in human-agent interaction, organized into three categories: challenges conveying information from agents to users (e.g., capabilities, current actions, side effects), from users to agents (e.g., goals, preferences, corrections), and overarching challenges (e.g., verifiability, consistency, detail level, interaction history). The work draws on communication grounding theory and highlights the need for new design patterns supporting transparency and control.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• Modern AI agents based on generative foundation models introduce novel communication challenges due to their complexity, wide-ranging failure modes, and tool-use capabilities
  • Twelve distinct communication challenges are identified across three categories: agent-to-user, user-to-agent, and general human-agent communication
  • Establishing common ground between humans and agents is critical for transparency and control but is made difficult by opaque architectures, stochastic outputs, and evolving capabilities
  • Users need to form accurate mental models of agent capabilities and monitor agent behavior, which current systems poorly support
  • Multi-agent workflows with different roles, privileges, and access further exacerbate communication and transparency challenges

docs.title: ChatBench: From Static Benchmarks to Human-AI Evaluation
Summary
docs.text: ChatBench converts standard MMLU benchmark questions into user-AI conversations through a user study, revealing that AI-alone accuracy fails to predict user-AI accuracy with significant divergences across math, physics, and moral reasoning subjects. The dataset includes 396 questions with 144K answers and 7,336 user-AI conversations across two LLMs (GPT-4o and Llama-3.1-8b), and shows that fine-tuning a user simulator on ChatBench improves correlation with real user-AI accuracy by over 20 points.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• AI-alone benchmark accuracy fails to predict user-AI interactive accuracy, with significant differences across subjects
  • There is a large distribution shift between benchmark questions and questions real users actually ask
  • Interactions change evaluation insights: user-AI performance diverges from AI-alone performance across models, methods, and conditions
  • Fine-tuning a user simulator on ChatBench data improves its ability to estimate user-AI accuracies by 22-26 points of correlation
  • The approach of converting benchmarks to conversations is general and could be applied to other QA benchmarks like HotPotQA or GSM8K

docs.title: CL-bench: A Benchmark for Context Learning
Summary
docs.text: CL-bench introduces "context learning" as a distinct capability from prompt engineering and in-context learning, requiring models to learn new knowledge from complex contexts and apply it to solve tasks. The benchmark consists of 500 complex contexts, 1,899 tasks, and 31,607 verification rubrics crafted by domain experts, and reveals that frontier LMs solve only 17.2% of tasks on average (GPT-5.1 achieves 23.7%), exposing a critical gap in models' ability to reason with novel context-dependent knowledge.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• Context learning -- acquiring and applying new knowledge from complex contexts -- is a fundamental but largely overlooked LM capability distinct from prompt engineering and ICL
  • Frontier LMs solve only 17.2% of CL-bench tasks on average; even the best model (GPT-5.1) achieves only 23.7%
  • Models perform substantially worse on harder categories like inducing laws from experimental data or simulating complex sandbox environments (11.8% average solve rate)
  • A higher proportion of failures stems from models ignoring context content rather than misunderstanding it
  • Insufficient long-context reasoning and instruction-following abilities also contribute to context learning failures

docs.title: CLaRa: Bridging Retrieval and Generation with Continuous Latent Reasoning
Summary
docs.text: CLaRa (Continuous Latent Reasoning) addresses RAG's fundamental structural issue—retrieval and generation are optimized separately in disjoint spaces—by performing embedding-based compression and joint optimization in a shared continuous space. Each document is encoded once into compact memory tokens; the reranker and generator are trained end-to-end via a single language modeling loss with gradients flowing through both modules. CLaRa achieves SOTA compression and reranking performance even at 16× text compression ratio.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• Standard RAG suffers from architectural mismatch: retrievers rank in embedding space while generators consume raw text, preventing joint optimization
  • Discrete document selection in RAG prevents gradients from flowing back to the retriever, hindering end-to-end training
  • CLaRa encodes each document once into compact memory tokens shared by both retrieval and generation, eliminating redundant encoding
  • SCP (key-preserving data synthesis) enables semantically rich, retrievable compressed vectors via QA and paraphrase supervision
  • SOTA compression and reranking performance at 16× text compression ratio, outperforming text-based fine-tuned baselines

docs.title: Beyond Knowledge to Agency: Evaluating Expertise, Autonomy, and Integrity in Finance with CNFinBench
Summary
docs.text: CNFinBench evaluates LLMs as autonomous financial agents across 29 subtasks spanning expertise, autonomy, and integrity — going beyond knowledge-focused benchmarks to test behavioral stability under adversarial pressure. A novel Harmful Instruction Compliance Score (HICS) measures safety degradation. Testing 22 models reveals a critical pattern: models scoring 66.4 on capability tasks drop to 34.4 on compliance and risk control, suffer a 15.4-point decline from isolated tasks to full execution chains, and collapse under adversarial multi-turn attack with compliance violations surging 172.3%.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• Capability-compliance divergence: models averaging 66.4 on capability tasks drop to 34.4 on compliance and risk control — a nearly 50% degradation invisible to standard capability benchmarks
  • 15.4-point accuracy decline from single modules to full execution chains, showing isolated task performance doesn't predict agentic behavior
  • Compliance violations surge 172.3% in adversarial Round 2, indicating rapid safety collapse under pressure
  • Novel HICS metric measures safety degradation across severity and consistency dimensions
  • 22 models evaluated across 29 subtasks with realistic agent workflows and adversarial multi-turn interactions

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: A survey framing code as the infrastructure layer ("harness") of agentic AI systems — not just the artifact produced. Organized across three connected layers: harness interface (code for reasoning, action, and environment modeling), harness mechanisms (planning, memory, tool use, feedback loops), and scaling the harness (multi-agent coordination, shared state, verification). Covers applications from coding assistants and GUI automation to embodied agents and enterprise workflows.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• Code is increasingly the operational substrate of agent systems — used for planning representation, action interfaces, environment modeling, and execution-based verification — not just the output artifact
  • The three-layer framing (interface → mechanisms → scaling) provides a unified taxonomy: what agents can perceive/do, how they plan/remember/act, and how multi-agent coordination and verification work
  • Code's executability and verifiability are the core properties that make it especially suited as an agent harness substrate, enabling agents to externalize reasoning into inspectable, runnable steps
  • Key open challenges: evaluation beyond final task success, verification under incomplete feedback, regression-free harness improvement, consistent shared state across agents, and safety oversight for destructive actions
  • The survey identifies a spectrum from single-agent coding assistants to multi-agent systems with shared repo state, PR workflows, and adversarial red-teaming roles

docs.title: Code Health in LLM-Based Test Generation: Effectiveness and Token Efficiency
Summary
docs.text: The authors ask whether more maintainable code gets better LLM-written unit tests. They measure maintainability with CodeScene's CodeHealth (CH) score, on about 24,600 competitive-programming solutions in Python, Java and C++. They generate tests with Qwen3-Coder-30B in a single attempt each, then score them by coverage and mutation score. Healthier code gets somewhat better tests, a weak but consistent effect that is strongest on mutation score. Less healthy Java and C++ also takes more input tokens, even at the same number of lines. Two caveats: CodeHealth is CodeScene's commercial product and two authors work there, and the code is contest solutions, not production code.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• Higher CodeHealth goes with more effective generated tests, but only weakly. The correlation with mutation score is ρ = 0.18 for Python, 0.21 for Java and 0.34 for C++; with coverage it is only 0.01–0.15. The Java and C++ correlations hold after controlling for lines of code. For Python they do not, but that result rests on only 251 files.
  • The correlation grows as the metric asks more of the tests, from line coverage to branch coverage to mutation score. That suggests healthy code mainly helps an LLM write tests that check behavior, not just tests that execute the code. The steepest single case is Java: median mutation score rises from about 35% in the least healthy bin to about 95% in the healthiest.
  • Unhealthy code is more expensive in tokens. For Java and C++, the least healthy files use about 44–45% more median input tokens than near-perfect ones. The correlation (ρ ≈ −0.25 to −0.30) is about the same across Qwen, OpenAI, Claude and Gemini tokenizers, and survives controlling for lines of code. Low-health Java also splits into more tokens per character, which the authors put down to camelCase names, generics and chained calls. Low-health C++ is costlier mainly because it is longer.
  • The authors call this a "double penalty" for poor maintainability: code that is hard for humans to work with also costs LLMs more context and money. They point to GitHub Copilot's switch to usage-based billing (June 2026) as why this matters now.
  • The effect is real but weak, and results vary widely from file to file, so it should not be read as a rule for any single file. The C++ results are also very low overall (median mutation score of 3–12%), which limits how much that strongest correlation is worth.

docs.title: Codified Context: Infrastructure for AI Agents in a Complex Codebase
Summary
docs.text: This paper presents a three-tier codified context infrastructure developed during construction of a 108,000-line C# codebase using Claude Code as the sole code-generation tool. The architecture scales beyond single-file manifests (CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md) by separating a hot-memory constitution (always-loaded), 19 domain-specialist agents (invoked per task), and a cold-memory knowledge base of 34 on-demand specification documents. Quantitative evidence across 283 development sessions shows how codified context propagates across sessions to prevent failures and maintain consistency.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• Single-file manifests don't scale beyond modest codebases; a tiered architecture is needed for large, multi-agent projects
  • Domain-specialist agents require substantial embedded project-specific knowledge (often >50% of agent content) to perform reliably — the "brevity bias" causes agents without pre-loaded context to produce significantly more errors
  • Hot/cold memory separation distinguishes always-loaded conventions from on-demand specification documents, balancing context efficiency with coverage
  • The project was built by a chemistry researcher (non-SE background) using AI agents, making it a test case for domain experts building software beyond their primary expertise
  • Presence of AGENTS.md files was associated with a 29% reduction in median runtime and 17% reduction in output token consumption (citing prior work)

docs.title: Cognitive Agency Surrender: Defending Epistemic Sovereignty via Scaffolded AI Friction
Summary
docs.text: This paper argues that "zero-friction" AI design exploits human cognitive miserliness, leading to cognitive agency surrender—users offloading not just tasks but reasoning itself to AI systems. The authors propose "Scaffolded Cognitive Friction," using multi-agent systems as computational Devil's Advocates to inject epistemic tension. An analysis of 1,223 HCI papers from 2023–2026 reveals an "agentic takeover" trend where research defending human epistemic sovereignty was suppressed by focus on autonomous agents.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• Frictionless AI interfaces exploit System 1 heuristics by providing fluent conclusions that bypass System 2 analytical reasoning
  • Literature analysis shows frictionless usability maintains 67.3% structural hegemony in HCI research; research defending epistemic sovereignty dropped from 19.1% (2025) to 13.1% (2026)
  • Multi-agent systems can be repurposed as cognitive forcing functions (Devil's Advocates) rather than efficiency maximizers
  • Intentionally designed friction is a foundational technical prerequisite for AI governance and preserving societal cognitive resilience
  • Proposes multimodal computational phenotyping (gaze, pupillometry, fNIRS, HDDM) to mathematically decouple decision outcomes from cognitive effort

docs.title: Complete CALM: A Coordination Criterion for Specifications
Summary
docs.text: Hellerstein generalizes the CALM theorem from relational transducers to arbitrary concurrent specifications. A specification is defined as an event universe, an observation function mapping histories to admissible outcomes, and a declared refinement order; the Complete CALM theorem states such a specification admits a coordination-free implementation if and only if its outcomes are monotone. The result subsumes the original CALM, CRDTs, I-confluence, and HATs as instances, and yields a bidirectional Complete CAP companion: consistent, available, partition-tolerant implementation exists iff the specification is distributed-monotone.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• One semantic theorem recovers several disjoint results. CALM, CRDTs, I-confluence, HATs and CAP had lived in separate formalisms with none reducing to another; monotonicity over a declared refinement order unifies them.
  • Operating on specifications rather than programs is what buys the generality — the test doubles as a proof technique for abstract properties like serializability or snapshot isolation.
  • The criterion handles any refinement order, not only set inclusion, which is the specific limitation of the original CALM being lifted.
  • It can verify proper coordination: resolve a non-monotone specification with coordination, then re-test the residual for monotonicity.
  • Identifies the coordination-free frontier — the strongest guarantees achievable without coordination for a given interface.

docs.title: Related
docs.text:
• Hydro — Hellerstein's group's framework, which applies this line of theory to distributed Rust.
  • The Dataflow Model Revisited — the streaming/dataflow side of the same tradition.

docs.title: Compressive Transformers for Long-Range Sequence Modelling
Summary
docs.text: The Compressive Transformer extends the Transformer architecture by compressing past hidden activations into a secondary compressed memory rather than discarding them, enabling the model to attend to both fine-grained recent memories and coarser long-term compressed memories. The model achieves state-of-the-art language modeling results (17.1 perplexity on WikiText-103 and 0.97 bpc on Enwik8) and can also serve as a memory mechanism for RL agents.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• The Compressive Transformer maps past activations to compressed representations using a learned compression function, reducing both space and compute costs
  • It achieves state-of-the-art results on character-level (Enwik8: 0.97 bpc) and word-level (WikiText-103: 17.1 ppl) language modeling
  • The model specifically improves modeling of rare words by retaining compressed long-range context
  • The architecture can serve as a memory component within RL agents, successfully compressing and utilizing past observations
  • A new book-level language modeling benchmark (PG-19) is proposed to promote long-context sequence modeling research

docs.title: Configuring Agentic AI Coding Tools: An Exploratory Study
Summary
docs.text: Systematic analysis of configuration mechanisms across 5 agentic coding tools (Claude Code, Copilot, Cursor, Gemini, Codex) based on 2,923 GitHub repositories. Identifies 8 configuration mechanisms (Context Files, Skills, Subagents, Commands, Rules, Settings, Hooks, MCP) and finds that Context Files dominate adoption with AGENTS.md emerging as an interoperable standard. Advanced mechanisms like Skills and Subagents are shallowly adopted — most repos define only 1-2 artifacts, and Skills rely on static instructions rather than executable workflows.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• Context Files dominate the configuration landscape and are often the sole mechanism; AGENTS.md is emerging as a cross-tool standard
  • Claude Code users employ the broadest range of configuration mechanisms (1,305 of 2,923 repos), followed by GitHub Copilot (957)
  • Skills and Subagents are shallowly adopted — Skills predominantly rely on static resources rather than executable scripts to extend behavior
  • Eight distinct configuration mechanisms exist spanning a spectrum from static context to executable integrations: Context Files, Skills, Subagents, Commands, Rules, Settings, Hooks, MCP servers
  • Distinct "configuration cultures" are forming around different tools

docs.title: Constitutional AI: Harmlessness from AI Feedback
Summary
docs.text: Constitutional AI (CAI) introduces a method for training harmless AI assistants using AI-generated feedback instead of human labels for harms, guided by a small set of principles (a "constitution"). The process combines a supervised learning phase (where the model critiques and revises its own outputs) with an RL phase using AI preference labels (RLAIF), producing models that are less harmful and less evasive than standard RLHF-trained models while achieving Pareto improvements on helpfulness-harmlessness tradeoffs.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• CAI can train harmless AI models using only ~10 natural language principles, without any human feedback labels for harms
  • The RL-CAI model achieves Pareto improvement over standard RLHF on the helpfulness-harmlessness tradeoff
  • Chain-of-thought reasoning in both SL and RL phases improves human-judged performance and transparency of AI decision making
  • AI supervision may be more efficient than collecting human feedback, enabling focus on higher-quality oversight
  • The method produces non-evasive assistants that explain objections to harmful queries rather than refusing

docs.title: Constraint Decay: The Fragility of LLM Agents in Backend Code Generation
Summary
docs.text: Evaluates LLM agents on constrained multi-file backend code generation across 8 web frameworks with 80 greenfield and 20 feature-implementation tasks. Introduces "constraint decay": as structural constraints (architectural pattern, database, ORM) accumulate on top of a fixed API spec, assertion pass rates drop by ~30 points on average for capable agents, approaching zero for weaker ones. Data-layer defects account for ~45% of failures.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• Constraint decay is real and severe: layering structural requirements (clean architecture, PostgreSQL, SQLAlchemy ORM) on a fixed API spec causes ~30-point average drop in assertion pass rates for capable agents
  • Framework choice matters significantly: agents perform much better with lightweight explicit frameworks (Flask) than with convention-heavy environments (FastAPI, Django) under identical API contracts
  • Data-layer defects — incorrect query composition and ORM runtime violations — are the leading root cause, driving ~45% of agent logic failures
  • Existing benchmarks (SWE-Bench, greenfield generators) overlook non-functional constraints, rewarding structurally arbitrary but functionally correct solutions and thus overestimating production readiness
  • Current agentic architectures (OpenHands, Mini-SWE-Agent) don't solve the problem — structural constraint adherence is orthogonal to the action/tool capabilities of current agents

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: This paper introduces Context Language Models (CLMs), language models that natively manage their own context: the context is mirrored into a file the model can freely edit via Bash, with edits synced to the live context on the next turn. Applied zero-shot to existing models, CLMs beat hand-designed context-management harnesses on long-horizon tasks at lower compute. Because context management becomes model behavior rather than harness code, it can also be steered by instructions, evolved as a skill, or trained with RL.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• Zero-shot CLMs outperform SOTA context-management strategies: +11.4% accuracy with 21.5% fewer FLOPs on BrowseComp-Plus, +5% with 59% fewer FLOPs on 12-hour EdgeBench, and 65% greater speedup at equal compute on a 24-hour six-repository agent-swarm task
  • Unrestricted edit access yields emergent strategies (framed as a Bitter Lesson for context management): an in-context multi-agent scoreboard maintained through 163 in-place edits at 6-8K tokens, a new "notes" chat role, and reusable helper functions such as compact_turns
  • Context management becomes steerable and learnable: one instruction sentence changes the strategy, a skill-evolution loop improves held-out ContextBench accuracy by up to 35.9 points at lower compute, and online GRPO RL with a success-gated efficiency advantage improves Qwen3.5-9B on BrowseComp-Plus by 47.6% with 12% fewer FLOPs
  • Mid-context edits break prefix caching; the paper introduces prefix-reuse FLOPs as a cost metric and Suffix Cache Reuse, which cuts server-side compute by 35% versus standard SGLang at matched performance
  • Model-editable context is a new attack surface where prompt injections or self-generated instructions can persist across turns; the authors frame harnesses as procedural memory that could later be distilled into CLM weights

docs.title: ContextBench: A Benchmark for Context Retrieval in Coding Agents
Summary
docs.text: CONTEXTBENCH is a process-oriented benchmark for evaluating context retrieval in coding agents, comprising 1,136 issue-resolution tasks from 66 repositories across eight programming languages, each annotated with human-verified gold contexts. Unlike end-to-end benchmarks that only measure final task success, CONTEXTBENCH tracks agent trajectories and measures context recall, precision, and efficiency at file, block, and line levels throughout issue resolution. Evaluation of four frontier LLMs and five coding agents reveals that sophisticated scaffolding yields only marginal retrieval gains, LLMs consistently favor recall over precision, and significant gaps exist between explored and utilized context.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• Sophisticated agent scaffolding does not consistently improve context retrieval over simpler baselines, echoing "The Bitter Lesson" -- more complex retrieval scaffolds can be over-engineered.
  • LLMs consistently favor recall over precision in context retrieval, retrieving broad context to maximize coverage while introducing substantial noise.
  • Significant gaps exist between explored and utilized context: agents often inspect gold-relevant code but fail to retain or use it in final patch generation, highlighting consolidation as a key bottleneck.
  • Balanced retrieval frequency and context granularity achieve higher Pass@1 at lower cost, while aggressive retrieval mainly increases token consumption.
  • CONTEXTBENCH provides intermediate gold-context metrics that complement end-to-end success rates, offering valuable signals for guiding and rewarding LLM reasoning in software tasks.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Bubeck's Foundations and Trends monograph presents the main complexity theorems of convex optimization together with the algorithms that achieve them. It moves from black-box optimization (cutting-plane methods, gradient descent and its accelerated variants) through non-Euclidean methods such as mirror descent and Frank-Wolfe, to structural optimization (FISTA, mirror prox, interior point methods) and stochastic optimization, emphasizing relevance to machine learning.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• Black-box convex optimization has matching upper and lower complexity bounds: cutting-plane methods (center of gravity, ellipsoid, Vaidya) for finite dimension, and dimension-free rates for projected subgradient and gradient descent on Lipschitz, smooth and strongly convex functions
  • Nesterov's accelerated gradient descent attains the optimal rate for smooth convex functions, closing the gap left by plain gradient descent
  • Non-Euclidean geometry matters: mirror descent, dual averaging and Frank-Wolfe achieve almost dimension-free rates in settings such as the simplex, which are common in machine learning
  • Exploiting structure beyond the black-box model (a smooth plus a simple non-smooth term via FISTA, saddle-point representations via mirror prox, self-concordant barriers via interior point methods) yields much faster rates than black-box methods allow
  • Randomness enables further gains: stochastic and mini-batch SGD, variance-reduced methods for sums of smooth strongly convex functions, random coordinate descent, and convex relaxation with randomized rounding

docs.title: CORAL: Towards Autonomous Multi-Agent Evolution for Open-Ended Discovery
Summary
docs.text: CORAL is the first framework for autonomous multi-agent evolution on open-ended problems, replacing rigid evolutionary search heuristics with long-running agents that explore, reflect, and collaborate through shared persistent memory and asynchronous execution. On Anthropic's kernel engineering task, four co-evolving CORAL agents improve the best known score from 1,363 to 1,103 cycles (133.9x speedup over baseline), achieving 3-10x higher improvement rates with far fewer evaluations than fixed evolutionary search baselines like OpenEvolve across 10 tasks.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• Existing LLM-based evolution methods (FunSearch, AlphaEvolve) rely on fixed heuristics and hard-coded exploration rules that limit agent autonomy; CORAL replaces these with agents that autonomously decide what to inspect, when to evaluate, and what to store
  • On Anthropic's kernel engineering task, CORAL (4 agents) achieves 1,103 cycles vs. OpenEvolve's 2,740 cycles and the previous best known 1,363 cycles — a 20% improvement over prior SOTA
  • Single-agent CORAL achieves 43% improvement rate (24/56 evaluations) vs. OpenEvolve's 3% (12/363), demonstrating that agent autonomy produces far more efficient search
  • Key architectural components: shared persistent memory for knowledge reuse, asynchronous multi-agent execution, heartbeat-based interventions, isolated workspaces, and evaluator separation for safety
  • Mechanistic analyses show gains arise from knowledge reuse across agents and diverse multi-agent exploration strategies rather than simply more compute

docs.title: Crashing Waves vs. Rising Tides: Preliminary Findings on AI Automation from Thousands of Worker Evaluations of Labor Market Tasks
Summary
docs.text: MIT FutureTech study of 17,000+ worker evaluations across 3,000+ O*NET labor market tasks finds that AI automation follows a "rising tide" pattern — broad, gradual improvement across many task types — rather than "crashing waves" of sudden capability surges on specific tasks (contradicting METR's findings). Frontier models achieved ~50% success on 3-4 hour tasks in 2024-Q2, rising to ~65% by 2025-Q3, with extrapolations suggesting 80-95% success on most text-based tasks by 2029 at minimally sufficient quality.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• The success-duration curve is relatively flat (logit slope β ≈ -0.31), indicating AI automation is a "rising tide" — broad improvement across task durations — rather than "crashing waves" that abruptly automate narrow task sets
  • Newer model vintages produce approximately parallel upward shifts in performance across all task durations, while larger models disproportionately improve on shorter tasks (outward rotation)
  • The implied feasible task duration at 50% success roughly doubles every 3.8 months; failure-rate halving times are 2.4-3.2 years depending on task duration
  • At minimally-sufficient quality (score ≥7), frontier models already succeed on ~50-75% of text-based labor market tasks, with substantial variation across job families (47% Legal to 73% Installation/Maintenance)
  • Achieving near-perfect success rates or superior quality will take considerably longer than reaching 80-95%, providing a window for worker adjustment

docs.text: This paper studies instruction-induction conflict: a user instruction to behave in a target way is followed by N hardcoded assistant turns demonstrating a competing pattern, and instruction-following is measured as N grows across 13 models and 16 instructions. Every model eventually drifts from following the instruction to following the in-context pattern, but the transition point varies enormously and is largely uncorrelated with capability benchmarks. docs.text:
• Average instruction-following rates range from 1% to 99% across models, and susceptibility to induction override is largely uncorrelated with standard capability benchmarks

  • Output diversity is the main factor separating robust from fragile conditions: instructions requiring long, varied responses resist override far better than a single repeated token, and follow-ups attribute this to response variety rather than semantic engagement

docs.title: Dream-RSI: Recursive Self-Improvement through Evolving Worlds
Summary
docs.text: Google/DeepMind paper on the meta-level of recursive self-improvement: not what a coding agent discovers in an algorithm-engineering, maths-optimisation or GPU-kernel search, but how its exploration policy improves over thousands of propose–evaluate cycles. Dream-RSI adds a lightweight orchestration layer that makes exploration explicit and programmable while leaving the underlying coding agent untouched. Its key move is to turn accumulated discovery history (the realised discovery trees) into a replay simulator, so candidate exploration policies can be evaluated off-policy by "dreaming" over past trajectories instead of paying for expensive online rollouts; the improved policy is then redeployed, growing the simulator pool in a closed loop.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• The bottleneck in long-horizon discovery is meta-level feedback: judging an exploration policy requires observing many proposal–evaluation cycles, so online meta-optimisation is delayed and expensive. Fixed hand-designed strategies avoid that cost but cannot learn from experience.
  • Discovery history is a simulator, not just context: replaying recorded discovery trees gives immediate, near-free off-policy feedback on alternative policies, which is what makes the meta-loop tractable.
  • Reported efficiency gains are large where the search is expensive: up to 162× fewer agent calls than SimpleTES on a Lasso-path solver, >50× budget savings on maths-optimisation tasks, 1.79–2.43× fewer generations to hit KernelBench targets or up to 2.09× better kernels at equal budget.
  • Separation of concerns is a design principle: the orchestration layer owns exploration strategy; the coding agent stays a black box, so the approach composes with any discovery agent.
  • Evidence is eight tasks across three domains with the authors' own baselines; "competitive or improved" in the abstract signals that gains are not uniform across settings.

Summary
docs.text: Using data from 52,000 chess players on an online platform over five years, this paper investigates how access to AI feedback affects learning, skill gaps, and intellectual diversity. The study finds that people predominantly seek AI feedback after successes rather than failures, which is detrimental to learning since feedback on failures is what improves future performance. Higher-skilled individuals benefit more from AI feedback and use it more effectively, causing the skill gap to widen rather than narrow with AI access.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• Individuals are far more likely to seek AI feedback after successes than failures, but only feedback on failures improves future performance -- feedback on successes actually decreases it
  • Higher-skilled decision-makers seek AI feedback more often, are more likely to seek it after failures, and benefit more from it, causing access to AI feedback to increase rather than decrease the skill gap

docs.text: This paper introduces Beam Retrieval, an end-to-end framework for multi-hop question answering that models the entire multi-hop retrieval process by jointly optimizing an encoder and two classification heads across all hops. docs.text: EverMemOS is a self-organizing memory operating system implementing an engram-inspired lifecycle for LLM memory. docs.title: Evolution with recombination as a Metropolis-Hastings sampling procedure
Summary
docs.text: This paper presents a population genetic model of evolution incorporating haploid selection, mutation, recombination, and drift, where the mutation-selection equilibrium can be expressed exactly in closed form for arbitrary fitness functions. The key simplification is using n-parent recombination (drawing alleles from the whole population independently per locus) instead of 2-parent recombination, which enforces linkage equilibrium among offspring while allowing analysis of the whole population under linkage disequilibrium. The model is shown to be formally identical to a Bayesian model -- specifically a Dirichlet process mixture model -- enabling exact analytical calculations of stationary distributions.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• The evolutionary model with n-parent recombination exactly satisfies detailed balance at its stationary distributions, enabling closed-form solutions for arbitrary fitness functions
  • The model is formally identical to a Monte-Carlo sampling procedure from a well-known Bayesian model (factorial Dirichlet process), providing an exact connection between evolution and Bayesian inference
  • A universal relationship is established between fitness fluctuations at stationarity and the gradient of a population's mean fitness with respect to selection intensity
  • Mutational robustness in the form of error-correcting codes (e.g., Hamming codes) can decrease genetic load and maintain fitness levels with less intense selection

docs.title: EvolveMem:Self-Evolving Memory Architecture via AutoResearch for LLM Agents

docs.text: EVOLVEMEM is a memory architecture that treats the retrieval infrastructure itself as an optimization target rather than a fixed configuration. An LLM-powered diagnosis module reads per-question failure logs, identifies root causes, and proposes adjustments to retrieval configuration (scoring weights, fusion strategies, context budgets); a guarded meta-analyzer applies accepted proposals with automatic revert-on-regression. docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• All prior memory systems (MemGPT, Mem0, A-MEM, MemoryBank, etc.) evolve stored content but keep retrieval infrastructure frozen — EVOLVEMEM is the first to co-evolve both
  • Different question types require fundamentally different retrieval strategies (factual lookup vs. temporal reasoning vs. multi-hop), making frozen one-size-fits-all retrieval configs suboptimal as memory scales
  • The 4-step EVALUATE→DIAGNOSE→PROPOSE→GUARD loop auto-reverts harmful proposals and can discover entirely new configuration dimensions not present in the original action space
  • Evolved configurations transfer positively across benchmarks (LoCoMo → MemBench), suggesting the system captures universal retrieval principles rather than benchmark-specific heuristics
  • Starting from a minimal baseline, self-evolution converges autonomously: F1 improves from 30.5% to 54.3% on LoCoMo over 7 rounds (78% relative improvement)

docs.title: EvoOntology: A Self-Evolving Ontology Layer for Data Agents
Summary
docs.text: EvoOntology addresses the "agent–data gap": data agents reach heterogeneous sources only through generic tools, so they explore blindly and discard grounding between tasks. It builds a three-layer ontology — a content layer of Terms, Mappings, Constraints, and Evidence; a schema layer defining the object model; and a tool layer exposed as an MCP server (browse/resolve) — constructed by a builder agent from workload-guided probe queries and refined by an evolution agent through single-level typed edits accepted only if they beat the parent on held-out paired validation. Across DDR-Bench, InsightBench, and BIRD with six backbones, it outperforms both plain ReAct and the same semantic layer injected statically into the prompt.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• Static prompt injection of a semantic layer does not reliably help and sometimes hurts (−15.0 Traj-Wise on DDR-Bench for Claude-Sonnet-5; up to −5.6 EX on BIRD), while serving the same content through queryable MCP tools gives +17.8 average Traj-Wise on DDR-Bench and +7.4 EX on BIRD — a static fragment "competes with the agent's other instructions and cannot be pruned per turn"
  • Typed, persistent structure beats episodic memory: ReAct + Memory (replaying past trajectories) reaches 75.8 Traj-Wise vs. 89.5 for EvoOntology
  • The validation gate and level attribution are the load-bearing parts of the evolution loop: removing the gate costs −11.2 ("unfiltered candidates admit regressions the next round cannot always undo"), removing attribution −6.3, while replacing typed patches with free-form rewrites costs only −1.7
  • Exposure matters more than content: Tool-level edits (how the ontology is surfaced) account for 57% of the evolution gain from 6 accepted rounds, vs. 34% from 11 Content rounds and 9% from 3 Schema rounds; in the structure ablation, Mappings (−13.4) and Evidence (−8.7) are the load-bearing families, supporting probe-grounded entries over prose-only descriptions
  • The layer is net cheaper and backbone-specific: per-turn input rises (3.2K → 4.6K tokens) but turns per task fall (14.6 → 8.4), cutting total tokens ~20%; evolved ontologies overlap at most 0.62 Jaccard across backbones, and transferring one to a different backbone costs 6.6–10.9 points

docs.title: Expert Personas Improve LLM Alignment but Damage Accuracy: Bootstrapping Intent-Based Persona Routing with PRISM

docs.text: This paper systematically investigates when and why expert persona prompts help or hurt LLMs, resolving conflicting findings in the literature. The key discovery: persona effectiveness is task-type dependent — expert prompts consistently improve alignment-dependent tasks (safety, preference, format-following) but reliably damage pretrained-knowledge retrieval (e.g., MMLU).   • PRISM self-generates expert persona descriptions, training queries, and answers, then uses self-verification to retain only behaviors where personas actually help
  • A binary gate routes queries to the base model when persona activation is not beneficial, preserving knowledge-retrieval accuracy while improving alignment
  • The pipeline requires no external data, models, or knowledge — it is fully bootstrapped from the model itself

docs.text: This paper introduces Position Interpolation (PI), a method to extend the context window of RoPE-based pretrained LLMs like LLaMA by linearly down-scaling position indices to fit within the original context window range, rather than extrapolating beyond it. With minimal fine-tuning (within 1000 steps), LLaMA models can be extended from 2048 to 32768 tokens while preserving quality on original-length tasks. • Position Interpolation extends context windows by down-scaling position indices to match the original pre-trained range, avoiding catastrophically high attention scores from extrapolation

docs.title: Externalization in LLM Agents: A Unified Review of Memory, Skills, Protocols and Harness Engineering
Summary
docs.text: A systems-level survey that introduces "externalization" as the unifying design principle behind modern LLM agent architecture. The paper argues that practical agent progress comes not just from stronger models but from progressively relocating cognitive burdens — state, procedural expertise, and interaction structure — into persistent external infrastructure. It organizes this into three externalization dimensions (memory, skills, protocols) unified by a fourth integrative layer (harness engineering), tracing a historical arc from capability-in-weights through capability-in-context to capability-in-infrastructure.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• Memory externalizes state across time (converting recall into recognition), skills externalize procedural expertise (converting improvised generation into structured composition), and protocols externalize interaction structure (converting ad hoc prompting into governed contracts)
  • The harness is not a fourth kind of externalization but the runtime environment that hosts and coordinates the other three, providing orchestration, sandboxing, observability, approval gates, and context budget management
  • Skills have boundary conditions that limit reliability: semantic alignment gaps between description and execution, portability/staleness across environments, unsafe composition risks (including prompt injection via skill files), and context-dependent degradation over extended interactions
  • Skill acquisition follows four pathways — authored, distilled from episodic traces, discovered through environment interaction, and composed from existing skills — forming an evolutionary loop mediated by harness feedback
  • The paper frames externalization through Norman's cognitive artifact theory: external structures don't merely add information, they perform representational transformations that change the form of the task the model faces

docs.title: FANToM: A Benchmark for Stress-testing Machine Theory of Mind in Interactions
Summary
docs.text: FANToM is a benchmark for stress-testing machine Theory of Mind (ToM) in interactive conversational contexts, consisting of 10K questions covering 256 multiparty conversations with information asymmetry. Unlike prior ToM evaluations that use passive narratives, FANToM grounds evaluation in conversations where characters join and leave, creating natural information gaps. The benchmark is specifically designed to identify "illusory ToM" -- cases where models answer some question formats correctly but fail others requiring the same underlying reasoning.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• State-of-the-art LLMs score significantly lower than humans on FANToM, with a gap exceeding 70% on the full question set
  • Chain-of-thought reasoning improves performance in most models but does not substantially bridge the gap with human performance
  • Fine-tuning can help models achieve higher scores on individual question types, but fine-tuned models still significantly underperform humans when coherent responses across multiple question types are required
  • Models exhibit "illusory ToM" -- different error patterns depending on question format despite all questions requiring the same underlying reasoning about who knows what information

docs.title: FD-NL2SQL: Feedback-Driven Clinical NL2SQL that Improves with Use
Summary
docs.text: FD-NL2SQL is a feedback-driven natural language to SQL assistant designed for oncology clinical trial databases. It decomposes user questions into schema-aligned predicate sub-questions, retrieves semantically similar expert-verified exemplars via sentence embeddings, and synthesizes executable SQL grounded in the schema. The system continuously improves through two feedback signals: clinician edits to generated SQL are added to the exemplar bank, and lightweight logic-based SQL augmentation (single atomic mutations) automatically expands the exemplar bank without additional annotation.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• Decomposing complex clinical queries into atomic, schema-aligned predicate sub-questions improves robustness of NL2SQL generation compared to flat prompt demonstrations
  • Retrieval-guided SQL synthesis grounded in expert-verified exemplars produces more reliable queries than naive LLM generation in specialized biomedical domains
  • A self-evolving exemplar bank that grows from both clinician edits and automated SQL augmentation enables continuous improvement without heavy annotation effort
  • Logic-based SQL augmentation using single atomic mutations (operator or column changes) retained only when returning non-empty results provides a lightweight way to expand training coverage

docs.title: Fine-Tuning Language Models from Human Preferences
Summary
docs.text: This early and influential paper from OpenAI demonstrates fine-tuning pretrained language models using reinforcement learning from human preferences (RLHF). A reward model is trained from human comparisons of model outputs, then used to optimize a policy via PPO with a KL penalty to prevent divergence from the pretrained model. The approach is applied to stylistic text continuation and summarization tasks using a 774M parameter GPT-2 variant, achieving strong results with as few as 5,000 human comparisons for style tasks.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• Human preference-based reward models can effectively guide RL fine-tuning of language models for tasks where programmatic reward functions are poor proxies for true goals
  • A KL penalty between the fine-tuned policy and pretrained model is essential for preventing mode collapse and maintaining coherence during RL training
  • For stylistic continuation, the fine-tuned model is preferred by humans 86% of the time vs. zero-shot and 77% vs. fine-tuning to a sentiment network, using only 5,000 comparisons
  • For summarization, models learn a "smart copier" behavior that skips irrelevant preamble, achieving good ROUGE scores with 60,000 human comparisons
  • Online data collection (interleaving reward model updates with policy training) outperforms offline collection for summarization but not for style tasks

docs.text: FinMaster benchmarks LLMs across full-pipeline financial workflows in accounting, auditing, and consulting. docs.title: Summary
docs.text: This paper introduces the concept of "first-person fairness" in chatbots -- evaluating fairness toward the user interacting with the chatbot, as opposed to traditional "third-person" fairness toward people being evaluated by AI systems. Using a Language Model Research Assistant (LMRA), the authors assess biases across six language models on 66 tasks in nine domains, spanning two genders and four races, based on millions of real-world chat interactions. docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• First-person fairness (bias toward the user based on their name's demographic correlates) is a distinct and understudied form of chatbot bias compared to third-person fairness in decision-making systems
  • The LMRA approach enables scalable bias evaluation across hundreds of thousands of response pairs, with human annotations corroborating its findings
  • Subtle but systematic biases exist in how chatbot responses differ based on user names associated with different genders and races
  • Post-training reinforcement learning techniques significantly reduce first-person fairness biases in chatbot systems

docs.title: Beyond the 80/20 Rule: High-Entropy Minority Tokens Drive Effective Reinforcement Learning for LLM Reasoning
Summary
docs.text: This paper investigates the mechanisms of Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) through the lens of token entropy, discovering that a small minority of high-entropy "forking tokens" in Chain-of-Thought reasoning act as critical decision points that steer the model toward diverse reasoning pathways. The authors show that restricting policy gradient updates to only the top 20% highest-entropy tokens achieves performance comparable to or exceeding full-gradient updates, while training on only the 80% lowest-entropy tokens causes severe degradation. The 32B model trained this way sets new state-of-the-art for RLVR on base models under 600B parameters.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• In CoT reasoning, only a small fraction of tokens exhibit high entropy; these "forking tokens" act as critical decision points guiding diverse reasoning paths
  • RLVR primarily adjusts the entropy of high-entropy tokens while the base model's overall entropy patterns are largely preserved during training
  • Training on only 20% of the highest-entropy tokens achieves competitive or superior reasoning performance compared to full-gradient updates, surpassing the 80/20 rule
  • The effectiveness scales with model size: the 32B model shows the largest gains from forking-token training, achieving 63.5 on AIME'24 and 56.7 on AIME'25

docs.title: Use of Formal Methods at Amazon Web Services
Summary
docs.text: Since 2011, AWS engineers have used TLA+ formal specification and model checking on 10+ large complex distributed systems (S3, DynamoDB, EBS, internal lock managers). In every case TLA+ found subtle bugs unreachable by testing/code review or gave sufficient confidence for aggressive performance optimizations. Engineers learned TLA+ in 2-3 weeks and the investment was less time-consuming than informal proofs.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• TLA+ model checker found a DynamoDB bug with a 35-step error trace that passed design reviews, code reviews, and extensive fault-injection testing — the authors are convinced it would not have been found by conventional methods
  • Engineers at all levels (entry to Principal) learned TLA+ in 2-3 weeks without formal training, especially once it was framed as "exhaustively testable pseudo-code" rather than "formal verification"
  • Formal specifications serve as living documentation: precise, testable system models enable rapid verification that design changes are safe, acting as a "what if" tool analogous to spreadsheets for financial models
  • TLA+ is not effective for emergent performance degradation (cascading slowdowns, feedback loops) — it verifies logical correctness but not real-time behavior on non-deterministic infrastructure
  • AWS initially evaluated Alloy but found it insufficiently expressive for real-world distributed systems; TLA+ (and PlusCal) provided the necessary expressiveness for rich data structures and fault-tolerant algorithms

docs.title: From Technical Debt to Cognitive and Intent Debt: Rethinking Software Health in the Age of AI
Summary
docs.text: Proposes a "triple debt model" for software system health comprising technical debt (in code), cognitive debt (erosion of shared team understanding), and intent debt (missing externalized goals, constraints, and rationale). Argues that generative AI may reduce technical debt through automated refactoring and testing, while simultaneously accelerating cognitive and intent debt — as AI generates code faster than teams can understand it, and developers engage in "cognitive surrender" rather than building mental models.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• Generative AI redistributes engineering challenges: it can reduce technical debt while quietly accelerating cognitive debt (loss of shared understanding) and intent debt (missing rationale/goals)
  • Cognitive debt is a team-level property — the erosion of shared "theory of the system" — distinct from individual comprehension gaps, and it accumulates invisibly because AI-inflated confidence masks the loss
  • Intent debt lives in missing or incomplete non-code artifacts (specs, ADRs, tests-as-intent); it becomes critical as AI agents need explicit context to work effectively — what practitioners call "context debt" is often a symptom of intent debt
  • The three debt types reinforce each other: intent debt causes cognitive debt (no docs → no mental models), cognitive debt causes technical debt (misunderstanding → bad decisions), and technical debt amplifies cognitive debt (messy code → harder to reason about)
  • Mitigations include treating understanding as a deliverable, intent-first workflows (capture rationale at decision time), and resisting the automation of understanding itself

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: GRAM (Generative Recursive reAsoning Models) extends recursive latent-state reasoning — where a compact model refines a hidden state iteratively instead of generating long token chains — by making transitions stochastic rather than deterministic. This enables exploring multiple parallel latent trajectories (reasoning "width") in addition to scaling via recursive depth, trained with amortized variational inference. On tasks like Sudoku, N-Queens, and ARC-AGI, GRAM outperforms deterministic recurrent baselines and can also operate as an unconditional generative model.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• Prior Recursive Reasoning Models (HRM, TRM) are deterministic — same input always produces the same latent trajectory and single answer; GRAM makes transitions stochastic via learned Gaussian perturbations, enabling multi-hypothesis exploration
  • Inference-time scaling has two orthogonal axes: recursive depth (more steps) and trajectory width (more parallel samples) — GRAM supports both simultaneously
  • Stochasticity is applied only at the slow, abstract high-level latent state; fine-grained low-level refinement remains deterministic — injecting noise at the low level empirically did not help
  • GRAM is trained with amortized variational inference (ELBO), where the posterior has access to the target during training but only the learned prior is used at inference time
  • The same architecture doubles as an unconditional generative model (pθ(x)) when conditioning input is absent, demonstrated on binarized MNIST

docs.text: This paper proposes Geometric-Mean Policy Optimization (GMPO), a plug-and-play improvement to GRPO that replaces the arithmetic mean of token-level rewards with the geometric mean to suppress outlier importance-weighted rewards. On five mathematical reasoning benchmarks, GMPO-7B improves average Pass@1 over GRPO by up to 4.1%.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• GRPO suffers from unstable policy updates due to extreme importance sampling ratios caused by outlier token-level rewards
  • Replacing the arithmetic mean with the geometric mean in GRPO's objective inherently suppresses outliers, yielding more stable importance sampling ratio distributions
  • GMPO-7B achieves 4.1% higher Pass@1 accuracy than GRPO-7B on five mathematical reasoning benchmarks and 1.4% higher on Geometry3K multimodal reasoning
  • GMPO maintains a smaller KL divergence from the pre-trained model and higher token entropy than GRPO, indicating enhanced stability and greater policy exploration

docs.text: This Meta-led paper proposes compounding inference: organizing inference-time compute so that intermediate work persists and can be inspected, extended, combined or challenged by later computation.   • Agents reuse earlier work in ways a fixed pipeline would not, including synthesizing independent discoveries and reviving initially refuted ideas

docs.text: The GPT-4 technical report presents a large-scale multimodal Transformer model that accepts both image and text inputs and produces text outputs. docs.text:
• GPT-4's performance can be accurately predicted from models trained with up to 10,000x less compute using power law scaling relationships for both loss and capability metrics

docs.title: Graph-Augmented Large Language Model Agents: Current Progress and Future Prospects
Summary
docs.text: This survey provides a comprehensive overview of Graph-augmented LLM Agent (GLA) methods, categorizing them by their primary functions in LLM agent systems: planning, memory, and tool usage. Graphs address key limitations of LLMs as autonomous agents—unreliable multi-step planning, poor long-term memory, tool management, and multi-agent coordination. The paper also covers how GLA solutions facilitate orchestration, efficiency, and trustworthiness in multi-agent systems.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• LLMs alone are insufficient for autonomous agent systems: they hallucinate during planning, lack long-term memory, and struggle with multi-agent coordination
  • Graphs serve as a powerful auxiliary structure for continuity, structure, and coordination in complex agent workflows
  • GLA methods improve planning by modeling task dependencies and state transitions as graphs
  • Graph-based memory enables structured, queryable knowledge retention beyond flat retrieval
  • Future directions include improving structural adaptability and enabling unified, scalable, multimodal GLA systems
