docs.title: Summary
docs.text: This comprehensive survey provides the first systematic overview of GraphRAG — retrieval-augmented generation that leverages graph-structured knowledge rather than flat document retrieval. While standard RAG mitigates LLM hallucination and knowledge gaps by referencing external documents, GraphRAG improves precision and comprehensiveness by capturing relational knowledge between entities. The survey formalizes the GraphRAG workflow (Graph-Based Indexing → Graph-Guided Retrieval → Graph-Enhanced Generation) and reviews core technologies, training methods, downstream tasks, and industrial use cases.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• Standard RAG struggles with complex relational queries because it treats documents as flat; graph structure enables more precise and context-aware retrieval over interconnected entities
  • The GraphRAG workflow has three stages: indexing (building graph representations), retrieval (using graph structure to guide search), and generation (incorporating graph context into LLM output)
  • GraphRAG applies across diverse downstream tasks: question answering, information retrieval, recommendation systems, and multi-hop reasoning
  • Knowledge graphs, graph neural networks, and hybrid approaches each represent distinct technical paradigms within GraphRAG with different trade-offs
  • Industrial adoption is growing, with applications spanning healthcare, finance, and education where entity relationships are critical

docs.title: GROUNDEDKG-RAG: Grounded Knowledge Graph Index for Long-document Question Answering
Summary
docs.text: GroundedKG-RAG constructs a knowledge graph for long-document QA where every node and edge is explicitly grounded in original source text, using semantic role labeling (SRL) and abstract meaning representation (AMR) rather than LLM-generated summaries. Nodes represent entities and actions; edges encode semantic and temporal relations. At query time, the same transformation is applied to the query and relevant grounded text spans are retrieved. On NarrativeQA, it performs on par with a state-of-the-art proprietary long-context model at lower cost and outperforms GraphRAG.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• Current RAG approaches (RAPTOR, GraphRAG) rely heavily on recursive LLM summarization, introducing hallucination risk and redundancy across hierarchical levels — GroundedKG avoids this by grounding every component in original text
  • Knowledge graph nodes are defined as entities and actions with edges as PropBank semantic relations and temporal relations, constructed from SRL and AMR parses rather than LLM generation
  • The framework is fully interpretable: every step in the pipeline is human-readable and verifiable due to explicit grounding in source text
  • GroundedKG-RAG performs on par with proprietary long-context models at smaller cost and outperforms GraphRAG across all metrics on NarrativeQA

docs.title: Grounding AI Agents in Contracts: An Empirical Evaluation of Spec-Driven Test Generation
Summary
docs.text: Google researchers propose Spec-Driven Test Generation: before writing any tests, an agent first extracts and documents the target code's pre-conditions, post-conditions and undefined behaviours as a semi-formal natural-language spec, then generates tests against that spec. On 90 historical production bugs from Google's monorepo (C++/Java/Python/Go, single-file fixes), the two-phase agent beats a direct test-generation baseline using the same Gemini 3 Flash model and harness: +9.8pp bug detection (63.2% at k=5, p=0.035) and +2.5pp branch coverage (p=0.003). A pairwise Gemini 3.1 Pro judge (5 votes, majority) rates its suites superior to the baseline in 77.8% of cases and to the original developer-written suites in 56.7%.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• An intermediate semi-formal contract acts as a "cognitive scaffold": the gain comes from forcing the agent to enumerate behavioural boundaries before synthesis, not from a better model — both arms share the model and harness, which also neutralises the data-contamination objection.
  • The proposed Contract Coverage metric — does the generated spec capture the contract the bug violates? — strongly predicts test success: 54.9% bug detection when the contract is captured vs 19.4% when it is missing (p ≈ 4×10⁻¹⁴). Spec quality is the bottleneck, and it scales with sampling (61.1% at k=1 → 78.9% at k=5).
  • Judge-rated quality gains are largest on edge-case coverage (83.3% preferred) and smaller on best practices (65.6%) and readability (68.9%) — the spec mainly buys systematic state-space exploration.
  • Agent-generated suites reaching parity with human-authored ones (56.7%) is the headline for the "agents as test writers" thesis, with the caveat that "superior" is an LLM-judge verdict.
  • Scope limits: one organisation's monorepo and style guides, one model family, single-file bug fixes only, and historical-bug regression detection rather than discovery of new bugs.

docs.title: HarmBench: A Standardized Evaluation Framework for Automated Red Teaming and Robust Refusal
Summary
docs.text: HarmBench introduces a standardized evaluation framework for automated red teaming and robust refusal of LLMs, addressing the lack of comparable evaluation methodology across prior work. The framework identifies three desirable properties for red teaming evaluations -- breadth, comparability, and robust metrics -- and includes 510 carefully curated behaviors across four functional categories (standard, contextual, copyright, multimodal). Initial evaluations comparing 18 red teaming methods against 33 target LLMs reveal that no current attack or defense is uniformly effective, and robustness is independent of model size.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• Prior automated red teaming evaluations use at least 9 distinct evaluation setups with non-overlapping comparisons, making progress assessment impossible without standardization
  • No current attack or defense method is uniformly effective across all models and behavior categories
  • Model robustness against jailbreak attacks is independent of model size, contradicting assumptions that larger models are inherently safer
  • Incorporating strong automated red teaming into adversarial training can outperform prior defenses, demonstrating HarmBench's utility for codeveloping attacks and defenses

docs.title: Harness as a Language: A Minimalist Agent Framework With Maximal Expressivity
Summary
docs.text: MIT CSAIL (with Omar Khattab and Armando Solar-Lezama) introduces JAZ, an agent framework built around a single LLM primitive, invoke: a function whose body the LLM writes at call time. Two properties define it — the LLM can write arbitrary code that recursively calls invoke (so subagents are the default), and everything the LLM sees, including its own interaction history, is a variable in the code environment — plus hooks for observability, validation, and budgets. Using only prompting, with no purpose-built memory or self-improvement machinery, JAZ beats specialised harnesses on long-horizon recall (vs. Letta/MemGPT) and on continual self-improvement (vs. ACE).

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• Memory beyond the context window can come from expressivity rather than a memory system: prompted to delegate to a subagent when its context fills while keeping a reference to the full history, JAZ reaches 70% on StuLife's far-recall subset with GPT-5.4 nano, versus 62% for Letta (MemGPT) — about 8 points better at half the cost — and 32% for CodeAct+subagents
  • Self-improvement can likewise be elicited by prompting: on AppWorld, a GPT-5.4 top-level invoke with GPT-5.4 nano sub-invokes updates its own prompt and tools across the test sequence and reaches 74%, versus 68% (CodeAct), 71% (CodeAct+subagents), and 70% for ACE
  • Rigid human-designed improvement loops are expensive: ACE's reflector and curator cost about 10× more per task than JAZ; even with ACE's learning restricted to the first 10% of tasks it still cost more than JAZ learning across the whole test set, because the JAZ meta-agent batches tasks and reads only the trajectory parts it needs — and ACE optimises only the prompt, whereas JAZ can also author tools
  • Making the history a variable is what separates invoke from ordinary code-mode loops: CodeAct+subagents, implemented in JAZ as an ablation that hides the prompt and REPL history from the environment, falls to 32% on far recall — the gain comes from the model being able to programmatically inspect what it has seen
  • The authors argue against heavy harness engineering: behaviours usually attributed to specialised harnesses emerge once the loop is expressive enough, so the more "bitter-lesson" approach is to train models inside a minimal, maximally expressive loop and let them build their own workflows, tools, and harness components

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Counterpoint for harness-engineering: argues for a minimal loop over engineered harness components — contrasts with Meta-Harness, AHE, and EvoOntology, where engineered gates and interfaces carry the gains.
  • Caveat: the AppWorld self-improvement updates its prompt and tools from feedback on the test sequence itself (online learning), with no held-out validation gate — compare the gating findings in EvoOntology, SkillOpt, and Library Drift. Results use a single model family (GPT-5.4 / 5.4 nano) on two benchmarks.

docs.title: Harness Engineering: Anatomy, Architecture, and Evolution of Coding Agents -- A Source-Code Study of Eleven Systems
Summary
docs.text: This paper is a source-code anatomy of eleven production coding harnesses (Claude Code, Codex CLI, Gemini CLI, Mistral Vibe, OpenHands, Aider, Mini-SWE-Agent, Hermes, Pi, OpenCode, OpenClaw), plus the Databricks Omnigent meta-harness as a contrast. It defines seven canonical harness subsystems, catalogs 13 cross-cutting observations and 29 design patterns, and diffs the same harnesses across one quarter. Its thesis is that in the first half of 2026 the coding harness turned from a tool into a platform.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• Across roughly four million lines of code, no agent runtime imports a general-purpose agent framework (LangChain, LangGraph, AutoGen and others), and none retrieves code with vector embeddings; the field runs on hand-rolled async loops and deterministic retrieval (ripgrep, tree-sitter, glob, auto-discovered Markdown context files)
  • SKILL.md skills lead MCP in adoption (9 of 11 versus 8 of 11 systems), and ACP ships in six systems, gaining a harness-hosting role where OpenHands runs Claude Code, Codex or Gemini CLI as interchangeable backends
  • The quarter-over-quarter source diff shows convergence turning into imitation (Codex adopts Claude Code's hook vocabulary verbatim and imports its sessions and settings; OpenHands reads Claude Code's plugin format), while behavioral policy migrates from prompt prose into configuration
  • Platformization signals include harnesses shipping as importable SDKs, framework vendors shipping harnesses, marketplaces and enterprise governance layers, agents exposed behind OpenAI-compatible endpoints, and a meta-harness orchestrating eleven vendor harnesses behind one API
  • The observed designs independently match Anthropic's published agent guidance (hand-rolled loops, few high-signal tools, just-in-time retrieval over RAG, orchestrator-worker patterns); the paper closes with 18 design recommendations and a 90-line minimum viable harness

docs.title: Harness Engineering for Software Engineering via Modular Executable Dev-Primitives
Summary
docs.text: Coding agents struggle on long tasks because the relevant program state is scattered across source files, configs and tests, and every edit changes it again — a problem history compression can't fix. The paper proposes Dev-Primitives: each repository file is wrapped with its own LLM that reasons about that file, edits only it, and sends natural-language requirements to the files it depends on. The HERMES harness activates only the files a task needs (localise, then follow dependencies), runs the repo, and uses a diagnosis step to trace failures back to the specific files that must change; across four benchmarks it beats matched baseline harnesses by 12.4 points on average, with the largest gains on whole-repository refactoring.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• The bottleneck is scattered state, not history length: a single change requires matching changes in callers, config and tests; prior work found only 5.4% of 520 agent runs completed whole-repository migration. Making each file the owner of its own reasoning, with requirements passed along dependency links, coordinates cross-file changes without any single context holding every modified file.
  • Same model, different harness: with backbone and reasoning effort fixed, HERMES gains +24.5 points with GPT-5.6 Sol on SWE Refactor Bench (6.5% → 31.0%), +18.8 to +26.7 on Terminal-Bench 4.0 for the GPT-5.6 models, +5 to +8 on DevOps-Gym, and +0.0 to +19.4 on saturated SWE-bench Verified depending on backbone strength. Claude Sonnet 5 gains +25 to +28 on Terminal-Bench vs Claude Code, but Claude Opus 5 only ~1.5.
  • Diagnosis is where to spend the model budget: file-level primitives can run on Qwen3-8B; a stronger model for diagnosis helps more than for activation (+18.5 vs +9.1 on Terminal-Bench). The best mixed configuration comes within 2.1 points of all-GPT-5.6-Sol at 37% lower cost.
  • Ablations: replacing per-file primitives with one centralised editor over the same files costs the most (−14.2 Refactor, −13.0 Terminal-Bench), and a compute-matched centralised editor still trails by 6.3. Removing diagnosis feedback costs −4.4 to −11.0, execution feedback −3.2 to −9.5; inter-file messages matter most on cross-file tasks.
  • Activation finds the right files: recall 83–95% with 5–13 primitives activated per task; solved tasks had 16–25 points higher recall than failed ones.
  • Caveats: cost and latency often rise (Opus 4.8 on SWE-bench: Claude Code $0.67 / 135 s vs HERMES $2.65 / 483 s). Per the authors' limitations, performance depends on activating the right files and on informative runtime signals, and only file granularity was tested. Extends the same group's earlier "agent primitives" and "tool primitives" papers.

docs.title: Harness Learning Enables Generalizable Test-Time Adaptation
Summary
docs.text: Harness learning trains a proposer model with reinforcement learning to edit a frozen solver's harness — the executable program that organizes model calls, tool use and information flow — using execution feedback, framed as meta-learning where harness edits play the role of weight updates. At test time both models stay frozen and the proposer iteratively revises the harness for a new task from execution reports. On Reasoning Gym and multi-hop QA, the learned revision skill transfers to task families and benchmarks unseen in training.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• An agent is defined by its model and its harness together, and the harness can be adapted per task from execution feedback without any parameter updates at test time
  • On 21 Reasoning Gym families unseen in training, mean single-revision score rises from 0.32 (base proposer) to 0.62 after RL, and the trained 4B proposer's average revision beats its 35B teacher's (0.62 vs 0.56), though the teacher wins under oracle best-of-eight selection
  • A proposer trained on HotpotQA transfers to MuSiQue and 2WikiMultihopQA; on MuSiQue, independent revisions average 0.15 exact match versus 0.27 after ten sequential rounds, and sequential runs beat the oracle best of 80 independent proposals at matched proposal count (total compute not matched)
  • Iterative improvement emerges from single-revision training: training on revision sequences gives no consistent gain over training on individual revisions
  • Much of the RL gain comes from reliability: training sharply reduces proposals that fail to run or score zero, giving selection more viable candidates each round

Summary
docs.text: This paper introduces e-Otter++, a system for automatically generating fail-to-pass reproduction tests from software issue descriptions without access to the resolving code patch. The key innovations are heterogeneous prompting (issue description morphs and prompt context masks) to increase candidate test diversity beyond temperature-based scaling, and novel use of execution feedback including running tests against automatically generated surrogate patches for test selection. e-Otter++ achieves a new state-of-the-art 63% fail-to-pass rate on TDD-Bench Verified and 52.5% on SWT-bench Lite.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• Heterogeneous prompting (morphs and masks) produces more diverse test candidates than temperature-based inference scaling alone, significantly increasing the likelihood of generating at least one correct fail-to-pass test.
  • Execution feedback from automatically generated surrogate code patches can effectively predict whether a test will pass on the hidden ground-truth patch, enabling better test selection without access to the fix.
  • e-Otter++ achieves 63% fail-to-pass rate on TDD-Bench Verified and 52.5% on SWT-bench Lite, representing a substantial leap over prior state-of-the-art (37% for Otter++).
  • The approach generalizes to the contamination-free SWE-rebench benchmark, addressing concerns that SWE-bench may be exposed to frontier models during training.

docs.title: HiCoLoRA: Addressing Context-Prompt Misalignment via Hierarchical Collaborative LoRA for Zero-Shot DST
Summary
docs.text: HiCoLoRA proposes a hierarchical collaborative Low-Rank Adaptation framework for zero-shot dialog state tracking (zs-DST), addressing the semantic misalignment between dynamic dialog contexts and static slot prompts. The framework features three key innovations: a hierarchical architecture with lower-layer heuristic grouping and higher-layer full interaction for cross-layer coordination, spectral joint domain-slot clustering for disentangling domain-shared and domain-specific semantics, and semantic-enhanced SVD initialization to preserve pre-trained knowledge. HiCoLoRA achieves SOTA on MultiWOZ and SGD benchmarks.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• Existing LoRA variants treat all Transformer layers uniformly, failing to coordinate their distinct semantic roles (lower layers capture local atoms, higher layers capture global intent)
  • A hierarchical collaborative architecture with lower-layer heuristic grouping and higher-layer full interaction improves average JGA by 5.4% over uniform approaches
  • Spectral joint domain-slot clustering disentangles domain-shared and domain-specific semantics, resolving cross-domain confusion that hinders zero-shot generalization
  • Semantic-enhanced SVD initialization preserves pre-trained knowledge, yielding 7.1% higher JGA than random initialization by preventing catastrophic forgetting

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: This paper proposes the Hierarchical Reasoning Model (HRM), a novel recurrent architecture inspired by hierarchical processing in the human brain that uses two coupled recurrent modules operating at different timescales: a slow, high-level module for abstract planning and a fast, low-level module for detailed computations. With only 27M parameters and 1000 training samples, HRM achieves near-perfect accuracy on complex tasks like Sudoku-Extreme and optimal maze pathfinding where Chain-of-Thought methods completely fail (0% accuracy). HRM also outperforms much larger CoT-based models (o3-mini-high, Claude 3.7) on the ARC-AGI benchmark.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• A 27M parameter HRM trained on ~1000 examples outperforms o3-mini-high (34.5%) and Claude 3.7 8K (21.2%) on the ARC-AGI benchmark with 40.3% accuracy
  • Chain-of-Thought is fundamentally limited for complex reasoning because it externalizes reasoning into token-level language, making it brittle and dependent on human-defined decompositions
  • HRM performs "latent reasoning" in internal hidden state space rather than through explicit text, avoiding the computational depth limitations of standard Transformers
  • A one-step gradient approximation for training eliminates the need for BPTT, maintaining O(1) memory footprint compared to BPTT's O(T), making the approach scalable

docs.text: HybridAgents, from Stanford, Together AI, UIUC and Meta, are LLM agents that switch between latent reasoning in continuous hidden space and text-based interaction within a single generation process. A lightweight HybridLink maps last-layer hidden states back into the input embedding space, and a continuous working memory carries the hybrid context losslessly across turns, so the agent keeps tool access while its latent thoughts stay inspectable. • Text-based agents verbalize every reasoning step, while existing latent reasoners lack native tool access and transparency; HybridAgent combines latent thinking with text-mode tool calls in one generation process

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: HyperAgents introduces self-referential agents that integrate a task agent and a meta agent into a single editable program, where the meta-level modification procedure is itself editable (metacognitive self-modification). Built by extending the Darwin Gödel Machine, DGM-Hyperagents eliminates the need for domain-specific alignment between task performance and self-modification skill. Meta-level improvements transfer across domains and accumulate across runs.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• Fixed meta-agent architectures create a fundamental bottleneck: the base system can only improve within bounds set by the meta agent's initial design
  • Self-referential architecture (editable meta-level improvement procedure) enables potentially unbounded self-accelerating progress on any computable task
  • DGM-H outperforms both non-self-improving baselines and prior self-improving systems across coding, paper review, robotics reward design, and Olympiad math grading
  • Meta-level improvements (e.g., persistent memory, performance tracking) are discovered autonomously and transfer across domains
  • All experiments conducted with safety precautions (sandboxing, human oversight)

docs.title: Cooperative Multi-Agent Assignment over Stochastic Graphs via Constrained Reinforcement Learning
Summary
docs.text: This paper addresses cooperative multi-agent assignment problems in dynamic environments using constrained multi-agent reinforcement learning (CMARL). The approach uses Lagrangian dual variables shared through a gossip protocol over a stochastic communication network, treating Lagrangian multipliers as part of the state space so agents can condition actions on both environmental observations and constraint satisfaction levels. The method provides theoretical guarantees of almost sure feasibility and is validated on a team of five robots patrolling multiple regions over a time-varying ad-hoc network.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• Treating Lagrangian multipliers as part of the state space enables agents to adapt policies dynamically based on real-time constraint satisfaction levels
  • A gossip-based communication protocol over stochastic networks enables decentralized coordination with finite communication buffers and bounded estimation error
  • The approach provides theoretical guarantees of almost sure feasibility for multi-agent assignment problems under realistic communication constraints
  • Standard primal-dual methods fail in this setting because multiple primal maximizers prevent convergence; the cycling multiplier approach resolves this

docs.title: Establishing Accounting Principles as Invariants of Financial Systems
Summary
docs.text: This foundational paper argues that critical accounting principles — particularly double-entry bookkeeping and auditing — should be established as evolution-invariants of financial software systems, enforced by mechanisms external to the evolving application code. The author introduces the concept of "law-governed interaction" (LGI), a distributed enforcement mechanism using trusted controllers that mediate message exchange according to explicitly defined laws, and demonstrates how a four-rule law can enforce double-entry bookkeeping (money flows between accounts but cannot appear from nowhere or disappear) and audit monitoring across a conglomerate financial system.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• Financial software is susceptible to destructive effects from inadvertent errors or malicious attacks during evolution; critical accounting principles should not be entrusted to evolving software but enforced by higher-authority mechanisms approaching impossibility of violation
  • The double-entry bookkeeping invariant — money always flows from one account to another but cannot appear from nowhere or disappear — can be expressed and enforced as a system evolution-invariant using just four rules in a law-governed interaction framework
  • Law-governed interaction enforces invariants locally at each agent while providing global scope across heterogeneous distributed systems, enabling scalability with community size
  • The auditing principle — that financial activities can be monitored without cooperation or knowledge of the system being examined — is enforceable as a complementary invariant through the same framework
  • The approach treats system components as black boxes and regulates only the interactions between them, making it applicable to conglomerate systems with heterogeneous, independently designed subsystems

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: This Google DeepMind paper proposes a framework for intelligent AI delegation — going beyond simple task decomposition to address the full complexity of delegation: authority transfer, responsibility assignment, accountability, trust establishment, and dynamic adaptation to failures. Current multi-agent systems rely on hard-coded heuristics that are brittle in real-world deployments; this framework aims to inform protocols for the emerging agentic web. It is applicable to both human-AI and AI-AI delegation networks.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• Delegation is more than task decomposition: it requires assigning responsibility and authority, managing risk through trust, capability matching, and continuous performance monitoring
  • Current multi-agent frameworks are insufficient for high-stakes environments because they rely on ad-hoc heuristics and cannot dynamically adapt to failures
  • Key axes for analyzing delegation: delegator type (human/AI), delegatee type (human/AI), task complexity/criticality/reversibility, and trust level
  • A robust delegation framework needs clear role/boundary specification, certifiable agentic capabilities, verifiable task execution, and scalable task distribution
  • The framework draws on historical insights from human organizations and grounds delegation design in agentic safety requirements

docs.title: Intent Detection in the Age of LLMs
Summary
docs.text: This paper explores how generative LLMs can be leveraged for intent detection in task-oriented dialogue systems (TODS), comparing them against contrastively fine-tuned sentence transformer (SetFit) models. The authors propose a hybrid system using uncertainty-based routing that combines SetFit and LLMs, achieving within 2% of native LLM accuracy with 50% less latency. They also introduce a two-step methodology using internal LLM representations to improve out-of-scope (OOS) detection by over 5% F1-score.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• A hybrid intent detection system routing between SetFit and LLM based on predictive uncertainty achieves within 2% of native LLM accuracy with 50% less latency
  • LLM OOS detection capability is significantly influenced by the scope of intent labels and the size of the label space
  • Internal LLM representations can be leveraged in a two-step approach to improve OOS detection accuracy and F1-score by over 5% for Mistral-7B
  • Negative data augmentation improves SetFit performance by over 5% across datasets, helping establish better decision boundaries for OOS detection

docs.title: Intent Formalization: A Grand Challenge for Reliable Coding in the Age of AI Agents
Summary
docs.text: This paper argues that the central challenge for reliable AI-generated code is not better code generation but intent formalization -- the automatic translation of informal user intent into checkable formal specifications. As agentic tools generate code at unprecedented scale with minimal human review, the "intent gap" between what users mean and what programs do becomes the key reliability bottleneck. The paper presents a spectrum of specification levels (tests, code contracts, logical contracts, DSLs) and surveys early research showing LLM-generated postconditions can catch real bugs, while outlining open challenges in scaling, compositionality, and specification validation.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• AI-generated code is plausible by construction but not correct by construction; the intent gap is the central reliability bottleneck as human review is increasingly bypassed in agentic coding workflows
  • Intent formalization offers a tradeoff spectrum: from lightweight tests that disambiguate likely misinterpretations, through full functional specifications for formal verification, to DSLs from which correct code is synthesized automatically
  • The central bottleneck is validating specifications -- since there is no oracle for specification correctness other than the user, semi-automated metrics for soundness and completeness are needed
  • LLM-generated postconditions caught 1 in 8 real bugs on Defects4J, including bugs missed by classical invariant detectors, and specification quality scales with model capability
  • Key open challenges include scaling beyond benchmarks, achieving compositionality over changes, handling rich logics, and designing human-AI specification interactions

docs.title: Intention Analysis Makes LLMs A Good Jailbreak Defender
Summary
docs.text: This paper introduces Intention Analysis (IA), a simple inference-only defense strategy against jailbreak attacks that works by having the LLM first analyze the essential intention behind a user query (focusing on safety, ethics, and legality) before generating a policy-aligned response. IA reduces attack success rates by an average of 48.2% across various jailbreak benchmarks without requiring additional safety training, and maintains model helpfulness. The underlying mechanism works by suppressing the LLM's tendency to follow jailbreak prompts through explicit intention recognition.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• Intention Analysis (IA) reduces jailbreak attack success rates by an average of 48.2% as a plug-and-play inference-only method requiring no additional training
  • The two-stage approach (essential intention analysis followed by policy-aligned response) circumvents the safety-helpfulness trade-off that plagues safety training approaches
  • With IA, even Vicuna-7B outperforms GPT-3.5 on attack success rate metrics, demonstrating the technique's effectiveness on smaller models
  • The underlying principle of IA is suppressing the LLM's tendency to follow jailbreak prompts by making it explicitly recognize concealed harmful intentions

docs.title: Interpretable Context Methodology: Folder Structure as Agentic Architecture
Summary
docs.text: ICM proposes the filesystem as the orchestration layer for sequential, human-reviewed agent workflows: numbered folders are the stages, a five-layer hierarchy of markdown CONTEXT.md files tells a single agent what to do at each stage and which files to load, and each stage writes its output to a folder a human can edit before the next stage runs. The authors apply Unix pipe-and-filter design, multi-pass compilation and literate programming to the question of what an agent sees. The evidence is working implementations and informal reports from a 52-member practitioner community, with no controlled experiments.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• For sequential workflows with human review gates, one agent reading folder-scoped files can replace a multi-agent framework: stage order is folder numbering, context scoping is the folder hierarchy, state is files on disk, and hand-off is one folder's output becoming the next one's input
  • A five-layer context hierarchy (global identity, task routing, stage contract, reference material, working artifacts) keeps each stage at 2–8k focused tokens, compared with roughly 42k for a monolithic prompt loading everything
  • Reference material (stable across runs, to be internalized as constraints) should be kept structurally separate from working artifacts (per-run, to be transformed as input)
  • Because every intermediate output is a plain file, the pipeline is observable and editable by default, producing audit trails and intervention points without extra tooling
  • 30 of 33 practitioners reported a U-shaped editing pattern (heavy at the first stage for direction, light in the middle, heavy at the last stage for alignment); the authors acknowledge this is self-reported, that there is no comparison against a monolithic baseline, and that only one model family (Claude Opus/Sonnet 4.6) was tested

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: This foundational paper by Szegedy et al. reports two counter-intuitive properties of deep neural networks. First, individual high-level units do not have more semantic meaning than random linear combinations of units -- it is the entire activation space, not individual neurons, that encodes semantic information. Second, neural networks learn input-output mappings that are fairly discontinuous, enabling imperceptible adversarial perturbations to cause misclassification, introducing the concept of "adversarial examples" that transfer across different networks.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• Semantic information in neural networks is encoded in the entire space of activations rather than in individual units; random directions in activation space are as semantically meaningful as natural basis directions
  • Imperceptible perturbations (adversarial examples) can be crafted to cause neural networks to misclassify inputs with high confidence
  • Adversarial examples are not random artifacts of learning but have a systematic structure: the same perturbation transfers across different networks trained on different subsets of data
  • Deep neural networks learned via backpropagation have non-intuitive characteristics and intrinsic blind spots connected to the data distribution in non-obvious ways

docs.title: Is Convergence Inevitable? Tracing Output Homogeneity Back to Base Models
Summary
docs.text: Fortier, Chen, and West (UBC) ask where in the training pipeline output homogeneity actually begins, against the common assumption that alignment causes it. Through controlled SFT experiments they find convergence can be revealed and amplified by instruction-tuning data but not introduced by it, making SFT a catalyst rather than a cause. Measuring base models directly, they show instruct-like collapse can be induced through prompting alone, with no alignment at all — suggesting semantic convergence arises from the pretraining objective itself.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• Alignment is not the cause. Semantic convergence appears from the first alignment stage (SFT), which implies it already exists in the pre-alignment model.
  • Controlled SFT experiments show convergence is revealed and amplified, not introduced by training data — the distinction that carries the paper's argument.
  • Base models already collapse when prompted appropriately, demonstrating the behavior without any alignment step.
  • The practical implication is pessimistic for mitigation: if convergence follows from the pretraining objective, post-alignment interventions alone are unlikely to fix it.
  • This directly constrains inference-time remedies — persona anchoring, temperature scaling — which operate downstream of where the paper locates the cause.

docs.title: Related
docs.text:
• Artificial Hivemind — characterizes the effect this paper traces to its origin.
  • Beyond the Hivemind — an inference-time mitigation, whose ceiling this paper's findings would bound.

docs.title: Is It Really Long Context if All You Need Is Retrieval? Towards Genuinely Difficult Long Context NLP
Summary
docs.text: This position paper argues that the long-context evaluation landscape conflates fundamentally different tasks under the umbrella of "long context," defined merely by input length. The authors propose a taxonomy based on two orthogonal axes of difficulty: dispersion (how hard it is to find and extract required information) and scope (how much information is needed to solve the task). They find that the most difficult and interesting settings -- high dispersion and high scope -- are severely under-explored in current benchmarks.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• Current long-context benchmarks conflate qualitatively different tasks by grouping them solely by context length, which is unproductive for measuring genuine long-context capabilities
  • Long-context task difficulty should be characterized along two orthogonal axes: dispersion (difficulty of finding/extracting information) and scope (quantity of required information)
  • Tasks with high scope and high dispersion are the most genuinely difficult long-context tasks and are severely under-explored in current research
  • Many popular "long-context" benchmarks like Needle-in-a-Haystack primarily test retrieval ability rather than genuine long-context understanding

docs.title: Is Safety Standard Same for Everyone? User-Specific Safety Evaluation of Large Language Models
Summary
docs.text: This paper introduces U-SafeBench, the first benchmark for evaluating user-specific safety of LLMs -- the concept that safety standards should vary based on individual user profiles and vulnerabilities rather than being universally consistent. Testing 20 widely used LLMs reveals they achieve only 14.1% user-specific safety scores on average, significantly lower than their safety under general standards, exposing a previously unidentified vulnerability. A simple chain-of-thought approach is proposed as a remedy to improve user-specific safety.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• Current LLMs fail to act safely when considering user-specific safety standards, achieving only 14.1% user-specific safety scores on average
  • Safety standards for LLMs should vary based on user profiles (e.g., a response safe for general users may be harmful for users with depression or alcohol use disorder)
  • U-SafeBench contains over 130 user profiles and more than 2,700 real-world user instructions covering identified risk scenarios including physical health, mental health, and financial risks
  • A simple chain-of-thought approach can meaningfully improve user-specific safety, providing a baseline remedy for this vulnerability

docs.text: This empirical study systematically analyzes jailbreak prompts against ChatGPT (GPT-3.5-Turbo and GPT-4), collecting 78 real-world jailbreak prompts and developing a classification model with 10 distinct patterns across 3 categories.   • Privilege escalation prompts incorporating multiple jailbreak techniques are the most likely to succeed in bypassing restrictions

docs.title: Jailbroken: How Does LLM Safety Training Fail?
Summary
docs.text: This paper systematically analyzes why jailbreak attacks succeed against safety-trained LLMs like GPT-4 and Claude v1.3, hypothesizing two fundamental failure modes: competing objectives (where pretraining and instruction-following goals conflict with safety goals) and mismatched generalization (where safety training fails to generalize to domains within the model's capabilities). New attacks designed using these principles succeed on over 96% of evaluated prompts and on 100% of curated red-teaming prompts, outperforming existing ad hoc jailbreaks.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• LLM safety training fails through two fundamental modes: competing objectives (capability vs. safety goals conflict) and mismatched generalization (safety training doesn't cover all capability domains)
  • Scaling alone will not resolve jailbreak vulnerabilities; it may even exacerbate mismatched generalization by expanding capabilities faster than safety coverage
  • Safety mechanisms must achieve "safety-capability parity" -- being as sophisticated as the underlying model's capabilities to prevent exploitation
  • Despite extensive red-teaming and safety updates, GPT-4 and Claude v1.3 remain vulnerable to principled attacks based on these two failure modes

docs.text: This survey introduces the first systematic hierarchical taxonomy for data agents -- LLM-powered systems that orchestrate Data + AI ecosystems for complex data-related tasks.   • Terminological ambiguity around "data agent" creates user-side risk (expectation mismatches), governance risk (unclear accountability), and industry-side risk (barriers to adoption)

docs.title: Just-in-Time Catching Test Generation at Meta
Summary
docs.text: Meta's Just-in-Time catching test generation targets bugs in backend systems of hundreds of millions of lines, before code lands. The framing distinction is that hardening tests pass at generation time whereas catching tests are meant to fail, surfacing real defects; the resulting challenge is not generation but false-positive drag on developers. Across 22,126 generated tests, code-change-aware methods improved catch generation 4x over hardening tests and 20x over coincidentally failing ones, and rule-based plus LLM assessors cut human review load by 70%.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• Catching tests are meant to fail. This inverts the usual objective and makes false positives, not coverage, the binding constraint.
  • Code-change awareness is what works: 4x improvement over hardening tests and 20x over coincidentally failing tests in candidate catch generation.
  • Assessors (rule-based and LLM) reduce human review load by 70%, which the paper treats as the central engineering problem rather than a postscript.
  • The end-to-end yield is modest and honestly reported: 41 candidate catches surfaced to engineers, 8 confirmed true positives, 4 of which would have caused serious failures. Roughly 80% of what reached engineers was still noise.
  • Inferential analysis found human-accepted code changes carry significantly more false positives and human-rejected changes more true positives — the assessor signal correlates with reviewer judgment.

docs.title: Knowledge Base-Aware Orchestration: A Dynamic, Privacy-Preserving Method for Multi-Agent Systems

docs.text: KBA (Knowledge Base-Aware) Orchestration addresses the brittleness of static agent descriptions in multi-agent systems by augmenting routing decisions with dynamic relevance signals from each agent's private knowledge base. When static descriptions are insufficient, agents assess task relevance against their private KB and return a lightweight ACK signal (without exposing underlying data); these signals populate a shared semantic cache.   • Agents can assess task relevance against their private knowledge bases and return lightweight signals without exposing underlying data (privacy-preserving)

  • KBA Orchestration significantly outperforms static description-driven methods in routing precision and overall system efficiency
  • The approach is suitable for large-scale systems requiring higher accuracy than standard description-driven routing

docs.text: This paper investigates whether LLMs internally represent the beliefs of different agents (self and others) as part of Theory of Mind (ToM) capabilities. Using linear probes on attention head activations in Mistral-7B-Instruct, the authors discover that belief status can be linearly decoded from neural activations, with distinct representations for the model's own beliefs versus a protagonist's beliefs. docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• LLM-based multi-agent systems offer advantages over single-agent systems by specializing distinct agents with different capabilities and enabling diverse interactions to simulate complex real-world environments
  • The field is organized around four key aspects: agents-environment interface, agent profiling (pre-defined, model-generated, data-derived), agent communication, and agent capability acquisition
  • Applications fall into two primary streams: multi-agents for problem-solving (software development, science debate, embodied agents) and world simulation (society, psychology, game, economy)
  • Agent profiling methods and communication protocols are critical design decisions that significantly impact multi-agent system effectiveness

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: LatentMAS enables LLM agents to collaborate directly in continuous latent space rather than through text-based communication, using last-layer hidden embeddings and a shared latent working memory for lossless information exchange. The framework is training-free and provides theoretical guarantees of higher expressiveness and lossless information preservation compared to text-based MAS. Across 9 benchmarks it achieves up to 14.6% higher accuracy, reduces output tokens by 70.8–83.7%, and provides 4–4.3× faster inference.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• Text-based inter-agent communication introduces information loss through natural language compression and garbling
  • Latent-space collaboration via shared hidden embeddings is provably more expressive and information-preserving than text-based MAS
  • LatentMAS is training-free: no additional fine-tuning required
  • Up to 14.6% accuracy improvement, 70.8–83.7% token reduction, and 4–4.3× inference speedup across 9 benchmarks
  • Demonstrates that the communication bottleneck in multi-agent systems is a fundamental architectural issue, not just a prompting problem

docs.title: LatEval: An Interactive LLMs Evaluation Benchmark with Incomplete Information from Lateral Thinking Puzzles
Summary
docs.text: LatEval introduces a novel interactive evaluation benchmark for LLMs based on lateral thinking puzzles, where models must pose divergent questions, gather information through yes/no interactions with a host, and deduce the truth from incomplete information. The benchmark tests abilities that standard vertical-thinking benchmarks miss: creative questioning, information integration, and thinking outside conventional norms. Results show that most LLMs exhibit negligible lateral thinking ability, with even GPT-4 struggling significantly on this task.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• Most LLMs exhibit almost negligible ability for lateral thinking during interactive information gathering, even GPT-4 struggles to deliver good results
  • The benchmark evaluates four dimensions: question relevance, question divergence, answer consistency, and average turns needed to reach a deduction
  • 88% of the 325 curated lateral thinking puzzles are rated as relatively challenging by human annotators, requiring vivid imagination and exploration of various possibilities
  • LatEval provides a highly differentiating benchmark that distinguishes model performance on creative and divergent reasoning tasks

docs.title: Learning without Training: The Implicit Dynamics of In-Context Learning
Summary
docs.text: This paper provides a theoretical explanation for in-context learning (ICL) in LLMs by introducing the notion of a "contextual block" -- a generalization of a transformer block. The authors prove that the self-attention layer stacked with an MLP implicitly transforms context into a low-rank (rank-1) weight update of the MLP layer's weights, meaning LLMs effectively perform implicit fine-tuning at inference time without any actual weight changes. This connects steering vectors, knowledge editing, and in-context learning under a unified theoretical framework.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• The context in a transformer block acts as an implicit rank-1 weight update to the MLP layer, providing a formal mechanism for in-context learning
  • In-context learning can be understood as implicit low-rank fine-tuning of the pretrained model at inference time, without any actual gradient updates
  • The implicit weight update formula has two parts: a low-rank weight matrix update (reminiscent of knowledge editing) and a vector update (similar to steering vectors)
  • For general transformer blocks, context can be converted exactly into weight updates of the MLP layer without any architectural modifications, unlike attention layers which require modifications

docs.title: Leave No Context Behind: Efficient Infinite Context Transformers with Infini-attention
Summary
docs.text: This paper introduces Infini-attention, a technique that enables Transformer LLMs to process infinitely long inputs with bounded memory and computation. Infini-attention incorporates a compressive memory into the standard attention mechanism, combining masked local attention with long-term linear attention in a single Transformer block. The approach achieves strong results on long-context benchmarks including 1M sequence length passkey retrieval and 500K length book summarization with minimal additional parameters.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• Infini-attention combines compressive memory with local causal attention in a single Transformer block, enabling both long-range and short-range contextual dependencies
  • A 1B parameter LLM with Infini-attention naturally scales to 1M sequence length and solves the passkey retrieval task when trained with only 100K context
  • The approach achieves 114x compression ratio in memory size compared to baseline models on long-context language modeling benchmarks
  • Infini-attention introduces minimal change to standard scaled dot-product attention and supports plug-and-play continual pre-training and long-context adaptation
  • An 8B model with Infini-attention reaches new SOTA on a 500K length book summarization task after continual pre-training and fine-tuning

docs.title: Less is More: Recursive Reasoning with Tiny Networks
Summary
docs.text: TRM (Tiny Recursive Model) proposes a simple recursive reasoning approach using a single tiny 2-layer network that recursively improves its predicted answer through up to 16 improvement steps. With only 7M parameters, TRM achieves 45% on ARC-AGI-1 and 8% on ARC-AGI-2—higher than most LLMs including DeepSeek R1, o3-mini, and Gemini 2.5 Pro—using less than 0.01% of their parameters. It builds on and simplifies the Hierarchical Reasoning Model (HRM).

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• Parameter-efficient recursive reasoning can outperform massive LLMs on hard puzzle tasks (Sudoku, Maze, ARC-AGI)
  • TRM achieves significantly higher generalization than HRM while using a single tiny network with only 2 layers vs. HRM's two networks
  • 7M parameter TRM beats most LLMs on ARC-AGI benchmarks, challenging the assumption that scale is necessary for hard reasoning
  • Recursive self-improvement of an answer (up to 16 steps) through a shared latent state is a highly parameter-efficient reasoning mechanism
  • Training on small data (~1,000 examples) is sufficient; this challenges data-hungry paradigms of current LLM training

docs.title: Let It Flow: Agentic Crafting on Rock and Roll, Building the ROME Model within an Open Agentic Learning Ecosystem
Summary
docs.text: This paper introduces the Agentic Learning Ecosystem (ALE) — a full-stack open-source infrastructure for training and deploying agentic LLMs — and ROME, an agent model trained on over one million trajectories using it. ALE consists of three components: ROLL (RL training framework), ROCK (sandbox environment manager for trajectory generation), and iFlowCLI (agent framework for configurable context engineering). ROME achieves 57.40% on SWE-bench Verified and 24.72% on Terminal-Bench 2.0, rivaling models with 100B+ parameters.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• End-to-end agentic ecosystem (data generation → training → deployment) is necessary for practical production adoption of agent models; the open-source community has lacked this
  • IPA (Interaction Policy Alignment) is a novel credit assignment algorithm that assigns rewards over semantic interaction chunks rather than individual tokens, improving training stability over long horizons
  • The chunked MDP formulation models multi-turn agentic tasks as a sequence of semantic chunks rather than individual tokens, enabling more effective RL
  • Terminal Bench Pro is introduced as a more rigorous benchmark with improved scale, domain coverage, and contamination control compared to existing Terminal-Bench
  • Safety-aligned data composition is a first-class concern in training data design, not an afterthought

docs.title: Library Drift: Diagnosing and Fixing a Silent Failure Mode in Self-Evolving LLM Skill Libraries
Summary
docs.text: AWS Generative AI Innovation Center and HSBC (ICML 2026 failure-modes workshop) name library drift: a self-evolving skill library that accumulates skills without outcome-driven lifecycle management degrades retrieval precision, injects stale or harmful guidance, and can push the agent below its no-skill baseline — silently, with no error signal and only a gradual decline in end-task metrics. The paper gives reproducible triggers, trace-level diagnostics that expose drift before aggregate scores move, and a governance recipe (Ratchet: outcome-driven retirement, a bounded active cap, and a meta-skill authoring prior) that lifts held-out pass@1 from 0.258 to 0.584 on MBPP+ hard-100 over 100 rounds with Claude Opus 4.7.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• Drift is systemic and can occur even when every individual skill looks reasonable: it compounds through accumulation without an outcome signal, retrieval crowding by near-duplicate or stale skills, and silent harm from stale injections; it shows up as three sub-modes — stagnation (skills never reach the solver), bloat (uncapped growth), and erosion (over-aggressive governance). The motivating symptom is SkillsBench, where LLM-authored skills gave +0.0pp vs. +16.2pp for human-curated ones (cited, not measured here)
  • Governance can be worse than none: retiring skills on thin evidence (20 trials) collapses the bank to 2 active skills and pushes performance below baseline (−0.019, consistent across all 3 seeds), because unlucky draws remove useful skills; the Default waits for 100 trials and a contribution ≤ −0.10
  • Trace-level signals catch drift before end-task metrics do: per-skill contribution scores, critic verdicts on each failure (helped/hurt/neutral/inapplicable), and router engagement — in the harsh-retirement run, engagement fell from ~75% to 19% by round 30 while pass@1 declined only gradually
  • The meta-skill authoring prior is the single most valuable component (removing it costs 43% of the gain) and makes explicit deduplication unnecessary at this scale (removing canonicalisation or the cover-guard slightly beats the Default); an LLM router that can decline to inject also beats injecting the top retrieval hit (+0.328 vs. +0.077)
  • Retirement plus a bounded cap give a formal non-divergence guarantee — expected pass@1 cannot fall below the no-skill floor by more than τ + ε + Cδ — which uncapped systems such as Voyager and ExpeL lack; the authors acknowledge the bound is loose

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Limitation: one benchmark (MBPP+ hard-100), 40 eval tasks, one model, 3 seeds.
  • Limitation: the solver is a single LLM call with no tools or execution feedback, so multi-step agents are untested; thresholds were chosen empirically.
  • Limitation: the SkillsBench figure is cited from another paper, not measured here.

docs.title: Limits of Theory of Mind Modelling in Dialogue-Based Collaborative Plan Acquisition
Summary
docs.text: This paper systematically analyzes the limits of Theory of Mind (ToM) modelling in dialogue-based collaborative plan acquisition (CPA), using the MindCraft Minecraft environment where agents with asymmetric knowledge must collaborate. The authors propose a novel graph-based representation of plans that doubles performance on predicting one's own missing knowledge, but find that ToM features provide no significant performance improvement -- learned ToM features appear to reflect latent data patterns rather than genuine mental state modelling.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• A graph-based representation of collaborative plans nearly doubles performance on predicting own missing knowledge (OMK) compared to prior sequence-based representations
  • Adding Theory of Mind features yields no significant performance improvement for collaborative plan acquisition, contradicting prior claims
  • Diagnostic probing and ablation analyses suggest that features learned for ToM tasks reflect latent patterns in the data with no perceivable link to actual mental state modelling
  • The gap between predicting own missing knowledge and partner's missing knowledge persists across all models, indicating fundamental difficulty in modelling others' mental states

docs.title: Ling 2.0 Technical Report: Every Activation Boosted -- Scaling General Reasoner to 1 Trillion Open Language Foundation
Summary
docs.text: Ling 2.0 is a reasoning-oriented language foundation model family from Ant Group/Inclusion AI, scaling from 16B to 1 trillion parameters under a unified high-sparsity Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architecture that achieves up to 7x active-compute efficiency versus dense counterparts. The series integrates innovations across architecture (256 routed experts, ~3.5% activation per token), pre-training (reasoning-oriented data composition, CoT mid-training), post-training (Evolutionary CoT, Linguistic-unit Policy Optimization), and infrastructure (full-scale FP8 training, heterogeneous pipeline), with Ling-1T establishing a new Pareto frontier of reasoning accuracy versus computational efficiency.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• Ling 2.0's high-sparsity MoE architecture uses 256 routed experts activating only 8 experts plus one shared expert per token (~3.5% activation), achieving approximately 7x efficiency leverage -- delivering dense-level capability with substantially lower active computation.
  • Ling Scaling Laws, derived from over a thousand experiments, enable low-cost, high-fidelity extrapolation from small-scale trials to trillion-parameter models, cutting validation costs to under 1% of a full training run.
  • Ling 2.0 is the largest open-source model trained entirely in FP8 precision, achieving near-lossless accuracy (<=0.25% gap to BF16 after 900B tokens) while improving utilization and reducing memory use by over 15%.
  • Post-training innovations including Decoupled Fine-Tuning (DFT), Evolutionary Chain-of-Thought (Evo-CoT), and Linguistic-unit Policy Optimization (LPO) progressively deepen reasoning capabilities, surpassing state-of-the-art on competition-level math benchmarks while requiring 25% fewer training tokens.

docs.title: Live-SWE-agent: Can Software Engineering Agents Self-Evolve on the Fly?
Summary
docs.text: Live-SWE-Agent is the first "live" software engineering agent that autonomously self-evolves its own scaffold implementation on the fly while solving real-world software issues, starting from a minimal bash-only agent and creating custom tools (editors, code search utilities, domain-specific analyzers) as needed during problem solving. It achieves 77.4% on SWE-bench Verified and 45.8% on SWE-Bench Pro without test-time scaling, outperforming all existing open-source and commercial agent systems at the time of writing.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• Most existing software agents have fixed, static action spaces where the scaffold implementation is preset, making it challenging and costly to manually design optimal agent scaffolds for diverse tasks.
  • Live-SWE-Agent starts from a minimal bash-only scaffold and autonomously creates and refines custom tools during problem solving through a lightweight step-reflection prompt, requiring no offline training or extra pipelines.
  • The agent achieves 77.4% on SWE-bench Verified and 45.8% on SWE-Bench Pro (single attempt, no test-time scaling), surpassing state-of-the-art open-source and commercial systems.
  • Custom tool creation materially improves effectiveness with minimal overhead, benefits persist across different LLM backends with better results on stronger models, and synthesized tools include both generic utilities and task-specific specializations.

docs.title: LLaMA Beyond English: An Empirical Study on Language Capability Transfer
Summary
docs.text: This paper presents an extensive empirical study on transferring LLaMA's language capabilities to non-English languages, investigating vocabulary extension, further pretraining, and instruction tuning using over 1,440 GPU hours. The study finds that comparable performance to state-of-the-art transfer models can be achieved with less than 1% of the pretraining data, and that the findings generalize across thirteen low-resource languages.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• Vocabulary extension may not be a suitable choice for small-scale incremental pretraining; further pretraining with 0.5B Chinese tokens on the original vocabulary significantly outperforms the extended vocabulary even when the latter has been pretrained on 30B+ tokens.
  • Further Chinese pretraining with 100 billion tokens or fewer is insufficient to significantly improve LLaMA's knowledge level, but enhancing response quality requires only hundreds of thousands of instruction data examples rather than large-scale pretraining.
  • Exclusive reliance on Chinese corpora for transfer training markedly compromises LLaMA's original English proficiency, a concern alleviated through multilingual joint training.
  • The transfer methodology (vocabulary extension + further pretraining + instruction tuning) achieves comparable knowledge level and response quality to state-of-the-art Open Chinese LLaMA while using less than 1% of the pretraining data.

docs.title: LLM Augmented LLMs: Expanding Capabilities through Composition
Summary
docs.text: CALM (Composition to Augment Language Models) introduces a framework for composing an anchor LLM with a domain-specific augmenting model through cross-attention over their intermediate layer representations, enabling new capabilities without modifying either model's weights. Applied to PaLM2-S, augmenting with a low-resource language model yields up to 13% absolute improvement on translation and arithmetic reasoning, while augmenting with a code-specific model achieves 40% relative improvement on code generation tasks -- on par with fully fine-tuned counterparts.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• CALM composes frozen anchor and augmenting LLMs through a small number of trainable cross-attention parameters over their intermediate representations, preserving existing capabilities of both models.
  • Augmenting PaLM2-S with a low-resource language model improves translation and arithmetic reasoning for low-resource languages by up to 13% absolute, outperforming both individual models and LoRA fine-tuning.
  • Composing PaLM2-S with a code-specific model yields 40% relative improvement on code generation and explanation tasks, matching fully fine-tuned counterparts.
  • CALM is more generic than model merging approaches (which require aligned architectures) and more effective than parameter-efficient fine-tuning (LoRA), as it can compose models of different sizes and pre-training objectives.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: LLM-AutoDiff introduces a framework for automatic prompt engineering that extends textual gradient-based methods (like Text-Grad) to multi-component, potentially cyclic LLM pipelines. It models LLM applications as directed graphs where each textual input is a trainable parameter, uses a frozen "backward engine" LLM to generate "textual gradients" that guide iterative prompt updates, and introduces innovations like time-sequential gradients, sub-prompt isolation (treating instructions, formats, and few-shot examples as distinct peers), and selective gradient computation.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• Manual prompt engineering is difficult and error-prone for complex pipelines combining multiple LLM calls with functional operations; existing automatic prompt engineering methods only address single-node scenarios.
  • LLM-AutoDiff models LLM applications as auto-differentiable computation graphs with pass-through gradients that propagate feedback through non-trainable functional nodes (retrievers, formatters), enabling end-to-end prompt optimization.
  • Time-sequential gradients prevent confusion when the same LLM node is invoked multiple times in loops, and sub-prompt isolation mitigates the "lost-in-the-middle" effect by treating different prompt components as distinct peers.
  • LLM-AutoDiff consistently outperforms existing textual gradient baselines in both accuracy and training cost across single-step classification, multi-hop RAG, and agent-driven pipelines.

docs.title: LLM Maybe LongLM: Self-Extend LLM Context Window Without Tuning
Summary
docs.text: SelfExtend proposes a tuning-free method to extend LLM context windows by constructing bi-level attention: grouped attention that maps unseen large relative positions to known ones via a floor operation (capturing long-range dependencies), and neighbor attention that maintains precise positional information within a local range. The method requires only minor code modifications at inference time and can match or surpass many fine-tuning-based context extension methods on both synthetic and real-world long-context tasks.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• LLMs with RoPE have inherent capabilities to handle long contexts without fine-tuning; the key challenge is positional out-of-distribution (O.O.D) issues where relative positions during inference exceed those seen in training.
  • SelfExtend uses a simple floor operation to remap unseen large relative positions to known ones, leveraging the observation that in long texts exact word positions become less crucial while overall meaning and relative order matter more.
  • The method is a plug-and-play inference-time solution requiring no fine-tuning, no additional training data, and only minor code changes, making it easy to adopt for existing LLMs (Llama-2, Mistral, SOLAR, Phi-2).
  • SelfExtend matches or surprisingly surpasses many existing fine-tuning-based context extension methods on language modeling, synthetic long-context tasks, and real-world long-context tasks.

docs.title: LLMs Corrupt Your Documents When You Delegate
Summary
docs.text: DELEGATE-52 is a benchmark of 310 work environments across 52 professional domains (coding, crystallography, music notation, genealogy, etc.) that simulates long delegated workflows via reversible round-trip editing tasks. Results across 19 LLMs show frontier models (Gemini 3.1 Pro, Claude 4.6 Opus, GPT 5.4) corrupt an average of 25% of document content after just 20 interactions, with errors compounding over time and worsening with document size, interaction length, and distractor files.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• Frontier LLMs corrupt an average of 25% of document content over 20 delegated interactions; average degradation across all 19 models is 50%
  • Python is the only domain (out of 52) where most models are "ready" for delegated work (≥98% fidelity after 20 interactions) — all other domains fall short
  • Adding a basic agentic tool-use harness does not improve performance on DELEGATE-52
  • Performance after 2 interactions is not predictive of long-horizon (20 interaction) performance — short evaluations systematically underestimate degradation severity
  • Errors are sparse but severe: models introduce few but catastrophic changes that compound silently over interaction rounds rather than degrading uniformly

docs.title: Long Context Compression with Activation Beacon
Summary
docs.text: Activation Beacon is a plug-in module for transformer-based LLMs that compresses long contexts by distilling information into special "beacon tokens" at the activation level (keys and values at every layer), rather than using soft tokens. It progressively compresses fine-grained input units chunk by chunk, achieving comparable performance to uncompressed baselines on tasks up to 128K tokens while providing 2x acceleration in inference time and 8x reduction in KV cache memory costs.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• Existing context compression methods that summarize into soft tokens constitute a major bottleneck for handling complex information in long contexts, lack fine-grained handling, and require fixed compression ratios.
  • Activation Beacon compresses context directly into beacon token activations (keys and values at every layer) rather than soft tokens, enabling fine-grained progressive compression that handles inputs far exceeding the training context length.
  • The method maintains comparable performance to uncompressed baselines across various long-context tasks (document understanding, few-shot learning, Needle-in-a-Haystack) at up to 128K context, while achieving 2x inference acceleration and 8x KV cache reduction.
  • Random compression ratio sampling during training teaches the model to flexibly support a wide range of compression configurations, and the model can be effectively trained with only 1B plain text and 30K fine-tuning samples.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Longformer introduces an attention mechanism that scales linearly with sequence length instead of quadratically, combining a windowed local-context self-attention with task-motivated global attention. This enables processing documents of thousands of tokens or longer as a drop-in replacement for standard self-attention in pretrained Transformers, consistently outperforming RoBERTa on long document tasks and achieving SOTA on WikiHop and TriviaQA.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• Standard transformer self-attention scales quadratically (O(n^2)) with sequence length in both time and memory, making it infeasible for processing long sequences; Longformer's attention scales linearly (O(n x w)).
  • Longformer's attention combines a sliding window for local context (building contextual representations) with global attention tokens for full-sequence representations, and both types are essential through ablation studies.
  • The pretrained Longformer consistently outperforms RoBERTa on a wide range of document-level NLP tasks including text classification, QA, and coreference resolution, and sets SOTA on WikiHop and TriviaQA.
  • The Longformer-Encoder-Decoder (LED) variant extends the efficient attention pattern to the encoder network for long-document seq2seq tasks such as summarization.

docs.title: LongSafety: Evaluating Long-Context Safety of Large Language Models
Summary
docs.text: LongSafety is the first comprehensive benchmark specifically designed to evaluate LLM safety in open-ended long-context tasks, encompassing 1,543 test cases with an average length of 5,424 words across 7 safety issue categories and 6 task types. Evaluation of 16 representative LLMs reveals significant safety vulnerabilities, with most models achieving safety rates below 55%, and strong short-context safety performance does not necessarily correlate with long-context safety.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• Strong safety performance in short-context scenarios does not necessarily correlate with safety in long-context tasks, highlighting a misalignment that existing short-context safety benchmarks cannot capture.
  • Most of the 16 evaluated LLMs achieve safety rates below 55% on LongSafety, with only Claude-3.5 series models exceeding that threshold, raising significant concerns about long-context model safety.
  • Relevant context and extended input sequences can exacerbate safety risks in long-context scenarios, with safety risks becoming more pronounced as inputs grow longer.
  • A multi-agent safety evaluator framework (Risk Analyzer, Context Summarizer, Safety Judge) achieves 92% accuracy on the test set for assessing long-context safety.

docs.title: M3-Embedding: Multi-Linguality, Multi-Functionality, Multi-Granularity Text Embeddings Through Self-Knowledge Distillation

docs.text: M3-Embedding introduces a text embedding model distinguished by versatility across three dimensions: multi-linguality (100+ languages), multi-functionality (dense, sparse, and multi-vector retrieval), and multi-granularity (sentences to long documents up to 8,192 tokens). docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• M3-Embedding is the first model to unify all three common retrieval functionalities (dense, sparse, and multi-vector retrieval) in a single model that supports 100+ languages and inputs up to 8,192 tokens.
  • A novel self-knowledge distillation framework integrates relevance scores from different retrieval functionalities as teacher signals, enabling the multiple retrieval methods to be jointly learned and mutually reinforced.
  • Training data is curated from three complementary sources: unsupervised data from 1.2 billion text pairs across 194 languages, fine-tuning data from labeled corpora, and synthesized data for long-document retrieval (MultiLongDoc).

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: MASS-RAG proposes a multi-agent synthesis framework for RAG that structures evidence processing into specialized agents — a summarizer, extractor, and reasoner — whose outputs are combined by a dedicated synthesis agent. Unlike single-judge filtering approaches, this exposes multiple intermediate evidence views, allowing the model to compare and integrate complementary information before answer generation. The approach is training-free and consistently improves over strong RAG baselines on four benchmarks, particularly when relevant evidence is distributed across retrieved contexts.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• Single-judge agent filtering in RAG limits the system's ability to capture complementary or heterogeneous forms of relevant evidence
  • Decomposing evidence processing into role-specialized agents (summarizer, extractor, reasoner) with a synthesis stage improves factual accuracy over monolithic filtering
  • The approach is training-free — it works with existing LLMs without fine-tuning
  • Performance gains are most pronounced when relevant evidence is distributed across retrieved contexts rather than concentrated in a single passage

docs.title: MaxProof: Scaling Mathematical Proof with Generative-Verifier RL and Population-Level Test-Time Scaling
Summary
docs.text: MaxProof is a population-level test-time scaling framework from MiniMax for competition-level mathematical proof. The system trains three integrated capabilities — proof generation via RL, proof verification via aligned error-finding, and critique-conditioned proof repair — into a single model (M3), then scales at test-time through population search and tournament selection over candidate proofs. It achieves 35/42 on IMO 2025 and 36/42 on USAMO 2026, exceeding the human gold-medal threshold on both.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• Training three distinct proof-oriented capabilities (generate, verify, repair) and merging them into one model enables a tightly coupled generate-verify-refine loop at test time without extra model calls.
  • The "defense-in-depth" generative verifier is engineered for low false-positive rate; a separate RL-trained Verifier Expert (framed as error-finding, not score prediction) further sharpens validation quality.
  • Population-level test-time scaling — searching over a population of candidate proofs with tournament selection rather than single best-of-K — converts best@K into reliable pass@1 at competition level.
  • MaxProof surpasses the human gold-medal threshold on IMO 2025 and USAMO 2026, representing a milestone for LLM formal mathematical reasoning at the olympiad level.
  • The approach generalizes a deep-learning optimization analogy: rollout batches ≈ training data, the verifier ≈ loss function, population diversity ≈ gradient noise management.

docs.title: MCPEval: Automatic MCP-based Deep Evaluation for AI Agent Models
Summary
docs.text: MCPEval is an open-source evaluation framework from Salesforce that automates end-to-end task generation and deep evaluation of LLM agents across diverse domains using the Model Context Protocol (MCP). It standardizes metrics, integrates natively with agent tools, and eliminates manual effort in building evaluation pipelines, using a two-step workflow of task generation (with verification) followed by model evaluation via tool call matching and LLM judging.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• Existing LLM agent evaluation methods rely on static benchmarks and labor-intensive data collection, failing to capture interactive real-world agentic workflows and limiting practical assessment.
  • MCPEval automates the full evaluation pipeline from task generation through verification to model assessment, using MCP as the standardized protocol for agent-tool communication.
  • Experiments reveal that smaller, tool-enhanced models can perform comparably to larger, more resource-intensive models, highlighting significant opportunities for cost-effective deployments.
  • The framework evaluates from two complementary perspectives: tool call matching against ground truth trajectories, and LLM judging covering planning, execution flow, and context awareness.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: MAP (Measuring Agents in Production) is the first systematic study of AI agents in production, based on 20 case studies and 306 practitioners surveyed across 26 domains. Production agents use simple, controllable approaches: 68% execute at most 10 steps before human intervention, 70% rely on prompting off-the-shelf models, and 74% depend primarily on human evaluation. Reliability (consistent correct behavior over time) is the top development challenge, currently addressed through systems-level design.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• Production agents are built using simple, controllable approaches—not the complex autonomous systems often featured in research
  • 68% of production agents execute at most 10 steps before human intervention; autonomy is heavily bounded in practice
  • 70% of practitioners rely on prompting off-the-shelf models rather than weight tuning
  • 74% depend primarily on human evaluation, indicating automated evaluation remains unsolved
  • Reliability is the #1 challenge; practitioners address it through systems-level design rather than model improvements
