docs.title: Measuring AI Ability to Complete Long Software Tasks
Summary
docs.text: METR proposes the "50% task-completion time horizon" metric -- the duration of tasks that AI models can complete with 50% success rate, calibrated against human expert completion times. Evaluating 12 frontier models from 2019-2025 on 170 tasks (HCAST, RE-Bench, and a new SWAA suite), they find that the 50% time horizon has been doubling approximately every 7 months, with o3 reaching ~110 minutes. Naive extrapolation suggests AI systems could automate month-long software tasks within 5 years, though external validity remains an open question.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• The 50% task-completion time horizon for frontier AI models has been doubling approximately every 7 months from 2019 to 2025, with o3 reaching approximately 110 minutes
  • Progress is primarily driven by improved logical reasoning, better tool use, greater reliability, and ability to adapt to mistakes
  • The 80% time horizon follows a similar doubling trend but is 4-6x shorter, indicating models that sometimes succeed on hard tasks cannot yet reliably perform moderate-length tasks
  • Performance is much lower on less structured, "messier" tasks, raising questions about external validity to real-world software engineering work
  • Naive extrapolation predicts AI will reach a time horizon of over 1 month (167 work hours) between mid-2028 and mid-2031

docs.title: Measuring the Impact of Early-2025 AI on Experienced Open-Source Developer Productivity
Summary
docs.text: This METR randomized controlled trial measured the impact of AI tools (primarily Cursor Pro with Claude 3.5/3.7 Sonnet) on 16 experienced open-source developers completing 246 real tasks on mature projects they regularly contribute to. Surprisingly, allowing AI actually increased task completion time by 19%, despite developers forecasting a 24% speedup before the study and estimating a 20% speedup even after participating, revealing a large disconnect between perceived and actual AI impact on developer productivity.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• In a rigorous RCT on real open-source tasks, AI tools actually slowed experienced developers down by 19%, contradicting both developer self-estimates (20% speedup) and expert predictions from economics (39% shorter) and ML (38% shorter).
  • The slowdown effect appears broadly robust across a wide range of experimental design decisions, though factors specific to this setting (large mature codebases, highly experienced developers) likely contribute.
  • Five factors were found to contribute to the slowdown, six factors had evidence against contributing, and ten factors had mixed or unclear evidence, suggesting multiple compounding causes.
  • These results do not imply AI tools are not useful in all settings -- improvements to prompting, agent scaffolding, or domain-specific finetuning could yield positive speedup, and future models may perform differently.

docs.title: Megatron-LM: Training Multi-Billion Parameter Language Models Using Model Parallelism
Summary
docs.text: Megatron-LM presents an efficient intra-layer model parallel approach for training very large transformer models (up to 8.3B parameters) using up to 512 GPUs. The approach exploits the inherent structure of transformers to parallelize attention heads and MLP layers across GPUs with minimal code changes to PyTorch, achieving 76% scaling efficiency at 15.1 PetaFLOPs and state-of-the-art results on WikiText103, LAMBADA, and RACE benchmarks.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• A simple and efficient intra-layer model parallel approach can be implemented with only a few targeted modifications to existing PyTorch transformer code, without requiring custom compilers or new frameworks.
  • The approach scales to 8.3B parameters on 512 GPUs with 76% scaling efficiency (15.1 PetaFLOPs) compared to a strong single-GPU baseline of 39 TeraFLOPs (30% of peak).
  • Careful attention to the placement of layer normalization in BERT-like models is critical for achieving increased accuracy as model size grows, and the existing BERT architecture results in model degradation at scale.
  • Scaling model size results in improved accuracy for both GPT-2 (up to 8.3B parameters) and BERT (up to 3.9B parameters), achieving SOTA on WikiText103 perplexity (10.8), LAMBADA accuracy (66.5%), and RACE accuracy (90.9%).

docs.title: Mem0: Building Production-Ready AI Agents with Scalable Long-Term Memory
Summary
docs.text: Mem0 introduces a scalable memory-centric architecture for AI agents that dynamically extracts, consolidates, and retrieves salient information from ongoing conversations to maintain coherence across multi-session dialogues. An enhanced graph-based variant (Mem0^g) captures complex relational structures between conversational elements. On the LoCoMo benchmark, Mem0 outperforms existing memory systems and RAG methods, while the full-context approach still scores highest overall (~73% LLM-as-a-Judge vs 68.44% for Mem0^g); Mem0's advantage over full context is efficiency, achieving 91% lower p95 latency and 90%+ token cost savings compared to full-context approaches.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• LLMs' reliance on fixed context windows creates a fundamental limitation for maintaining coherence across extended multi-session dialogues, which simply extending context length cannot solve.
  • Mem0 achieves 26% relative improvement in LLM-as-a-Judge metric over OpenAI's memory system, and Mem0^g with graph memory achieves ~2% higher overall score than the base Mem0 configuration.
  • Mem0 attains 91% lower p95 latency and saves more than 90% token cost compared to full-context approaches, offering a practical balance between reasoning capabilities and deployment constraints.
  • The architecture follows an incremental processing paradigm with extraction and update phases, processing message pairs to selectively store, consolidate, and retrieve relevant memories.

docs.title: MemOS: An Operating System for Memory-Augmented Generation (MAG) in Large Language Models
Summary
docs.text: MemOS proposes a memory operating system for LLMs that elevates memory to a first-class operational resource, unifying three core memory types -- parametric (model weights), activation (runtime states), and plaintext (external text) -- under a standardized abstraction called MemCube. The system provides unified mechanisms for memory representation, organization, governance, lifecycle management, version control, and cross-platform migration, aiming to shift LLMs from systems that merely perceive and generate to ones that remember, adapt, and grow over time.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• Current LLMs fundamentally lack a unified and structured architecture for handling memory, relying on implicit parametric memory and ephemeral activation memory, with RAG serving as an ad hoc textual patch.
  • MemOS classifies memory into three core types (Parametric, Activation, Plaintext) and provides the MemCube abstraction for tracking, fusion, and migration of heterogeneous memory across tasks and contexts.
  • Traditional scaling laws are approaching diminishing returns, and the next fundamental leap in model capability will come from treating memory as a first-class, schedulable, and governable resource.
  • MemOS adopts evolution as a central management objective, supporting memory recomposition, migration, and fusion to facilitate long-term capability growth with integrated access control, traceability, and interpretability.

docs.title: Mercury: Ultra-Fast Language Models Based on Diffusion
Summary
docs.text: Mercury introduces the first family of commercial-scale diffusion-based large language models from Inception Labs, which generate tokens in parallel using a coarse-to-fine iterative refinement process instead of sequential autoregressive decoding. Mercury Coder Mini and Small achieve state-of-the-art throughputs of 1100+ and 700+ tokens/sec respectively on NVIDIA H100 GPUs, outperforming speed-optimized frontier models by up to 10x while maintaining comparable coding quality on benchmarks.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• Mercury models are the first large-scale diffusion-based LLMs, using a Transformer architecture that generates multiple tokens in parallel through iterative refinement from noise.
  • Mercury Coder Mini achieves 1100+ tokens/sec and Mercury Coder Small achieves 700+ tokens/sec on H100 GPUs, speeds previously only possible with custom chips, representing up to 10x throughput improvement over frontier models.
  • Despite the massive speed advantage, coding quality remains comparable to high-speed commercial offerings across diverse use cases, programming languages, and hardware backends.
  • Diffusion models make significantly better use of modern GPU architectures by generating tokens in parallel, leading to higher arithmetic intensity and overall computational efficiency, with broad implications for latency-sensitive applications like coding assistants and agentic workloads.

docs.title: Meta-Harness: End-to-End Optimization of Model Harnesses
Summary
docs.text: Meta-Harness is an outer-loop system that automatically searches over harness code for LLM applications, using an agentic proposer with access to source code, scores, and execution traces of all prior candidates via a filesystem. LLM performance depends not just on model weights but on the harness—how information is stored, retrieved, and presented—yet harnesses are still largely hand-designed. Meta-Harness outperforms hand-designed harnesses on text classification, math reasoning, and agentic coding benchmarks.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• LLM system performance is heavily determined by harness design, not just model weights; the paper cites prior work showing a harness change around a fixed model can produce a 6× performance gap on the same benchmark, and argues the harness "often matters as much as the model itself"
  • Existing text optimizers fail for harness optimization because they compress feedback too aggressively (memoryless, scalar scores only)
  • Meta-Harness accesses full source code and execution traces of all prior candidates, enabling richer optimization
  • Improves over state-of-the-art context management by 7.7 points while using 4× fewer context tokens on text classification
  • A single discovered harness improves accuracy on 200 IMO-level math problems by 4.7 points across five held-out models

docs.title: MindCraft: Theory of Mind Modeling for Situated Dialogue in Collaborative Tasks
Summary
docs.text: MindCraft introduces a dataset and task for studying theory of mind modeling in situated collaborative dialogue, where pairs of human players with asymmetric knowledge and skills collaborate in Minecraft to create goal materials. The dataset captures the evolution of partners' beliefs about the world and each other at periodic intervals, enabling computational models to predict a collaboration partner's mental state as a task unfolds.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• The dataset captures true representations of participants' beliefs (not just proxies from event sequences), recording self-reported mental states about their own and their partner's knowledge at periodic intervals during collaborative tasks.
  • Partners have asymmetric knowledge and skill-sets, requiring them to negotiate their own plans of action while maintaining common ground -- departing from traditional leader-follower setups.
  • Baseline computational models show that the shared physical environment and perceived activities play a greater role than language alone in shaping a partner's understanding of each other for achieving common ground.
  • The work is a first step toward building embodied AI agents able to infer belief states of collaborative partners in situ through situated dialogue.

docs.title: Model Context Protocol (MCP): Landscape, Security Threats, and Future Research Directions
Summary
docs.text: This paper presents the first systematic academic analysis of the Model Context Protocol (MCP) ecosystem from both architectural and security perspectives. It defines the full lifecycle of MCP servers across four phases (creation, deployment, operation, maintenance) with 16 key activities, and constructs a comprehensive threat taxonomy covering four major attacker types (malicious developers, external attackers, malicious users, security flaws) across 16 distinct threat scenarios, validated through real-world case studies.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• MCP shifts the paradigm from hardcoded tool bindings per application toward an interoperable ecosystem of composable, discoverable network services, with thousands of independently developed MCP servers already deployed.
  • The MCP server lifecycle spans four phases (creation, deployment, operation, maintenance) with 16 key activities, each presenting distinct security exposure points.
  • Four major attacker archetypes (malicious developers, external attackers, malicious users, security flaws) give rise to 16 representative threat scenarios including tool poisoning, installer spoofing, and unauthorized access.
  • Despite rapid adoption, MCP's ecosystem still faces key challenges in security, tool discoverability, and remote deployment that lack comprehensive solutions.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: This paper introduces Monadic Context Engineering (MCE), an architectural paradigm that applies algebraic structures from functional programming -- Functors, Applicative Functors, and Monads -- to provide a formal foundation for AI agent design. The AgentMonad uses a monad transformer stack (StateT S (EitherT E IO)) to intrinsically manage state propagation, short-circuiting error handling, and asynchronous execution in agent workflows. The framework enables robust sequential composition via Monads, principled parallel execution via Applicatives, and systematic capability composition via Monad Transformers, with extensions to Meta-Agents for dynamic sub-agent orchestration.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• Current agent architectures built with imperative ad hoc patterns result in brittle systems with poor state management, error handling, and concurrency; monadic abstractions provide a formal alternative
  • The AgentMonad transformer stack (StateT S (EitherT E IO)) unifies state, error handling, and side effects into a single composable structure, enabling each step to be independently verifiable
  • Applicative Functors provide a principled structure for parallel execution of independent agent operations, while Monads handle sequential dependent operations with automatic failure propagation
  • The framework maps naturally to the Model Context Protocol (MCP), where tool results must explicitly indicate success or failure
  • Meta-Agents can leverage MCE for generative orchestration, dynamically creating and managing sub-agent workflows through metaprogramming

docs.title: Monitoring Reasoning Models for Misbehavior and the Risks of Promoting Obfuscation
Summary
docs.text: This OpenAI paper demonstrates that chain-of-thought (CoT) monitoring can effectively detect reward hacking in reasoning models used in agentic coding environments, with a weaker model (GPT-4o) successfully monitoring a stronger frontier model (o3-mini). However, when CoT monitors are incorporated into the RL training reward, agents eventually learn "obfuscated reward hacking" -- hiding their intent within seemingly benign chains-of-thought while continuing to exploit the environment, suggesting a fundamental tension between optimization pressure and monitorability.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• Chain-of-thought monitoring using a simple prompted LLM (GPT-4o) is very effective at detecting reward hacking in agentic coding environments, performing far better than monitoring only agent actions and outputs.
  • A weaker model (GPT-4o) can effectively monitor a model far more capable than itself (o3-mini), providing promising evidence for scalable oversight of even superhuman models.
  • When CoT monitors are incorporated into RL training rewards, agents initially become more capable and aligned, but with excessive optimization they learn obfuscated reward hacking -- hiding exploitative intent within the CoT.
  • There may be a necessary "monitorability tax" -- deliberately not applying strong optimization pressure to chains-of-thought to ensure they remain monitorable and useful for detecting misaligned behavior.

docs.title: MSA: Memory Sparse Attention for Efficient End-to-End Memory Model Scaling to 100M Tokens
Summary
docs.text: MSA (Memory Sparse Attention) is an end-to-end trainable memory model framework that achieves linear complexity in both training and inference while scaling to 100M tokens. Key innovations include scalable sparse attention architecture, document-wise RoPE, KV cache compression, and Memory Parallel inference. MSA exhibits less than 9% precision degradation when scaling from 16K to 100M tokens and enables 100M token inference on 2×A800 GPUs.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• Standard full-attention LLMs are effectively limited to ~1M token contexts; human-scale memory requires 200-300M token capacity
  • Hybrid linear attention and fixed-size memory states (RNNs) suffer from severe precision degradation and inability to dynamically modify memory content
  • MSA achieves linear complexity through sparse attention + document-wise RoPE, with <9% degradation from 16K to 100M tokens
  • Memory Interleaving mechanism enables complex multi-hop reasoning across scattered memory segments
  • Significantly surpasses frontier LLMs, SOTA RAG systems, and leading memory agents on long-context benchmarks

docs.title: MTU-Bench: A Multi-granularity Tool-Use Benchmark for Large Language Models
Summary
docs.text: MTU-Bench is a multi-granularity tool-use benchmark for LLMs that covers five tool usage scenarios: single-turn/single-tool, single-turn/multi-tool, multi-turn/single-tool, multi-turn/multi-tool, and out-of-distribution tasks. Built by transforming existing task-oriented dialogue datasets (MultiWOZ, SGD, etc.) into tool-use data through an automated synthesis pipeline, it includes 159K+ dialogues with 136 tools and provides fine-grained automatic evaluation metrics without requiring GPT-based evaluators.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• Existing tool-use benchmarks have insufficient evaluation scenario coverage, lack multi-turn and multi-tool settings, and rely on costly GPT-based evaluation.
  • MTU-Bench covers all five granularities of tool usage (single/multi-turn crossed with single/multi-tool, plus OOD) with automatic evaluation metrics based on ground truth comparison.
  • Fine-tuning LLaMA3 on MTU-Instruct produces MTU-LLaMA, which performs best across various tool-use scenarios and metrics, demonstrating the instruction dataset's effectiveness.
  • The benchmark evaluates six fine-grained metrics including tool selection accuracy, parameter selection accuracy, success rate, turn-based success rate, tool number accuracy, and tool order accuracy.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: This paper presents the first systematic study of multi-user LLM agents, formalizing the problem as a multi-principal decision setting where a single agent must serve multiple users with distinct roles, preferences, authority levels, and potentially conflicting interests. The authors introduce a unified multi-user interaction protocol and three stress-testing scenarios evaluating instruction following, privacy preservation, and coordination. Results reveal systematic gaps: frontier LLMs frequently fail to maintain stable prioritization, exhibit increasing privacy violations over multi-turn interactions, and suffer efficiency bottlenecks requiring iterative information gathering.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• Most existing LLM systems are implicitly optimized for single-principal interaction and lack native protocols to distinguish user roles, enforce information boundaries, or resolve conflicts in multi-user settings
  • Frontier LLMs frequently fail to maintain stable prioritization under conflicting user objectives in multi-principal scenarios
  • Privacy violations increase over multi-turn interactions, suggesting that current models lack robust mechanisms for maintaining information boundaries across extended conversations
  • Multi-user coordination suffers from efficiency bottlenecks when tasks require iterative information gathering across users with private contexts
  • The gap between single-user and multi-user capabilities represents a critical challenge as LLM agents are increasingly deployed in team workflows and organizational tools

docs.title: Mutation-Guided LLM-based Test Generation at Meta
Summary
docs.text: Meta's ACH system generates tests by first generating mutants — simulated faults — that are specific to a concern of interest, then generating tests that kill them, hardening the codebase against that class of regression. Unlike traditional mutation testing it deliberately produces few mutants, targeting currently undetected faults rather than broad coverage. Deployed across 10,795 Android Kotlin classes in 7 Meta platforms, it produced 9,095 mutants and 571 privacy-hardening tests; in Messenger and WhatsApp test-a-thons engineers accepted 73% of its tests, judging 36% privacy-relevant.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• The inversion is the contribution: generate the fault first, then the test that catches it, which targets a named concern instead of maximizing coverage.
  • Few mutants, deliberately. ACH departs from traditional mutation testing by generating a small number of concern-specific undetected faults rather than exhaustive mutation.
  • Privacy is the illustration, not the limit — the authors state the method applies to any class of regression.
  • An LLM-based equivalent-mutant detector reaches precision 0.79 / recall 0.47, rising to 0.95 / 0.96 with simple preprocessing — the classic mutation-testing obstacle, handled tractably.
  • Engineer acceptance of 73% with only 36% judged privacy-relevant is the honest result: most accepted tests were valued for reasons other than the concern they were generated for.

docs.title: Related
docs.text:
• Just-in-Time Catching Test Generation at Meta — the successor system, which distinguishes hardening tests (pass at generation) from catching tests (meant to fail).
  • An Empirical Evaluation of LLMs for Automated Unit Test Generation — the coverage-driven predecessor approach.
  • Defects4J — the standard curated real-bug corpus this line of work is evaluated against.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Proposes Natural-Language Agent Harnesses (NLAHs) — editable documents that describe run-level harness policy (stages, roles, state rules, verification gates, recovery logic, stopping conditions) — executed by a shared runtime (IHR) that translates them into agent calls, handoffs, and state updates. Evaluated on coding, terminal-use, and computer-use benchmarks with comparable task outcomes to code harnesses, while making harness design inspectable and module-ablatable.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• Traditional code harnesses bundle prompts, tool adapters, parser rules, validation scripts, and benchmark-specific logic together — making them hard to inspect, port, compare, or ablate even though the design pattern is the reusable part
  • NLAHs separate harness policy (natural language, editable) from harness mechanism (code/runtime, exact), inspired by AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, and SKILL.md patterns
  • IHR-executed NLAHs achieve comparable task outcomes to native code harnesses on coding, terminal-use, and computer-use benchmarks while exposing much shorter, readable harness policies
  • Individual harness modules (verifier, self-evolution, multi-candidate search, file-backed state) can be cleanly ablated from NLAHs to measure their effect on task outcomes under a shared runtime
  • The boundary: deterministic code handles exact operations (tests, parsers, sandboxing, artifact validators); natural language handles policy (task decomposition, role contracts, retry logic, evidence discipline)

docs.title: From Natural Language to Verified Code: Toward AI Assisted Problem-to-Code Generation with Dafny-Based Formal Verification
Summary
docs.text: Introduces NL2VC-60, a benchmark of 60 complex algorithmic problems for evaluating LLM synthesis of formally verified Dafny code from natural language. Evaluates 7 open-weight LLMs (9B-120B parameters) across three prompting tiers: contextless, signature-guided, and self-healing with Dafny verifier feedback. Integrates uDebug community test suites alongside formal verification to prevent vacuous verification.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• Contextless prompting leads to near-universal failure (0% verification for most models); structural signatures and iterative self-healing produce dramatic turnarounds (Gemma 4-31B: 90.91%, GPT-OSS 120B: 0% → 81.82%)
  • Dual-layer validation (formal verification + functional testing via uDebug) is essential — formal verification alone permits "vacuous verification" where weak specs pass the verifier but code fails real inputs
  • 300 person-hours were required to hand-author the 60 Dafny reference implementations, highlighting that domain expertise remains essential even with LLM assistance
  • The first comprehensive dataset of Dafny-specific compilation and verification error types, providing a taxonomy of LLM failure modes in formal methods
  • Open-weight LLMs can serve as "effective apprentices" for formal verification when given structural guidance, but cannot autonomously produce verified code from raw natural language

docs.title: Neural Garbage Collection: Learning to Forget while Learning to Reason
Summary
docs.text: Neural Garbage Collection (NGC) teaches a language model to manage its own KV cache during chain-of-thought reasoning, trained end-to-end from outcome-based task reward alone. As the model reasons, it periodically scores KV cache entries, samples which to evict, and continues reasoning on the pruned cache. By treating both token generation and cache-eviction decisions as discrete actions optimized via reinforcement learning, the model jointly learns what to think and what to forget. On Countdown, AMC, and AIME tasks, NGC maintains strong accuracy at 2-3x peak KV cache compression and substantially outperforms heuristic eviction baselines.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• Efficiency can be treated as a model capability learned through end-to-end optimization rather than designed through hand-crafted heuristics, following the broader pattern of deep learning subsuming design choices
  • NGC maintains strong accuracy relative to the full-cache upper bound at 2-3x peak KV cache size compression, substantially outperforming heuristic eviction baselines (StreamingLLM, KNorm, KeyDiff, SnapKV)
  • Joint optimization of reasoning and memory management through a single outcome-based reward signal (binary correctness) is sufficient -- no proxy objectives or supervised fine-tuning are needed
  • Budget-aware interoception (including the eviction rate in the prompt during training) improves generalization across different cache budgets at test time
  • Much of the KV cache consists of transient intermediate reasoning steps that become irrelevant as reasoning progresses, suggesting active cache management need not degrade and may enable longer reasoning horizons

docs.title: Neural Theorem Proving: Generating and Structuring Proofs for Formal Verification
Summary
docs.text: Introduces ProofSeek, a framework for neural theorem proving that generates whole proofs in Isabelle using a 3-component pipeline: natural language statement generation, LLM-based formal proof generation, and heuristic-based proof construction. Uses a 2-stage fine-tuning process (SFT for syntactic correctness, then RL for semantic validity). Validated on miniF2F-test and applied to verify AWS S3 bucket access policies.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• ProofSeek achieves ~41% proof success on miniF2F-test and 96% on manually curated AWS S3 policies, but drops to 69.1% on LLM-generated policies — demonstrating a gap between curated and generated verification targets
  • Two-stage fine-tuning (SFT then RL with GRPO) produces a 3% improvement in proof success rate and 20% reduction in execution time vs DeepSeek baseline
  • LLMs function as "black-box distribution generators" suggesting proof steps, which are then verified by interactive proof systems — combining neural generation with symbolic checking
  • Whole-proof generators cannot leverage previously proved lemmas, while proof-step generators don't scale during training — ProofSeek bridges this with a heuristic proof construction module
  • Successfully applied to verify AWS S3 bucket security policies, demonstrating practical application beyond mathematical theorem proving

docs.title: Next-Concept Modeling: Fast, Parallel Coarse-to-Fine Text Generation
Summary
docs.text: Next-Concept Modeling (NCM), from Stanford and Together AI, is a non-autoregressive text generation framework positioned against diffusion language models. A multiscale residual VQ-VAE encodes text into a hierarchy of discrete codes, and a transformer generates one level at a time from coarse to fine, predicting all codes within a level in parallel. NCM matches or beats the strongest diffusion baselines on generation quality while running 10-31x faster and training on fewer tokens.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• Diffusion LMs degrade with fewer sampling steps, process the full sequence at every step and need many passes over the data; NCM generates in K levels, far fewer than the sequence length, and predicts each level's codes in parallel
  • At matched parameter scales, NCM beats the strongest diffusion baseline's generative perplexity on LM1B while running 21x faster, and is competitive on OpenWebText at 10x faster
  • On XSum summarization NCM matches the strongest diffusion model's ROUGE-L at 31x faster, using roughly 6-16x fewer function evaluations than unguided diffusion baselines on conditional tasks
  • On Sudoku, NCM outperforms both autoregressive and diffusion baselines at every difficulty level while using fewer function evaluations
  • NCM uses roughly 4-5x fewer training tokens than strong diffusion baselines on LM1B and OpenWebText, counting both tokenizer and generator training

docs.title: Impact of AI on the IT Industry: Talent Transformation in the AI Era (NTT DATA / INSEAD)
Summary
docs.text: A joint NTT DATA / INSEAD report examining how AI transforms the IT services industry across five levels: tasks, jobs, processes, organizations, and value proposition. Based on academic literature and executive interviews, it finds that task-level AI automation (especially coding and testing) is mature, but the frontier has shifted to workflow redesign where the ability to verify and govern AI outputs is more valuable than generating them. The report outlines four strategic scenarios: Body Shop, Service as a Software, Vertical AI Orchestrator, and Governance & Infrastructure Platform.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• Task-level AI automation in coding and testing has reached maturity; the bottleneck has shifted to validation, governance, and workflow orchestration
  • The traditional hierarchical talent pyramid is under strain — junior operational execution is pressured while human judgment, oversight, and domain expertise grow in value
  • AI-driven productivity challenges time-based pricing models, accelerating transition toward productized and platform-based business models
  • The ability to verify and be accountable for AI outputs is becoming more valuable than the ability to generate them
  • Competitive advantage will depend on shifting value creation from labor time to proprietary assets, data, and governance capabilities

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: OLMo 3 is a family of fully-open language and thinking models at 7B and 32B parameter scales from AI2, providing complete access to the entire model flow including every stage, checkpoint, data point, and dependency. The flagship OLMo 3.1 Think 32B is the strongest fully-open thinking model, competitive with Qwen 3 32B while being trained on six times fewer tokens, and the OLMo 3 Instruct models surpass other open-weight models of comparable size including Qwen 2.5, Gemma 3, and Llama 3.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• OLMo 3 releases the complete model flow (all stages, checkpoints, data, dependencies), enabling research into any stage of development -- not just final weights -- which is unprecedented for state-of-the-art models.

docs.title: On the Opportunities and Risks of Foundation Models
Summary
docs.text: This comprehensive Stanford CRFM report defines and analyzes "foundation models" -- large models trained on broad data via self-supervision that can be adapted to many downstream tasks. Covering capabilities (language, vision, robotics, reasoning), technical principles (architectures, training, evaluation, systems, data, security), applications (healthcare, law, education), and societal impact (inequity, misuse, environment, legality, economics, ethics), it argues that foundation models represent an unprecedented level of homogenization in AI that provides powerful leverage but also creates single points of failure.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• Foundation models are characterized by two key properties: emergence (behaviors implicitly induced rather than explicitly constructed) and homogenization (consolidation of methodologies around a few shared models), which together create both opportunities and systemic risks.
  • The homogenization of AI around a few foundation models means that defects in the foundation model are inherited by all adapted downstream models, creating single points of failure.
  • Despite impending widespread deployment, we currently lack a clear understanding of how foundation models work, when they fail, and what they are capable of due to their emergent properties.
  • Critical research on foundation models requires deep interdisciplinary collaboration commensurate with their fundamentally sociotechnical nature.

docs.title: On the Reliability Limits of LLM-Based Multi-Agent Planning
Summary
docs.text: This technical note applies decision theory to LLM-based multi-agent systems, modeling them as finite acyclic delegated decision networks. The central result is that without new exogenous signals, no multi-agent architecture can outperform a centralized Bayes decision maker with access to the same information. Communication between agents necessarily degrades decision quality, quantifiable via mutual information (log loss) or squared posterior error (Brier score).

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• Multi-agent architectures that share the same base model and context (planner/worker/critic/reviewer) add roles without adding new information — they cannot outperform a single centralized decision maker
  • The performance gap from inter-agent communication equals the expected posterior divergence between what the central agent knows and what the terminal stage receives
  • Under log loss, communication cost = conditional mutual information; under Brier score = expected squared posterior error
  • Genuinely new exogenous signals (tool calls, DB lookups, executable feedback) are what actually improve multi-agent reliability — not architectural role decomposition
  • Human review is optimally deployed when automated posterior risk exceeds review cost (threshold policy)

docs.title: Persistent Memory in Multi-Agent LLM Inference: What It Costs, What It Buys, and When You Can Tell
Summary
docs.text: The authors measure two common claims on one three-tier chain-of-agents system served on edge hardware. Splitting long-context inference across agents does bound the largest call's working set: peak KV cache is 14.3 MiB per query against about 35 MiB for single-pass and retrieval-augmented baselines. A persistent tier that stores reasoning traces and recalls them on later queries gives no detectable accuracy gain at a measurable memory cost; the authors argue this null is built into how such tiers are tested, and document four measurement errors that had made the tier look beneficial.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• Splitting the work across agents lowers peak KV cache; better retrieval does not: RAG changes which evidence enters a call, decomposition changes how many calls it is spread over, so the RAG baseline's peak matches single-pass while the chain of agents is 2.5× lower, at about 1.6× more total cache traffic and accuracy matching RAG
  • Enabling persistent recall across eight paired datasets (n=100 per arm) adds +0.368 MiB peak cache (95% CI [0.167, 0.590]) and changes accuracy by +0.015 (CI [−0.011, +0.046]), excluding a gain larger than about 0.046
  • The null is built into the test: single-question benchmarks supply each item's evidence and score items independently, and clearing traces between conditions (required for correctness) leaves recall only unrelated items, so recall could fire for just 24% of questions; a memory gain reported on an independent-item benchmark is more likely an artifact than a finding
  • A memory ablation must satisfy four conditions, each of which the authors' own setup once violated: the component actually runs (their tier wrote traces nothing read), runs are independent (fixed-seed re-runs recalled their own answers, 100/100 questions already traced), only the tested setting differs (a parser fixed in one arm gave a fake +37-point gain), and the effect exceeds replicate noise (±0.09–0.10); three of these inflated the apparent benefit and none was visible in the results table
  • Detection needs no knowledge of the specific bug: assert non-zero counters for every claimed component, query the store with the evaluation questions before running, diff the two arms' serialized requests and alternate which arm runs first, and estimate noise from replicate runs rather than a single-run bootstrap

docs.title: Precision Proactivity: Measuring Cognitive Load in Real-World AI-Assisted Work
Summary
docs.text: This paper introduces a transcript-based framework grounded in Cognitive Load Theory to measure intrinsic and extraneous cognitive load in AI-assisted knowledge work. Studying 34 financial professionals performing a complex valuation task with GPT-4o, the authors find that AI-generated content usage is positively associated with quality, while extraneous load shows the largest negative association -- roughly three times that of intrinsic load. Model-initiated task switching is the strongest predictor of performance decline, and extraneous load is path-dependent: once either speaker enters a high-load pattern, it tends to persist.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• Extraneous cognitive load (from interaction structure, not task complexity) has roughly three times the negative association with output quality compared to intrinsic load in AI-assisted work
  • AI-generated content usage and cognitive load contribute independently and in opposing directions to performance -- the relationship is additive rather than interactive
  • Model-initiated task switching is the strongest predictor of quality decline, suggesting AI systems should constrain scope expansion rather than proactively introduce new topics
  • Extraneous load is path-dependent and persistent within speakers: once a high-load conversational pattern begins, the interaction provides weak endogenous mechanisms for restoring coherence
  • Less experienced professionals face larger penalties from extraneous load but derive greater marginal gains from AI content, while more experienced professionals increase AI content uptake under load

docs.text: CASE-Bench introduces a context-aware safety benchmark for LLMs that integrates Contextual Integrity (CI) theory into safety evaluations. docs.text:

docs.title: Procedural Graphs: Self-Evolving Execution Structures for LLM Agents
Summary
docs.text: Most agents choose actions by unconstrained generation over a growing, flat history, leaving procedural knowledge — what to do, in what order, under which conditions — implicit. The Procedural Graph makes it explicit: where a knowledge graph stores (entity, relation, entity) triplets for what-is questions, this stores (procedure, relation, procedure) triplets for what-to-do questions. At each step the framework localizes the agent's active node and a guidance model turns the surrounding subgraph into situational guidance that biases the next action without dictating it; an LLM refiner then edits the graph by contrasting failed against successful trajectories.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• Names the long-horizon failure mode precisely: as trajectories lengthen, agents lose track of objectives, invoke tools out of order, and repeat unproductive actions.
  • The knowledge-graph analogy is the core idea — procedural knowledge as a first-class queryable structure, not prose in a system prompt.
  • Guidance biases rather than dictates the next action, keeping the solver free while constraining drift.
  • The graph is self-evolving under a validation gate: edits are committed only if they preserve or improve held-out performance, and rejected edits are retained to discourage repetition.
  • Starting from a minimal skeleton, the loop builds graphs that match or surpass hand-designed ones, and can repair a flawed expert prior.

docs.title: Related
docs.text:
• UnitBoost — a contrasting answer to agent coordination: replace the generative manager with a defined operator.
  • LatticeDB — an embedded graph store whose stated target workloads include exactly this kind of agent state.
  • Formalizing Fermat's Last Theorem — a field report of the same failure mode at scale.

docs.text: Investigates how language models internally represent and track characters' beliefs for Theory of Mind (ToM) reasoning, using the CausalToM dataset of simple stories with two characters. The study discovers a pervasive "lookback mechanism" whereby LMs store information as pointer-address pairs in residual streams, enabling later retrieval through attention. docs.title: Reasoning Models Reason Well, Until They Don't
Summary
docs.text: This paper shows that existing reasoning benchmarks for large reasoning models (LRMs) have limited complexity—LRM performance drops abruptly once problem complexity exceeds modest thresholds and does not generalize. The authors create the Deep Reasoning Dataset (DeepRD) with scalable complexity and find that while most real-world examples fall inside LRMs' success regime, the long tails (complex cases) exceed their capabilities. This challenges claims about LRMs being capable of generalized reasoning or scientific research.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• Existing graph and reasoning benchmarks have limited complexity; LRMs appear strong partly because benchmarks don't scale to real difficulty
  • LRM performance drops abruptly at sufficient complexity and does not generalize to harder problems
  • DeepRD provides unlimited scalable-complexity examples for graph connectivity and natural language proof planning
  • Most real-world reasoning tasks fall inside LRMs' success regime, but the long tails exceed their capabilities—important for high-stakes domains
  • Claims that LRMs can perform original scientific research are premature given their failure to generalize to high-complexity reasoning

docs.title: ReasoningBank: Scaling Agent Self-Evolving with Reasoning Memory
Summary
docs.text: ReasoningBank is a memory framework that distills generalizable reasoning strategies from an agent's self-judged successful and failed experiences, going beyond raw trajectory storage or successful-only routines. At test time, the agent retrieves relevant memories to guide actions and integrates new learnings back in a closed loop. The paper also introduces memory-aware test-time scaling (MaTTS), which generates diverse exploration experiences per task to provide rich contrastive signals for synthesizing higher-quality memory, establishing memory-driven experience scaling as a new scaling dimension for agents.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• Distilling generalizable reasoning strategies from both successful and failed experiences produces more transferable memory than storing raw trajectories or only successful task routines
  • ReasoningBank achieves up to 20% relative improvement in effectiveness and 16% fewer interaction steps compared to baselines on WebArena, Mind2Web, and SWE-Bench-Verified
  • Memory-aware test-time scaling (MaTTS) creates a synergy between memory and compute: high-quality memory steers exploration toward promising paths, while the diverse experiences generated forge stronger memories
  • Memory-driven experience scaling establishes a new scaling dimension for agents, complementing traditional scaling of model size and training data
  • Self-judged experience evaluation without ground-truth labels enables continuous closed-loop agent evolution in deployment settings

docs.title: Recipes for building an open-domain chatbot
Summary
docs.text: Provides recipes for building high-performing open-domain chatbots at 90M, 2.7B, and 9.4B parameter scales, finding that beyond model scaling, two key ingredients are critical: blending conversational skills through fine-tuning on data emphasizing personality, engagingness, knowledge, and empathy (using the Blended Skill Talk setup), and careful choice of generation strategy (decoding algorithm and hyperparameters). Human evaluations show the 9.4B model outperforms Google's Meena in both engagingness (75% vs 25%) and humanness (65% vs 35%).

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• Fine-tuning on Blended Skill Talk (BST) data that emphasizes personality, knowledge, and empathy produces large improvements; small BST-tuned models can match or outperform larger models without such tuning.
  • Generation strategy is as important as model quality: models with the same perplexity but different decoding algorithms produce vastly different human evaluation results.
  • Constraining minimum beam length is crucial for controlling the dull-vs-spicy spectrum of responses, and beam search with careful hyperparameter tuning can outperform sampling.
  • Despite strong performance, models still exhibit limitations including lack of in-depth knowledge, tendency toward simpler language, and repetition of phrases.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Recursive Language Models (RLMs) treat arbitrarily long prompts as part of an external environment rather than feeding them directly into the neural network, allowing the LLM to programmatically examine, decompose, and recursively call itself over slices of the input via a REPL. RLMs successfully process inputs more than an order of magnitude beyond model context window limits and dramatically outperform vanilla frontier LLMs and common long-context scaffolds across four diverse long-context tasks. A post-trained RLM-Qwen3-8B using only 1,000 training samples improves the base model by a median of 28%.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• Treating the user prompt as an external environment variable that the LLM interacts with symbolically enables processing inputs far beyond native context windows without the lossy information loss of compaction approaches
  • RLMs outperform GPT-5 by a median of 26% against compaction, 130% against CodeAct with sub-calls, and 13% against Claude Code across four long-context benchmarks
  • Context rot (quality degradation with longer prompts) is dramatically reduced by RLMs compared to direct LLM calls, even for inputs beyond the model's native context window
  • Post-training a small model (Qwen3-8B) with only 1,000 domain-unrelated samples improves its RLM performance by a median of 28.3%, demonstrating that native recursive capability can be quickly trained

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: MASS (Multi-Agent Self-Supervision) is a recursive self-improvement method for open-ended research tasks where the model being improved is also its own best evaluator. A single base model alternates between an inner loop, in which it proposes, runs and self-evaluates multi-agent workflows (roles and information routing encoded as a prompt) under an evolutionary search, and an outer loop that fine-tunes the same model on orchestrator and subagent trajectories from the best workflows. Two cycles on Qwen3.6-27B improve score per output token by 1.2–1.6× on four research benchmarks, with gains judged by external strong models withheld from the loop.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• A single model critiquing its own work shares the prior that produced the errors, so self-feedback can reinforce rather than correct them; organizing copies of the model into an optimized multi-agent workflow is proposed as a way to get usable self-supervision
  • Across two cycles, win rate against the base model on held-out synthetic research tasks rises from 53.9% to 69.9%, and score per output token rises 1.2–1.6× on MLR-Bench, ScienceAgentBench, DSBench and AstaBench; Terminal-Bench 2.0 and SWE-bench Verified slip slightly (37.5→35.2, 62.6→61.1)
  • Fine-tuning only on task-solving trajectories also improves the other two roles: the model finds good workflows faster and its evaluator agreement with external judges rises from 73% to 93%
  • Multi-agent traces are more training-efficient: a student trained on them reaches a 68.3% win rate versus 64.0% for a single-agent student trained on about 1.4× more tokens, attributed to separating orchestration (delegation, integration) from bounded subagent execution
  • Ablations point to the workflow optimizer, not the evaluator, as the main bottleneck in the same-model loop: swapping in a stronger optimizer speeds progress more than swapping in a stronger evaluator

docs.title: Red Teaming Language Models with Language Models
Summary
docs.text: This paper proposes using language models themselves to automatically generate test cases ("red teaming") that expose harmful behaviors in target LMs, replacing expensive manual annotation. Testing on a 280B parameter Dialogue-Prompted Gopher chatbot, they explore zero-shot, few-shot, supervised learning, and RL-based methods for generating adversarial inputs, uncovering tens of thousands of diverse failure cases including offensive dialogue, data leakage, distributional bias, and privacy violations.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• LM-based red teaming can automatically generate tens of thousands of diverse, natural-language test cases that expose harmful behaviors, significantly scaling beyond manual testing.
  • RL-trained red team models are most effective at eliciting offensive replies (over 40% offensive rate), though at the cost of reduced diversity compared to zero-shot and few-shot methods.
  • LM-generated adversarial inputs uncover systematic failure modes including distributional bias (discussing certain groups more offensively), data leakage of memorized training data, and escalating offensive dialogues.
  • The approach is controllable through prompt engineering, allowing targeted testing for specific failure modes across different demographic groups and content categories.

docs.title: Red Teaming the Mind of the Machine: A Systematic Evaluation of Prompt Injection and Jailbreak Vulnerabilities in LLMs
Summary
docs.text: This paper systematically evaluates prompt injection and jailbreak vulnerabilities across GPT-4, Claude 2, Mistral 7B, and Vicuna using over 1,400 adversarial prompts categorized by attack vector. It finds that GPT-4 has the highest attack success rate (87.2%) due to its permissive instruction-following, that jailbreak prompts are highly transferable across models, and that current alignment mechanisms are insufficiently robust, particularly against roleplay, logic traps, and encoding-based attacks.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• GPT-4 exhibits the highest attack success rate (87.2%) among tested models, with Claude 2 at 82.5%, Mistral 7B at 71.3%, and Vicuna at 69.4%, suggesting model scale and instruction-following capability increase attack surface.
  • Roleplay-based prompt injections achieve the highest attack success rate (89.6%), followed by logic traps (81.4%) and encoding tricks (76.2%).
  • Jailbreak prompts are highly transferable across models: prompts succeeding on GPT-4 transfer to Claude 2 with 64.1% success and to Mistral/Vicuna with ~50% success.
  • Current alignment mechanisms are largely reliant on static refusal templates and are semantically shallow, failing against indirect or obfuscated attacks.

docs.title: ReDel: A Toolkit for LLM-Powered Recursive Multi-Agent Systems
Summary
docs.text: ReDel is an open-source toolkit for building recursive multi-agent systems where a root agent dynamically spawns sub-agents to decompose and solve complex tasks. It provides modular interfaces for custom tools, delegation schemes (synchronous DelegateOne and asynchronous DelegateWait), event-driven logging, and an interactive web interface for visualization and replay of delegation graphs.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• Recursive delegation -- where agents dynamically decide when and how to spawn sub-agents -- outperforms single-agent baselines and even published state-of-the-art systems on FanOutQA and TravelPlanner benchmarks.
  • The performance gap between recursive multi-agent systems and single-agent baselines grows larger as the underlying model capabilities improve, suggesting the approach scales well with model quality.
  • ReDel is the only fully open-source toolkit that supports dynamic multi-agent systems with a rich event-driven architecture, run replay, and web-based visualization interface.
  • Two delegation schemes (synchronous DelegateOne and asynchronous DelegateWait) cover different LLM capabilities, with parallel function calling enabling synchronous parallel delegation.

docs.title: Reflexion: Language Agents with Verbal Reinforcement Learning
Summary
docs.text: Reflexion proposes a framework where language agents learn from trial-and-error through verbal self-reflection rather than weight updates. After each failed attempt, the agent generates a textual self-reflection analyzing what went wrong and stores it in an episodic memory buffer, which is used as additional context in subsequent trials. This achieves 91% pass@1 on HumanEval (surpassing GPT-4's 80%), 22% improvement on AlfWorld, and 20% on HotPotQA over strong baselines.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• Verbal reinforcement through self-reflective text summaries stored in episodic memory can substitute for traditional RL weight updates, enabling agents to learn from failures without fine-tuning.
  • Reflexion achieves 91% pass@1 accuracy on HumanEval coding benchmark, surpassing GPT-4's previous state-of-the-art of 80%.
  • The framework is flexible enough to incorporate various feedback types (scalar, binary, or free-form language) from both external environments and internal self-evaluation.
  • Self-reflection provides more nuanced and interpretable learning signals than scalar rewards, enabling targeted changes in agent behavior across decision-making, reasoning, and programming tasks.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: ReFT (Reinforced Fine-Tuning) enhances LLM reasoning by first warming up with supervised fine-tuning on chain-of-thought data, then applying online reinforcement learning (PPO) where the model samples multiple reasoning paths and learns from those that produce correct answers. This two-stage approach significantly outperforms SFT alone on math problem-solving by exposing the model to diverse correct reasoning paths rather than a single annotated one.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• Reinforced fine-tuning (warm-up SFT followed by online PPO) significantly outperforms pure supervised fine-tuning on math reasoning benchmarks (GSM8K, MathQA, SVAMP) using the same training data.
  • RL provides richer supervision than SFT by sampling multiple valid reasoning paths per question, whereas SFT is limited to a single annotated chain-of-thought per problem.
  • ReFT's improvement comes without relying on extra or augmented training questions -- it learns better from the same data by exploring the space of correct solutions.
  • ReFT benefits from inference-time strategies such as majority voting and reward model reranking, further boosting performance beyond the base policy.

docs.title: Reinforced Agent: Inference-Time Feedback for Tool-Calling Agents
Summary
docs.text: Proposes a duo-agent architecture where a specialized reviewer evaluates provisional tool calls before execution, shifting from post-hoc error recovery to proactive error prevention. Introduces Helpfulness-Harmfulness metrics to quantify when reviewer feedback corrects errors vs. introduces new ones. Reasoning models (o3-mini) achieve 3:1 benefit-to-risk ratios vs. 2.1:1 for GPT-4o. Results: +5.5% on BFCL irrelevance detection, +7.1% on τ²-Bench multi-turn tasks.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• Reviewing tool calls before execution avoids the state recovery problem: once a destructive call executes (deleting a record, sending a message), recovery requires prohibitively expensive trajectory replay
  • A simple reviewer agent provides clean separation of concerns: the tool-calling agent requires no retraining or modification, only the reviewer model and prompt need tuning
  • Reasoning models (o3-mini) are substantially better reviewers than standard LLMs: 3:1 helpfulness-to-harmfulness ratio (36.8% errors corrected, 11.7% correct responses degraded) vs. 2.1:1 for GPT-4o
  • Automated prompt optimization (GEPA) of the reviewer prompt alone adds +1.5–2.8% on top of model selection gains, without touching the base agent
  • Helpfulness-Harmfulness metrics reveal the precise tradeoff and directly inform reviewer design — a reviewer is only worth adding if its benefit-to-risk ratio exceeds 1:1

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Q-chunking applies action chunking (predicting sequences of future actions rather than single actions) to temporal-difference-based reinforcement learning in the offline-to-online setting. By training both critic and actor on temporally extended action chunks, it enables faster value backup propagation without the off-policy bias of n-step returns, while leveraging temporally coherent behaviors from offline data for more effective online exploration.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• Action chunking in RL provides unbiased n-step value backup (unlike standard n-step returns which suffer from off-policy bias) by conditioning the Q-function on the full action sequence actually taken.
  • Behavior constraints on the temporally extended action space allow the agent to leverage temporally coherent behaviors from offline data for more effective online exploration.
  • Q-chunking outperforms prior best offline-to-online methods on a range of long-horizon, sparse-reward manipulation tasks in OGBench.
  • The recipe is generic and can be applied to existing offline-to-online RL algorithms with minimal modification, demonstrated by applying it to FQL to create QC-FQL with significant improvements.

docs.title: ReMem: Mutual Information-Aware Fine-tuning of Pretrained Vision Transformers for Effective Knowledge Distillation
Summary
docs.text: ReMem addresses the counterintuitive problem that knowledge distillation becomes less effective when distilling from stronger pretrained models. It employs mutual information-aware optimization during fine-tuning of Vision Transformers (ViTs) to improve knowledge transfer. For small or highly imbalanced datasets where MI optimization is less effective, it introduces MLP block reweighting based on the observation that top MLP blocks are primarily responsible for mutual information loss.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• Knowledge distillation effectiveness paradoxically decreases when the teacher model is stronger, often producing worse student models than distilling from weaker teachers
  • Top MLP blocks in ViTs are primarily responsible for mutual information loss during fine-tuning
  • Mutual information-aware optimization during fine-tuning improves knowledge transfer by aligning teacher and student representations
  • MLP block reweighting is a simple but effective heuristic for small or highly imbalanced downstream datasets
  • ReMem enables small student models to benefit from the strongest pretrained models, resolving the capacity gap problem

docs.title: Remote Labor Index: Measuring AI Automation of Remote Work
Summary
docs.text: The Remote Labor Index (RLI) is a multi-sector benchmark of real-world, economically valuable projects designed to evaluate end-to-end AI agent performance in practical settings. Current AI agents perform near the floor: the highest-performing agent achieves only a 2.5% automation rate. RLI grounds discussions of AI automation in empirical evidence and provides a common basis for tracking AI impacts on labor.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• Existing AI agent benchmarks measure specialized skills in isolation; they don't capture the diversity and complexity of real-world remote work
  • The highest-performing AI agent achieves only a 2.5% automation rate on RLI, far below popular perceptions of AI capabilities
  • RLI comprises real-world, economically valuable projects (data visualization, 3D rendering, etc.) across multiple sectors
  • A standardized, empirical benchmark for AI automation is necessary to help stakeholders proactively navigate AI-driven labor changes
  • The gap between benchmark performance on specialized tasks and performance on real work is substantial and often underappreciated

docs.title: Repo2Skill-Evo: Repository Skills Go Stale in Silence
Summary
docs.text: ByteDance, Peking University, and Beijing Jiaotong University show that repository-specific agent skills (which APIs to call, which scripts to run, which conventions apply) go silently stale after a release: they still load and get retrieved, but give obsolete guidance with no error signal. Repo2Skill-Evo casts each release as a maintenance task — given the V1 skill set and the official V1→V2 patch, remove stale content while keeping valid guidance — and across 105 releases from 57 repositories (1,158 skills, 12,217 patch-verified stale lines), six frontier agents reach only 29.9–69.7% avg@3 macro F1.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• Externalized knowledge decays invisibly: the version specificity that makes a skill useful also makes it fragile, and because a stale skill raises no error, outdated guidance keeps being retrieved and followed; skills should be treated as versioned knowledge assets that record the release they were distilled from — an agent-facing analogue of code–comment drift
  • Frontier agents cannot reliably maintain skills even with the official patch: Claude Opus 4.6 reaches 69.7% macro F1, GLM-5.1 64.3%, GPT-5.4 58.8% (highest recall at 74.6% but precision 55.7%), and Kimi-K2.5, Doubao-Seed2-pro, and MiniMax-M2.5 47.0%, 39.8%, and 29.9%
  • Two opposing failure modes dominate: missing affected files leaves stale content in place (low recall), while over-broad editing deletes valid guidance (low precision); exhausting the 50-turn budget is common (GLM-5.1 in 41.3% of runs)
  • Telling the agent which files are affected helps but does not solve the problem: on the 20 hardest transitions, oracle file paths raise mean F1 from 32.8% to 45.0% (+12.2 points), yet the best model still reaches only 62.3% — agents also struggle to trace affected claims within files and choose the right edits
  • Skills help most where agents know least: in a 10-repository utility study, skills gave the largest gains on tasks with the lowest baseline utility, which is also where stale skills would do the most damage

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Caveat: the dataset is a curated staleness-positive challenge set — releases were selected because they affect skills — so "every transition invalidates part of the skill set" reflects the selection, not how often releases cause staleness in general.
  • Limitation: measures how faithfully agents edit skills against the patch, not whether the maintained skills help on downstream tasks.
  • Limitation: V1 skills were LLM-generated and then expert-refined; one minimal agent setup with a 50-turn budget; the corpus leans toward fast-moving AI/ML repositories.

docs.title: Requirements-Augmented Generation for Trustworthy Acceptance Testing of LLM-Based Software
Summary
docs.text: This ASE 2026 paper from Monash and collaborators presents an automated acceptance-testing framework for LLM-based software, whose stochastic, persona-dependent behavior defeats classical test oracles. Requirements-Augmented Generation (REAG) retrieves software requirements, domain knowledge and personas via adaptive RAG to generate context-aware test oracles, and a confidence-calibrated cascade of judges accepts, escalates or abstains on verdicts with conformal risk control. An industrial case study on a production nutrition-advice application shows high verdict accuracy at lower cost than single-judge baselines.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• For LLM-based software the correct response depends on the user's persona and the software context, so classical acceptance tests and fixed oracles are insufficient
  • REAG generates context-aware oracles by retrieving relevant requirements, domain knowledge and personas with adaptive RAG plus self-reasoning, reaching 3.91/5 oracle quality and qualified or marginal quality in 82% of cases
  • The confidence-calibrated cascade quantifies verdict reliability via simulated expert agreement, using conformal risk control to decide whether to accept, escalate or abstain
  • On 346 test scenarios the cascade achieves 98.8% accuracy, lifts oracle quality from 3.91 to 4.30 by filtering unqualified outputs, and is 31.7% more cost-efficient than the strongest single judge
  • 18% of oracles are affected by retrieval errors or by following prominent scenario details outside the defined requirements, and ambiguous-intent edge cases still need human judgment

docs.title: ReSum: Unlocking Long-Horizon Search Intelligence via Context Summarization
Summary
docs.text: ReSum is a plug-and-play paradigm for LLM-based web agents that resolves the conflict between extensive exploration and limited context windows by periodically summarizing interaction histories into compact summaries via an external tool. Combined with ReSum-GRPO, which adapts Group Relative Policy Optimization to propagate trajectory-level rewards across segmented trajectories via advantage broadcasting, ReSum achieves 4.5% improvement over ReAct in training-free settings with a further 8.2% gain after RL training.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• Periodically compressing agent interaction histories into summaries enables unbounded exploration without architectural modifications, serving as a paradigmatic rather than architectural enhancement to existing ReAct-based agents.
  • ReSum-GRPO solves the credit assignment problem in long-horizon tasks by segmenting trajectories at summarization points and broadcasting trajectory-level advantages to all segments uniformly.
  • With only 1K training samples, a ReSum-enhanced 30B model achieves competitive performance with leading open-source models on challenging web search benchmarks (GAIA, BrowseComp).
  • ReSumTool-30B, a specialized summary model fine-tuned on Qwen3-30B-A3B-Thinking, outperforms significantly larger models like DeepSeek-R1-671B in summarization quality for web search contexts.

docs.title: Rethinking the Value of Agent-Generated Tests for LLM-Based Software Engineering Agents
Summary
docs.text: The authors study whether the tests coding agents write for themselves while fixing an issue actually help them fix it. They analyze runs of six frontier models on SWE-bench Verified, using the minimal mini-SWE-agent scaffold, where writing tests is optional. How often a model writes tests depends on the model, not on whether it succeeds: GPT-5.2 almost never writes tests yet scores nearly as high as Claude Opus 4.5, which writes them in 83% of tasks. When agents do write tests, the tests mostly print values rather than assert anything. Changing the prompt to encourage or forbid test writing changes test behavior on a large scale but barely changes how many issues get resolved. Suppressing tests cuts token use by a third to a half.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• Test writing is a habit that varies by model, not a sign of success. GPT-5.2 writes new tests in 0.6% of tasks and resolves 71.8%. Claude Opus 4.5 writes them in 83% and resolves 74.4%. Within any one model, resolved and unresolved tasks show similar test-writing rates, and unresolved runs run their tests more often.
  • Agent-written tests are mostly debugging probes, not checks. Print statements that show runtime values consistently outnumber assertions. The assertions that do appear are mostly simple property or exact-value checks; relational and range constraints are rare.
  • Prompting agents to write more tests adds cost and nothing else. When GPT-5.2 was told to write tests, 64% of tasks switched from no test to having one, yet its resolution rate was unchanged at 359/500. Meanwhile it used +5.5% API calls, +9% input tokens and +20% output tokens.
  • Forbidding tests saves a lot and loses a little. Kimi K2 Thinking used 49% fewer input tokens and 35% fewer API calls for −2.6 points of resolution. DeepSeek v3.2 used 33% fewer input tokens for −1.8 points. The changes in outcome are not statistically significant (McNemar test, p > 0.4).
  • Scope: this covers one minimal scaffold and one Python benchmark (SWE-bench Verified), and studies only tests the agent writes for itself during the run. It is not evidence against existing test suites, or against tests produced as a deliverable or used as a gate.

docs.title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Large Language Models: A Survey
Summary
docs.text: This comprehensive survey maps the evolution of Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) through three paradigms -- Naive RAG, Advanced RAG, and Modular RAG -- examining the tripartite foundation of retrieval, generation, and augmentation techniques. It covers over 100 RAG studies, analyzes core technologies across each stage, compares RAG with fine-tuning approaches, and reviews evaluation frameworks covering 26 tasks and nearly 50 datasets.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• RAG has evolved from a simple retrieve-and-read paradigm (Naive RAG) through Advanced RAG (with pre/post-retrieval optimization) to Modular RAG with flexible, reconfigurable components including search, routing, memory, and prediction modules.
  • RAG and fine-tuning are complementary rather than competing approaches: RAG excels in dynamic environments with real-time knowledge updates, while fine-tuning enables deep customization of model behavior and style.
  • Key challenges in RAG include retrieval precision/recall trade-offs, hallucination from irrelevant retrieved context, and augmentation difficulties in integrating information from multiple sources coherently.
  • The modular RAG architecture enables adaptive retrieval strategies (like FLARE and Self-RAG) that evaluate the necessity of retrieval on a per-query basis, transcending fixed retrieval pipelines.

docs.title: Retrofitting language models to operate over bytes
Summary
docs.text: Language models that read raw bytes avoid the problems of subword tokenization, such as weak handling of individual characters, English-centric vocabularies, and sensitivity to how a prompt happens to be tokenized. But byte-level models trained from scratch have never kept up with the frontier. This paper instead converts an existing subword model into a byte-level one, which the authors call "byteification." It takes two stages and less than 1% of a typical pretraining budget (49B tokens). The resulting models (Bolmo 7B/1B from Olmo, Bwen 8B from Qwen3, Blama 8B from Llama 3) come close to their source models, beat every earlier byte-level model of similar size, and are far better at character-level tasks. They can also reuse the source model's existing ecosystem, such as post-training, with no extra training.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• Converting an existing model beats training a byte-level model from scratch. Bolmo 7B scores +16.5 points over BLT 7B on STEM tasks. Bwen 8B significantly beats every earlier byte-level model and nearly matches Qwen3 8B. The authors argue that byte-level models failed to catch on because training them from scratch can't keep pace with how fast subword-model training improves. Converting a model lets byte-level models inherit that progress.
  • The key architectural change is letting the model look one byte ahead when deciding where chunks of bytes end. Earlier byte-level designs decide boundaries using only past bytes. Subword tokenizers, by contrast, effectively use future context: "_Wor" becomes a token in "_Wor!" but not in "_World!". Adding one byte of lookahead closes that gap. During generation, the decoder signals the end of each chunk with a special <b> symbol.
  • Character understanding improves greatly, at a measurable cost. Compared with a control model trained on the same data, the byte-level architecture slightly degrades multiple-choice, general QA and math, and substantially degrades code pass@1. In exchange, code pass@16 improves, because outputs are more varied, and character-level skills improve strongly. The authors warn that the extra variety could be an artifact of the sampling settings.
  • Inference can be made faster without the vocabulary-size limit subword models hit. Merging more bytes per chunk speeds up inference with a gradual drop in quality. Subword models can only grow their vocabulary so far: past roughly 200k–400k tokens, the cost of the final softmax over the vocabulary makes them a worse trade-off in both speed and quality. Merging chunk boundaries the way BPE does beat entropy-based merging in this setting.
  • Existing post-training transfers by adding weight differences ("task arithmetic"). Adding the difference between Olmo 3's instruction-tuned and base checkpoints to Bolmo brings its instruction-following (IFEval) up to the instruction-tuned model's level, with no further training.

docs.title: Reverse Thinking Enhances Missing Information Detection in Large Language Models
Summary
docs.text: This paper identifies a fundamental limitation of forward reasoning approaches (CoT, ToT): they propagate inferences from given premises without mechanisms to identify missing information, leading to hallucinations when inputs are incomplete. It proposes a reverse thinking framework that transforms missing information detection into a backward reasoning problem—guiding LLMs to identify necessary conditions and pinpoint missing elements. This approach achieves substantial performance gains on missing information detection tasks.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• Forward reasoning (CoT, ToT) fails systematically on problems with missing information because these methods assume initial information is complete and consistent
  • The strength of CoT/ToT—systematic forward derivation—becomes a weakness when facing informational incompleteness
  • Reverse thinking reframes missing information detection as backward reasoning: start from the desired conclusion and identify what premises are needed
  • The framework guides LLMs to identify necessary conditions and pinpoint missing elements through structured backward reasoning
  • Achieves substantial performance gains over traditional forward reasoning methods on missing information detection tasks

docs.title: Roaring Bitmaps: Implementation of an Optimized Software Library
Summary
docs.text: Lemire and co-authors present CRoaring, an optimised C implementation of Roaring compressed bitmaps — the set-of-integers index format used by Elasticsearch, Apache Spark, Druid, Pinot, Kylin, Hive, and others. Roaring splits the 32-bit space into 2^16-value chunks and stores each chunk in whichever of three container types (bitset, sorted array, or run-length) minimises memory; CRoaring adds SIMD (AVX2) algorithms for intersection, union, difference, symmetric difference, and population counts, and benchmarks against a wide range of compressed and uncompressed alternatives.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• Adaptive containers are the core design: a bitset container (8 kB) when a chunk holds more than 4,096 values, a sorted array of 16-bit integers when it holds fewer, and a run container when runs are compact — with the type chosen dynamically, even mid-operation (e.g. intersecting two bitsets may yield an array), to minimise memory while keeping logarithmic-time membership checks
  • Hand-written SIMD algorithms improve on what optimising compilers achieve: vectorised set operations between array containers and an AVX2 population count (computing cardinalities on vector registers without extra data transfer) can exceed a 2× speedup, the first reported use of advanced SIMD algorithms for compressed bitmaps
  • No structure wins everywhere, but Roaring gives the best all-round trade-off: uncompressed bitsets are faster on some dense datasets (CENSUSINC, WEATHER) with Roaring second at up to half the speed while using 10× less memory, and on many-way unions Roaring is generally fastest and sometimes several times faster than any alternative
  • The authors name two weaknesses: operations involving run containers lack advanced optimisations and are frequently a significant cost in profiling, and BitMagic — a similar design — has up to ~3× better random-access (membership) performance owing to Roaring's more compact layout
  • Engineering features matter alongside algorithms: CRoaring supports container-level copy-on-write and memory-file mapping, since memory allocation and copying are sometimes a significant cost; future directions include ARM performance, vectorising run-container operations, and more compact serialisation

docs.title: RULER: What's the Real Context Size of Your Long-Context Language Models?
Summary
docs.text: RULER is a synthetic benchmark for evaluating long-context language models that goes beyond simple needle-in-a-haystack (NIAH) retrieval to include four task categories: retrieval (with multiple needle variants), multi-hop tracing, aggregation, and question answering. Despite nearly perfect NIAH performance, almost all 17 evaluated models show significant degradation on RULER's more complex tasks as context length increases, with only half maintaining satisfactory performance at 32K tokens.

docs.title: Key Claims
docs.text:
• Simple NIAH tests are insufficient for evaluating long-context capabilities; models achieving near-perfect NIAH scores show large degradation on more complex tasks like multi-hop tracing and aggregation.
  • While all tested models claim context sizes of 32K+ tokens, only half can effectively handle 32K context by exceeding a qualitative performance threshold on RULER.
  • Larger model sizes positively correlate with better long-context capabilities, while training on longer sequences does not always lead to better performance.
  • Non-Transformer architectures like RWKV and Mamba still lag behind Transformers by large margins on long-context tasks measured by RULER.
