docs.title: What is it
docs.text:
Agent-driven test generation is the use of coding agents to autonomously identify test gaps, write tests, and open PRs — shifting test quality improvement off the critical path of feature development. A typical design is a continuous improvement loop: a scheduled agent scans for coverage gaps, assesses which gaps matter, generates targeted tests, gates them on a quality check, and opens PRs for review.

This page covers how such loops should be designed: what to use as the quality gate, what the agent should write tests against, which failure modes constrain the design, and what industrial deployments show about yield and review load. The wider problem of verifying agent-written code is Testing and Compliance for Coding Agents.

The short answer: generate tests against a written specification rather than the implementation, iterate with execution feedback, gate on mutation kill rate rather than coverage, and budget for review — precision, the cost of dismissing a false positive and reviewer capacity, not generation, set the limit.

docs.title: Mutation scoring is a better gate than coverage
docs.text:
Mutation scoring directly addresses the most documented failure mode in agent-generated tests: gaming. Agents naturally write mocks, stubs, and hardcoded values to pass assertions rather than testing actual behavior (Quality Code with AI). One practitioner source attributes part of this to RLHF-trained sycophancy, which also undermines the agent's review of its own output (Your LLM Doesn't Write Correct Code).

A mutation gate (e.g., PIT for Java) validates that new tests actually detect behavioral changes in production code; Google's coverage paper notes that safety-critical projects already use mutation testing as "a more rigorous adequacy criterion" than coverage (Code Coverage at Google). That it catches gaming in agent tests is this page's reasoning, not a measured result. A test that calls a method and asserts no exception won't kill mutants. A test that validates specific behavior will. Mutation kill rate measures detection power; coverage measures surface area.

Coverage is a useful input signal for prioritization but a poor outcome metric. In a single, contested example (readers noted the project was unfinished), a 576,000-line Rust reimplementation of SQLite passed functional tests but ran up to 20,000x slower because it missed performance invariants that only emerge from profiling real workloads (Your LLM Doesn't Write Correct Code). Google's testing guidance makes the same point from the other side: coverage measures that code was invoked, not that it was checked, and teams treat coverage floors as ceilings (SWE at Google: Testing).

Where coverage does help is as a review signal on the change itself. Google computes line and branch coverage for a billion lines daily, but its most useful form is delta coverage on the changeset, surfaced during code review. Only 0.5% of developers invoke coverage manually on a daily basis, but once it appears automatically in review, 45% of survey respondents (512) report using it often when authoring and 40% when reviewing. Google sets no global threshold; projects opt into voluntary levels (60–90%), and the authors suspect their adoption explains rising coverage (Code Coverage at Google). For a test-generation loop, that suggests using coverage to show reviewers what a generated test exercises, not as the loop's objective.

Mutation scoring's own limit: it catches the worst cases (no-assertion tests, trivial assertions) but misses subtler adaptation where the agent tests implementation quirks rather than intended contracts — the problem the next two sections address.

docs.title: Tests should be written against a specification, not the implementation
docs.text:
The strongest evidence concerns what the agent writes tests against. Google's Spec-Driven Test Generation adds one step: before writing any tests, the agent writes down the target code's pre-conditions, post-conditions and undefined behaviours as a semi-formal natural-language contract. It then generates tests against that contract. On 90 historical production bugs from Google's monorepo, with the same Gemini 3 Flash model and harness in both arms, the two-phase agent detected 9.8 percentage points more historical bugs than direct generation at k=5 (63.2%, p=0.035; 4.2 points at k=1) and added 2.5 points of branch coverage (Grounding AI Agents in Contracts).

The mechanism is the useful part. The authors' Contract Coverage metric asks whether the written spec captures the contract the bug violates, and it strongly predicts success: 54.9% detection when it does, against 19.4% when it doesn't. Spec quality, not test-writing, is the bottleneck, and it improves with sampling (61.1% at k=1 to 78.9% at k=5). An LLM judge preferred the spec-driven suites over the baseline agent's in 77.8% of cases, with the largest advantage on edge-case coverage (83.3%), and over the developer-written originals in 56.7% — which the authors call parity. That is a judge verdict, scoped to single-file fixes in one organisation.

This fits the wider intent-formalization argument: AI-generated code is "plausible by construction but not correct by construction", and the reliability bottleneck is translating intent into checkable specifications. LLM-generated postconditions caught 1 in 8 real bugs on Defects4J, including bugs that classical invariant detectors missed (Intent Formalization). The same paper names the catch: there is no oracle for whether a specification is correct other than the user, so specs need their own validation.

Less formal intent helps too. TiCoder's test-based intent clarification raised code-generation pass@1 by 45.97 points on average within 5 interactions, with a simulated user (TiCoder). By analogy, a concrete gap description ("write an integration test for the gRPC boundary when downstream returns UNAVAILABLE") should beat "improve coverage," though no source tests that directly. Practitioners at OpenAI report a related effect — constraining the solution space increased trust in agent output — but that is a practitioner claim, not a measured one (Charlie Guo).

Specs come in different weights:

  • Lightest: acceptance criteria written in plain English before the agent starts, then verified independently, one browser agent per criterion (Agents That Run While I Sleep).
  • Middle: Google's semi-formal contracts.
  • Heaviest: executable specifications that turn review into deterministic verification, leaving AI review only for what the spec cannot express (Specification as Quality Gate).

docs.title: Tests written alongside the code inherit its blind spots
docs.text:
When the same agent reads production code and writes tests, it adapts tests to match implementation details rather than intended behavior. The recommended countermeasure is cross-context interface tests — a separate agent context with minimal implementation knowledge writes the tests (Quality Code with AI, Executable Context Practices).

The gaming problem is a special case of a broader one. When the same model, or models trained on the same distribution, both write the code and judge it, their errors correlate rather than cancel. The review then checks the code against itself rather than against intent (Specification as Quality Gate). A practitioner puts it more bluntly: an agent that writes both the code and its own tests is a "self-congratulation machine" that validates what the agent thought you wanted (Agents That Run While I Sleep). Both arrive at the same remedy: an external specification, written before generation, that the tests are checked against.

If agents write both the tests and the production code for the same components over time, the two may co-evolve toward mutually compatible but jointly wrong solutions. This risk is amplified when the improvement loop targets components that already receive agent code PRs. No empirical resolution exists in the literature — it remains an open question.

The evidence here is practitioner argument; no source measures the correlation of errors between agent code and agent tests.

docs.title: Iterating with execution feedback beats single-shot generation
docs.text:
Single-shot workflows (assess → generate → gate) underperform iterative approaches. e-Otter++ reached 63% fail-to-pass on TDD-Bench Verified, against 37–39% for the prior state of the art, by combining heterogeneous prompting with execution feedback — running tests against surrogate patches and using the results to select better candidates. Against the prior system on the same model (Otter++, Claude-3.7-Sonnet, 38.8%) the gain is about 24 points, but that bundles heterogeneous prompting with execution feedback; in the paper's own ablations, execution-augmented repair alone adds roughly 3–10 points (typically 5–8) depending on prompt and model (e-Otter++). Self-Refine reports ~20% absolute improvement from generate-critique-refine loops using the model's own feedback, with no execution (Self-Refine). TestPilot's re-prompt-on-failure loop (below) points the same way.

The numbers aren't comparable with each other, but the direction is consistent, and the cost is a few additional LLM calls per component — likely modest next to mutation scoring, though no source here measures either cost.

docs.title: Property-based tests are harder to game and catch different bugs
docs.text:
Agentic PBT reports a 56% valid bug rate (from a manually reviewed subset) at an extrapolated ~$10/bug across 100 Python packages, with real bugs found and patched in NumPy, aws-lambda-powertools, and tokenizers (Agentic PBT). Two refinements matter for a production loop:

  • Ranking cut noise. An LLM-scored rubric raised precision to 86% valid and 81% reportable among the top-ranked reports (Property-Based Testing, Anthropic).
  • Self-reflection quality depends on the model. A self-reflection loop reduced false alarms, notably more with Opus 4.1 and Sonnet 4.5 than with Sonnet 4 (Property-Based Testing, Anthropic).

PBT generates random inputs, making gaming structurally difficult — you can't hardcode return values when the inputs are randomized. The complement to example-based tests is measurable. On HumanEval problems where standard solutions fail extended tests, LLM-generated property-based and example-based tests each caught 68.75% of bugs, and together 81.25% (LLM-Generated PBT Characteristics):

  • property-based tests found performance issues and edge cases through broad input exploration;
  • example-based tests caught specific boundary conditions.

The study is small (16 problems, one model), but it points the same way: generate both kinds of test, not one.

docs.title: AI-written tests have their own structural smells
docs.text: Empirical analysis of 2,232 commits shows AI-generated tests have higher assertion density (median 2.0 vs 1.0 for humans) but lower cyclomatic complexity — linear logic with many assertions (Testing with AI Agents). This risks Assertion Roulette: multiple assertions in a single test make failure diagnosis harder. Mutation scoring doesn't catch maintainability issues, so structural checks — max assertions per test method, test method length — are needed alongside it.

docs.title: Fault-targeted generation reframes the objective, but acceptance doesn't show it works better
docs.text:
Three industrial-scale reports — one benchmark evaluation and two Meta deployments — show how the objective has shifted. None compares fault-targeted with coverage-targeted generation directly, and ACH's acceptance rate matched earlier coverage-focused test-a-thons.

Coverage-driven generation is the 2023 baseline. TestPilot generates JavaScript unit tests from the function signature, implementation, and documentation-derived usage snippets, re-prompting with the failing test and its error message when generation fails — reaching 70.2% median statement coverage against 51.3% for the prior feedback-directed technique. The re-prompt loop is the durable contribution. The absolute numbers are gpt-3.5-era and should be read as a historical floor.

Fault-targeted generation replaces the coverage objective. Meta's ACH inverts the order: generate mutants — simulated faults specific to a concern — then generate tests that kill them. It deliberately produces few mutants, unlike traditional mutation testing, targeting currently undetected faults rather than exhaustive mutation. Across 10,795 Android Kotlin classes it produced 9,095 mutants and 571 privacy-hardening tests; in Messenger and WhatsApp test-a-thons, engineers accepted 73% of the tests they reviewed — very similar to earlier test-a-thons that focused only on coverage, and mostly because the tests added coverage of non-trivial code or a tricky corner case. The instructive figure is the other one: only 36% of the tests reviewed were judged possibly or definitely relevant to the concern they were generated for. Most tests were valued for unrelated reasons, which is worth knowing before treating acceptance rate as evidence that targeting worked.

ACH uses mutants as the generation target, not only as the verification gate. Its LLM-based equivalent-mutant detector reaches 0.79 precision / 0.47 recall, rising to 0.95 / 0.96 with preprocessing — the classic obstacle to mutation testing, handled tractably enough to deploy.

Catching tests invert the success criterion. Meta's successor system, Just-in-Time catching test generation, draws a distinction worth adopting: hardening tests pass at generation time; catching tests are meant to fail. Code-change-aware methods improved candidate catch generation 4× over hardening tests and 20× over coincidentally failing ones, and rule-based plus LLM assessors cut human review load 70%. Assessors labelled significantly more false positives on diffs humans accepted, and more true positives on diffs they rejected — the assessor signal correlates with reviewer judgment, which is what makes a triage layer viable at all — though the LLM and rule-based assessors agreed only modestly with each other.

docs.title: Review capacity, not generation, sets the limit
docs.text:
The end-to-end yield of catching tests is the number to internalize: 41 candidates surfaced to engineers, 8 confirmed true positives (19.5%), four of which would have caused serious failures. Separately, the assessors cut human review load about 70% in a study of 600 diffs. Meta kept the cost of the remaining false positives low by making each quick to dismiss — engineers are asked whether the change was intended and answer in minutes — and the authors report negligible drag on velocity (JIT Catching). For a loop whose tests are meant to fail, precision and the cost of a dismissal are the numbers to manage.

Review capacity is scarce, and agent output inflates the load on it. A synthesis of 2024–2026 industrial evidence finds that agents raise commit-level activity far more than releases: +180% at the commit level, +50% at the project level, +30% at release. In Stanford's dataset of 6,000 real agent sessions, only 44% of agent-produced code survived into user commits. The synthesis frames the downstream cost — CI, reviewer time, security analysis, rework — as a verification tax that grows with generation volume (Beyond Code Generation; these figures come from the studies it cites). A test-generation loop is not exempt: every generated test PR draws on the same reviewer budget as the code it protects. In a practitioner survey (N=31, multi-select), 74% of teams with deployed agents rely on human-in-the-loop evaluation (MAP).

Reviewers may also approve too easily. A position paper argues that frictionless interfaces exploit cognitive miserliness — the tendency to accept plausible output without analytical reasoning (Cognitive Agency Surrender); well-formatted, CI-passing test PRs fit that pattern. This is consistent with a grey-literature review of vibe-coding accounts, where skipping QA was the most common practice reported (36% of QA-practice mentions) (Vibe Coding). Professional developers behave differently: field observations and surveys find they plan before and validate agentic output after (Professional Developers Don't Vibe).

Perception is no substitute for measurement here either. The METR RCT found experienced developers were 19% slower with AI tools while believing they were 20% faster (METR), so a loop's quality has to be defined by measured outcomes — mutation kill rate, caught defects — rather than reviewers' impressions.

A phased review strategy (dedicated team → distributed → auto-merge) builds trust, but the transition points need explicit quality thresholds. The HULA framework at Atlassian achieved 82% plan approval, but PRs were raised for only a quarter of code-generated issues and 59% of those merged, so about 8% of issues ended in a merged PR (HULA) — suggesting 80%+ accept-rate targets for distributed review are optimistic without deliberate friction in the review process.

docs.title: Generated tests need a selection story
docs.text:
Generation is only half the economics. Test Impact Analysis is the pre-LLM answer to suites that outgrow the time available to run them: map changes to tests and run only the relevant subset, including impacted tests, previously failing tests, and newly added ones, with a safe fallback to the full suite whenever the analysis cannot reason about a change.

That fallback is what makes it deployable rather than merely clever, and it is the design pattern any generated-test loop should copy — a loop that adds tests without a selection story eventually makes CI the bottleneck it was meant to relieve. Defects4J remains the standard substrate for evaluating whether the tests being added actually detect real defects: 854 reproducible bugs across 17 Java projects, where reproducibility of the infrastructure, not the size of the bug list, is the product.

docs.title: What the evidence supports
docs.text:
• Write the spec before the tests. Spec-driven generation detected 9.8 points more historical bugs at k=5 (4.2 at k=1) with the same model and harness, and whether the spec captured the violated contract predicted success (54.9% vs 19.4%). One controlled study at one company, on single-file fixes (Grounding AI Agents in Contracts).
  • Iterate with execution feedback. e-Otter++, TestPilot and Self-Refine all gain from feedback loops; execution-augmented repair alone adds about 3–10 points in e-Otter++'s ablations.
  • Gate on mutation kill rate; show coverage in review. Mutation scoring targets gaming directly (this page's reasoning), and Meta's ACH deploys mutant-targeted generation at scale. Google's data shows delta coverage is useful to reviewers, not as an objective (Code Coverage at Google).
  • Generate property-based and example-based tests together. They catch different bugs (81.25% together vs 68.75% each), in a small study (LLM-Generated PBT Characteristics).
  • Plan for review, not generation, as the limit. About 1 in 5 of Meta's catching-test candidates that reached engineers was a true positive, kept affordable by making dismissal quick (JIT Catching); HULA merged about 8% of issues (HULA). Acceptance rate is a weak proxy: engineers accepted 73% of ACH's tests, but only 36% of the tests reviewed were relevant to the target concern (ACH).

docs.title: In practice
docs.text:
A loop design that follows the evidence: deterministic gap scan → assessment with full code access → written contract → generation from the contract only → execution feedback → mutation gate plus structural checks → review with delta coverage.

  1. Start with a deterministic scan. Produce a concrete gap list before any LLM call — cheap, objective checks first, LLM judgment second (Demystifying Evals).
  2. Separate assessment from generation. The assessment agent needs full code visibility to prioritize; the generation agent should see only interface contracts (API signatures, proto definitions, error codes). A written contract is the natural boundary object: the assessment agent produces it, the generation agent consumes only it (Tests should be written against a specification).
  3. Generate both property-based and example-based tests, especially for pure functions and data transformations with no integration tests (Property-based tests).
  4. Run, observe and iterate before gating (Iterating with execution feedback).
  5. Gate on mutation kill rate plus structural checks (assertions per test, test length) (Mutation scoring, Structural smells).
  6. Triage before humans see it, and make dismissing a false positive cheap; set explicit thresholds for each step from dedicated review to auto-merge (Review capacity, not generation, sets the limit).
  7. Add test selection with a full-suite fallback (Generated tests need a selection story).

Checking a loop design against the evidence:

Design choice What the evidence says Risk if ignored Mutation scoring gate Reasoned, not measured; ACH shows mutant-targeted generation is deployable (ACH) Low Written spec before generation +9.8pp bug detection at k=5; contract coverage predicts success (Grounding AI Agents in Contracts) Medium Specific gap assessments Indirect — by analogy to TiCoder; practitioner reports Low Deterministic scan first Practitioner guidance (Demystifying Evals) Low Quality defined by measured outcomes Indirect — self-perception misled on productivity (METR, n=16) Low Separate generation context Practitioner recommendation (Quality Code with AI) Medium Execution feedback loop Consistent direction, incomparable numbers: ~3–10pp from repair in e-Otter++'s ablations; ~20% for Self-Refine on non-test tasks Medium Property-based tests alongside examples Both together catch more bugs (LLM-Generated PBT Characteristics) Medium Coverage as review signal, not objective Delta coverage is used in review (Code Coverage at Google) Low Realistic review acceptance targets 59% of raised PRs merged, ~8% of issues (HULA) Medium Structural quality checks Assertion Roulette risk (Testing with AI Agents) Low

docs.title: Open questions
docs.text:
• Does mutation scoring suffice to prevent subtle test gaming? It catches no-assertion and trivial tests, but does it catch tests that assert on implementation quirks rather than intended behavior? Empirical data from a real deployment would answer this.
  • What is the optimal context boundary for the generation agent? Full code visibility produces more relevant tests but enables gaming. Interface-only visibility prevents gaming but may miss important edge cases. The right boundary is likely domain-specific.
  • How does test quality degrade over repeated loop iterations on the same component? SlopCodeBench finds agent code 2.0–2.3× more eroded and verbose than human code, with erosion rising in 77% of trajectories (SlopCodeBench). Does this apply to test code added incrementally?
  • Can mutation scoring and PBT be combined in the quality gate? PBT as a generation strategy with mutation scoring as a verification gate could be complementary — but the interaction is unexplored. The nearest evidence is that LLM-generated property-based and example-based tests catch different bugs (68.75% each, 81.25% together), but that is a small HumanEval study with no mutation gate.
  • Who validates the specification? Spec-driven generation moves the bottleneck from test-writing to spec quality: contract coverage predicts bug detection, and there is no oracle for a spec's correctness except the user (Intent Formalization). How much human review a generated contract needs, and whether sampling several contracts (k=5) substitutes for it, is untested outside Google's single-file bug fixes.
  • Does an external spec break the co-evolution loop? Correlated blind spots between agent code and agent tests are the reason for an external spec. Whether an agent-written spec, from the same model family, actually breaks that correlation or just moves it one step upstream has not been measured.

docs.title: What is it
docs.text:
An agent's memory is everything it can know that is not in its weights or its current prompt: facts about a user, the history of a long task, lessons from earlier attempts, the state of a codebase it is changing. Retrieval is how that material gets back into the context window when it is needed. The two are one design problem. A memory that cannot be found is lost, and retrieval over a store full of stale or wrong entries returns confident errors.

This page covers how agent memory is built (what is stored, in what structure, and when it is consolidated), how retrieval fails, why memories go stale, and — as its own section — how agents lose track of state over long runs and what has been proposed against it. It is distinct from Context Engineering, which asks what should be in the window at any moment. Memory is the question of what persists between windows.

The short answer: long context doesn't replace memory; many of the largest losses happen at write time; stale entries go undetected; and structured external state is the most common answer to long-run coherence — though the one clean ablation here found no gain, and most reported gains haven't been tested that way.

docs.title: Bigger context windows don't replace memory
docs.text:
The obvious alternative to memory is to keep everything in context. The evidence says that works less well than advertised window sizes suggest.

  • Advertised context is not usable context. RULER finds that models with near-perfect needle-in-a-haystack scores degrade sharply on multi-hop tracing and aggregation; of 17 models claiming 32K+ windows, only half perform satisfactorily at 32K.
  • Most long-context benchmarks test retrieval, not understanding. Is It Really Long Context? separates dispersion (how hard the needed information is to find) from scope (how much of it is needed). The hard corner — high on both — is barely benchmarked. OOLONG targets aggregation over the whole input and finds frontier models below 50% at 128K.
  • Models can't see what's missing. AbsenceBench asks models to spot deliberately omitted content; F1 falls 56.9% relative to needle-in-a-haystack, and the best model scores 69.6%. Marking omissions with placeholders helps by 35.7%, which points at attention having nothing to attend to.
  • Recall decays as context grows, gradually. Anthropic's context engineering post calls this context rot — a gradient rather than a cliff, across all models — and concludes bigger windows don't remove the need to curate.
  • Conversational memory specifically. On LoCoMo, both long-context models and RAG improve over base models but trail humans by 56%, and by 73% on temporal reasoning. Long-context models are also prone to attributing events to the wrong speaker.

There is also cost, which is where memory systems earn their place. Mem0 reports 91% lower p95 latency and over 90% token savings against full-context approaches, at a modest accuracy cost: full context still scores highest on LoCoMo (about 73% vs 68.44% for Mem0's best variant).

docs.title: Memory designs differ in tiering, linking and when they compile
docs.text: The systems in this wiki differ on three choices: how memory is tiered, how entries are linked, and when raw history is compiled into something smaller.

docs.title: Tiers borrowed from operating systems and psychology
docs.text:
Several designs split memory by recency and stability. MemoryOS uses short-, mid- and long-term stores with heat-based paging, borrowed from OS memory management. LightMem follows the Atkinson–Shiffrin model — sensory filtering, topic-aware short-term memory, and a long-term store updated offline in a "sleep-time" pass so consolidation never blocks inference — and reports up to 38× fewer tokens. EverMemOS turns dialogue into episodic traces plus atomic facts, then consolidates them into thematic scenes that guide retrieval. MemOS goes furthest, treating parametric, activation and plaintext memory as one governed resource with versioning and migration.

The same split shows up in a practitioner setting. Codified Context, built over 283 sessions on a 108,000-line codebase, separates an always-loaded "hot" constitution from 34 "cold" specification documents loaded on demand, with 19 domain-specialist agents in between.

docs.title: Links and structure
docs.text:
A-MEM organizes memories as a Zettelkasten: each new note gets keywords, tags and links to related notes, and can trigger rewrites of older ones. It argues fixed graph schemas like Mem0's limit adaptability. MemPalace makes the opposite bet on what to store: it keeps everything verbatim and relies on a spatial hierarchy for findability, reporting a +34% retrieval gain from structure alone. That figure is self-reported by the project.

LinkedIn's data context layer uses hierarchy for retrieval rather than storage. Curated documents sit under a tree of indexes, each holding summaries of its children, and the indexes are regenerated from the leaves upward whenever content changes. An agent can walk the tree with MCP calls, search it semantically, or fetch a known document by identifier. Its worked example reaches the right document in four index reads.

docs.title: Compile ahead of time, or just in time
docs.text:
The sharpest design split is when raw history gets condensed. Most systems summarize or extract at write time. GAM argues this ahead-of-time compression is irreversible and always loses information; it keeps light highlights plus a complete page store and runs a deep-research agent over it at query time. Anthropic's post makes the same move for agent context generally: keep lightweight references such as paths and queries, and load on demand.

The same argument is happening over LLM wikis — the pattern this wiki itself uses. Proponents describe compilation at ingest as the difference between a search engine and an encyclopedia. The Hidden Flaw counters that LLM-written summaries indexed beside originals make the store self-referential, and recommends synthesizing at query time from immutable originals. RAG vs. Agent Memory vs. LLM Wiki treats the three as complementary layers.

docs.title: Teaching the model what to keep
docs.text:
A separate line of work moves memory management into the model. MemAgent reads documents in segments and overwrites a fixed-size memory, with RL teaching it what to retain; with an 8K context window and trained on 32K-token documents, it extrapolates to 3.5M tokens with under 5% loss. Neural Garbage Collection has the model evict its own KV cache during reasoning, learned from task reward alone, and holds accuracy at 2–3× compression. AgentFold has a web agent "fold" its own trajectory at each step, choosing between fine-grained condensation and deep consolidation. MSA builds memory into attention and scales to 100M tokens with under 9% degradation.

Harness as a Language challenges the need for any dedicated memory system. Its JAZ framework exposes the agent's own history as a variable the model can inspect in code, and beats Letta/MemGPT on far recall (70% vs 62%) at about half the cost. Hiding the history from the code environment drops it to 32%.

docs.title: Agents can remember experience, not just facts
docs.text:
Some memory stores lessons rather than facts. Reflexion is the early form: after a failure the agent writes a self-reflection into an episodic buffer and reads it on the next attempt. ReasoningBank distills strategies from both successes and failures and reports up to 20% relative improvement; it argues that this transfers better than storing raw trajectories or successful routines alone.

How such a memory is maintained matters. ACE names two failure modes of iteratively rewritten context: brevity bias (summaries drop domain detail) and context collapse (each rewrite erodes what earlier rounds kept). It answers with incremental, structured updates. SkillX organizes experience into a three-tier skill hierarchy that transfers from a strong agent to weaker ones.

The clearest production account is Uber's legal redlining agent. Plain RAG over playbooks failed; storing each lawyer's final decision, edit and reasoning — retrieved with recency weighting — made the agent much more accurate with no fine-tuning. Uber's 91% accuracy figure is self-reported without a stated method.

docs.title: Retrieval fails in several distinct ways
docs.text:
The search key doesn't match the content. Uber's first system failed because a counterparty's redline is phrased nothing like the playbook passage that governs it. The fix was choosing keys: index feedback by the counterparty's intent, and anchor rules to sentences in Uber's own template.

Agents find the right material and then don't use it. ContextBench traces coding agents' retrieval against human-verified gold context. Agents often inspect the relevant code but fail to use it in the final patch, so consolidation, not only search, is a key bottleneck. More elaborate retrieval scaffolding gives only marginal gains, and agents consistently favor recall over precision.

Retrieval and reasoning get conflated in evaluation. BrowseComp-Plus fixes the corpus so the two can be measured separately. Better retrievers raise accuracy and cut search calls, while agents mostly buy accuracy with more searches. Retrieval doesn't help uniformly: on BrowseComp-ZH, enabling web search drops DeepSeek-R1 from 23.2% to 7.6%.

Structure helps when the domain is relational. Asking questions over a knowledge graph rather than raw SQL lifts GPT-4 from 16.7% to 54.2% on an enterprise insurance schema. GroundedKG-RAG builds its graph from linguistic parses rather than LLM summaries, so every node traces to source text, and outperforms GraphRAG. Prometheus turns a repository into a knowledge graph plus working memory, cutting LLM inference cost 45.4% while raising its resolution rate 25%. The graph side is covered in Ontologies.

Autonomous retrieval loops add their own risks. The Agentic RAG SoK lists compounding hallucination, memory poisoning and retrieval misalignment, and argues answer accuracy alone can't evaluate them — the trajectory has to be assessed.

The retrieval configuration is usually frozen. EvolveMem notes that memory systems evolve their content but not their retrieval settings, even though factual, temporal and multi-hop questions need different strategies. Its diagnose-propose-guard loop, which reverts any change that regresses, improves LoCoMo F1 from 30.5% to 54.3% over seven rounds.

docs.title: Stale memory goes undetected
docs.text:
Memory that was right and is now wrong may be the hardest failure, because nothing signals it.

STALE tests whether agents revise a belief when new evidence implicitly invalidates it. Most memory frameworks score below 10%; the best model reaches 55.2%. The mechanism is precise. In LightMem, updated evidence is retrieved 77.5% of the time and the matching old entry is often recalled alongside it, yet only 3.3% of those old entries get flagged for update, so stale and current memories coexist with nothing deciding which is authoritative. Models that correctly identify an outdated belief when asked directly still accept a question that presupposes it (Gemini 3.1 Pro: 92% vs 30%). The authors' prototype, which marks entries active or stale at write time and propagates changes to dependent facts, raises accuracy from 8.7% to 68.0% on the same backbone.

The same failure appears in procedural memory. Repo2Skill-Evo shows repository skills go silently stale after a release: they still load and get retrieved, but give obsolete guidance. Even given the official patch, the best frontier agent reaches 69.7% F1 at removing stale content, and agents fail in both directions — missing affected files, or deleting valid guidance.

Practitioner sources converge on the same rule. Meta's tribal-knowledge agents treat automated maintenance as essential because "context that decays is worse than no context at all." LLM Knowledge Base for Coding Agents says the same of wikis: "A stale wiki misleads agents confidently." LLM Wiki v2 prescribes freshness metadata and trust scores that decay without verification. In enterprise stores, the same document often exists in 3–5 versions and RAG retrieves whichever is semantically closest, not most current.

LinkedIn's data context layer splits freshness by who can maintain it. A pipeline regularly regenerates dataset profiles from schemas, query logs and code, while what automated signals can't capture — business rules, exceptions, known data-quality issues — is written by asset owners and reviewed through pull requests. The two layers are stored separately so a refresh never overwrites a human correction, and the corrections in turn show where the generated profiles are wrong.

docs.title: Agents lose track of state over long runs
docs.text:
Agents that run for a long time lose the plot. Procedural Graphs states the failure precisely: as trajectories lengthen, agents lose track of their objectives, invoke tools out of order, and repeat unproductive actions. Its diagnosis is structural — most agents choose actions by unconstrained generation over a flat, growing history, which leaves procedural knowledge (what to do, in what order, under which conditions) implicit and fragile.

On that diagnosis the problem is not only window size: a growing log is a poor representation of state whether or not it is retained.

docs.title: The failure is well measured
docs.text:
Degradation compounds across iterations. SlopCodeBench has agents repeatedly extend their own code across 196 checkpoints. No agent solves any problem end-to-end; the best passes 14.8% of checkpoints. Agent checkpoints are 2.3× more verbose and 2.0× more eroded than human code, and structural erosion rises in 77% of trajectories even when pass rates hold. Measuring Code Sloppiness reports the same design yielding a 0% strict pass rate for state-of-the-art models.

Delegated documents corrupt silently. On DELEGATE-52, frontier models corrupt an average of 25% of document content over 20 delegated interactions. Errors are sparse but severe, and performance after 2 interactions doesn't predict performance after 20 — short evaluations understate the problem. Adding a basic tool-use harness doesn't help.

Isolated-task scores overstate long-horizon ability. GPT-5.4 with OpenHands reaches only 25% on SWE-EVO, whose tasks span about 21 files each; the authors set this against 72.8% for GPT-5.2 on SWE-Bench, so the comparison crosses models as well as benchmarks.

It shows up in real, large-scale runs. The Fermat's Last Theorem formalization initially failed because agents "quickly lost track of the project's state and stopped collaborating effectively," contributing about 7% of non-boilerplate lines. Success required a shared coordination platform, not a better model.

It has a signature mid-run. The Cognitive Companion detects looping, drift and stuck states with a parallel monitor, cutting repetition 52–62%. Its probe-based version reads hidden states at no measured inference overhead, so degradation is visible in the model's internals, not only its output.

docs.title: Five strategies, distinguished by what they treat as unreliable
docs.text:
1. Externalize the procedure. Procedural Graphs stores procedural knowledge as (procedure, relation, procedure) triplets. At each step it locates the agent's active node and turns the surrounding subgraph into guidance that biases the next action without dictating it. The graph evolves under a validation gate: edits commit only if held-out performance holds or improves, and rejected edits are kept to discourage repeating them.

2. Externalize the memory. EverMemOS consolidates history into structured scenes; ReSum takes the cheaper route of periodic summarization, with an RL variant that propagates reward across the summarized segments. Kosmos attributes its ability to stay coherent over about 200 agent rollouts to a structured world model shared between its agents.

3. Decompose until state barely accumulates. MAKER completes a task of over one million LLM steps with zero errors by decomposing it so finely that each micro-agent holds almost no state, then voting at every step. Extreme modularity is what makes per-step error correction affordable. This is the one approach that removes the need to hold state rather than helping the agent hold it.

4. Replace the coordinator. UnitBoost replaces the usual LLM manager — which reads worker outputs, writes the answer, allocates further calls and decides when to stop, all in one opaque, order-sensitive call — with a defined merge operator. Outputs become slot–value proposals, a constrained argmax assembles the result, and unfilled slots become an explicit residual for the next round. It states a guarantee (absent coupling constraints, unit-wise maximization dominates picking any single complete candidate) and maps its own failure region: one indivisible unit, unavailable unit identity, or per-unit pricing.

5. Share state laterally. AgentRadio keeps agents passively aware of teammates' discoveries through a background message layer. Four agents reach 62.1% on long-horizon codebase questions against 32.3% for one agent, and beat a compute-matched best-of-6 single-agent baseline (37.9%) — so the gain is structural, not extra spend. They also top the single-agent leaderboard entry on the newer Opus 4.8 (57.2%), though that entry's cost isn't reported. The multi-agent side of this is covered in Multi-Agent Systems.

docs.title: Memory ablations can manufacture gains that a clean test removes
docs.text:
Many of the gains on this page come from ablations: switch the memory off and report the drop. Persistent Memory in Multi-Agent Inference shows how such an ablation can mislead. On its own chain-of-agents system, a tier that stores reasoning traces and recalls them on later queries cost +0.368 MiB of peak KV cache and changed accuracy by +0.015 (95% CI [−0.011, +0.046]) across eight datasets.

The authors argue that null is built into the test. Single-question benchmarks supply each item's evidence and score items independently, and stored traces must be cleared between conditions so re-runs can't recall their own answers. That leaves recall nothing useful to retrieve: it could fire for only 24% of questions. Their conclusion is that a memory gain reported on an independent-item benchmark is more likely an artifact than a finding. LoCoMo and LongMemEval exist because multi-session settings are needed to test memory at all.

Reaching the null took four corrections, three of which had inflated the apparent benefit and none of which showed in the results table: - the memory tier wrote traces that nothing ever read - fixed-seed re-runs recalled their own earlier answers (100 of 100 questions already had a stored trace) - a parser was fixed in one arm only, producing a fake 37-point gain - run-to-run noise (95% bands of ±0.09–0.10 before stored traces were reset between runs) was larger than every effect they had planned to report

Their checks need no knowledge of the specific bug: assert a non-zero counter for every claimed component, query the store with the evaluation questions before running, diff the two arms' requests, and alternate which arm runs first.

A related finding concerns lossless recovery. In a controlled study of coding-agent harnesses, making elided tool output recoverable through a recall_event tool gave no accuracy gain over plain elision (−0.36 points on average), because models almost never called it. In 56% of the settings where it was available it was never used, and use fell to near zero at 64k and larger windows. Keeping originals retrievable only helps if the agent actually goes back for them.

docs.title: What the evidence supports
docs.text:
• Long context complements memory; it doesn't replace it. Usable context is shorter than advertised, recall degrades gradually with length, and aggregation and absence detection fail well before the window fills.
  • Many of the largest losses happen at write time. STALE's biggest gain came from deciding at write time which entry is current. Brevity bias, context collapse and irreversible compression are all write-time losses. The open choice is between compiling early (cheaper queries, lossy) and compiling late (lossless, costlier per query).
  • Stale memory goes undetected. Benchmarks (STALE, Repo2Skill-Evo) show agents retrieve or keep obsolete entries without flagging them. One practitioner source (Meta) goes further and calls decaying context worse than none, though no source measures that.
  • Structured external state is the most common answer to long-run coherence. Procedural Graphs, EverMemOS and Kosmos each attribute it to a structured, external state representation rather than a growing log, and Externalization in LLM Agents frames memory as relocating state into persistent infrastructure. JAZ and MemAgent show in-context or learned alternatives can also work.
  • Self-modifying memory can be gated. Procedural Graphs and EvolveMem commit changes only after held-out or regression checks. Ungated systems (A-MEM, ReasoningBank, ACE) also report gains, so whether the gate is necessary is open.

docs.title: Open questions
docs.text:
• Compile early or late? GAM and The Hidden Flaw argue for query-time synthesis from originals; ACE, LLM-wiki proponents and most memory systems compile at write time. No source compares them on the same task at matched cost. One data point cuts against "late": coding agents given a tool to recover elided originals almost never used it (Harness Design). GAM puts a dedicated research agent over the store instead of leaving retrieval to the working agent, which may be what makes the difference.
  • How many reported memory gains survive a clean ablation? Persistent Memory found four confounds in its own ablation, three of which inflated the effect, and argues independent-item benchmarks can't show a real gain. Systems on this page that report ablation gains outside multi-session benchmarks haven't been checked against those conditions (Persistent Memory).
  • Can staleness be detected without being told? STALE's prototype and Repo2Skill-Evo both assume a signal that something changed (new dialogue, a release patch). Most real staleness arrives with no such signal.
  • Do the long-horizon strategies compose? Procedural structure, externalized memory, decomposition and lateral messaging act on different layers, but no source evaluates them together. More structure is also more to keep consistent.
  • Does a validation gate arrest degradation? SlopCodeBench and DELEGATE-52 measure ungated iteration. Whether a held-out gate of the kind Procedural Graphs uses slows agents' degradation — SlopCodeBench finds agent code 2.0–2.3× more eroded and verbose than human code — is untested.
  • Monitor or prevent? The Cognitive Companion detects degradation cheaply but helps on loop-prone, open-ended work while being neutral or harmful on structured tasks. Nobody has compared detect-and-recover against prevent-by-structure on one benchmark.
  • Where is the crossover against model improvement? AgentRadio beat a newer model on one task family. When memory and coordination engineering is a better investment than waiting for capability has one data point, not a curve.
  • Learned or engineered memory? MemAgent, NGC and JAZ suggest models can learn or improvise what to keep; MemoryOS, EverMemOS and LightMem engineer it. The sources don't compare the two families directly.

docs.title: What is it
docs.text:
Context engineering is the discipline of managing what information an LLM sees — selection, structure, compression, and delivery — as a first-class engineering concern. It sits above prompt engineering (which focuses on individual instructions) and below model training (which changes weights). The framing is: given a fixed model, the quality of outputs is largely determined by what you put in the context window and how you put it there.

The term appears across research groups and practitioners in 2025–2026 (ACE, Everything is Context, OPENDEV, Effective Context Engineering). Anthropic frames it as superseding prompt engineering once agents run in loops: the object of design is the whole context state, curated cyclically, not a one-shot prompt. This page covers what belongs in the window at each step and how to organize and maintain it; what persists between windows is Agent Memory and Retrieval, and the runtime that manages the window is Harness Engineering.

The short answer: relevant, minimal, on-demand context beats comprehensive context — static context files barely help on their own (unless the repository has little other documentation), while curated knowledge the agent actually lacks can help a lot.

docs.title: More context degrades reasoning
docs.text:
LLMs have bounded context windows. Even as windows grow, quality degrades as they fill — "context rot": recall degrades as tokens grow, across all models, as a gradient rather than a cliff (Effective Context Engineering). Anthropic treats context as an attention budget that every token depletes, so the goal is the smallest set of high-signal tokens that produces the desired behaviour. At the same time, agentic tasks naturally accumulate information across many turns. The tension is fundamental: you need more context to do complex work, but more context degrades reasoning.

Two failure modes show up repeatedly when context is compressed or rewritten (ACE):

  • Brevity bias: prompt and context optimizers drift toward concise, generic summaries, dropping domain-specific knowledge that turns out to be critical. ACE argues that LLMs, unlike humans, benefit from long, detailed contexts
  • Context collapse: iterative rewriting of context erodes details from prior rounds, causing cumulative degradation

The two pull in opposite directions — shrink the context and lose detail, keep it and lose attention — which is why the rest of this page is about which context, not how much.

docs.title: Context spans much more than the prompt
docs.text:
What can go into the window:

  • System prompts and instructions
  • Project-specific knowledge (conventions, architecture, known failure modes)
  • Retrieved documents (RAG)
  • Tool schemas and capabilities
  • Conversation/task history
  • Human contributions and tacit knowledge (Everything is Context)

Everything is Context treats all of this as a governed, file-system-mounted resource; Codified Context calls it infrastructure — load-bearing artifacts the agent depends on, not advisory documentation.

docs.title: Relevant context beats comprehensive context
docs.text:
Context files barely help and can hurt. Developer-provided context files improve task success by about 4% on average, LLM-generated ones reduce it by about 3%, and both increase inference cost by over 20%. Unnecessary constraints actively hurt performance. The practical implication: context files should describe minimal requirements, not everything you know. The exception is a repository with no other documentation: there, LLM-generated context files improved performance by 2.7% on average and outperformed developer-written ones (Evaluating AGENTS.md). This is a controlled evaluation.

But the right content may help a lot. In a single-developer experience report, specialist agents embedding substantial project knowledge (often over half of each agent's content) were observed to make fewer errors in bug-prone domains than agents without pre-loaded context (Codified Context). That suggests relevant context matters more than comprehensive context, though no controlled comparison was run.

LinkedIn's data context layer points the same way at larger scale: agents already wrote valid SQL, and what they lacked was which dataset to trust, which filters were required and what a row meant. In one business-area benchmark the permission-adjusted acceptable-answer rate rose from 25.9% to 79.5%; in a separate comparison, median time to answer fell from 10.7 to 4.7 minutes. These are early internal figures measured against an earlier version of the analytics agent, so they don't isolate the effect of context alone (LinkedIn).

docs.title: Load context on demand, in structure
docs.text:
The organizing principles that recur across sources all keep the always-loaded core small and fetch the rest when needed:

  • Hot/cold separation. Always-loaded essentials vs. on-demand retrieval. A single-file manifest (CLAUDE.md) doesn't scale beyond modest codebases; large projects need tiered architectures with domain-specialist agents and separate specification documents (Codified Context).
  • Modular, conditionally loaded sections. Sections load based on context relevance (OPENDEV); keep the core prompt small and let the model load skills at runtime, so context is demand-paged rather than preloaded (Towards a Harness That Can Do Anything).
  • Just-in-time over pre-loading for dynamic environments: keep lightweight identifiers (paths, queries, links) and load on demand; for tasks that outrun the window, use compaction, structured notes kept outside the window, and sub-agents that return distilled summaries (Effective Context Engineering).
  • Durable state in files. Long-horizon artifacts outgrow the window, so durable state belongs in files — and reading and writing files is a core trained capability that improves with the base model (Harness Engineering for Self-Improvement).
  • Structured formats resist inappropriate edits. Anthropic found JSON beat Markdown for feature-tracking state because agents were less likely to overwrite it (Charlie Guo). Procedural Graphs goes further, storing procedural knowledge as a queryable graph rather than prose in a system prompt.
  • Scope context per stage, and keep rules apart from inputs. ICM gives each stage of a workflow its own folder and a contract listing exactly which files to load, keeping each stage at 2–8k tokens against roughly 42k for a prompt that loads everything. It also separates reference material (stable across runs, to be followed as constraints) from working artifacts (per-run, to be transformed). The quality benefit is argued from the lost-in-the-middle literature and practitioner reports, not measured against a monolithic baseline.
  • Navigate by summary indexes instead of loading the corpus. LinkedIn's data context layer arranges curated documents under a tree of indexes, each holding summaries of its children. An agent walks the tree through MCP calls and reaches the right document in about four reads, without unrelated files entering the window.

Most of these are design reports and practitioner experience. The measured support is indirect: the context-file evaluation above (less is better) and the harness-search results below (selection beats volume).

docs.title: Context can be maintained by hand, by the agent, or by search
docs.text:
Context is maintained in one of three ways:

  • Static — written once, updated manually
  • Adaptive — updated by the agent based on execution feedback (ACE)
  • Automatically optimized — outer-loop search over harness configurations (Meta-Harness)

Automated selection has the strongest numbers. Meta-Harness, citing prior work, notes that changing only the harness around a fixed model can produce a 6× gap on the same benchmark. Its own outer-loop search beats the best context-management baseline by 7.7 points with 4× fewer context tokens (Meta-Harness).

Generated and curated context can also live in separate layers. LinkedIn has an LLM pipeline write baseline profiles of datasets from schemas, query logs, code and sample rows, while owners add business rules, exceptions and known data-quality issues as Markdown reviewed through pull requests. The two layers are stored apart so that pipeline refreshes never overwrite human corrections, and are returned together at retrieval (LinkedIn).

docs.title: Constraint may beat freedom
docs.text: OpenAI's experience, as reported by Charlie Guo, is that trust in AI-generated code rose when the solution space was constrained — a strict layered architecture enforced by linters. This is a practitioner report, not a measured result, but it is consistent with the finding that more instructions don't help: what constrains the agent mechanically works where prose that asks it to behave doesn't. The evidence for executable over static context is gathered in Executable Context.

docs.title: What the evidence supports
docs.text:
• Keep always-loaded context minimal. In the one controlled evaluation, developer-written context files gave about +4% on average and LLM-generated ones about −3%, at over 20% extra cost, and unnecessary constraints hurt. Where a repository has no other documentation, LLM-generated files instead helped (+2.7%) (Evaluating AGENTS.md).
  • Spend context on what the agent can't infer. Domain knowledge the agent lacks (which data to trust, project-specific failure modes) is where the large reported gains are — LinkedIn's 25.9% → 79.5% (LinkedIn) and Codified Context's fewer errors (Codified Context) — though neither isolates context from other changes.
  • Load on demand rather than up front. Every architecture surveyed keeps a small core and fetches the rest; the support is design reports plus Anthropic's account of context rot from needle-in-a-haystack studies (Effective Context Engineering).
  • Automated harness search beats hand-designed context-management harnesses. On text classification, Meta-Harness beat ACE by 7.7 points with about 4× fewer context tokens. That is one domain in one paper (Meta-Harness).
  • Don't let rewriting erode context. Brevity bias and context collapse are documented failure modes of iterative compression (ACE); layering generated and curated context separately is one defence (LinkedIn).

docs.title: In practice
docs.text:
The harness engineering playbook distills to four practices (Charlie Guo):

  1. Architecture as guardrails — enforce structure mechanically (linters, schemas), not just via instructions
  2. Tools as feedback — custom error messages that teach the agent while it works; remediation instructions embedded in tooling
  3. AGENTS.md as living system of record — updated every time the agent makes a mistake; points to deeper sources of truth rather than containing everything
  4. Plan before execute — agents should never write code without an approved written plan

Beyond those: write context files as a short index of pointers rather than a manual (Relevant context beats comprehensive context); scope context per stage and per sub-agent (Load context on demand, in structure); and keep machine-generated and human-curated context in separate layers (Context can be maintained by hand, by the agent, or by search).

docs.title: Open questions
docs.text:
• How do you maintain context quality over time? Agent-generated code accumulates cruft differently than human code; the "garbage collection" problem for context is unsolved (Charlie Guo).
  • How do you verify completeness? Agents mark things complete without proper end-to-end validation (Charlie Guo).
  • Does any of this transfer to brownfield codebases? The success stories surveyed by Charlie Guo all involve greenfield projects.
  • Where is the Pareto frontier of context size vs. quality? More data is needed on when adding context stops helping and starts hurting (Evaluating AGENTS.md).
  • Does selective loading still matter as windows grow? ICM's authors note that if models attend reliably over 200k tokens, the efficiency case for stage-scoped context weakens, though inspectability and editability remain. Whether structurally separating rules from inputs improves output over a flat context of the same content is also untested (ICM).
