docs.title: What is it
docs.text:
Executable context practices are concrete ways to give AI coding agents feedback they can run against — executable specs, property tests, type systems, linter rules, teaching tool output, review gates and outcome metrics — in place of instructions they have to read and remember. This page is a how-to guide for engineering teams integrating AI coding agents into professional workflows: backend services (Java), data pipelines (Scala) and ML systems (Python), using tools such as Claude Code, Copilot or similar agents.

The evidence behind each practice is on the companion page, Executable Context; each practice below states its evidence and links the section it rests on. Practices are grouped by what they do, and each can be adopted independently. Code examples alternate between Java, Scala and Python. Where a practice is extrapolated rather than measured, it says so.

The short answer: start with executable specs before implementation, linter rules as guardrails, separated test authorship, performance gates and plan approval; stop writing monolithic context files and stop judging adoption by how it feels.

docs.title: Executable specs before implementation
docs.text:
Evidence: strongest effect size here, +46pp pass@1 for interactive test clarification — though TiCoder measured clarification with simulated users, not this exact workflow (Executable Context).

Write failing tests that define the requirement before asking an agent to implement. The tests are the spec — executable, unambiguous, and verifiable. It has the strongest supporting effect size in this document (+46pp in TiCoder), though TiCoder measured interactive clarification rather than this exact workflow.

Python — ML feature store

# spec_test_feature_store.py — human-authored, agent cannot edit
def test_feature_freshness_sla():
    """Features older than 6h must trigger a refresh, not serve stale."""
    store = FeatureStore(staleness_threshold=timedelta(hours=6))
    store.ingest("user_spend", value=100.0, ts=now() - timedelta(hours=7))

    with pytest.raises(StaleFeatureError):
        store.get("user_spend", strict=True)

def test_feature_backfill_is_idempotent():
    store = FeatureStore()
    store.backfill("user_spend", date(2026, 1, 1), date(2026, 1, 31))
    store.backfill("user_spend", date(2026, 1, 15), date(2026, 1, 31))  # overlap
    assert store.count("user_spend", date(2026, 1, 15)) == 1  # no duplicates

Anti-pattern — NL-only specification:

## Feature Store
- Features should be fresh
- Backfill should work correctly

This tells the agent what but not how much, when, or what happens at the boundary. The agent fills in the gaps with plausible but unverified assumptions.

Sources: TiCoder, Intent Formalization

docs.title: Property-based tests for invariants
docs.text:
Evidence: practitioner reports of hardcoded and mocked test-passing (Executable Context); agentic PBT found real bugs (56% valid in a sample, 86% of top-ranked) but did not measure resistance to gaming (Agentic PBT).

Example-based tests are gameable — an agent can hardcode return values that match specific assertions. Property-based tests generate hundreds of random inputs, making cheating structurally difficult. Agentic PBT found real bugs in NumPy and aws-lambda-powertools. In a random sample of 50 reports (drawn from the top 80% by an initial LLM score), 56% were valid bugs; under a refined ranking rubric, 18 of the 21 top-scoring reports (86%) were valid.

Scala — data pipeline

// Properties the agent's implementation must satisfy — agent cannot edit this file
class CurrencyConversionSpec extends ScalaCheckSuite {

  property("conversion roundtrip preserves value within tolerance") {
    forAll(genPositiveAmount, genCurrencyPair) { (amount, (from, to)) =>
      val converted = convert(amount, from, to)
      val roundtripped = convert(converted, to, from)
      assert(Math.abs(roundtripped - amount) / amount < 0.001)
    }
  }

  property("zero amount converts to zero in any currency") {
    forAll(genCurrencyPair) { case (from, to) =>
      assertEquals(convert(0.0, from, to), 0.0)
    }
  }

  property("conversion is monotonic — larger input yields larger output") {
    forAll(genPositiveAmount, genPositiveAmount, genCurrencyPair) {
      (a, b, (from, to)) =>
        if (a > b) assert(convert(a, from, to) >= convert(b, from, to))
    }
  }
}

The key: these properties are hard to satisfy by accident. An agent that hardcodes return values will fail on random inputs. An agent that implements correctly will pass on all of them.

Sources: Agentic PBT, Property Based Testing

docs.title: Choose a level of formalization
docs.text:
Evidence: LLM-generated postconditions caught 1 in 8 real Defects4J bugs (Intent Formalization); the table is a guide, not a measured ranking.

Tests are not the only form of executable specification. The spectrum runs from lightweight to heavy:

Level Example Effort Verification strength Unit tests assert f(2) == 4 Low Spot checks Property tests forAll(x => f(f_inv(x)) == x) Medium Invariant coverage Code contracts @requires x > 0 @ensures result > x Medium Pre/post conditions Type constraints sealed interface + exhaustive match Low Compiler-enforced Formal specs TLA+, Alloy High Model checking

LLM-generated postconditions caught 1 in 8 real bugs on Defects4J, including bugs missed by classical invariant detectors. The further down this table you move, the stronger the guarantees.

Source: Intent Formalization

docs.title: Type systems as verification layers
docs.text:
Evidence: type-constrained decoding more than halves compilation errors in one controlled study (Type-Constrained Code Generation).

94% of compilation errors in LLM-generated TypeScript are type errors rather than syntax errors. Type-constrained decoding, which enforces well-typedness during generation, cuts compilation errors by more than half and raises functional correctness by 3.5–5.5% (relative). Use the type system to make invalid states unrepresentable — the compiler becomes a verification layer that runs on every build.

Java — backend payment service

// Sealed types force exhaustive handling — agent can't forget a case
public sealed interface PaymentResult
    permits PaymentSuccess, PaymentDeclined, PaymentRequiresAction {

  record PaymentSuccess(TransactionId id, Instant settledAt)
      implements PaymentResult {}

  record PaymentDeclined(DeclineReason reason)
      implements PaymentResult {}

  record PaymentRequiresAction(URI redirectUrl, Duration expiry)
      implements PaymentResult {}
}

// Compiler enforces every branch — no "default: throw" needed
public String toUserMessage(PaymentResult result) {
  return switch (result) {
    case PaymentSuccess s      -> "Settled: " + s.id();
    case PaymentDeclined d     -> "Declined: " + d.reason();
    case PaymentRequiresAction a -> "Action needed: " + a.redirectUrl();
  };
}

Anti-pattern — stringly-typed APIs:

// Agent will happily generate invalid status strings
public void handlePayment(String status, Map<String, Object> details) {
    if (status.equals("success")) { /* ... */ }  // typo? casing? missing case?
}

Source: Type-Constrained Code Generation

docs.title: Linter rules as architecture guardrails
docs.text:
Evidence: practitioner view only (OpenAI, via the harness engineering playbook); no controlled study (Harness Engineering Playbook).

Custom linter errors double as remediation instructions — they teach the agent while it works. The .because() message is what the agent sees when it violates the rule, turning enforcement into feedback. This is the "architecture as guardrails" practice from the harness engineering playbook: enforce structure via executable rules, not prose instructions.

Java — ArchUnit

@AnalyzeClasses(packages = "com.spotify.payments")
public class ArchitectureRules {

    @ArchTest
    static final ArchRule domain_must_not_depend_on_infrastructure =
        noClasses().that().resideInAPackage("..domain..")
            .should().dependOnClassesThat()
            .resideInAPackage("..infrastructure..")
            .because("Domain layer must stay portable — "
                + "use a port/adapter interface instead");

    @ArchTest
    static final ArchRule controllers_must_not_call_repositories =
        noClasses().that().areAnnotatedWith(RestController.class)
            .should().dependOnClassesThat()
            .areAnnotatedWith(Repository.class)
            .because("Controllers call services, not repositories — "
                + "add a service method");
}

OpenAI's view, relayed in the harness engineering playbook, is that increasing trust in agent output requires constraining the solution space. It is presented as an insight, not a measured result.

Source: Harness Engineering Playbook

docs.title: Schema-level constraints
docs.text:
Evidence: extrapolated from the type-system and linter practices on this page; no source measures it directly.

The same principle applies to data schemas: enforce invariants at the schema level, not in application code. This is a practice recommendation extrapolated from the sections above; no source here measures it directly.

Scala — Spark schema enforcement

val transactionSchema = StructType(Seq(
  StructField("transaction_id", StringType, nullable = false),
  StructField("amount_cents", LongType, nullable = false),  // cents, not dollars
  StructField("currency", StringType, nullable = false),
  StructField("timestamp", TimestampType, nullable = false)
))

// Fail fast on schema violations — agent sees exactly what's wrong
def validateBatch(df: DataFrame): DataFrame = {
  val validated = spark.createDataFrame(df.rdd, transactionSchema)
  require(
    validated.filter(col("amount_cents") < 0).isEmpty,
    "Negative amounts found — check upstream currency conversion"
  )
  validated
}

An agent that tries to use DoubleType for monetary amounts or allows nullable transaction IDs gets an immediate, actionable error.

docs.title: Tool output that teaches
docs.text:
Evidence: +10.7pp on SWE-bench Lite from interface design alone (Executable Context).

SWE-agent's 10.7pp improvement came from interface design alone. The principle: every error message should be a remediation instruction. Custom tool output teaches the agent while it works, compounding over the course of a session.

Python — ML training harness

class TrainingHarness:
    def validate_config(self, config: TrainConfig) -> None:
        if config.learning_rate > 1e-2:
            raise ConfigError(
                f"learning_rate={config.learning_rate} is dangerously high. "
                f"Typical range for this architecture: 1e-5 to 1e-3. "
                f"If intentional, set force_high_lr=True."
            )
        if config.batch_size % 8 != 0:
            raise ConfigError(
                f"batch_size={config.batch_size} not divisible by 8. "
                f"Wastes GPU memory on A100s due to tensor core alignment. "
                f"Nearest valid: {(config.batch_size // 8 + 1) * 8}"
            )
        if config.warmup_steps > config.total_steps * 0.2:
            raise ConfigError(
                f"warmup_steps={config.warmup_steps} is >{20}% of "
                f"total_steps={config.total_steps}. This leaves too little "
                f"time for lr decay. Typical: 5-10% of total steps."
            )

Anti-pattern — raw exceptions:

# Agent can't learn from this
raise ValueError("invalid config")

Sources: SWE-agent, The Art of Tool Interface Design

docs.title: Iterative execution over one-shot generation
docs.text:
Evidence: ~20% on average across seven mostly non-code tasks from self-feedback with no execution (Self-Refine); trace-fed optimizers beat score-fed ones (Executable Context).

Self-Refine reports ~20% absolute improvement on average across seven tasks (up to 13% on code generation) from generate-critique-refine loops — using the model's own feedback, with no execution. Meta-Harness shows that optimizers with access to full execution traces beat ones fed compressed scalar scores. Together they suggest the loop is the mechanism, and that richer feedback helps: give the agent the ability to run its output, observe the result, and iterate.

Scala — iterative schema evolution

// Don't generate the final schema in one shot from a description.
// Let the agent iterate against executable validation.

def validateSchema(schema: StructType, sample: DataFrame): SchemaReport = {
  val nullViolations = sample.columns.filter { col =>
    !schema(col).nullable &&
      sample.filter(F.col(col).isNull).count() > 0
  }
  val typeCoercions = detectImplicitCoercions(schema, sample)
  val cardinalityAnomalies = detectCardinalityAnomalies(schema, sample)

  SchemaReport(
    violations = nullViolations,
    warnings = typeCoercions ++ cardinalityAnomalies,
    suggestion =
      if (nullViolations.nonEmpty)
        s"Mark ${nullViolations.mkString(", ")} as nullable, or fix upstream"
      else "Schema consistent with sample data"
  )
}

Run validation after each schema change. The agent sees what broke, why, and what to try next.

Sources: Self-Refine, Meta-Harness

docs.title: Context files as an index to executable checks
docs.text:
Evidence: inferred from the AGENTS.md evaluation (+4% / −3%, broader exploration); the +37.5pp KG result is indirect (Executable Context).

Use AGENTS.md as an index that points to executable checks, not as a knowledge container. This is this page's inference from the AGENTS.md evaluation, which found context files encourage broader exploration while unnecessary requirements in them hurt performance.

Practical example:

## Payment Service — AGENTS.md

### Architecture
Enforced by ArchUnit: `src/test/java/arch/ArchitectureRules.java`
Run: `./gradlew archTest`

### Domain invariants
Property tests: `src/test/java/properties/PaymentProperties.java`
Run: `./gradlew propertyTest`

### API contracts
Contract tests: `src/contractTest/`
Run: `./gradlew contractTest`

### Boundaries
- Do NOT add retry logic without checking `RetryPolicy.java` (central policy)
- Do NOT call payment providers directly (use `PaymentGateway` port)
- Do NOT store card data outside `SecureVault` (PCI scope)

Twenty lines. Every claim is verifiable. The agent knows where to look and what to run, not just what to believe.

Anti-pattern — monolithic documentation:

## Rules
- Use Java 21
- Use Spring Boot 3.4
- Use constructor injection not field injection
- Use records for DTOs
- Always use var for local variables
- Never use Optional.get() without isPresent()
... (47 more rules)

Most of these should be linter rules. Putting them in documentation means they're only enforced when the agent reads them, remembers them, and chooses to comply. Linters enforce them every time, automatically, with feedback.

Sources: Evaluating AGENTS.md, Good Spec, KG Benchmark

docs.title: Separate test authorship from implementation
docs.text:
Evidence: practitioner reports of test gaming when one context writes both (Executable Context).

Agents adapt tests to match their implementation when both are in the same context. The structural countermeasure: write interface tests in a separate agent context with minimal knowledge of the implementation. The test knows the contract, not the code.

Java — contract test in a separate module

// Lives in :payment-contract-tests, separate from :payment-service
// Agent implementing the service never sees this code
@SpringBootTest(webEnvironment = RANDOM_PORT)
class PaymentApiContractTest {

    @Test
    void charge_idempotency_key_prevents_double_charge() {
        var key = UUID.randomUUID().toString();
        var charge = new ChargeRequest("tok_visa", 1000, "SEK");

        var first  = post("/v1/charges", charge,
            header("Idempotency-Key", key));
        var second = post("/v1/charges", charge,
            header("Idempotency-Key", key));

        assertThat(first.statusCode()).isEqualTo(201);
        assertThat(second.statusCode()).isEqualTo(200);  // not 201
        assertThat(second.body().id()).isEqualTo(first.body().id());
    }

    @Test
    void charge_with_expired_token_returns_402() {
        var charge = new ChargeRequest("tok_expired", 500, "SEK");
        var response = post("/v1/charges", charge);

        assertThat(response.statusCode()).isEqualTo(402);
        assertThat(response.body().error().code())
            .isEqualTo("card_declined");
    }
}

The agent implementing the payment service sees failing contract tests as a signal to fix, not as a template to reverse-engineer.

Source: How To Effectively Write Quality Code With AI

docs.title: Performance invariants alongside correctness
docs.text:
Evidence: a single, contested case: test-passing code about 20,000x slower on one benchmark (Executable Context).

Functional tests are necessary but not sufficient. The SQLite case (about 20,000x slower on one benchmark, despite passing its tests) shows that correctness tests say nothing about performance. Add executable performance gates to CI.

Python — ML inference performance gate

@pytest.mark.benchmark
def test_inference_latency_p99(trained_model, benchmark_inputs):
    """p99 latency must stay under 50ms for single-item inference."""
    latencies = []
    for x in benchmark_inputs:  # 1000 representative samples
        start = time.perf_counter_ns()
        trained_model.predict(x)
        latencies.append((time.perf_counter_ns() - start) / 1e6)

    p99 = sorted(latencies)[int(len(latencies) * 0.99)]
    assert p99 < 50.0, f"p99={p99:.1f}ms exceeds 50ms SLA"

@pytest.mark.benchmark
def test_batch_throughput(trained_model, benchmark_batch):
    """Must process 10k items in under 5 seconds on CPU."""
    start = time.perf_counter()
    trained_model.predict_batch(benchmark_batch)
    elapsed = time.perf_counter() - start
    assert elapsed < 5.0, f"Batch took {elapsed:.1f}s, budget is 5s"

These tests fail before deployment. A regression from an agent-generated optimization that speeds up one path while degrading another is caught immediately.

Source: Your LLM Doesn't Write Correct Code

docs.title: Audit trails for unreviewed code
docs.text:
Evidence: practitioner recommendation; no source measures it (Quality Code with AI).

Maintain explicit markers on AI-generated code that has not been human-reviewed. Code that looks reviewed but wasn't is worse than code that's visibly unreviewed.

Java — review annotation

@HighRiskUnreviewed(
    generatedBy = "claude-2026-04",
    reason = "Retry logic with exponential backoff — "
        + "verify jitter bounds and max retry cap"
)
public RetryPolicy buildRetryPolicy(RetryConfig config) {
    return RetryPolicy.builder()
        .maxRetries(config.maxRetries())
        .initialDelay(config.initialDelay())
        .multiplier(config.backoffMultiplier())
        .jitter(config.jitterFactor())
        .build();
}

Add a CI check: grep -r @HighRiskUnreviewed --include='*.java' | wc -l as a reported metric. Track the count over time. Set a threshold if appropriate for your risk profile.

Source: How To Effectively Write Quality Code With AI

docs.title: Plan-then-execute with review gates
docs.text:
Evidence: HULA approved 82% of generated plans, 59% of raised PRs merged, and about 8% of issues ended in a merged PR — the gate is necessary, not sufficient (HULA; (Executable Context).

Have a human review the agent's plan before it writes code. The HULA framework at Atlassian uses this pattern on real JIRA issues: 82% of generated plans were approved, but only 25% of code-generated issues produced a PR and 56 of 663 issues (about 8%) ended in a merged PR — though 59% of the PRs it raised were merged. Plan review catches bad plans early; it doesn't make the code that follows correct.

The GEICO post relays Faros AI telemetry on AI adoption (10,000+ developers): task completion up 21%, but PR review time up 91% and bugs per developer up 9%. It is secondhand vendor data, and the post notes it does not prove harm.

Practical gate — GitHub Actions:

- name: Check plan approval
  run: |
    APPROVED=$(gh pr view $PR --json comments -q \
      '.comments[] | select(.body | contains("PLAN APPROVED"))')
    if [ -z "$APPROVED" ]; then
      echo "::error::Agent plan not yet approved. Add PLAN APPROVED comment."
      exit 1
    fi

Sources: Spec-Driven Development, HULA

docs.title: Worktree isolation with test-gated merge
docs.text:
Evidence: +26.7% on PaperBench and +14.3% on Commit0 over a single agent (CAID).

CAID demonstrates +26.7% on PaperBench and +14.3% on Commit0 by combining git worktree isolation with test-based merge verification. Each agent works in an isolated copy of the repository. Merges are gated on passing tests — both in the branch and after integration.

# Agent A: payment retry logic
git worktree add ../payment-retry feature/payment-retry
cd ../payment-retry
# ... agent works ...
./gradlew test                    # branch gate

# Agent B: notification service (parallel, isolated)
git worktree add ../notifications feature/notifications
cd ../notifications
# ... agent works ...
./gradlew test                    # branch gate

# Integration — sequential, after both branch gates pass
git merge --no-ff feature/payment-retry
git merge --no-ff feature/notifications
./gradlew test                    # integration gate

The pattern maps directly from human software engineering primitives (git, CI, code review) to agent coordination. Nothing novel is required — just discipline.

Source: CAID

docs.title: Give each agent its own signal
docs.text:
Evidence: role decomposition over the same model and context cannot beat a single decision maker in theory; empirical exceptions exist (Executable Context, Multi-Agent Systems).

Multi-agent is valuable when each agent interacts with a different part of the environment. Agent A runs tests on module X while Agent B runs tests on module Y — each gets exogenous signal the other doesn't have. But Agent A "planning" and Agent B "reviewing" with the same context adds roles, not information. Deploy human review where automated posterior risk exceeds review cost — not as a blanket policy, but targeted at the highest-risk decisions (Reliability Limits).

docs.title: Measure outcomes, not perceptions
docs.text:
Evidence: developers were 19% slower while believing they were 20% faster (Executable Context).

Measure outcomes, not opinions:

Metric What it captures How to collect Cycle time (commit to production) End-to-end velocity Git + deployment pipeline Defect escape rate Correctness of shipped code Bug tracker, post-deployment incidents Rework rate Maintainability, first-time quality PRs that revert or immediately follow-up fix Review turnaround Overhead of human verification PR timestamps Test coverage delta Agent testing discipline CI coverage reports, diffcov @HighRiskUnreviewed count Audit trail completeness grep + trend

Collect per-team, per-task-type. Compare before and after agent adoption. Do not aggregate across teams — the variance is the signal.

Do not use lines of code, number of PRs, or "time to first commit" as proxies. The SQLite case — 576,000 lines that passed their tests but ran about 20,000x slower on one benchmark — shows that volume measures nothing about value (Your LLM Doesn't Write Correct Code).

Source: Your LLM Doesn't Write Correct Code

docs.title: Evaluate in tiers
docs.text:
Evidence: Anthropic's eval guidance (Demystifying Evals) and a practitioner survey (N=31) in which 74% rely on human evaluation (MAP).

Production agent evaluation follows three tiers, each with different cost/fidelity tradeoffs:

Tier 1 — Deterministic / code-based graders. Fast, cheap, objective, brittle. Compile checks, test suites, linter passes, type checks. Run on every commit. Catches regressions reliably but misses semantic correctness.

Tier 2 — Model-based graders. Flexible, slower, more expensive. LLM judges evaluate output quality, planning coherence, code style. Useful for subjective dimensions, but vague rubrics produce inconsistent judgments.

Tier 3 — Human evaluation. Ground truth, expensive, slow. In a survey of practitioners with deployed agents (N=31, multi-select), 74% rely on human-in-the-loop evaluation. This is not a sign of immaturity — it reflects the current state of automated evaluation.

Evaluations compound in value: they serve as regression testing, upgrade confidence, and a product-research feedback channel. Start with Tier 1 (free, immediate), add Tier 2 for dimensions Tier 1 can't cover, and use Tier 3 strategically for the highest-stakes decisions.

Rigid graders can fail valid solutions — frontier models find policy loopholes the eval authors didn't anticipate — and loose graders can be exploited. Graders need to be both flexible and bypass-resistant, and the suite needs to evolve alongside the models it evaluates.

Sources: Demystifying Evals, Measuring Agents in Production

docs.title: Where to start
docs.text:
Ordered by evidence strength and implementation cost:

  1. Executable specs before implementation (Executable specs). +46pp. Zero tooling cost — you already have a test framework. Requires discipline, not infrastructure.

  2. Linter rules as architecture guardrails (Linter rules). Practitioner-reported (OpenAI); not measured in a controlled study. One-time setup (ArchUnit, pylint custom rules, scalafix). Compounds over time as rules accumulate.

  3. Separate test authorship from implementation (Separate test authorship). Prevents test gaming. Organizational change — put contract tests in a separate module with a separate owner.

  4. Performance gates in CI (Performance invariants). Catches the class of bug that correctness tests miss. Requires representative benchmark data.

  5. Plan-then-execute gates (Plan-then-execute). In HULA, 18% of generated plans were not approved, so no code was written for them. The end-to-end merge rate was about 8% of issues (56 of 663), though 59% of the PRs it raised were merged (HULA).

docs.title: What to stop
docs.text:
1. Stop writing monolithic context files. LLM-generated context hurts (−3%) and developer-written context files give a marginal benefit (+4% on average), both at 20%+ cost increase (Evaluating AGENTS.md). Replace with 20-line index files pointing to executable checks.

  2. Stop relying on developer surveys for AI tool evaluation. The 19% vs +20% perception gap makes self-reported data unreliable. Use observable metrics (Measure outcomes).

  3. Stop letting agents author and verify in the same context. This is the structural root cause of test gaming (Executable Context). Separation is non-negotiable for high-stakes code.

  4. Stop treating multi-agent as a default improvement. Under matched compute, single agents match or beat multi-agent systems on multi-hop reasoning benchmarks (Executable Context). Use multi-agent when the work decomposes into parallel parts; see Multi-Agent Systems.

  5. Stop using lines of code as a productivity metric. Volume measures nothing about value: a 576K-line generated codebase passed its tests yet ran about 20,000x slower on one benchmark (Your LLM Doesn't Write Correct Code).

docs.title: Organizational implications
docs.text:
The research points to a structural shift in engineering roles:

One practitioner frames the overall shift directly: more capable code generation raises, not lowers, the requirement for engineering rigor.

Specification becomes the critical path. As code generation becomes cheaper, the ability to precisely specify what to build becomes more valuable than the ability to build it. This shifts leverage toward senior engineers, architects, and domain experts who can write executable specs. The Spec-Driven Development literature calls this "shifting the specifier-to-implementer ratio."

Review changes character. With plan-then-execute gates, review happens before code exists, at the spec and plan level. Post-implementation review shifts from "is this code correct?" to "does this code match the approved plan?" — arguably a more tractable question, though spec review adds its own burden and the payoff is "plausible but not yet proven at scale" (Spec-Driven Development).

Testing becomes an architectural discipline. Where to place tests, what to make property-based vs. example-based, how to isolate test contexts from implementation contexts — these are architectural decisions, not afterthoughts.

Measurement infrastructure is prerequisite. Without the outcome metrics, you cannot distinguish real improvement from the perception gap. Invest in measurement before investing in agent tooling.

Sources: Spec-Driven Development, Professional Developers Don't Vibe, Measuring Agents in Production

docs.title: Quick reference
docs.text: # Practice Mechanism Evidence Details 1 Executable specs before implementation Tests as partial intent formalization +46pp pass@1 (simulated users) Go 2 Property-based tests for invariants Random inputs, auto-shrinking 56% valid (random sample); 86% of top-ranked Go 3 Type system as verification layer Compiler-enforced exhaustiveness Compilation errors more than halved Go 4 Linter rules as architecture guardrails Executable rules with remediation Practitioner report only Go 5 Tool output that teaches Compact, actionable error messages +10.7pp from ACI design Go 6 Iterative execution loops Generate-critique-refine ~20% avg over 7 tasks, ≤13% on code (self-feedback, no execution) Go 7 Structured context as index Pointers to executable checks Inferred; +37.5pp KG result is indirect Go 8 Separate test and impl contexts Cross-context interface tests Prevents test gaming Go 9 Performance invariant tests Benchmark gates in CI Catches 20,000x regressions Go 10 Audit trail annotations @HighRiskUnreviewed markers Explicit review state Go 11 Plan-then-execute gates Human approves before code 82% plan approval; ~8% of issues merged Go 12 Worktree isolation + test gates Git-based agent coordination +14-27% task completion Go 13 Measure actual impact Observable metrics, not surveys 19% slower vs 20% perceived Go

docs.title: Open questions
docs.text:
• What makes plan approval translate into merged code? HULA approved 82% of plans but merged PRs for about 8% of issues. Where the drop-off happens after approval is not broken down.
  • Can measurement close the perception gap? METR shows self-assessment is unreliable; whether the outcome metrics actually change team decisions has not been studied.
  • Do the code-level practices transfer across stacks? The examples span Java, Scala and Python, but the evidence behind them comes mostly from Python and TypeScript benchmarks; none of the practices has been measured in a JVM codebase.

docs.title: What is it
docs.text:
Executable context is the practice of giving AI coding agents feedback they can act on — tests, type checkers, linters, REPL output, structured exploration of the codebase — instead of, or in addition to, static markdown instructions. The tests, checks and tool output are context the agent can run against, rather than prose it has to interpret and remember.

This page examines the claim that executable and interactive context produces materially more correct, robust and maintainable code than documentation alone, and that the engineer's leverage lies in designing the environment the agent works in rather than in writing prompts. It draws on controlled comparisons of context formats, agent-computer interface and harness design, the measured effect of repository context files, and the failure modes — plausible-but-wrong code, gamed tests, misjudged productivity — that appear when verification is missing. How to apply the findings in a team is the companion page, Executable Context Practices.

The short answer: several independent lines of evidence point the same way — interactive tests, structured representations and designed tool interfaces outperform their non-interactive or unstructured baselines (plain prompting, raw SQL schemas, a default shell), and the one study that measures static context files directly finds marginal gains at best — but the studies measure different tasks with different metrics, and no study compares the two head-to-head on one coding benchmark.

docs.title: Interactive tests clarify intent better than prose
docs.text:
The most direct evidence comes from Microsoft Research's TiCoder study. Interactive test-based intent clarification — where the user and the LLM iteratively refine understanding through executable unit tests — produces a 45.97% absolute improvement in pass@1 over code generation without clarification, across four state-of-the-art LLMs on two Python datasets within five interactions — with user feedback simulated by an idealized proxy. (The 15-programmer user study measured how well users judged code and their cognitive load, not pass@1.) Note what is being compared: LLM-proposed tests clarified with (simulated) user feedback, not human-written failing tests against documentation. Tests serve as partial formalization of intent: executable, verifiable, unambiguous. Static natural-language descriptions leave the intent gap open.

As a side effect, the interaction produces a test suite — the specification artifact is the verification artifact.

Source: TiCoder: LLM-Based Test-Driven Interactive Code Generation

docs.title: Structured representations beat flat text for relational questions
docs.text:
The starkest controlled comparison in the corpus. GPT-4 answering questions about an enterprise SQL database achieves 16.7% accuracy when querying the SQL schema directly and 54.2% accuracy when the database is exposed as a knowledge graph — a 37.5 percentage point delta. The KG setup includes an ontology layer with business context, so this compares a representation plus added semantics, not format alone. The task is enterprise question answering, not coding.

GraphRAG work points the same way for relational queries: it improves precision and comprehensiveness by capturing relational knowledge that flat retrieval misses, particularly for multi-hop queries that require reasoning across entities.

Sources: KG Benchmark for Enterprise SQL QA, Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation: A Survey

docs.title: Interface design moves agent performance without changing the model
docs.text:
SWE-agent demonstrated that designing interfaces specifically for LLM agents — compact feedback, guardrails against error propagation, informative but concise responses — produced, as the paper reports, 10.7 percentage points of improvement over a default Linux shell in ablations on SWE-bench Lite (its own table puts the gap at about 7 points when the shell-only agent also gets demonstrations). Separately, SWE-agent reached 12.47% on full SWE-bench against a previous best of 3.8% from non-interactive retrieval-augmented systems — a different comparison. Claude 3 Opus achieved 10.5% despite SWE-agent being developed for GPT-4 Turbo, indicating these gains are portable across models.

Four ACI design principles emerged: simple and easy to understand, compact and efficient, informative but concise feedback, and guardrails that prevent error cascades.

The Art of Tool Interface Design reinforces this: its Thinker framework — state-machine augmented generation, delegated sub-task tools and adaptive context management — achieved 82.6% success on tau-bench retail with GPT-4o (vs 68.3% baseline) and 81.9% with Llama-3.1 405B (vs 49.6% baseline), all through prompting and tool design rather than fine-tuning.

Sources: SWE-agent, The Art of Tool Interface Design

docs.title: The harness matters as much as the model
docs.text:
Meta-Harness argues the harness "often matters as much as the model itself," citing prior work in which changing only the harness around a fixed model produced up to a 6× gap on the same benchmark. Its own key insight: optimizers that access full execution traces outperform text-only optimizers, which are poorly matched to the problem because they compress feedback too aggressively (scalar scores lose the signal); in its ablation, full access to execution traces was the most important component. On online text classification, Meta-Harness improved over the best prior hand-designed harness (ACE) by 7.7 points while using 4x fewer context tokens, and a single discovered harness improved accuracy on 200 IMO-level math problems by 4.7 points across five held-out models.

This aligns with the broader harness engineering discipline synthesized from OpenAI, Stripe, and Anthropic practices: the engineer's job is increasingly building the environment (constraints, tools, feedback loops) rather than writing code directly. See Harness Engineering.

Sources: Meta-Harness, Harness Engineering Playbook

docs.title: Static context files have a low ceiling
docs.text:
The ETH Zurich evaluation of AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md files — the first rigorous empirical study of repository-level context files — found that developer-provided context improves agent performance by only +4% on average, while LLM-generated context actually hurts performance by -3%. Both increase inference cost by 20% or more. Unnecessary constraints in context files actively degrade performance — agents follow instructions faithfully, and bad instructions produce bad outcomes. The exception: in repositories with their other documentation removed, LLM-generated files helped by 2.7% on average.

The study did find that context files encourage broader exploration (more file traversal, more thorough testing), which suggests they have value as pointers to executable checks rather than as containers of knowledge.

Codified Context, an experience report on a 108K-line C# codebase over 283 sessions, argues single-file manifests don't scale and proposes hot/cold memory separation plus 19 domain-specialist agents. It cites prior work associating AGENTS.md presence with a 29% reduction in median runtime and 17% fewer output tokens.

Sources: Evaluating AGENTS.md, Codified Context

docs.title: The gains point the same way but are not comparable
docs.text:
Signal Comparison Delta Source Interactive test clarification vs none (simulated users) pass@1 code generation +46pp TiCoder Knowledge graph + ontology vs raw SQL schema QA accuracy +37.5pp KG Benchmark Designed ACI vs default shell SWE-bench Lite solve rate +10.7pp SWE-agent Optimized vs hand-designed harness (ACE) Text-classification accuracy +7.7 pts, 4× fewer tokens Meta-Harness Developer context files vs none Agent task completion +4% Evaluating AGENTS.md

The direction is consistent: executable, structured and interactive context outperforms its baselines, and the one direct measurement of static documentation finds marginal gains at best and negative returns at worst. The magnitudes come from different tasks and metrics, so they shouldn't be ranked against each other.

docs.title: Without executable checks, plausible code passes for correct
docs.text:
The evidence is not just that executable context works better — the absence of executable verification produces specific, documented failure modes. The first is that LLM-generated code optimizes for plausibility, not correctness.

The most vivid demonstration, though a single and contested one (the project was unfinished and its README has since been revised): a 576,000-line LLM-generated Rust reimplementation of SQLite that passed all its tests but was about 20,000x slower than SQLite on the author's primary-key lookup benchmark. It missed performance invariants (INTEGER PRIMARY KEY lookups, page-cache behaviour) that only executable benchmarks would catch.

At the benchmark level, this manifests as a dramatic gap between single-attempt and filtered performance. Codex-12B solved 28.8% of HumanEval problems with a single sample and 70.2% when any of 100 samples counted. For Codex-S, picking the sample that passes the unit tests solved 77.5%, but picking by the model's own mean log-probability solved only 44.5%. The model can generate correct code but cannot reliably identify which of its outputs is correct without external verification.

Sources: Your LLM Doesn't Write Correct Code, Codex/HumanEval

docs.title: Agents game the tests they can see
docs.text:
Agents adapt their output to pass the tests they can see. They write mocks that simulate expected behavior rather than testing actual integration. They hardcode return values that match test assertions. RLHF-trained sycophancy makes this worse: agents generate what users describe rather than what's needed, and the same sycophancy bias infects self-review.

Users often don't catch it. The vibe-coding review (101 grey-literature sources, 518 behavioural accounts) found skipped QA was the most common QA practice (36% of QA accounts), and 10% delegated quality checks back to the same AI; it does not measure test gaming directly. The review also cites an earlier study (Pearce et al.) finding about 40% of 1,689 Copilot-generated programs contained security vulnerabilities, and another (Majdinasab et al.) finding that even additional safety layers frequently produce insecure code.

The countermeasure is structural: separate test authorship from implementation context, use property-based tests that are hard to game with hardcoded values, and place interface tests in a separate agent context with minimal knowledge of the implementation.

Sources: How To Effectively Write Quality Code With AI, Your LLM Doesn't Write Correct Code, Vibe Coding in Practice

docs.title: Developers misjudge their own productivity
docs.text:
The METR randomized controlled trial with 16 experienced open-source developers across 246 real tasks found that AI tools increased task completion time by 19%. Developers had predicted a 24% speedup before the study and still estimated a 20% speedup after participating — despite the measured slowdown. Economists predicted 39% shorter task times; ML researchers predicted 38%.

This is the most dangerous finding in the corpus. Without executable measurement, even experts cannot accurately assess the impact of AI tools on their own productivity. Every claim of "I'm faster with AI" that lacks measurement is suspect.

The finding is specific to large, mature codebases with highly experienced developers. It does not imply AI tools are useless — improvements to prompting, agent scaffolding, and domain-specific adaptation could yield speedups. But it does imply that subjective assessment is unreliable.

Source: METR Study

One possible explanation comes from the cognitive agency surrender literature, which argues frictionless interfaces exploit System 1 heuristics and bypass the analytical reasoning that would catch the discrepancy. That paper is a literature analysis and doesn't study METR's result directly. Either way, the feeling of productivity is not productivity.

Implication: any AI adoption evaluation that relies on developer surveys or self-reported time savings is measuring perception, not reality.

Sources: METR Study, Cognitive Agency Surrender

docs.title: Frictionless tools invite cognitive surrender
docs.text:
Frictionless AI interfaces exploit cognitive miserliness — the tendency to offload reasoning to the easiest available path. An automated classification of 1,223 high-confidence AI-HCI papers (2023-2026) found 67.3% structural hegemony for frictionless usability, while research on epistemic sovereignty dropped from 19.1% (2025) to 13.1% (2026).

The implication: tools that feel most productive may be the ones that most effectively bypass analytical reasoning. The paper argues for intentional friction in interface design as a prerequisite for cognitive resilience; review gates, mandatory test execution and plan-then-execute workflows are this page's extrapolation of that to engineering practice.

Field observations (N=13) and surveys (N=99) of professional developers offer a contrasting picture: experienced developers do not "vibe code." They carefully control AI agents through planning and supervision, retain agency over software design, and insist on quality attributes — in other words, they resist the surrender the HCI analysis warns about. The same paper cites HULA's deployment, where about 8% of issues ended in a merged PR (see Executable Context Practices).

Sources: Cognitive Agency Surrender, Professional Developers Don't Vibe, They Control

docs.title: Extra agents add overhead unless they bring new signal
docs.text:
Information-theoretic analysis proves that multi-agent architectures sharing the same base model and context cannot outperform a centralized decision maker. Communication between agents degrades decision quality, quantifiable via mutual information loss. Under fixed reasoning-token budgets, single-agent systems match or outperform multi-agent systems on multi-hop reasoning — though multi-agent systems become competitive when a single agent's context utilisation degrades.

Multi-agent message-passing is lossy compression of full context. Adding agents without adding information is adding overhead without adding capability.

Sources: Reliability Limits, Single-Agent Outperforms Multi-Agent

The corollary: the main lever for multi-agent reliability is genuinely new exogenous signals (the paper also credits preserving decision-relevant information and non-redundant review) — tool calls, database lookups, test execution results, linter output, file system reads. These provide information the model does not already have.

This means: multi-agent is valuable when each agent interacts with a different part of the environment. Agent A runs tests on module X while Agent B runs tests on module Y — each gets exogenous signal the other doesn't have. But Agent A "planning" and Agent B "reviewing" with the same context is theater.

Human review is optimally deployed when automated posterior risk exceeds review cost — not as a blanket policy, but targeted at the highest-risk decisions.

This is the theoretical argument. Some empirical results complicate it: one multi-agent system gains without any tools, and another gains from how its agents communicate under a compute-matched baseline. See Multi-Agent Systems for that evidence.

Source: Reliability Limits

docs.title: Other sources point the same way
docs.text:
Sources that inform this page without anchoring a specific finding above:

  • Benchmarks and baselines. SWE-bench set the real-world bar (the best model solved 1.96% at launch). Agentless showed a fixed localize-repair-validate pipeline reaching 32% on SWE-bench Lite at about $0.70 per task. METR's time-horizon study finds the length of tasks agents complete doubling about every 7 months.
  • Context retrieval and reuse. ContextBench finds agents explore more context than they use, making consolidation a key bottleneck. ACE evolves contexts incrementally (+10.6% on agent benchmarks). Everything is Context proposes a file-system abstraction for governed context. An analysis of Claude Code's traffic traces one SWE-bench Verified task: 92 LLM calls with 92% prefix reuse.
  • How tools are configured and built. A study of 2,923 repositories finds static configuration dominates and executable integrations are still rare. OPENDEV and Dive into Claude Code describe harness designs with layered safety and context compaction. Environment Scaling argues static datasets are insufficient for adaptive agents.
  • Verification tooling. MCPEval automates agent evaluation through tool-call matching and LLM judging. Verify turns specs into Playwright checks run by parallel browser agents. Testing with AI Agents finds AI authored 16.4% of test commits in the repositories studied.
  • Why outputs need checking at all. Sleeper Agents shows trained-in backdoors persist through safety training, and monitoring reasoning models finds chain-of-thought monitoring works but optimizing against it teaches obfuscation.

docs.title: What the evidence supports
docs.text:
• Executable feedback beats non-interactive baselines. Interactive test clarification (+46pp pass@1 with simulated users, TiCoder), designed agent interfaces (+10.7pp over a plain shell, SWE-agent) and automated harness search (+7.7 points over ACE on text classification, where access to full execution traces was the key ingredient, Meta-Harness) all beat their baselines, while context files add about +4% on average (Evaluating AGENTS.md). Each is a controlled result on its own task; the magnitudes can't be ranked against each other.
  • Static context files should be short pointers, not manuals. Developer-written files gave +4% on average, LLM-generated ones −3%, both at 20%+ extra cost; that they encourage broader exploration suggests their value is in pointing at checks. The exception: with no other documentation, LLM-generated files helped by 2.7% (Evaluating AGENTS.md).
  • Models can generate correct code but can't pick it out. Codex-S solved 77.5% when the unit tests chose the sample and 44.5% when its own log-probability did; external verification is what closes the gap (Codex/HumanEval).
  • Don't trust perceived productivity. In the METR RCT, experienced developers were 19% slower while believing they were 20% faster (METR). It is one study, of mature codebases and experienced developers.
  • More agents help mainly with new information. The theoretical result is that role decomposition over the same model and context cannot beat a single decision maker (Reliability Limits); empirical exceptions are covered in Multi-Agent Systems.

docs.title: In practice
docs.text: The practices that follow from this evidence — with code examples for Java, Scala and Python, adoption order and a quick-reference table — are on Executable Context Practices. Its highest-leverage starting points are executable specs before implementation, linter rules as architecture guardrails, separating test authorship from implementation, performance gates in CI, and plan-then-execute review gates.

docs.title: Open questions
docs.text:
• How much of each gain survives on the same task? The headline numbers (TiCoder, the KG benchmark, SWE-agent, Meta-Harness, AGENTS.md) come from different tasks and metrics. No study compares executable context against static documentation head-to-head on one coding benchmark.
  • Does writing failing tests first beat TiCoder-style clarification? The strongest effect size here is for LLM-proposed tests refined with (simulated) user feedback. Whether human-authored failing tests given upfront perform as well is untested.
  • Does constraining the solution space measurably help? The linter-as-guardrail practice rests on a practitioner report. A controlled comparison of constrained and unconstrained agents on the same codebase would settle it.

docs.title: Related topics
docs.text:
• Executable Context Practices — how to apply this evidence: specs, types, linters, feedback loops, measurement
  • Harness Engineering — the runtime layer where executable feedback is implemented
  • Testing and Compliance for Coding Agents — verification as the bottleneck, and evaluation tiers in more depth
  • Context Engineering — what to put in the window, including static context files
  • Multi-Agent Systems — when coordination helps, including evidence that complicates the new-signal argument

docs.title: Change log
docs.text:
• 2026-10-26 — Fact-checked against the raw sources: corrected figures, attributions and evidence-strength wording; every evidence-summary claim now links its source
  • 2026-10-26 — Created by splitting the evidence half (formerly sections 2, 3, 8.2–8.3 and 9.1) out of Executable Context Practices

docs.title: What is it
docs.text:
A harness is the runtime layer that wraps an LLM agent: it handles tool dispatch, context management, safety enforcement, session persistence, and feedback loops — everything that happens after the first prompt. Harness engineering is the discipline of deliberately designing this layer rather than leaving it as scaffolding glue. The term was coined by @mitchellh and synthesized into a playbook by Charlie Guo: "anytime you find an agent makes a mistake, you take the time to engineer a solution such that the agent never makes that mistake again." The key shift is treating the environment as the primary artifact, not the code the agent produces.

Distinct from context engineering (what goes in the window), harness engineering is about the surrounding system: constraints, feedback loops, tool design, safety layers, and orchestration protocols. This page asks how much that layer matters next to the model, which of its components earn their cost, and whether harnesses can be designed or optimized systematically rather than by trial and error.

The short answer: the harness can matter as much as the model, but no single component helps everywhere — the right harness depends on the model, the task and the budget, and it can increasingly be searched for or learned rather than hand-built.

docs.title: The harness can matter as much as the model
docs.text:
LLM system performance is heavily determined by harness design, not just model weights. Harness changes alone can produce up to a 6× performance gap on the same benchmark with a fixed model — prior work cited by Meta-Harness, which argues the harness "often matters as much as the model itself." Meta-Harness's own measured gains over hand-designed baselines (below) are consistent with this.

The practitioner consequence is that the engineer's job splits into two halves (Charlie Guo):

  1. Building the environment — constraints, tools, documentation, feedback loops
  2. Managing the work — planning with agents, reviewing rather than writing code, orchestrating parallel sessions

These aren't sequential. The agent's failures tell you what the environment is missing; a better environment lets you manage with less friction.

docs.title: Separating setup from runtime makes components replaceable
docs.text:
OPENDEV draws a useful line:

  • Scaffolding — assembly before the first prompt: system prompt compilation, tool schema construction, subagent registration. Done once per session.
  • Harness — runtime orchestration: tool dispatch, context compaction, safety enforcement, state persistence across turns. Runs continuously.

OPENDEV makes this split its organizing principle, so that each component is independently configurable and replaceable. The split is a design description, not a measured result.

docs.title: Constraint and feedback increase trust in agent output
docs.text:
Guo synthesizes four recurring practices from OpenAI, Stripe, and Anthropic (Charlie Guo):

  • Architecture as guardrails. Enforce structure mechanically via linters and schemas, not just via instructions. OpenAI enforced a strict layered architecture with rigid dependency rules via custom linters. Stripe ran agents in isolated, pre-warmed "devboxes" with access to 400+ internal tools via MCP servers. The practitioners' counterintuitive lesson: constraining the solution space increased trust in agent output.
  • Tools as feedback. Custom linter error messages double as remediation instructions — the tooling teaches the agent while it works. OpenAI's Greg Brockman, as relayed by Guo, recommends maintaining a list of tools your team relies on and making sure someone takes point on making each agent-accessible (CLI or MCP server).
  • AGENTS.md as living system of record. A Markdown file at repo root, automatically read by agents at session start, updated every time the agent does something wrong. It points to deeper sources of truth (design docs, architecture maps, execution plans) rather than containing everything inline. Background agents can periodically scan for stale docs and open cleanup PRs.
  • Plan before execute. Guo's own advice, which he files under managing the work rather than the harness: agents propose, humans approve, then agents execute. Anthropic's related approach: an initializer agent generates 200+ individual features from a high-level prompt, each with explicit test steps.

All four come from practitioner reports relayed in one synthesis, not from controlled comparisons. The evidence that executable feedback beats static instructions is covered in Executable Context.

docs.title: No component helps every model and task
docs.text:
Most harness comparisons pit complete systems against each other, which can't say which part made the difference. An Empirical Study of Harness Design holds the run loop fixed and varies one component at a time across 176 settings (three Nemotron-3 sizes plus Mistral-Medium-3.5-128B, on SWE-Bench Verified and Terminal-Bench 2.1). No component helps everywhere:

  • Context management pays off mostly by preventing overflow. Its advantage on SWE-Bench falls from 35.7 points at a 32k window to 2.7 at 128k. Cheaply dropping stale tool output before falling back to LLM summarization gives the best cost; making dropped content recoverable adds nothing, because models almost never ask for it back.
  • Planning helps weak models and saves money on strong ones. It adds 11.6 points for the 30B model by keeping runs alive long enough to attempt an edit. For the strongest models it cuts cost about 30% at a 0.4–2.0 point loss, mostly by trimming redundant checking after an edit.
  • Predefined tools help models that are weak at bash. A bash-capable model (Nemotron-3 550B) does better with bash only, +3.6 and +5.6 points at 53% and 30% lower cost, because it combines several operations per call. Mistral prefers the full tool set on SWE-Bench but bash only on Terminal-Bench, so the crossover also depends on the task.

The authors' conclusion is that each component should be chosen for the model, task type and budget rather than adopted by default. Caveats: every setting was run once, Terminal-Bench has only 89 tasks, and planning and tools were only tested at one context configuration.

docs.title: Good harnesses build on what the model already knows
docs.text:
A recurring claim in the practitioner literature is that the harness should be decoupled from any particular model. What is a Harness? gives the clearest anatomy — system prompt, tools, agentic loop, and a translation layer that lets the same harness run different models — and argues the translation layer is what moves leverage from AI labs to end users, who can own, modify, and run the harness locally. Ante is that position as a working artifact: a harness evaluated continuously across model families on Terminal-Bench 2.1 rather than pinned to one hero model, with each result linking a raw audit run and a pinned build. Its comparative efficiency figures are vendor self-reported.

The practitioner design notes converge on a few principles (Towards a Harness That Can Do Anything):

  • Exploit what the model already knows. Coding and systems administration are overrepresented in training data, so a harness built from familiar primitives costs fewer tokens than one teaching a novel environment. The bash-only result above is a measured case of this.
  • Determinism where possible — the model picks the goal, but deliberation toward it should be well-defined steps.
  • Keep the core prompt small, loading skills into context at runtime rather than preloading them.
  • Feel light to the model, do heavy work underneath — logging, sanity checks, failsafes, sanitization.

Harness Engineering for Self-Improvement organizes this as an operating-system analogy: encapsulate complicated logic behind a simple interface, and expect configs, tool interfaces, and protocols to standardize across the industry. It also notes the coding-agent loop has already converged across Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, and Cursor-style agents.

docs.title: The surfaces agents act on are part of the harness
docs.text:
Harness design does not stop at the harness. Designing APIs for Agents argues that API design for agents inverts the human-facing defaults: agents read entire documentation sets up front and generate thousands of lines in seconds, so onboarding friction is no longer the cost to minimize — debugging cost is. Concretely: defaults are bad (explicitness is cheap when the consumer fills every field), errors are good (forgiving APIs that coalesce sloppy input produce codebases where different call sites use different values for the same thing), and error messages should tell the agent to read the docs, because modern harnesses will.

This is the same principle as constraining the solution space, applied one layer out. It is a practitioner argument, not a measured comparison.

docs.title: Safety needs independent layers
docs.text:
Production harnesses need defense in depth — a single safety layer is insufficient when agents can execute arbitrary shell commands. OPENDEV describes five independent layers:

  1. Prompt-level guardrails (security policy, action safety)
  2. Schema-level tool restrictions (plan-mode whitelist, per-agent allowed tools)
  3. Runtime approval system (manual/semi-auto/auto with persistent permissions)
  4. Tool-level validation (dangerous pattern blocklist, stale-read detection, timeouts)
  5. Lifecycle hooks (pre-tool blocking, argument mutation)

Each layer operates independently, so failure of one doesn't compromise the rest. This is one system's design, described rather than evaluated against simpler alternatives.

docs.title: Structure can replace generative coordination
docs.text:
Three sources propose structural fixes for long-horizon drift and coordination.

Procedural Graphs makes procedural knowledge explicit — (procedure, relation, procedure) triplets for what-to-do questions, the way a knowledge graph holds what-is — and translates the active subgraph into step-level guidance that biases the next action without dictating it. The graph self-evolves under a held-out validation gate, which is the detail that distinguishes it from unconstrained self-modification.

UnitBoost questions a structural assumption in multi-agent harnesses: that the manager must be generative. Replacing it with a defined merge operator — unit map, constrained argmax, explicit residual — makes coordination order-free and provenance-recording, and beats input-matched generative managers. It also states where it does not help: one indivisible unit, unavailable unit identity, or an endpoint charging per emitted unit.

ICM takes the opposite route for sequential, human-reviewed workflows and drops the orchestration code entirely: numbered folders are stages, a markdown contract in each says what to read and write, and one stage's output folder is the next one's input. Every intermediate state is a file a human can open and edit, so observability comes for free. The authors scope it out of real-time multi-agent work, high concurrency and automated branching, and their evidence is practitioner reports, not controlled comparisons.

Procedural Graphs is treated in depth under Agent Memory and Retrieval; UnitBoost's place among coordination mechanisms is covered in Multi-Agent Systems.

docs.title: Evals belong inside the harness
docs.text:
Anthropic argues evals should be a core component of agent development, not an afterthought. Without them you're "flying blind" — catching issues only in production, where fixing one failure creates others (Demystifying Evals). Two eval categories work together:

  • Capability evals — start low, hill-climb; measure what the agent can do
  • Regression evals — near 100% pass rate; catch backsliding after changes

Evals also become the highest-bandwidth channel between product and research teams: they define metrics researchers can optimize against. They are also the precondition for the automated optimization below, which needs a score to search against.

docs.title: Harnesses can be searched for or learned
docs.text:
Rather than hand-designing harnesses, an outer loop can search over harness configurations automatically. Meta-Harness does this using an agentic proposer with access to source code and full execution traces of all prior candidates. It beats hand-designed baselines in all three domains it tests: +7.7 points over ACE on online text classification with 4× fewer context tokens, +4.7 points on 200 IMO-level math problems across five held-out models, and above Terminus-KIRA on TerminalBench-2 (76.4% vs 74.7% with Opus 4.6). On TerminalBench-2 it searched and evaluated on the same 89 tasks, and another hand-built harness, ForgeCode, still scored higher (81.8%). Existing text optimizers fail here because they compress feedback too aggressively (scalar scores only, no trajectory access).

Meta-Harness searches afresh for each task. Harness Learning instead trains the reviser, so the skill of revising harnesses carries over to new tasks. A proposer model is trained with RL to edit a frozen solver's harness code from execution reports, rewarded by how the edited harness scores; at test time both models stay frozen and only the harness changes. On 21 Reasoning Gym families unseen in training, mean single-revision score rises from 0.32 to 0.62, and the 4B proposer's average revision beats its 35B teacher's (0.62 vs 0.56). A proposer trained on HotpotQA keeps improving harnesses over ten rounds on MuSiQue and 2WikiMultihopQA. Two details matter for practice: much of the gain is reliability (far fewer edits that break the harness), and training on revision sequences adds nothing consistent over training on single revisions.

docs.title: Verification improves when the checker gets the environment
docs.text:
The harness can also be pointed at checking work rather than doing it. VeriHarness turns the generator's own model into a verifier for long-horizon workspace tasks (reports, spreadsheets) by giving it a workspace, evidence tools and reusable verification skills, with no reference answers, rubrics or stronger judge. Across several rollouts, a disagreement resolver checks disputed claims against source files and data, and a consensus challenger tries to refute claims all rollouts share and looks for requirements none of them met. Selection plus evidence-backed revision adds about 6 points over a single rollout with both Gemini 3.5 Flash and Claude Opus 4.8, beating the verification baselines it was compared against. Its verification skills also improve from failure feedback: skills evolved from an empty library beat a human-authored one on held-out tasks.

The gain comes from the environment, not the model: majority voting and LLM-as-a-judge only re-read what the model already believes. The cost is several full rollouts per task (VeriHarness).

docs.title: What the evidence supports
docs.text:
• Treat the harness as a first-class lever. A fixed model can show up to a 6× gap across harnesses (prior work cited by Meta-Harness), and automated harness search beat its hand-designed starting baselines in all three domains Meta-Harness tested — though on TerminalBench-2 it searched and evaluated on the same tasks, and a hand-built harness still scored higher.
  • Choose components per model, task and budget. The one component-level study (Harness Design) finds context management, planning and predefined tools each help some models and hurt or cost others. It ran each setting once, so the direction is more reliable than the magnitudes.
  • Build on primitives the model already knows. Practitioners argue for familiar primitives such as files, logs and the Linux filesystem (Towards a Harness That Can Do Anything); the component study separately measured a bash-capable model doing better and cheaper with bash alone (Harness Design).
  • Give verifiers the environment, not more votes. VeriHarness (VeriHarness) gains about 6 points by checking claims against files and data, where voting and LLM judges cannot add information. It is one paper on workspace tasks.
  • Constraint and mechanical feedback are practitioner advice, not measured. Custom linters, teaching error messages and an approved-plan gate come from one synthesis of practices at OpenAI, Stripe and Anthropic (Charlie Guo).

docs.title: In practice
docs.text:
Ordered roughly by evidence strength and cost:

  1. Instrument before you tune. Keep capability and regression evals alongside the harness (Evals belong inside the harness); without a score, neither manual tuning nor automated search has anything to optimize.
  2. Ablate components on your own model and tasks instead of adopting a full-featured harness by default (No component helps every model and task). Try bash-only for strong models, planning for weak ones, and cheap truncation of stale tool output before summarization.
  3. Encode mistakes as mechanical constraints. Each time the agent errs, add a linter rule, schema or teaching error message rather than another instruction, and keep AGENTS.md short and pointing at the checks (Constraint and feedback).
  4. Gate execution on an approved plan for non-trivial work (Constraint and feedback).
  5. Layer safety independently — prompt policy, tool restrictions, approvals, tool-level validation and hooks (Safety needs independent layers).
  6. Choose attended or unattended parallelism deliberately. Attended parallelization — actively managing several sessions, checking in and redirecting — gives more control but is cognitively demanding. Unattended parallelization (Stripe's "Minions") — post a task, walk away, let CI carry it, re-enter at review — scales better but needs substantially more harness investment up front (Charlie Guo).

docs.title: Open questions
docs.text:
• How do you keep agent-written code from accumulating entropy? Agent-generated code accumulates cruft differently than human-written code; "garbage collection" agents are an emerging practice but not yet mature (Charlie Guo). A longitudinal comparison of codebases with and without them would settle whether they work.
  • Does any of this retrofit onto brownfield codebases? The success stories Guo surveys all involve greenfield projects (Charlie Guo). No source reports applying these practices to a large existing codebase.
  • Is environment-backed verification affordable outside benchmarks? Agents mark features complete without proper end-to-end testing (Charlie Guo). VeriHarness shows a same-model verifier with environment access helps on workspace tasks, but at the cost of several full rollouts per task (its released pool cost over $100,000) (VeriHarness). A cost-matched comparison against cheaper checks would answer it.
  • Search per task, or learn to revise? Meta-Harness optimizes each task from scratch; Harness Learning trains a reusable reviser that transfers. No source compares them on the same tasks at matched cost (Harness Learning).
  • What does organizational adoption take? None of this happens by accident; the practices require deliberate organizational adoption (Charlie Guo), and no source studies what makes it stick.
