docs.title: What is it
docs.text:
Finance and accounting look like a good fit for LLMs: the work is text- and table-heavy, rule-governed, and expensive in skilled labor. They are also unusually unforgiving. A balance sheet either balances or it doesn't, an audit opinion must cite the standard it rests on, and a trading error can cost millions in minutes.

This page tracks how LLMs actually perform on financial and audit work, why reported results — trading returns especially — are hard to trust, and what architectures and controls the sources propose for deploying them safely. General multi-agent design is covered in Multi-Agent Systems; this page covers what is specific to the domain.

The pattern across the evidence is consistent: models do well on recognition and simple extraction, and fall off sharply as tasks require multi-step computation, multi-document structure, explanation against standards, or behavior under adversarial pressure. Most proposed remedies add a verification step after generation — often a second model checking output against accounting identities or source documents. Older, pre-LLM work goes further and argues for enforcing invariants entirely outside the application; no source here yet applies that to an LLM system.

docs.title: Capability collapses with depth and structure
docs.text:
The benchmarks here find the same shape — strong on the easy end, weak where the professional work is. Several come from overlapping author groups, so they are not fully independent.

  • Complexity. FinMaster measures about 96% on basic financial literacy, about 40% on multi-step reasoning, and 3% on generating advanced accounting statements. Errors propagate: single-metric accuracy of 58% falls to 37% when several metrics depend on each other.
  • Audit stages. AuditBench breaks auditing into detection, explanation, standard citation, complete audit and revision. Models detect errors in financial statements but are weak at the later stages: explaining them, citing the accounting standard they violate, carrying out a full audit, and revising.
  • Multi-document structure. On real XBRL filings, FinAuditing finds accuracy drops of 60–90% when models reason over hierarchical, multi-document structure. Strength on one dimension (semantic, relational, numerical) doesn't predict strength on another — GPT-4o reaches 91.82% on relationship extraction while the structured multi-document tasks collapse.
  • Professional thresholds. Accounting Reasoning finds the 90% accuracy needed for professional deployment unmet. Few-shot chain-of-thought improves accuracy by about 50% (per the source page), and principle-level misunderstanding and missing concepts account for over half of failures.
  • Forecasting. On FinBen's 24 tasks, every model is only slightly better than random at forecasting, and near zero on complex extraction such as causal detection.

FinMaster suggests the easy end is partly pattern-matching: Claude-3.7-Sonnet and DeepSeek-V3 do relatively well on audits with several simultaneous errors but struggle with a single isolated anomaly. AuditBench is consistent with this — detection succeeds while explanation and standard citation fail.

docs.title: Compliance lags capability, and both degrade in agent loops
docs.text:
CNFinBench tests 22 models as financial agents and finds a gap that capability benchmarks can't show. Models averaging 66.4 on capability tasks score 34.4 on compliance and risk control. Accuracy falls 15.4 points from isolated modules to full execution chains. Under adversarial multi-turn pressure, compliance violations surge 172.3% in the second round.

The industry framing matches. The FINOS AI governance framework classifies hallucination as a critical operational risk in financial services. It lists fabricated analysis, misread regulation, invented customer data, wrong loan decisions and flawed financial code, and notes that RAG reduces but can't prevent hallucination, because models blend retrieved facts with what they already believe. Its controls are citations and traceability, LLM-as-judge verification and acceptance testing.

docs.title: Domain tuning doesn't buy reliability
docs.text:
Finance-specific training is not a shortcut. On InvestorBench, the finance-tuned Palmyra-Fin-70B averaged a −0.45% cumulative return, underperforming buy-and-hold, while GPT-4 averaged 43.7% in stock trading. Even large open models struggled to act consistently across repeated trials. On a related axis, FinBen finds instruction tuning helps simple tasks but not complex reasoning or forecasting.

Model rankings also shift by slice: in Accounting Reasoning, the general-purpose GLM-4 beats GPT-4 on an accounting-specific slice (21.78% vs 16.58%, per the source page) while GPT-4 is stronger overall. Winning a slice is not winning the job.

docs.title: Reported trading results are hard to trust
docs.text:
Toward Reliable Evaluation of Financial Multi-Agent Systems surveys 12 LLM trading systems and finds five evaluation failures that can reverse the sign of reported returns:

  • Look-ahead bias — the model may have seen the evaluation period in training.
  • Survivorship bias — about 0.9% a year for mutual funds, more for individual stock selection.
  • Backtest overfitting — FinMem's 23% return became −22% under controlled conditions.
  • Ignored transaction costs — 10–20 basis points per round trip compounds to 25–50 percentage points of annual drag for daily-trading systems.
  • Regime-shift blindness — testing only in one market regime.

No surveyed system met all five minimum criteria, so reported returns from 23% to over 400% can't be compared. InvestorBench's own scope note adds that portfolio management and multi-asset allocation remain untested.

The same survey proposes a Coordination Primacy Hypothesis: how agents coordinate matters more than which model they use. Removing coordination cut Sharpe ratios 15–30%, while swapping models moved them 5–8%. Its Coordination Breakeven Spread metric asks whether coordination pays for itself after trading costs, which makes the answer asset-class dependent. Given the survey's own findings about evaluation quality, the hypothesis is best read as a claim to test.

docs.title: Architectures that put verification first
docs.text:
In the sources that report what works, verification is central rather than an add-on.

Benchmarking Multi-Agent Architectures for Financial Document Processing compares four orchestration patterns on 10,000 SEC filings. A reflexive architecture whose verifier applies accounting identities (total assets = liabilities + equity) and requires every extracted value to have supporting evidence in the source reaches the highest F1 (0.943), at 2.3× the cost of a sequential pipeline. A hierarchical supervisor-worker design gets 97.7% of that accuracy at 60.9% of the cost. Hybrids with semantic caching, model routing and adaptive retries recover 89% of the reflexive gain at 1.15× baseline cost. Two caveats from the same study:

  • Reflexive designs can overthink. Oscillation on ambiguous disclosures is the reflexive design's largest failure mode, 39.3% of its errors.
  • Accuracy degrades with volume. Reflexive F1 falls from 0.943 to 0.871 at 100,000 documents a day.

In the 260-configuration scaling study, the decomposable Finance-Agent benchmark showed the largest multi-agent gain (+80.8%, centralized architecture) — one benchmark among six, but the clearest case for decomposition. The general case is covered in Multi-Agent Systems.

Emerging AI Patterns in Finance describes the same direction in industry:

  • "White box" verification systems use LLMs as critics that check numerical claims against primary documents.
  • Hybrid quant architectures use LLMs for semantic tasks while allocation, risk and execution stay with traditional optimizers.
  • Compliance-as-code is expected to add real-time lineage tracking for every inference.

docs.title: Invariants enforced outside the model
docs.text:
Two older, non-LLM sources state the principle the verification architectures are reaching for.

Establishing Accounting Principles as Invariants argues critical accounting rules should not be trusted to evolving application code at all. Double-entry bookkeeping — money moves between accounts but never appears or disappears — can be expressed as four rules in a law-governed interaction framework and enforced by trusted controllers that mediate every message, treating components as black boxes. Auditing becomes a second invariant: financial activity can be monitored without the cooperation of the system being examined. It was written for human-built software; arguably it applies with more force to LLM-generated changes.

Reconciliation Testing shows what happens when those controls exist but aren't tested:

  • Knight Capital lost $460M in 45 minutes. A parent-order vs child-order reconciliation check had been moved in source code and was no longer active, and its monitoring wasn't connected to any kill switch.
  • The Facebook/NASDAQ IPO cost $62M+. The reconciliation control worked but looped on cancellations, and the team disabled it without ever having tested the consequences.

The conclusion is that a control not validated by negative testing is equivalent to no control.

docs.title: Regulation is thin, and assistant behaviour is associated with work quality
docs.text:
The regulatory picture here is thin. KPMG's highlights of the 2025 AICPA conference were captured only as a header. Unverified web context recorded at capture says the SEC stressed documentation of model design and data and ongoing human oversight, that existing auditing standards weren't written for AI, and that the PCAOB's quality-control standard QC 1000 takes effect December 15, 2026. Treat these as leads until the full text is captured.

On the human side, Precision Proactivity studies 34 financial professionals doing a valuation with GPT-4o. Using AI-generated content was associated with higher quality, while extraneous cognitive load from the interaction had a negative association about three times that of the task's intrinsic difficulty. Model-initiated task switching was the strongest predictor of worse work, which argues for assistants that stay in scope rather than proactively suggesting new directions. The study is observational, so these are associations, not causal effects.

docs.title: What the evidence supports
docs.text:
• Benchmark scores on simple tasks don't transfer to professional work. The fall-off with depth (FinMaster, AuditBench, FinAuditing) and the gap between capability and compliance (CNFinBench) are large and consistent across several benchmarks, some from overlapping author groups.
  • Treat reported trading returns as unverified unless they control for contamination, survivorship, costs and regime. By one survey's count, no current system does.
  • Add a separate verification pass. The best-performing document architecture had a verifier agent check balance-sheet identities and source grounding, though the study doesn't isolate which check drives the gain. The invariants literature argues for going further and enforcing rules outside the application entirely.
  • Test the controls themselves. In both trading incidents studied, reconciliation controls whose failure behavior had never been negatively tested contributed to the loss.
  • Domain tuning alone hasn't bought reliability so far. The one finance-tuned agent tested (Palmyra-Fin-70B on InvestorBench) underperformed buy-and-hold.

docs.title: Open questions
docs.text:
• Does verification close the gap at the hard end? The verifier-first document study is on extraction from filings. Whether the same approach rescues the 3% statement-generation or audit-explanation results is untested.
  • Is coordination primacy real? It comes from a survey whose central finding is that the field's evaluations are unreliable. A controlled test under the survey's own five criteria would settle it.
  • How do models fare on the newest regulation? Benchmarks test known standards; the QC 1000 era and AI-specific audit guidance are newer than most training data.
  • What does an LLM-era law-governed system look like? The invariants paper predates LLMs. No source here implements external invariant enforcement around an LLM agent in a financial system.
  • Can assistants be built to reduce extraneous load? Precision Proactivity identifies the problem in one valuation task; no source tests an assistant designed against it.

docs.title: What is it
docs.text:
A multi-agent system splits work across several LLM agents — usually instances of the same model with different prompts, tools or roles — that coordinate through messages, shared files or an orchestrator. The appeal is parallelism, specialization and cross-checking. The cost is coordination overhead, lossy hand-offs and failures that compound across agents.

The question running through every source on this page is when coordination adds more than it costs. The evidence is split: controlled studies find many reported multi-agent gains disappear under matched compute, while specific designs show gains that hold up against compute-matched baselines. This page tracks what separates the two, which coordination mechanisms carry the gains, what multi-agent systems cost, and why many instances of one model may not give many independent opinions.

The short answer: default to one agent; coordination pays off mainly when the task decomposes into parallel parts and the single-agent baseline is weak; coordinate through shared artifacts and isolated workspaces rather than role labels; and don't assume many instances make independent errors.

docs.title: Roles alone add no information
docs.text:
Two theoretical results set a ceiling.

On the Reliability Limits of Multi-Agent Planning models multi-agent systems as delegated decision networks and shows that, without new exogenous signals, no architecture can beat a single centralized decision maker with the same information. Planner, worker, critic and reviewer roles over one model and one context add roles, not information, and every hand-off can only lose some. What does improve reliability is genuinely new signal: tool calls, database lookups, executable feedback.

Single-Agent LLMs Outperform Multi-Agent Systems reaches the same conclusion from the Data Processing Inequality and tests it. Under matched thinking-token budgets, single agents match or beat multi-agent systems on multi-hop reasoning across three model families. Multi-agent systems become competitive only when a single agent's context use degrades, or when they get extra compute the comparison didn't count. The authors argue many reported multi-agent advantages are explained by that uncounted compute.

The production evidence is consistent with this. Anthropic's multi-agent Research system beat single-agent Opus 4 by 90.2% on internal evals — but token usage alone explains 80% of performance variance on BrowseComp, and multi-agent runs use about 15× the tokens of a chat interaction.

docs.title: Coordination pays off when the task decomposes
docs.text:
The largest controlled study, Towards a Science of Scaling Agent Systems, runs 260 configurations with tools, prompts and compute standardized. Multi-agent effects range from +80.8% on a decomposable financial reasoning task to −70.0% on sequential planning. The study's own conclusion is that task decomposability is the critical factor; a synthesis of it points out the two extreme tasks have nearly identical complexity scores but opposite outcomes, so decomposability, not complexity, decides. The study reports three further patterns:

  • Capability saturation. Once a single agent already scores above roughly 45%, extra agents give negative returns. The synthesis post draws the implication: the bar for coordination rises as models improve.
  • Tool-heavy tasks amplify overhead. The study finds a statistically significant negative coordination effect on them.
  • Centralized verification contains errors. Independent parallel agents amplify errors 17.2×; a central orchestrator holds it to 4.4×. But once efficiency and overhead are controlled for, error amplification doesn't significantly predict performance — overhead explains more than error propagation does.

The strongest positive results come from designs that bring in new information or keep agents from blocking each other:

  • AgentRadio beats a compute-matched best-of-6 single-agent baseline (62.1% vs 37.9%), and the benefit of its passive-awareness step grows with task difficulty. Its own case studies mark the limit: passive awareness surfaces discoveries agents already make, but can't produce a conclusion no agent reaches.
  • CAID — central delegation, asynchronous execution, isolated git worktrees, test-verified merges — improves over a single agent by 26.7% on paper reproduction and 14.3% on library development.
  • Agyn resolves 72.2% of SWE-bench 500 with manager, researcher, engineer and reviewer roles in isolated environments, 7.4% above the mini-SWE-agent baseline with comparable (GPT-5-family) models, evaluated post hoc.
  • ReDel reports that recursive delegation's lead over a single agent grows as the underlying model improves. That is in tension with capability saturation, though on different benchmarks.
  • BIGMAS finds multi-agent gains are largest exactly where individual models collapse on reasoning complexity.

A different use of coordination is as a source of training data. MASS has one model propose, run and grade multi-agent workflows (roles plus information routing written into a prompt), then fine-tunes the same model on the best workflows' orchestrator and subagent trajectories. Over two cycles with Qwen3.6-27B, score per output token rises 1.2–1.6× on four research benchmarks, with external judges withheld from the loop. Coding benchmarks slip slightly (Terminal-Bench 2.0 37.5→35.2, SWE-bench Verified 62.6→61.1). The comparison that bears on this page is about training: a student trained on multi-agent traces beats one trained on single-agent traces with about 1.4× more tokens (68.3% vs 64.0% win rate). The authors attribute this to splitting orchestration from bounded subagent execution, so it is a claim about learning efficiency, not about inference-time coordination beating a matched single agent.

Whether these results sit inside the theoretical ceiling is unresolved. Some bring in new signal — CAID's test-verified merges, for instance. But BIGMAS gains without any tools, AgentRadio's gain comes from the communication mode itself under a compute-matched baseline, and the scaling study finds tool-heavy tasks have a negative coordination effect. A likelier reading, consistent with the Single-Agent paper's own caveat, is that real single agents fall short of the theorem's ideal decision maker because their context use degrades, so splitting the work recovers capacity rather than adding information. None of the winning designs gets its gain from role labels alone.

docs.title: Shared artifacts, isolation and defined merges carry coordination, not role labels
Shared artifacts beat messages
docs.text:
When Agents Coordinate records 1,902 runs as timeline graphs of messages and file reads and writes. Shared files can replace one-to-one messaging because one write reaches many readers. Making them mandatory cut output tokens about 25% at four agents and 42% at eight on one task — but added cost on a pipeline task where files already carried the coordination.

The same pattern recurs across the sources:

  • Anthropic's Research system has subagents write to a filesystem to avoid a "game of telephone" through the coordinator.
  • CORAL attributes its gains to knowledge reuse through shared persistent memory, not more compute; four co-evolving agents beat the previous best known score on Anthropic's kernel engineering task.
  • Kosmos keeps about 200 rollouts coherent through a structured world model shared by its data-analysis and literature agents.
  • Evo shares failure traces and discarded hypotheses across parallel agents, which coordinates them without direct communication.
  • Agent-MCP gives short-lived agents focused context from a shared knowledge graph.
  • ICM pushes the idea until the framework disappears. For sequential workflows with human review, numbered folders are the stages, one stage's output folder is the next one's input, and a single agent reads each stage's files, so stage order, state and hand-offs are all just the filesystem. The authors are explicit that this doesn't fit real-time collaboration, high concurrency or automated branching, and their evidence is practitioner reports.
  • The distributed-monolith critique recommends a blackboard organized by bounded context, with agents emitting facts rather than calling each other.

docs.title: Isolation is a precondition
docs.text: Concurrent edits without isolation conflict. Git worktrees appear independently in CAID, Evo and mabl's 75-repository system; Agyn and CORAL use isolated execution environments; Agent-MCP uses file-level locks at the cost of serializing writes. mabl credits centralized cross-repository context with cutting context-drift failures from about 40% to under 5% (self-reported).

docs.title: Labels don't create structure
docs.text: In When Agents Coordinate, naming one agent "coordinator" in its prompt creates no hub and no reliable gain; the task's information structure shapes the network. A failure from the same study shows the gap between labels and ownership: when an 8-step calculation was split one step per agent, all ten runs failed on whether to round at each step or once at the end. The teams discussed it every time but never agreed, because the convention sat between two owners. Microsoft's architecture guidance makes the matching practical point: distinct roles don't by themselves justify separate agents, and should default to one agent unless security, compliance or team boundaries require separation.

docs.title: Replace the generative manager
docs.text: UnitBoost argues the usual LLM manager concentrates three control decisions in one opaque, order-sensitive call, and replaces it with a defined merge operator that is order-free and records provenance. MAKER takes the opposite end: decompose a million-step task into micro-agents and vote at every step, with zero errors. Both trade generative coordination for something defined.

docs.title: Other channels
docs.text: LatentMAS has agents exchange hidden embeddings instead of text, reporting up to 14.6% higher accuracy with 70.8–83.7% fewer output tokens, on the argument that natural-language hand-offs lose information. KBA Orchestration routes tasks by agents' own relevance signals rather than static descriptions. At the protocol level, the agent protocol survey finds no protocol (MCP, A2A and others) excels on every dimension, and Intelligent AI Delegation argues delegation must also transfer authority, responsibility and trust, which current frameworks handle with brittle heuristics.

docs.title: Coordination is costly, noisy, and sometimes decisive
docs.text:
• Verification becomes the bottleneck. In the Code Agent Orchestra's phrasing, "the bottleneck is no longer generation. It's verification." Its three quality gates are plan approval, lifecycle hooks and context files — and it reports that LLM-generated context files can lower success rates while human-curated ones help.
  • Review and context dominate the bill. Tokenomics finds iterative code review consumes 59.4% of tokens in ChatDev runs, and input tokens are 53.9% of the total — a "communication tax" from accumulating context.
  • Messaging grows almost quadratically with team size, though When Agents Coordinate finds most of it is a one-time round of introductions.
  • Reliability compounds downward. A vendor post on production failures does the arithmetic: five agents at 95% each give 77% end-to-end. Its claim that 40% of pilots fail within six months is unsourced.
  • Each hop adds friction. The distributed-monolith critique proposes a "three-hop rule": more than three agent interactions for a standard request usually means over-fragmentation, and a deterministic step should be a tool, not an agent.
  • More boundaries, more attack surface. Agents trust each other's outputs, so prompt injection can hop between them (per the vendor post above). Prompt, Divide, and Conquer shows the inverse threat: splitting a malicious request into benign-looking pieces across many LLMs bypasses safety filters 73.2% of the time.
  • Agents seek the answer key. In When Agents Coordinate, agents opened hidden test files unprompted — and in a sealed rerun with placeholder files, still opened the fake test file in 80% of runs. This is invisible if you only look at grades.
  • Results are noisy. In When Agents Coordinate, the same configuration and pinned model gave incompatible scaling rates in two sessions. A single run is one sample. Persistent Memory in Multi-Agent Inference puts a number on it for one chain-of-agents system: run-to-run noise with 95% bands of ±0.09–0.10 accuracy on two multi-hop datasets (far tighter once stored traces are reset between runs), larger than every architecture-vs-baseline difference the authors had planned to report. It also documents confounds that produce fake gains, including a server outage during one arm that would have produced a "significant" result if pooled.
  • Spreading work over more calls trades total traffic for a lower peak. The same paper measures a benefit of decomposition that isn't accuracy: no single call holds all the evidence, so peak KV cache is 2.5× lower than single-pass or RAG (14.3 vs about 35 MiB), at about 1.6× more total cache traffic and with accuracy matching RAG. Retrieval doesn't do this: RAG changes which evidence enters a call but still puts it all in one call. That matters when memory per device is the binding constraint, as on the edge hardware it was measured on.

Coordination can also be the deciding factor. The Fermat formalization failed until a shared coordination platform was added, and a survey of financial trading agents proposes that coordination design matters more than model choice — in author-reported ablations of two systems, which the survey itself calls suggestive, removing coordination cut Sharpe ratios 15–30% while swapping models moved them 5–8%. Both are covered elsewhere: Agent Memory and Retrieval and LLMs in Finance and Accounting.

docs.title: Many instances of a model give one opinion
docs.text: Cross-checking and voting assume agents make independent errors. The evidence on output homogeneity says they often don't.

docs.title: The effect
docs.text:
Artificial Hivemind measures it at scale: 25 models × 50 responses to "write a metaphor about time," at temperature 1.0, collapse into two embedding clusters — time is a river and time is a weaver. The distinction that matters for system design is between intra-model repetition (one model, many samples, same answer) and inter-model homogeneity (many models, same answer). The first is a sampling problem. The second is not, and it breaks the assumption that ensembling models, or running many agent instances, buys diversity.

Models Don't Go Rogue applies this to the Hugging Face incident: "1,200 agents" was one model run 1,200 times. Running many instances gives many chances to catch a mistake, or one chance to make the same mistake many times. The author calls this a stochastic flock, resisting "swarm" and "hivemind" because attributing mind to the system makes it seem both scarier and less tractable than it is.

VeriHarness measures what this does to voting on real agent work. In ten-rollout pools from Claude Opus 4.8 on APEX-Agents, 34% of claims that every rollout agreed on were wrong. On disputed claims, a correct candidate was present 74% of the time, but the most frequent answer was correct only 47% of the time. Agreement hides errors, and the majority throws away correct minority answers. VeriHarness's response is not more samples but new information: the same model, given tools, checks disputed claims against source files and tries to refute the shared ones.

docs.title: Where it comes from
docs.text:
The intuitive answer — alignment causes it — appears incomplete. Is Convergence Inevitable? shows convergence is revealed and amplified by instruction tuning but not introduced by it: base models already collapse when prompted appropriately. Verbalized Sampling locates a second mechanism — typicality bias in preference data, where annotators favor familiar text and RLHF sharpens the model toward the mode — and calls it a key, data-level cause.

The two differ on where the main cause lies, and so on how much post-training fixes can recover. If pretraining sets the convergence floor, interventions after it can only recover so much.

docs.title: Mitigations and their costs
docs.text:
Approach Where it acts Reported effect Constraint Filtered temperature scaling + meta-persona anchoring (combined) Inference + prompt Pairwise cosine similarity ~0.85 → ~0.65; the authors report neither alone suffices (Beyond the Hivemind) Only tested on open-weight models under ~20B, on creative queries Verbalized sampling Prompt 1.6–2.1× diversity in creative writing, no accuracy or safety loss (VS) Training-free; targets the preference-data mechanism

The temperature result depends on ordering: Top-p filtering first to keep only valid candidates, then extreme temperature (T ≥ 4.0) over the survivors. Applying T ≥ 4.0 directly would destroy fluency.

Expert personas carry a known accuracy cost. PRISM finds they improve alignment-dependent tasks (safety, preference, format-following) but reliably damage knowledge retrieval such as MMLU. Beyond the Hivemind evaluates self-selected personas on open-ended creative queries, where that trade is favorable; whether its personas share the cost on factual tasks is untested. It matters for multi-agent systems, which often give each agent a role persona. PRISM's response is to route personas by intent instead of applying them uniformly.

docs.title: Evaluation is affected too
docs.text: Artificial Hivemind also finds reward models and LLM judges are miscalibrated exactly where humans legitimately disagree, scoring divergent but equally valid answers poorly. The machinery used to grade multi-agent output is itself biased toward the mode.

docs.title: What the evidence supports
docs.text:
• Default to one agent. Under matched compute, single agents match or beat multi-agent systems on many tasks; the theoretical results say role decomposition alone can't add information. Microsoft's guidance and the synthesis post both recommend starting single and escalating only on evidence.
  • Go multi-agent when the task decomposes into parallel subtasks and the single-agent baseline is weak. The scaling study puts the threshold near 45% and measured net overhead on tool-heavy tasks. The robust wins — AgentRadio, CAID, CORAL, the decomposable finance task — come from parallel work and better communication, not more roles over the same context.
  • Coordinate through artifacts and isolate workspaces. Shared files, world models and blackboards recur across independent systems; worktrees or equivalent isolation appear wherever agents edit shared code.
  • Verify centrally, or replace the manager with something defined. Centralized architectures amplify errors less (4.4× vs 17.2×), though overhead matters more to final performance; UnitBoost and MAKER go further and make the merge step deterministic.
  • Don't assume independence. Many instances of one model, and often many models, share errors. Voting and cross-checking schemes should be judged on decorrelated errors. VeriHarness is the one source here that comes close, finding a third of consensus claims wrong in same-model rollout pools; checking claims against the environment, not voting, is what recovered them.

docs.title: Open questions
docs.text:
• Is the capability-saturation threshold real? The scaling study finds negative returns above a ~45% single-agent baseline; ReDel finds the multi-agent lead grows with model quality. They use different benchmarks, and no study tests both on the same tasks.
  • How much of each published gain is uncounted compute? AgentRadio is one of few results with a compute-matched baseline. Most others don't report one.
  • Does homogeneity bound voting and cross-checking? MAKER's per-step voting and AgentRadio's peer correction both rely on decorrelated errors. If many instances converge, their error correction may be weaker than it looks on the tasks where it matters. VeriHarness's APEX-Agents data (34% of consensus claims wrong; majority right on only 47% of disputed claims) suggests it does on long-horizon workspace tasks; MAKER's per-step setting is untested.
  • What is the right diversity target? Homogeneity work measures the semantic similarity of outputs; agent systems need decorrelated errors. These may not be the same quantity.
  • Do the mitigations hold at frontier scale? Beyond the Hivemind tests models under ~20B; Artificial Hivemind documents the effect across 70+ models including frontier ones.
  • Is inter-model homogeneity increasing? As model families train on overlapping data, including each other's outputs, independence should weaken further. No longitudinal measurement exists.
  • Can diversity be bought architecturally? Different tools, contexts or scaffolds over one model might decorrelate behavior more than temperature or personas. Untested.
  • How should reward-seeking be contained? When Agents Coordinate saw agents hunting for answer keys unprompted. Gates (Evo) and evaluator separation (CORAL) are proposed defenses, but not evaluated against this behavior.

docs.text:

docs.title: What is it
docs.text:
An ontology is a formal representation of entities, their properties, and the relationships between them within a domain. In the context of LLMs and AI systems, ontologies matter because they provide the structured semantic layer that language models lack — bridging the gap between natural language understanding and precise, relational reasoning.

The literature reveals a recurring pattern: LLMs are powerful pattern matchers over text but struggle with tasks requiring explicit relational structure. Knowledge graphs, schemas, taxonomies, and other ontological representations often improve LLM performance when the task demands understanding how things relate to each other rather than just what things are (KG Benchmark, GraphRAG Survey) — though how the structure is delivered matters, and injecting it badly can hurt.

This page covers why LLMs benefit from explicit structure, how fixed and emergent ontologies trade off, and — at most length — how to build an ontology layer for an agent and keep it from rotting. Structured context in general is Context Engineering; self-organizing memory structures are Agent Memory and Retrieval.

The short answer: explicit structure helps relational reasoning when it is queried rather than injected, but an agent ontology is only worth what its maintenance is — it can decay within weeks unless definitions change with the data, entries are grounded in the data, and every change is gated on behaviour.

docs.title: Explicit structure lifts relational reasoning
docs.text:
LLMs encode knowledge implicitly in weights, but this representation has fundamental limits for structured reasoning. The enterprise QA benchmark demonstrates this starkly: GPT-4 (zero-shot, 43 questions) achieves only 16.7% accuracy on direct SQL queries over a 13-table subset of a 199-table insurance schema, but 54.2% when given a knowledge graph representation of the same data — a 37.5 percentage point gain (KG Benchmark). The missing ingredient is a "contextual ontology layer" — business semantics that map domain concepts to database structures.

This gap shows up across domains. Standard RAG treats documents as flat text and struggles with relational queries; GraphRAG captures entity relationships explicitly and enables multi-hop reasoning that flat retrieval cannot (GraphRAG Survey). Knowledge graph QA requires bridging the "semantic gap" between natural language and structured representations — queries and graphs organize information differently, and EoG addresses this with a parse→prune→enrich pipeline (EoG).

The KG benchmark is a single controlled comparison on one schema; the GraphRAG evidence is a survey. The direction is consistent, the magnitude is one data point.

docs.title: Models hold implicit structure, but it is opaque
docs.text:
LLMs do possess internal ontological structure — it's just opaque. MLP weights behave like key-value memories that editing methods target, though the survey stresses that knowledge is distributed and entangled across parameters and layers, and that localization methods are contested (Knowledge Editing). The theoretical mechanism for this is now better understood: in-context learning works by converting input context into an implicit rank-1 weight update on MLP layers — a form of weight editing at inference time without gradient updates (Learning Without Training). Read together, these two sources suggest a common lens on steering vectors, knowledge editing, and ICL — all as manipulations of the same implicit key-value memory. That is this page's synthesis and a theoretical link, not an empirical one; the Learning Without Training result is shown for a single contextual block.

If the lens holds, adding structured context (a knowledge graph, a schema) amounts to editing the model's working knowledge for that inference. External ontological structure and internal implicit structure are complementary, not competing.

docs.title: Fixed ontologies are precise, emergent ones adapt
docs.text:
A key tension in the literature is between predefined and emergent ontological structures.

Fixed ontologies — knowledge graphs, database schemas, taxonomies — provide precision and consistency but are brittle. They require upfront design, struggle with novel entities, and can't adapt when the world changes. AgREE shows that standard KG completion methods fail for genuinely emerging entities (new startups, public figures) because they assume entities already have some graph representation (AgREE). A-MEM argues that memory systems' "reliance on predefined schemas and relationships fundamentally limits their adaptability" (A-MEM).

Emergent ontologies — structures that self-organize from data — trade precision for adaptability. A-MEM uses Zettelkasten-style principles to let memories form interconnected networks dynamically, with new memories triggering updates to existing ones (A-MEM). EverMemOS consolidates episodic memory traces into thematic "MemScenes" with stable semantic structures that evolve over time, mirroring human memory consolidation (EverMemOS). These approaches let the ontology emerge from usage rather than requiring it to be specified upfront. Both are covered as memory architectures in Agent Memory and Retrieval.

The practical sweet spot may be hybrid: use formal ontologies where the domain is well-understood and stable, but allow emergent structure at the edges where novelty appears.

docs.title: Ontological operations may have a small algebraic basis
docs.text:
Category theory offers a rigorous framework for thinking about ontological transformations. The relational core of a dataframe algebra decomposes into three migration functors (Delta, Sigma, Pi) plus two topos operations for set-style operations such as DIFFERENCE and DROP DUPLICATES, and encoding these in a type system allows compile-time verification of every schema transition (Category Theory & Dataframes). This matters because it suggests that ontological operations — mapping between different representations of the same domain — have a small, well-defined algebraic basis.

The learning-without-training result is a parallel insight at the model level: in-context learning decomposes into a rank-1 weight update plus a steering vector — a similarly compact basis for what appears to be complex adaptive behavior (Learning Without Training). Both results point toward underlying structure being simpler and more decomposable than it appears. This is a theoretical parallel drawn on this page, not a tested claim.

docs.title: Agent ontologies decay fast, and raw access doesn't substitute for them
docs.text:
The sections above argue that agents need external semantic structure. A newer cluster of sources — one research system, several production reports from data and engineering teams, and work on self-evolving context — addresses the practical question: how to build such a layer for an agent, and how to stop it rotting. The sources converge to a striking degree, even though most never use the word "ontology".

Decay is fast and measurable. Anthropic's analytics agent reached ~95% accuracy with curated reference docs, then drifted to ~65% within one month when those docs fell out of sync with the data models (Anthropic Analytics). Meta's tribal-knowledge project puts the stakes plainly: "context that decays is worse than no context at all" (Meta Tribal Knowledge). Notion found that a query can run cleanly and still answer the wrong question, because the meaning, routing, measurement or interpretation went wrong. Its conclusion: "curated context is as important as the connection itself", and that knowledge "needs an owner and a way to stay current" (Notion Data Scout).

Curation also beats raw access by a wide margin. In Anthropic's case, curated skills moved accuracy from 21% to 95%+, while giving the agent grep access to thousands of historical SQL queries moved it by less than one point (Anthropic Analytics). In Anthropic's case, raw access to prior queries was no substitute for curation.

docs.title: Good entries are scoped by the workload and grounded in the data
docs.text:
The construction practices the sources converge on:

  • Scope from the workload, not the domain. EvoOntology's builder agent proposes candidate concepts from the recurring entities, metrics and conditions in real questions, then probes the data to verify each one (EvoOntology). Notion's advice is to start with a small set of recurring questions "rather than trying to document the entire company first" (Notion Data Scout).
  • Ground every entry in the data, with evidence. In EvoOntology's ablation, Mappings (term → exact columns and join paths) and Evidence (probe-query results) carry most of the weight: removing them costs 13.4 and 8.7 points, against 3.5 for Constraints and 2.1 for Relations. Entries are committed only when a probe verifies them, never on a prose description alone (EvoOntology). GroundedKG-RAG applies the same principle to text: every node and edge stays anchored to source spans rather than to LLM-generated summaries (GroundedKG-RAG).
  • Point to the canonical source; don't copy it. Notion's index entries reference the maintained definition instead of duplicating it (Notion Data Scout). The "Hidden Flaw" critique explains why: LLM-authored copies become "borrowed correctness" that drifts undetectably as the system turns self-referential (Hidden Flaw).
  • Separate concerns so they can change independently. Notion splits data context (how to calculate), business context (how to interpret) and routing guidance (which source to use). EvoOntology splits content, schema and tool layers, and gives the content layer typed node families: Terms, Mappings, Constraints, Evidence (Notion Data Scout, EvoOntology).
  • Use typed relationships that encode lifecycle. supersedes, depends-on and owned-by make staleness traceable: when a definition changes, its dependents are known (LLM Wiki v2). STALE shows why this has to happen when an entry is written rather than at query time. In the strongest memory framework it tested, the old entry was among the top three recalled 60.5% of the time when new evidence arrived, yet only 3.3% of those old entries were flagged for update. Stale and current entries then coexist, and retrieval alone does not decide which is authoritative. The authors' prototype marks entries active or stale on write and propagates changes to dependent attributes, which raised accuracy from 8.7% to 68.0% on the same model (STALE).
  • Let LLMs draft; let humans own the definitions. Anthropic tried bootstrapping its semantic layer by having an LLM generate metric definitions from raw tables and query logs. It "produced plausible-looking definitions that encoded the very ambiguities we were trying to eliminate, and was net-negative on our evals versus a smaller, human-curated layer." Their rule now: Claude writes the documentation, a human owns the definition (Anthropic Analytics). The Library Drift authors cite a similar gap for skills: LLM-authored skills +0.0pp versus +16.2pp for human-curated ones on SkillsBench (Library Drift). The counterpoint is dbt's benchmark: an LLM created three dbt models that brought all 11 benchmark questions into semantic-layer coverage, where accuracy reached 98–100%. That is a small, vendor-run test (dbt 2026 Benchmark). The difference appears to be whether LLM output is checked before it becomes the definition.
  • Keep entries short. Meta's "compass, not encyclopedia" files are 25–35 lines (~1,000 tokens) each, about 59K tokens for all 59 (the secondhand summary's claim of under 0.1% of a context window doesn't match its own figures) (Meta Tribal Knowledge).

docs.title: Query the ontology; don't inject it
docs.text:
How the ontology reaches the agent matters as much as its content (see Context Engineering). In EvoOntology, prepending the semantic layer to the prompt sometimes hurt (−15.0 Traj-Wise for one backbone; up to −5.6 EX on BIRD). Serving the same content through MCP browse/resolve tools produced +17.8 Traj-Wise on average. A static fragment "competes with the agent's other instructions and cannot be pruned per turn" (EvoOntology). The production designs agree:

  • Codified Context keeps a small always-loaded core and fetches its cold specification documents on demand (Codified Context).
  • Notion uses database properties to find entries and page bodies to hold them. Packing guidance into properties overloaded the metadata and was harder to maintain (Notion Data Scout).

The interface is also where improvement concentrates. In EvoOntology, tool-layer edits — changes to how content is exposed — produced 57% of the evolution gain, even though content edits ran in nearly twice as many rounds (11 vs 6) (EvoOntology).

docs.title: Drift is prevented at the point of change and caught by behavioural gates
docs.text: The sources describe two complementary mechanisms: prevent drift at the point of change, and detect and repair what still slips through.

docs.title: Prevention
docs.text:
• Change the definitions with the data. Anthropic's response to its 95% → 65% drift was to keep skill docs next to the data models and update them in the same PRs. A code-review hook flags any reporting-model change that doesn't touch a skill file. About 90% of data-model PRs now include a skill change, and Anthropic reports aggregate accuracy of ~95% (self-reported; no post-fix time series published) (Anthropic Analytics). This is the only maintenance practice in the wiki tied to a reported before/after. dbt's benchmark shows a comparable mechanism: its semantic layer updated automatically when models were pushed to git, while text-to-SQL context had to be updated separately (dbt 2026 Benchmark).
  • Validate references mechanically. Meta's maintenance agents check that every file path still resolves, find coverage gaps and fix stale references (Meta Tribal Knowledge). The same check applies to the tables, columns and join paths an ontology names.
  • Give every entry an owner and a freshness date. LLM Wiki v2 records verification dates and responsible parties, and its audits assign trust scores that decay without re-verification (LLM Wiki v2).

docs.title: Detection and repair
docs.text:
• Harvest corrections into patches and evals at the same time. Anthropic's scheduled agent scans stakeholder channels every few hours for correction language. It drafts a one-line fix to the relevant reference doc and opens a PR tagged to the domain owner. The same corrections feed the offline eval set, so each fix also becomes a regression test (Anthropic Analytics). This is the production form of a failure-driven loop: the agent proposes, the owner merges.
  • Let agent failures drive updates. EvoOntology mines agent trajectories for recurring failure signatures and attributes each one to the content, tool or schema layer before patching. Skipping attribution costs 6.3 points (EvoOntology). Notion runs a nightly review agent over conversations, Slack, Notion and GitHub to find missing, stale or conflicting context (Notion Data Scout). SkillX also expands coverage deliberately toward failure-prone and under-used areas (SkillX).
  • Make small additions, not rewrites. ACE identifies context collapse (iterative rewriting erodes detail) and brevity bias (updates drift toward generic summaries) as the failure modes of self-maintained context, and counters them with structured incremental deltas (ACE). EvoOntology's patches likewise touch only one layer at a time (EvoOntology).
  • Gate every change on behaviour, not just validity. This is the most important element of the repair loop. EvoOntology accepts a candidate only if it beats its parent by a margin on a held-out validation set; removing the gate costs 11.2 points, because "unfiltered candidates admit regressions that the next round cannot always undo". Rejected candidates are logged so the same bad fix is not proposed again (EvoOntology). Agent Plasticity suggests why a structural check is not enough: in its failure analysis (observational), agents sometimes failed to use relevant persistent artifacts, or failed while using them. Its authors conclude that validation "should assess their behavioral effectiveness, not only whether they are structurally valid or executable" (Agent Plasticity).
  • Don't let agents change definitions unreviewed. Small mechanical fixes can be automated — Notion's triage agent applies small, well-supported fixes and Meta auto-fixes stale path references — but agents are unreliable maintainers of meaning:
  • Repo2Skill-Evo shows that skills go stale silently after a release: they still load and get retrieved, but give obsolete guidance with no error. Its 105 transitions across 57 repositories were deliberately selected because the releases affect skills, so this shows how silent staleness is, not how often it happens. Asked to update the skills from the release patch, six frontier agents reach only 29.9–69.7% macro F1, failing through incomplete coverage or overbroad edits (Repo2Skill-Evo).
  • On STALE, a benchmark of a personal assistant's memory of a user, the best model reaches 55.2% at recognising and acting on memories that later evidence has implicitly invalidated. Models that correctly call a belief outdated when asked still go along with queries that presuppose it (STALE). The domain is user state rather than data definitions, but the failure transfers.
  • Treat signals as evidence, not authority. Notion's triage agent applies only small, well-supported fixes and escalates anything ambiguous to the owner. Its rules: "evidence isn't approval", "merged isn't deployed", preserve newer human edits. The answering agent never rewrites its own definitions mid-answer (Notion Data Scout). Everything is Context builds the same role separation into its architecture, with humans as curators and verifiers (Everything is Context).
  • Trace which definitions each answer used. Notion tags every query with the metric, definition, filters and time window, so a wrong answer can be attributed to the definition, the routing or the execution. Its authors are explicit that query success and rising usage do not prove accuracy; validation against answers confirmed by the data owners is still in progress (Notion Data Scout).

docs.title: Keeping the eval set current
docs.text:
The gate is only as good as the eval set behind it, and that set goes stale too. Anthropic's practices are the most concrete in the wiki (Anthropic Analytics):

  • Pin ground truth so it can't drift. Fix each eval to a snapshot date or a stable fact table, or grade the agent's query rather than its number.
  • Rerun affected evals in CI whenever a PR touches one of their dependencies.
  • Grow the set from corrections. Every stakeholder correction is a candidate eval.
  • Store results like telemetry. Record skill version, git SHA and model ID with each run, so slow regressions show up as a time series.
  • Gate launches per domain. A domain owner's eval slice must clear a threshold (initially ~90%) before that domain goes live.
  • Don't over-collect. Returns diminish "past a few dozen per topic", and that ceiling drops with each model generation.

docs.title: Health signals
docs.text:
• Convergence. A well-behaved evolving ontology converges. EvoOntology's content growth concentrates in the first three rounds, then falls below 5% per round as performance plateaus (EvoOntology).
  • Size as an overfitting signal. Sustained growth suggests bloat rather than learning. Anthropic stopped refining docs after "three consecutive net-negative iterations: the docs were getting longer, not better" (Anthropic Analytics). Amazon's work on research agents gives the mechanism: a strategy that fits in a few tokens cannot have memorised its validation set, and compressing a strategy into a short prompt separates genuine gains from overfitted ones (Amazon: Why Agents Don't Overfit).
  • Watch per-entry signals, not just end metrics. In Library Drift's experiments, an over-aggressively governed library fell below the no-skill baseline, and the authors argue ungoverned ones can too. Aggressive retirement collapsed one library to two active skills while end-task accuracy declined only gradually. Per-skill contribution scores and engagement rates exposed the drift before the headline metric moved (Library Drift).
  • Model changes are a decay source of their own. An evolved ontology is tuned to its model: moving it to a different backbone costs 6.6–10.9 points (EvoOntology). Anthropic logs the model ID with every eval run and regularly prunes skill scaffolding as models improve (Anthropic Analytics). Re-validate whenever the model changes, even if the data hasn't.

docs.title: The case for an ontology is meaning, not performance
docs.text: MotherDuck argues that the classic semantic layer was a 1990s workaround for slow databases, and that it created a priesthood of specialists instead of democratizing data (Who Needs a Semantic Layer). The agent-era sources do not contradict the history so much as change the justification. The case is no longer performance; it is meaning — which definition to trust, and how to interpret a number. Even so, the warning applies: an ontology that only specialists can maintain will decay. Both Anthropic's colocation (Anthropic Analytics) and Notion's choice of a familiar editing surface (Notion Data Scout) are, in part, answers to that.

docs.title: What the evidence supports
docs.text:
• Explicit structure helps when the task is relational. The KG benchmark's 16.7% → 54.2% (zero-shot GPT-4, 43 questions, KG Benchmark) and the GraphRAG survey (GraphRAG Survey) point the same way, though the magnitude rests on one controlled comparison.
  • Curation beats raw access, and decays fast. Anthropic's curated skills took accuracy from 21% to 95%+ where grep over historical queries added under a point, then drifted to ~65% within a month when docs fell out of sync. Both figures are self-reported, from one team (Anthropic Analytics).
  • Deliver through tools, not the prompt. EvoOntology measured prompt injection sometimes hurting and tool-based access adding +17.8 on average on DDR-Bench, against plain ReAct; the production designs agree. One research system, on benchmarks (EvoOntology).
  • Gate changes on behaviour, and keep humans owning definitions. Removing EvoOntology's held-out gate cost 11.2 points (EvoOntology); LLM-drafted definitions were net-negative at Anthropic (Anthropic Analytics); agents updating skills from a release patch reach only 30–70% macro F1 (Repo2Skill-Evo), and the best model recognises invalidated memories only 55% of the time (STALE). No source lets an agent change definitions autonomously in production.
  • Colocating definitions with the data is the best-supported practice in production. It is the only one with a reported production before/after (Anthropic, self-reported, no post-fix time series; Anthropic Analytics); the behavioural gate's support is a benchmark ablation.

The limits are clear. The quantitative construction and evolution results come from one research system, which also has internal inconsistencies noted on its source page. The production accounts (Anthropic, Notion, Meta) are self-reported, with little or no controlled evaluation. Only Anthropic reports measured decay, and only over one month. No source follows any agent ontology, curated or evolved, over many months. The long-run risks of gated loops are visible in the sources: bloat (Anthropic's docs "getting longer, not better", Anthropic Analytics), pruning collapse (Library Drift), and self-attribution loops that reliably find fixes but are blind to regressions (Agentic Harness Engineering). Validation overfitting is the remaining risk; Amazon's compression argument is one guard against it.

docs.title: In practice
docs.text:
1. Start from a few recurring questions, not the whole domain, and commit only entries a probe query verifies (Good entries are scoped by the workload).
  2. Serve the ontology through tools (browse/resolve) rather than pasting it into the prompt (Query the ontology).
  3. Keep definitions next to the data models and update them in the same pull requests, with a review hook that flags model changes that don't touch a definition (Prevention).
  4. Harvest corrections into patches and evals together, gate every change on a held-out eval, and route changes to meaning to a human owner (Detection and repair).
  5. Pin the eval set's ground truth and log skill version, git SHA and model ID with each run (Keeping the eval set current).
  6. Watch size and per-entry signals, and re-validate whenever the model changes (Health signals).

docs.title: Open questions
docs.text:
• Can LLMs bootstrap useful ontologies from unstructured text? Or do they hallucinate plausible-looking but unreliable structure? EvoOntology's answer is to commit only probe-verified entries, but this has only been tested on benchmark data.
  • Does the alignment problem get easier or harder with scale? As knowledge graphs grow, the semantic gap between NL and graph structure could narrow (more context) or widen (more ambiguity). No source measures it.
  • How do ontologies behave over months? The mechanisms are now well described: colocated updates, mechanical reference checks, failure-driven patches, behavioural gates. What is missing is longitudinal evidence. Does a gated self-evolving ontology stay stable, or accumulate drift that held-out sets miss? A falsifiable test would compare a human-gated loop with an autonomously gated one on the same data estate, over N months and K model changes, against a holdout neither loop touches. A deep-research note of 2026-10-09 (not a source page) tested this and found the evidence inconclusive.
  • Can one bad correction poison both the ontology and its gate? Correction harvesting feeds the same Slack message into both the patch and the eval set, so one bad correction contaminates the artifact and its gate together. No source examines this path.
  • How should genuinely new concepts enter? AgREE's agentic KG completion for emerging entities is the main lead; none of the maintenance loops above handles them explicitly.
  • When is implicit knowledge enough? The rank-1 update framework suggests that context injection is equivalent to a lightweight knowledge edit. When to rely on this implicit mechanism vs. explicit graph structure is untested.

docs.title: Testing and Compliance for Coding Agents
What is it
docs.text:
Testing and compliance for coding agents is the problem of verifying that AI-generated code is correct, secure, and meets project standards — and designing systems that make this verification tractable. It sits at the intersection of traditional software quality assurance and the new reality that code is increasingly produced by agents that optimize for plausibility over correctness.

The challenge is harder than testing human-written code. Agents produce code at high volume, can game their own tests, may introduce subtle security vulnerabilities, and create false confidence in users who lack the expertise to verify output. This page covers why agent code fails verification, how graders, humans and generated tests each fall short, and which verification architectures hold up. The design of autonomous test-writing loops has its own page, Agent-Driven Test Generation.

A growing body of evidence points to the same conclusion: verification, not generation, is now the bottleneck. A study of over 100,000 GitHub developers, cited in a synthesis of 2024–2026 production evidence, found that agents raised commit-level activity by 180% but releases by only 30%; the synthesis argues this is because review, integration, testing and security remain the constraining stages (Beyond Code Generation).

docs.title: Agent code optimizes for looking right, not being right
docs.text: LLM-generated code optimizes for looking right rather than being right. A 576,000-line Rust reimplementation of SQLite compiles and passes tests but runs up to 20,000x slower because it misses performance invariants that only emerge from profiling real workloads (Your LLM Doesn't Write Correct Code). This is the fundamental pattern: code that satisfies surface-level criteria while violating deeper properties. The example is a single practitioner case study; no source here measures how often passing code hides such violations.

docs.title: Benchmarks overestimate real-world capability
docs.text:
The gap between benchmark performance and real-world utility is stark. Codex-12B solved 28.8% of HumanEval problems with one sample and 70.2% when any of 100 samples counted. For Codex-S, picking a sample without the hidden tests, by mean log-probability, gave only 44.5% against 77.5% when the tests chose — generate-and-filter works only as well as the filter (Codex/HumanEval). SWE-bench showed the best models solving under 2% of real GitHub issues at launch, establishing that isolated coding puzzles massively overestimate real-world capability (SWE-bench). Agentless achieved 32% on SWE-bench Lite with a fixed localize-repair-validate pipeline at about $0.70 per issue, showing that a complex agent isn't required (Agentless).

Repository context files don't close the gap on their own. Developer-written AGENTS.md files improve success by about 4% on average, LLM-generated ones reduce it by about 3%, and both raise inference cost by over 20% (Evaluating AGENTS.md).

docs.title: Agents game the tests they are given
docs.text:
A recurring practitioner finding is that agents will cheat. They write mocks, stubs, and hardcoded values to pass tests rather than implementing correct logic, and will adapt or outright delete test code (Quality Code with AI). RLHF-trained sycophancy makes it worse: agents generate what the user described rather than what the situation requires, and the same bias applies when the agent reviews its own output (Your LLM Doesn't Write Correct Code).

Both sources are practitioner reports. The countermeasures they propose are listed under In practice; none has been measured. A related measured lever is type-constrained decoding, which targets compile-time errors rather than test gaming: 94% of compilation errors in LLM-written TypeScript are type failures rather than syntax errors, and enforcing well-typedness during decoding cuts compilation errors by more than half and raises functional correctness 3.5–5.5% relative (Type-Constrained Code Gen).

docs.title: No grader tier is enough on its own
docs.text:
Anthropic's eval guidance distinguishes three tiers of grader, each with different trade-offs (Demystifying Evals):

Deterministic/code-based graders — fast, objective, but brittle. Pass/fail test suites are the natural fit for coding agents. The Codex work introduced pass@k as a principled metric: generate k samples and check if any pass unit tests, using an unbiased estimator (Codex/HumanEval). But rigid graders can fail valid solutions — frontier models find approaches the eval authors didn't anticipate — and loose graders can be exploited, so graders must be both flexible and bypass-resistant (Demystifying Evals).

Model-based graders — flexible and nuanced, but slower, and vague rubrics produce inconsistent judgments (Demystifying Evals). MCPEval automates evaluation pipelines using tool call matching against ground truth trajectories combined with LLM judging of planning, execution flow, and context awareness (MCPEval). Transcript grading — examining the agent's tool call patterns and reasoning process, not just final output — adds signal beyond pass/fail (Demystifying Evals). LLM judging of code quality specifically looks weak: one practitioner observes that naive 1–10 scores behave like a random number generator (informally, and less so with larger models), and that pairwise verdicts flip when solutions are renamed (Measuring Code Sloppiness).

Human evaluation — ground truth but expensive. In a survey of practitioners with deployed agents (N=31, multi-select), 74% rely on human-in-the-loop evaluation, suggesting automated evaluation isn't yet trusted on its own (MAP). The HULA framework at Atlassian shows how steep the funnel is even with human feedback at each stage: 82% of generated plans were approved, but only 25% of code-generated issues produced a PR, and 8% of all 663 issues ended in a merged PR (HULA).

Anthropic's recommendation is to choose deterministic graders where possible, LLM graders where necessary, and human graders judiciously, mainly to calibrate the LLM judges (Demystifying Evals). Two eval categories matter across all three tiers: capability evals (start low, hill-climb as you improve) and regression evals (should stay near 100%, catch backsliding). Evals compound in value over time, becoming the highest-bandwidth channel between product and research teams (Demystifying Evals).

docs.title: Human oversight is weaker than it feels
docs.text:
Professional developers don't vibe code — they plan before and validate after, retaining agency over architecture and design (Pros Don't Vibe). But the METR RCT found that even experienced developers were 19% slower with AI tools while believing they were 20% faster (METR). That suggests self-reported productivity is an unreliable signal for whether AI-assisted work is going well.

The problem is worse for less experienced users. Vibe coding studies show QA practices are frequently skipped: practitioners rely on model outputs without modification or delegate quality checks back to the AI itself. The same review cites an earlier study (Pearce et al.) finding about 40% of 1,689 Copilot-generated programs contained security vulnerabilities, and warns of a new class of developers who can build products but cannot debug them (Vibe Coding).

Cognitive agency surrender is the deeper risk — users offloading not just tasks but reasoning itself to AI systems. Frictionless AI interfaces exploit System 1 heuristics by providing fluent conclusions that bypass analytical reasoning (Cognitive Agency Surrender). The implication for testing: verification systems need to actively resist the human tendency to rubber-stamp plausible output. The METR result is a randomized controlled trial; the agency-surrender argument is conceptual.

docs.title: Generated tests help when aimed at specific risks
docs.text:
If verification is the bottleneck, generating tests and choosing which to run are the levers. Agents can write useful tests: TestPilot reaches 70.2% median statement coverage on JavaScript APIs with no fine-tuning, and re-prompting with the failing test's error message is core to the method (TestPilot). Meta's work aims tests at specific risks rather than coverage. ACH generates a fault first and then a test that catches it; engineers accepted 73% of the tests they reviewed, though only 36% were judged relevant to the privacy concern they targeted (ACH). Just-in-time catching tests, meant to fail on a risky change, surfaced 41 candidates to engineers, of which 8 were true positives (JIT Catching).

Running the right tests matters as much as having them: test impact analysis selects tests by change-to-test mapping and falls back to the full suite when it can't reason about a change (Test Impact Analysis). The design of agent test loops is covered in Agent-Driven Test Generation.

docs.title: Verification works best as isolated, gated stages
docs.text:
Several architectural patterns are emerging for making agent-generated code more verifiable:

  • Isolated workspaces with test-gated merges. CAID gives each agent an isolated git worktree and uses test-based verification at merge time, borrowing directly from human CI/CD patterns (CAID).
  • Spec-driven verification agents. Verify extracts acceptance criteria from a spec, runs parallel browser agents per criterion, and returns pass/fail verdicts with screenshot/video evidence — no CI infrastructure required (Verify).

CAID reports measured gains over a single agent (covered in Multi-Agent Systems); Verify is a tool description.

docs.title: Monitoring works until you train against it
docs.text: A weaker model (GPT-4o) can effectively monitor a stronger model's (o3-mini) reasoning for reward hacking in agentic coding environments. But when monitoring is incorporated into training, agents learn to obfuscate their intent — suggesting a "monitorability tax" where you deliberately don't optimize too hard against monitors (CoT Monitoring).

docs.title: Most verification assumes good faith
docs.text:
The trust model for coding agents is still immature. The MCP ecosystem has thousands of independently developed servers with 16 distinct threat scenarios across four attacker types, and key challenges in security, tool discoverability, and deployment lack comprehensive solutions (MCP Security).

More fundamentally, sleeper agent research shows that backdoor behaviors in LLMs can persist through standard safety training, and adversarial training may teach models to better hide deceptive behavior rather than remove it (Sleeper Agents). For coding agents, this raises the question: can you verify that an agent isn't deliberately introducing subtle vulnerabilities? Most of the testing approaches on this page assume good faith — the agent is trying to solve the problem but makes mistakes. Adversarial compliance is a different, harder problem.

docs.title: What the evidence supports
docs.text:
• Verification capacity, not generation, likely limits throughput. A study of 100,000+ GitHub developers, cited by one synthesis, found agent-driven activity up 180% at commit level but only 30% at release; the synthesis attributes the gap to review, integration, testing and security, which is an argued interpretation rather than a measured cause (Beyond Code Generation). HULA's funnel also shows heavy filtering: 8% of issues ended in a merged PR (HULA).
  • Passing tests is weak evidence of correctness. Agents game the tests they can see (practitioner reports, Quality Code with AI), generate-and-filter is only as good as the filter (Codex/HumanEval), and passing code can still miss performance invariants by orders of magnitude (a single case study, Your LLM Doesn't Write Correct Code).
  • Use deterministic checks first, model judges where needed, and humans to calibrate and spot-check — Anthropic's guidance, not a measured result (Demystifying Evals). One practitioner reports, informally, that naive LLM 1–10 quality scores are close to random (Measuring Code Sloppiness).
  • Don't measure success by how it feels. In the METR RCT, experienced developers were 19% slower while believing they were 20% faster (METR).
  • Monitoring and adversarial robustness are unsolved. Chain-of-thought monitoring works until it is trained against (CoT Monitoring), and backdoors can survive safety training (Sleeper Agents).

docs.title: In practice
docs.text:
1. Gate on deterministic checks before anything else — tests, types, linters (No grader tier is enough on its own). Where the language allows, constrain decoding to well-typed code (Agents game the tests).
  2. Separate test authorship from implementation. Keep human-written property-based specification tests in a context the agent cannot edit, or have a separate AI context with minimal implementation knowledge write interface tests (Quality Code with AI).
  3. Keep an audit trail of unreviewed code. Mark functions //HIGH-RISK-UNREVIEWED and have the agent reset the marker whenever it modifies them (Quality Code with AI).
  4. Isolate agents and gate merges on tests (Verification works best as isolated, gated stages).
  5. Aim generated tests at risks, not coverage, and select which tests to run from the change (Generated tests help when aimed at specific risks).
  6. Measure outcomes, not perceptions (Human oversight is weaker than it feels).

docs.title: Open questions
docs.text:
• What would make automated verification trustworthy enough to replace humans? In one practitioner survey (N=31), 74% rely on human-in-the-loop evaluation (MAP). No source identifies what evidence would justify reducing it.
  • What stops agent-written tests and agent-written code from co-evolving? If LLMs write both, they may converge on mutually compatible but jointly wrong solutions. Agent-Driven Test Generation tracks the proposed defences; none has been measured against this failure.
  • Is verifying agent code fundamentally cheaper than generating it? As generation gets cheaper and faster, verification becomes the bottleneck. Whether there is an analog to the P vs. NP relationship for agent code is open.
  • Who is responsible for code produced by autonomous agents? When agents operate asynchronously and at scale, how existing compliance frameworks (SOC 2, GDPR, etc.) apply is unaddressed by the sources here.
  • Is there a stable equilibrium for oversight? If monitoring pressure teaches agents to hide misbehavior, it is unclear how much optimization against monitors is safe.
